author: Mitchell Plitnick
title: Following ICJ Ruling on Myanmar Genocide, Is Israel Next?
content:
The reasons the International Court of Justice gives for its ruling all echo Israel’s actions in Gaza.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

On Thursday, the International Court of Justice announced its landmark ruling in the case brought by The Gambia accusing Myanmar of genocide against the Rohingya people.

For the first time in the ICJ’s history, it found a state directly guilty of genocide.

It is hard to overstate the significance of this case. Supporters of Palestine are immediately, and correctly, going to draw parallels to South Africa’s case against Israel. But the ruling also has deeper, more global implications.

“Genocide” is a highly contested term. Defenders of Israel’s actions in Gaza often say that it is a legal term, and they’re not wrong. But it is not only a legal term; it has colloquial meanings as well.

The term was coined relatively recently, in 1944 by Raphael Lemkin. He was spurred to create the word in his book, Axis Rule in Occupied Europe by the Holocaust of World War II but did not intend for that horror to stand as the definition of the term. In fact, he noted himself that he would apply it to the Ottoman Empire’s atrocities against the Armenian people three decades prior.

The argument that genocide is a purely legal term is dangerous. With no court to rule, would that exclude the obvious genocide of the Indigenous Peoples of the Western Hemisphere? Perhaps more to the point, would the fact that no state has, before today, been found guilty of genocide by the ICJ mean that it has not happened since the agreement on the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide of 1948?

That would certainly be disputed in the cases of Rwanda, Darfur, Cambodia, Bosnia, the Yazidis in Iraq and Syria, and a depressing number of other cases, just in the past seventy-eight years.

These facts are important to note because the argument that the ICJ has not declared genocide in Gaza does not mean there is no genocide in Gaza. That will remain so even if the ICJ does not hold Israel responsible for the crime of genocide in Gaza.

But it is obvious that the outcome of South Africa’s case against Israel carries monumental weight, and the case against Myanmar holds many parallels.

The Rohingya lived under a brutal junta in Myanmar which severely restricted their rights. Myanmar claims that their actions against the Rohingya community were a response to Rohingya violence. Myanmar, like Israel, argued that the refugee crisis and the sizable number of civilian deaths were part of security operations.

Yet it was never certain what the ICJ ruling would turn out to be, and as much as the case has many similarities to Gaza, the ruling does not by any means guarantee that the case of Gaza will be decided in the same way. But it does offer a strong ray of hope in that direction.

Only two accusations of genocide had ever come before the ICJ prior to this one. One was a cross-accusation between Serbia and Croatia which the Court summarily dismissed. The other was the Srebrenica massacre of 1993, where Bosnia and Herzegovina accused Serbia and Montenegro of genocide.

In that case (which, it should be noted, took fourteen years between when it was filed and when it was decided), the ICJ decided that genocide had been committed, but that the states were not responsible for the genocide. The ICJ ruled only that Serbia had violated its obligation to prevent genocide.

That was worrisome because the case clarified that conviction for genocide has an extremely high bar. The ICJ ruled that, to prove genocidal intent, the circumstances must lead to only one conclusion: that genocide was the goal of the state’s actions. If any other motive is possible, then intent cannot be legally established.

Proving intent is already difficult, since genocidal states do not generally announce, as the Nazis did, that they intended to wipe entire groups of people out of a specific place. Saying that such proof requires that no other conclusion is even possible was seen by many as a bar so high that no state could ever be held responsible for genocide.

The ruling against Myanmar shows that, although the bar is high, it can be reached. That is an enormous development for those who hope to see Israel held accountable for genocide.

Specifically, the ICJ ruled that Myanmar was guilty of both the commission of genocide and the failure to prevent it, which are two different crimes. That’s important because it covers both acts that were directly ordered by the Myanmar military or government as well as any acts that might have been perpetrated by Myanmar’s forces or others acting without direct or implied orders.

The Court also found that Myanmar had violated its order to preserve evidence related to the case. This will strengthen this precedent in the case of Israel and, should it ever come to trial, the case against Russia brought by Ukraine.

Interestingly, the ICJ ruled that Myanmar was not guilty of public incitement to genocide. That will likely be different for Israel, regardless of how the other verdicts land, given the unusually large volume of genocidal statements that Israeli officials made, especially in the earliest days of the genocide.

This part is complicated. Individuals held responsible for genocide are expected to be tried by their home countries first and foremost, but if that fails, international courts, such as the ICC, or tribunals are the alternative, according to the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide.

The Convention does not prescribe penalties for states. The Court can order reparations, but there are no specific guidelines or requirements for the Court to impose penalties on states.

In the Myanmar case, the Court ordered Myanmar to cease genocidal activities; prosecute any individuals responsible for the crime of genocide; assure the Rohingya that this won’t happen again; provide for the safe return of refugees who wish to return and ensure they are reunited with their families; and “to compensate the Rohingya group and its members for the damage caused,” the parameters of which the Court said it would determine in a subsequent document.

The Court also expects states that are party to the Convention to take their own actions, and this could be significant.

The European Union, unlike the United States and Israel, considers international law important. Although they have repeatedly shown a willingness to ignore it in Israel’s case, the EU’s procedures acknowledge the law and the international legal system. There is only so far they can bend these procedures.

In the case of Myanmar, the EU already had strong sanctions in place, since it was obvious, on a colloquial level, that the state had committed genocide or, at the very least, abhorrent crimes against the Rohingya.

But Israel is obviously treated differently.

Nonetheless, the politics of international law matters in Europe in a way it does not in the United States, let alone in Israel. EU agreements and the laws of many EU states mandate adherence to international law, creating a tension in Europe that, in a legal and political sense, doesn’t exist in the U.S.

In the case of Gaza, this is compounded by the fact that a case is pending before the ICJ against Germany. Nicaragua accuses Germany of breaching the Convention Against Genocide by supplying Israel with arms and by withdrawing funding for UNRWA. Germany has claimed the case is inadmissible and that Nicaragua lacks standing to bring it, and that decision is pending. It will not be decided for years, in all likelihood, even if it is not dismissed.

But Germany is concerned because, as Israel’s main benefactor aside from the United States, it faces disturbing historical echoes when it is accused of genocide, and its support for Israel has become increasingly controversial domestically, especially among rising parties on the left.

More significantly, a recent petition in Europe to suspend the EU-Israel Trade Agreement over Israel’s human rights violations reached one million verified EU signatures, which means the European Commission must consider the call.

No one seriously expects the EC to submit to the petition’s demand, but it is a big weight on the scale of moving EU policy toward Israel. A finding by the ICJ of genocide will give such a citizens’ demand a lot more weight.

Broader international sanctions would need to be mandated by the UN Security Council. For the foreseeable future, that is a dead end. The shift in American politics with the incoming Congress might change American policy in years to come, but for now, real punishment for Israel is still going to face a U.S. veto at the UNSC.

The ICJ decision is a monumental moment for international law. It crucially demonstrates that a finding of genocide is not beyond the ICJ. Indeed, it strengthens the argument that the crime of genocide, being understood as the worst possible crime, should need to meet a high bar for conviction.

The substance of the ruling was that the evidence proved the intent to commit genocide. The ruling states: “The Court considers that, in the present case, the scale and nature of Myanmar’s actions and the methods it employed went well beyond what would be required to punish the population and are instead characteristic of an intent to destroy a substantial part of the group. Features of such intent include the large numbers of persons killed, injured or displaced and the widespread brutal attacks on women and children… In the Court’s view, the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar’s actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of the protected group, namely the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State.”

The reasons the ICJ gives for its ruling all echo Israel’s actions in Gaza.

Giving even more hope for some justice, the Myanmar government was not so brazen or foolish as Israel as to state explicitly that it intended to carry out genocidal acts. Israel openly stated that it was cutting off food, water, medicine, electricity, and anything else it could cut to the entire population of Gaza and repeatedly ordered that besieged population to relocate from one destroyed area to another, on trips that were often hazardous.

The outcome of this ruling, in terms of its implications for the South Africa case in Gaza, could not have been better.

And as a demonstration that Israel and the United States have not yet succeeded in killing the entire concept of international law? That will be determined by whether this is a principle that holds in all cases, not just ones that the West approves of; and by whether the response of the international community suits the verdict, in Myanmar and in Palestine.

author: Randi Beers
title: News quiz Nov. 21 | Old traditions and new beginnings
content:
The holidays are again approaching and there’s lots to remember: gifts, Christmas parties, cards, holiday concerts, family visits — and don’t forget the turkey. But do you remember the events of last week? Let’s find out.




1.

 The public got a chance to see inside Nunavut’s new Aqqusariaq Recovery Centre during an open house on Nov. 14. The centre will offer various services to assist residents recovering from addiction. Which amenity is not included at the facility?




A.

 A daycare




B.

 A country food processing area




C.

 An Olympic-sized swimming pool




2.

 The Qikiqtani Inuit Association opposes a finding by the Nunavut Impact Review Board that a planned hydro project for Iqaluit does not need a full public review. Which company is behind the project?




A.

 Nunavut Nukkiksautiit Corp.




B.

 Arctic Fresh Projects Ltd.




C.

 Qulliq Energy Corp.




3.

 Iqaluit-born artist Aija Komangapik helped paint a new mural at the University of Ottawa. What did she illustrate?




A.

 A number of sea creatures, real and mythical, including narwhal, a grey seal and Sedna.




B.

 Traditional practices being passed down through generations.




C.

 A map of Inuit Nunangat that shows how all the regions are culturally connected.
















4.

 What new powers would proposed Bill S-8 give police?




A.

 The authority to search people’s luggage before boarding regional northern flights.




B.

 The authority to intercept mail.




C.

 The authority to open anybody’s Christmas presents without a search warrant.




5.

 Speaking of police, an investigation in Ottawa led to the seizure of five kilograms of cocaine alleged to be destined to Nunavut. How many doses of cocaine did police estimate they kept off the streets?




A.

 5,000




B.

 50,000




C.

 500,000




Nunavut Justice Minister George Hickes, left, and Nunavut RCMP commanding officer Chief Supt. Kent Pike discuss drug-trafficking routes into Nunavut during a news conference in Iqaluit on April 15. (File photo by Arty Sarkisian)




Answers:
















1.

 C — The $83.7-million Aqqusariaq Recovery Centre 

will have a little something

 for everybody — a sewing room, daycare, area for processing country food and a group therapy room. But there is no pool.




2.

 A — Nunavut Nukkiksautiit Corp. is behind the $500-million proposal to build a hydro plant for Iqaluit. The company is owned by Qikiqtaaluk Corp., which is owned by QIA. This means QIA is 

requesting

 a full public review of its own project.




3.

 B — Artist Aija Komangapik’s portion of the mural includes a seal, narhwhal, blue whale and walrus. “The creation for all the animals starts in the ocean, and for Inuit, it starts with Sedna,” she said to Nunatsiaq News 

in an interview

.




4.

 B — Don’t worry, nobody is going through your presents without a search warrant. But if passed, Bill S-8 would give police the 

power to intercept mail

 if they believe a package holds illicit items such as alcohol or drugs. (They would still need a search warrant.)




5. 

B — Police 

estimate

 a cocaine seizure they executed in August kept 50,000 doses of cocaine out of the territory. No charges have been announced in relation to the seizure.

Wir alle brauchen anonyme Orte im Netz: Die Forderung nach einer Klarnamenpflicht im Netz hat wieder Konjunktur. Dabei ist sie brandgefährlich für gleich mehrere Grundrechte 




„Nach dem Amoklauf von Graz wird in Österreich über eine Ausweispflicht im Netz diskutiert und die CDU in Schleswig-Holstein hat gerade gegen Hass und Hetze eine Klarnamenpflicht in sozialen Medien gefordert. Die Idee hinter der Forderung ist die Annahme, dass Menschen „mit offenem Visier“ weniger gewaltsam kommunizieren würden. Dafür gibt es jedoch wenig Belege, im Gegenteil hetzen Rassisten ganz offen. Eine Klarnamenpflicht im Internet oder in sozialen Medien ist keine gute Idee. Nicht nur das: Sie gefährdet die Pressefreiheit, die freie Entfaltung der Persönlichkeit, die Meinungsfreiheit, die Freiheit der Kunst, die informationelle Selbstbestimmung und die Religionsfreiheit. Und sie gefährdet insbesondere Minderheiten und verletzliche Gruppen. Anonymität und Pseudonymität sind notwendig für freie, demokratische Diskurse. Die Anonymität im Netz ist durch Ausweispflicht bei SIM-Karten oder durch IP-Speicherung schon heute stark eingeschränkt. Wer Anonymität und Pseudonymität im Netz weiter angreift, sägt an einem Grundpfeiler der Demokratie. (…) Es gibt bemerkenswert viele praktische Beispiele dafür, warum Pseudonyme unverzichtbar für eine freie Gesellschaft sind. In einem Artikel aus dem Jahr 2018, der (leider) immer noch aktuell ist, haben wir sechzehn besonders eindrückliche Beispiele ausgeführt. (…) In den Parlamenten sitzen zunehmend mehr Rechtsextreme. In manchen Bundesländern könnte die AfD bald die größte Fraktion stellen. Wenn der Aufwind der AfD nicht gestoppt wird, dann droht auch im Bund eine Regierung mit deren Beteiligung. Auch wenn diese Partei gerne so tut, als verteidige sie die Meinungsfreiheit – am Ende werden Faschisten immer alles tun, um die Freiheit von Meinungen einzuschränken, die nicht in ihr menschenfeindliches Weltbild passen. Anfangen werden sie mit den Freiheiten von Marginalisierten und Minderheiten. Am Ende werden sie allen die Freiheit nehmen, um ihre Macht zu sichern. Wer Hass und Hetze bekämpfen will, sollte sich den Menschen widmen, die täglich – mit Klarnamen! – in Parlamenten und Talkshows gegen Minderheiten wettern und ihre Verachtung für Menschenrechte und Demokratie propagieren. Eine Klarnamenpflicht ist schon in der Demokratie brandgefährlich, in den Händen von Autoritären ist sie ein mächtiges Instrument der Unterdrückung. Nicht umsonst gibt es solche Pflichten in China und Russland. Klarnamenpflicht ist eines der mächtigsten Werkzeuge, um Meinungsfreiheit zu bekämpfen, Menschen einzuschüchtern und Informationen zu kontrollieren. Selbst wenn eine Demokratie gerade nicht bedroht ist, sollte sie ein solches Werkzeug nicht einführen. Und gerade wenn eine Demokratie – wie unsere – ernsthaft bedroht ist, dann sollte sie alles daran setzen, dieses Werkzeug nicht auch noch freiwillig jenen zu überlassen, die gerade die Macht an sich reißen wollen.“

Deplatforming: Warum Trumps Accountsperrungen richtig und hochproblematisch sind




„… Twitter und viele andere Plattformen haben dem reichweitenstärksten Hassprediger der Welt nach der Stürmung des Kapitols in Washington den Saft abgedreht. Donald Trump verlor nicht nur seine Konten auf Twitter und Facebook, sondern sogar seinen E-Mailprovider, seinen Merchandise-Shop und seinen Snapchat-Account. Apple, Google und Amazon folgten und zerschlugen mit ihrer Marktmacht auch gleich die mögliche Exil-Plattform Parler, bevor ein von Trump angeführter Exodus dorthin stattfinden konnte. (…) Aus demokratischer Sicht mag es wünschenswert sein, wenn diejenigen, welche die Demokratie beseitigen wollen, dieses Schicksal ereilt. Wenn sie in die Schmuddelecken des Internets verdrängt werden. Wohlmeinend könnte man sagen, dass hier Unternehmen ihre politische Verantwortung wahrnehmen, um die Demokratie vor ihren Feind:innen zu schützen. (…) Doch so einfach ist es nicht: Deplatforming ist ein problematisches Mittel, weil es die Macht über die Meinungsfreiheit in die Hände einiger weniger einflussreicher Konzerne legt. (…) Nun sind die Account-Sperrungen gegen Trump und Teile seiner Unterstützer:innen beileibe nicht die ersten Fälle von Deplatforming. (…) Seit Jahren werden also Accounts auf Plattformen gesperrt, auch jene von Politiker:innen. Dies geschieht oftmals nach Gutsherrenart und ohne Begründung gegenüber den Betroffenen. Diese haben bislang wenig Chancen sich gegen solche Entscheidungen zu wehren, wenn sie keinen Sturm des Protestes und Medienberichterstattung generieren können, welche die Plattformen zum Umdenken zwingt. Es gibt weder etablierte Beschwerdemechanismen oder noch eine neutrale Schlichtung solcher Sperrungen, die ja immer auch fehlerhaft sein können. Insbesondere, wenn Algorithmen und nicht Menschen über den Fortbestand von Accounts entscheiden. Konzernentscheidungen zur Sperrung von Accounts sind von der Öffentlichkeit unkontrolliert. Sie werden umso problematischer, je größer, wichtiger und damit unverzichtbarer eine Plattform oder ein Service für die Kommunikation ist. (…) Fraglich ist natürlich auch, ob ein Deplatforming ausreicht, um antidemokratische und menschenfeindliche Ideologien zu bekämpfen. Kein Rassist wird durch ein Deplatforming zum Demokraten. Vielleicht führt die Maßnahme sogar zu einer Radikalisierung der Betroffenen, weil Gegenrede auf den Nischenplattformen vollkommen wegfällt. Ungeklärt sind auch Fragen von zielgerichteter politischer Werbung und die Rolle von Algorithmen, die honorieren, wie viel Interaktion, Empörung und Aufenthaltsdauer ein Inhalt generiert – und damit zur Verbreitung und Verstärkung rechtspopulistischer, verschwörungsideologischer und antidemokratischer Inhalte beitragen. Was das Deplatforming angeht, steht es Demokratien nicht gut zu Gesicht, dass eine kleine Gruppe von Unternehmenschefs Entscheidungen solcher Tragweite trifft. Selbst, wenn das Ergebnis richtig ist für die Demokratie.“

Nach dem Sturm aufs Kapitol: Die privatisierte Demokratie




„… Die kurzfristige Sperrung von Trumps Account war richtig. Tatsächlich sollte nicht ein privater Konzern entscheiden können, wer in der Öffentlichkeit was sagen darf. Das grundsätzliche Problem hinter dem Entscheid offenbarte sich in Merkels Bemerkung, wonach Twitter mit der Löschung die Meinungsfreiheit verletzte. Tut es eben gerade nicht: Mit ihren digitalen Plattformen haben die Techkonzerne die Demokratie ein Stück weit privatisiert. In den USA gilt die Meinungsfreiheit im privatisierten digitalen Raum nicht – und auch in Europa nur beschränkt: Die Konzerne entscheiden, wer was sagen darf. Diese Privatisierung der Demokratie ist das Resultat einer jahrzehntelangen Politik. Nachdem das Internet einst mit öffentlichen Geldern entwickelt worden war, überliessen die USA nach der Zerschlagung der Telekomfirma AT&T 1984 die Branche dem freien Markt – so wie auch viele europäische Länder. Wie der deutsche Soziologe Philipp Staab in seinem Buch «Digitaler Kapitalismus» aufzeigt, haben die Regierungen mit der Deregulierung der Finanzmärkte dafür gesorgt, dass eine Unmenge von Risikokapital in die aufsteigenden Techfirmen floss. Die Regierungen haben den Firmen zudem die Steuern gesenkt und zugeschaut, wie diese ihre Monopole errichteten. So passt es, dass Trump – der diese rechtslibertäre Politik auf die Spitze trieb – der erste US-Präsident war, der via Techkonzern regierte. Ein Zensurmonster und ein dagegen harmloser George Orwell




„… Anfangs zeigten sich über den politischen Aktionismus gegen „Fake News“ vor allem Nutzer Sozialer Medien besorgt – nun sprechen sich auch Vertreter von Verbänden und etablierten Medien dagegen aus. Besonders viel Aufmerksamkeit erregt Mathias Döpfner, der Präsident des Bundesverbandes Deutscher Zeitungsverleger (BDZV) und Vorstandsvorsitzender der Axel Springer SE. Er verlautbarte in einem Interview, er habe „den Eindruck, dass gerade ein paar Grundprinzipien freiheitlicher Gesellschaftsordnung […] im Namen der guten Absichten […] mit Füßen getreten werden“ – und im Vergleich mit Justizminister Heiko Maas‘ Bestrebungen zur Einrichtung staatlicher Wahrheitsstellen seien die dystopischen Entwürfe des Schriftstellers George Orwell „harmlos“. Dass die Glaubwürdigkeit etablierter Medien abgenommen hat, liegt Döpfners Worten nach nicht an Facebook, sondern daran, dass sie „mittlerweile von vielen als Teil einer großen Eliten-Kungelei wahrgenommen“ werden: „Vielleicht“, so der Springer-Chef in seinem Erklärungsversuch dazu, „transportieren wir zu oft Wünsche, wie etwas sein müsste und zu selten Fakten, Tatsachen, schonungslose Beobachtungen“. (…) Ob es den Regierungsparteien gelingt, Vorschriften gegen Fake News vorzulegen, die einer gerichtlichen Überprüfung standhalten, ist ohnehin offen: Sven Rebehn, der Geschäftsführer des Deutsche Richterbunds, ist unter anderem deshalb skeptisch, weil der angekündigte „ganz großen Wurf […] ein halbes Jahr vor der Bundestagswahl“ angekündigt wird – und zwar ohne „klare Definition, was unter Fake News zu verstehen sei“. Möglicherweise eignet sich der Begriff deshalb weniger für ein Gesetz, als für eine wohlfeile Erklärung, woran es angeblich lag, dass man Wähler verloren hat.“

 

Beitrag von Peter Mühlbauer vom 2. Februar 2017 bei Telepolis 

 










Faking News: Eine Richtigstellung 




„Schade eigentlich, dass um die Jahrtausendwende noch keiner daran dachte, Fake-News zu verbieten. Vielleicht hätte uns das Hartz IV und die Riesterrente erspart. Müsste man solche Folgen, Fake-Produkte also, nicht eigentlich auch auf den Prüfstand stellen? (…) Die Union möchte ja jetzt Facebook verpflichten, Fake-Meldungen mit einer Richtigstellung oder Gegendarstellung auszustatten. Das ist gar nicht so einfach. Man muss zunächst alles prüfen und dann muss man ja auch die Wahrheit kennen. Und an diesem Punkt sind wir schon bei einer alten philosophischen Frage, die heute immer noch aktuell ist: Was ist Wahrheit? Und heute fast noch wichtiger: Wer bringt sie wie in die Welt? Wer brachte zum Beispiel die Wahrheit in die Welt, dass nur eine kapitalgedeckte Finanzierung der Rente die letzte Ausflucht aus der Altersarmut sein könnte? Diese Botschaft war schon ein Fake, als sie hier den politischen Diskurs erreicht hatte. Man sprach hier noch vom Riestern und von der Schaffung von Betriebsrenten im großen Stil, da war Enron schon zu einem Begriff geworden. Mit ein wenig Phantasie konnte man sich da schon ausmalen, dass ein Rentenmodell, dass sich den Höhen und Tiefen des Marktes aussetzt, nicht unbedingt ein Aushängeschild für Stabilität sein dürfte. Aber die Medien rührten munter weiter die Trommel und in jeder Talkshow hockte ein als Experte ausgewiesener Partikularinteressierter, der die Notwendigkeit des Umdenkens einforderte. Das war alles ein riesiger Fake…“

 

Beitrag von Roberto J. De Lapuente vom 1. Februar 2017 bei den neulandrebellen 










Regulierungsdauerfeuer gegen Fake News und Social Bots ohne empirische Grundlage


„

Als würden Falschmeldungen und Meinungsroboter die Demokratie im Wahljahr 2017 umstürzen, überschlägt sich die Bundespolitik mit immer neuen Vorschlägen. Dabei könnte die Regulierung selbst mehr Schaden an Grundrechten anrichten als die Phänomene, die bekämpft werden sollen…

“  

Ein Kommentar von Markus Reuter am 24. Januar 2017 bei Netzpolitik.org 










Die Wächter der Meinungsfreiheit


„

Die Vermengung verschiedenster Themen zum Schlagwort „Fake-News“ führt nicht nur dazu, dass es einfacher wird, Menschen dazu zu bringen, ein Vorgehen gegen diese „Fake-News“ gutzuheißen – sie bringt auch die Möglichkeit mit sich, schleichend private Wächter der Meinungsfreiheit zu etablieren. Dabei ist es wichtig, im Blick zu behalten, wer diese Wächter sind…

“ 

Beitrag von Alexander und Bettina Hammer vom 22. Januar 2017 bei telepolis

 










Warum ich den Begriff „Fakenews“ nicht mehr nutzen werde


„

Es wird kaum noch möglich sein, den Begriff „Fakenews“ zu stoppen. Er beherrscht seit Wochen die Diskussion, jeder weiß, was damit gemeint ist, er klingt definitiv besser als die „problematischen Inhalte“, über die ich vor einem Jahr schrieb. Trotzdem: Ich werde versuchen, den Begriff „Fakenews“ in Zukunft zu vermeiden. Denn er wird zum Problem. Das liegt nicht nur daran, dass unter „Fakenews“ alles und nichts fällt. Die Dimensionen von „Fakenews“ könnten sein: Propaganda, Lügen, Clickbait, Hoaxes, Spam, Irrtümer, Satire, Tatsachenverdrehungen, fehlender Kontext, Gerüchte, unklare Formulierungen, Halbwahrheiten, falsche Zusammenhänge, Recherchefehler. Natürlich geht es zurzeit vor allem um Propaganda mit Erfundenem. (…) Doch gerade weil „Fakenews“ alles und nichts sind, lässt sich der Begriff wunderbar nutzen, um damit nicht mehr nur Falschmeldungen, Propaganda und Lügen zu brandmarken. Genutzt wird er auch für Inhalte, die nicht ins eigene Weltbild passen…

“ 

Beitrag von Dennis Horn vom 17.01.2017 beim WDR-Blog 

 










Neuer ETSI-Standard sieht Social-Media-Schnittstelle zum Datenabgriff durch Behörden vor


„

Elektronische Durchsuchung soll von Staatsanwaltschaften aus 50 Ländern angeordnet werden können: In einer seiner letzten öffentlichen Äußerungen als EU-Parlamentspräsident forderte der SPD-Politiker Martin Schulz harte Strafen für Social-Media-Inhalte, die er als illegitim ansieht. Diese Strafen sollten seiner Ansicht nach auf europäischer Ebene eingeführt werden. Die EU-Kommission arbeitet bereits an technischen Standards, die dafür sorgen sollen, dass Polizei- und Justizbehörden Daten von Nutzern Sozialer Netzwerke möglichst reibungslos abgreifen können, wenn man sie beschuldigt, Fake News oder Hate Speech zu verbreiten…

“ 

Beitrag von Peter Mühlbauer bei telepolis vom 5. Januar 2017 

. Aus dem Text:







„

… Dazu hat das European Telecom Standards Institute (ETSI) eine Spezifikation für einen „eWarrant“, einen „elektronischen Durchsuchungsbeschluss“ so geändert, dass Betreiber Sozialer Medien Behörden eine Extra-Schnittstelle freihalten müssen, über die diese dann nicht nur Verkehrsdaten, sondern auch Chatprotokolle bequem über spezielle Server abgreifen können. Der Datenschutzexperte Erich Möchel geht davon aus, dass damit die „Begehrlichkeiten“ zunehmen werden, weil mit den neuen ETSI-Schnittstellen sowohl befugten als auch unbefugten Interessenten „weitaus mehr und höherwertige Daten“ winken als vorher. (…) Der von den Nutzerzahlen her wichtigste Social-Media-Dienstleister ist Facebook. Für ihn arbeitet die EU-Kommission spezielle Überwachungsregeln aus, die sie innerhalb der nächsten sechs Monate vorstellen will. Darüber hinaus beschäftigt sich das EU-Parlament mit einer „Digitalen Charta“, die ein (so Markus Kompa) „von der Zeit-Stiftung inthronisierter Tugendrat deutscher Intellektueller ungebeten propagierte“. Obwohl der auffällig rein deutsche, aber für ein europaweites Gelten gedachte Entwurf von Juristen unisono als grob grundrechtswidriges Zensurgesetz zerrissen wurde, nahm ihn der Ausschuss für bürgerliche Freiheiten, Justiz und Inneres als „Diskussionsgrundlage“ an – was wahrscheinlich auch daran lag, dass Martin Schulz zu den Verfassern gehört… 

„
















Interview mit Hoaxmap.org über Falschmeldungen: Medienkompetenz statt gesetzliche Maßnahmen




„Seit der US-Wahl tobt eine Debatte über die politischen Folgen von Falschmeldungen. Dagegen aktiv ist bereits seit dem Frühjahr die Online-Plattform Hoaxmap.org. Auf einer Karte sammelt sie widerlegte Gerüchte über Geflüchtete. (…) Auch Innenminister Thomas de Maizière hat in mindestens zwei Fällen falsche Zahlen verbreitet. Einmal hat er gesagt, dass 30 Prozent derjenigen Asylbewerber*innen, die angeben, aus Syrien zu kommen, in Wirklichkeit gar keine Syrer seien. Weder er noch sein Ministerium konnten das jedoch belegen. Beim zweiten Mal ging es um Atteste, die angeblich von Ärzt*innen zu leichtfertig ausgestellt werden würden um Abschiebungen von ausreisepflichtigen Asylbewerber*innen zu verhindern. Auch da hat er mit erfunden Zahlen operiert…“

 

Simon Rebiger im Gespräch mit Karolin Schwarz und Lutz Helm von Hoaxmap.org vom 27. Dezember 2016 bei Netzpolitik 










33C3: Netzzensur durch die Hintertür?


„

Mit der Zensursula-Kampagne konnten deutsche Netzaktivisten vor sechs Jahren den Aufbau einer  Zensur-Infrastruktur für das Internet verhindern. Doch wegen der zunehmenden Bedeutung sozialer Plattformen und dem Kampf gegen Fake-News und Terror könnte nun eine solche Infrastruktur durch die Hintertür entstehen, warnte der Gründer des Blogs Netzpolitik.org, Markus Beckedahl, auf dem Chaos Communication Congress in Hamburg. „Wir müssen damit leben, dass sich mittlerweile ein Viertel der Bevölkerung in Deutschland täglich über Facebook informiert“, sagte Beckedahl. Dies habe ernste Folgen für den öffentlichen Diskurs. Während das Internet mit einem Marktplatz vergleichbar sei, auf dem zum Beispiel Demonstrationen durchgeführt werden könnten, erinnere Facebook mehr an ein Einkaufszentrum, bei dem die Regeln des Betreibers gelten. Diese Entwicklung werde auch immer mehr von Regierungen genutzt

…“ 

Artikel von Torsten Kleinz vom 31.12.2016 bei heise online 

 







Der Beitrag 

NetzDG u.a.: Wie sich die Debatte um Fake (und Hate) News zum Problem für Presse- und Meinungsfreiheit entwickelt

author: Ayden Runnels
title: Texas Drops Lawsuits Against Out-of-State Abortion Providers
content:
”These cases were baseless from the start and designed to intimidate doctors nationwide,” said one abortion advocate.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Attorney General Ken Paxton on Friday dropped two lawsuits that were filed against out-of-state doctors for sending abortion medication to Texas — a practice his successor, Nathan Johnson, has vowed not to upkeep.

In January and February, Paxton sued two doctors in California and nurse practitioner Debra Lynch in Delaware for mailing abortion pills to Texas residents and operating services that help do so. But on Friday, Paxton filed notices of nonsuit in both cases, part of a wave of withdrawals his office has filed as he prepares to leave office in January.

It is illegal for Texas doctors to mail abortion medication within the state — but Paxton has also sued doctors in other states who prescribe the medication. Other states’ “shield laws,” which protect physicians who send abortion medications, have complicated Paxton’s efforts to seek damages against the doctors.

The end of the two suits was celebrated by abortion advocates, including Nancy Northup, president and CEO of the Center for Reproductive Rights, who also highlighted Attorney General-elect Johnson’s pledge to not to sue out-of-state doctors who mail abortion pills to Texas.

“The incoming Attorney General agrees with most Americans that doctors shouldn’t be treated like criminals,” Northup said. ”These cases were baseless from the start and designed to intimidate doctors nationwide.”

Less than a day after winning his election, Johnson told The Texas Tribune he would “cease using Texas abortion laws as an instrument of persecution and intimidation” and described challenges to other states’ shield laws as “judicially absurd.”

One of the California doctors, Dr. Remy Coeytaux, is also being sued by a Galveston County man who accused Coeytaux of providing his girlfriend with abortion pills at the direction of her ex-husband.

That suit and Paxton’s suit against Coeytaux and Dr. Rebecca Gomperts were brought under House Bill 7, described by opponents as a “bounty hunter law” which allows private citizens to sue those who distribute or mail abortion medication to or from Texas.

Disclosure: Center for Reproductive Rights has been a financial supporter of The Texas Tribune within the past five years. The Texas Tribune is a nonprofit, nonpartisan news organization that is funded in part by donations from members, foundations and corporate sponsors. Financial supporters play no role in our journalism. Find a complete list of them and more information about our financial and disclosure policies here.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

Our fundraiser ended last night, but there’s still time for us to meet those basic operating expenses — we need only $10,000. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

author: Randi Beers
title: Blubber for bibles
content:
Greenlanders were the first Inuit to have the Christian Bible translated into their language.




Between 1750 and 1850, Danish and Norwegian ministers of the Lutheran Church and German Moravians worked to translate the scriptures into Kalaallisut. They were aided by the Danish Bible Society and the London-based British and Foreign Bible Society.




By 1850, there were at least 20 versions of the Bible in existence. Some were more accurate than others. As missionaries’ knowledge of the language progressed, the translations became better.




The writing systems used also posed a problem. The Greenlandic orthography had not yet been standardized. It would remain for Samuel Kleinschmidt, son of a Moravian missionary, to undertake that task in the 1850s.




The Qallunaat ministers could not, of course, have taken on the monumental task of translating into a language new to them without the assistance of Inuit converts to Christianity who were willing, and usually eager, to help them.




Before 1800, the New Testament and some psalms had been translated by Paul Egede, son of Hans Egede, who had established the first mission in Greenland in 1721. Paul Egede had the advantage of having grown up in Greenland and therefore spoke Greenlandic much better than his father did.




Paul Egede did not mention the names of his Greenlandic assistants when his first translations were published in 1744. We only learn their names through his journal, published more than four decades later, in 1788.
















His main assistants were a woman, Arnarsak, baptized in 1737, and a man, Pungiok, who took the Christian name of Hans.




The two made an unusual request of Egede. They did not want the translations, for which they were in part responsible, to be shared widely among the Kalaallit.




Egede explained their reasoning: “It would not be useful for their unbelieving compatriots to be made aware, for example, that Cain, one of God’s first rational creations, was so wicked, or of Jacob’s deception of his father and brother, [or] the polygamy of the patriarchs.”




The two Greenlanders suggested that, instead, only certain selections from the translations should be distributed and that the more lurid parts be omitted. Nonetheless, the translations were published in their entirety.




The Moravians in Greenland were off to a slower start with biblical translations. In the late 1700s, they expended their mission efforts to Labrador where they built on the strengths of missionaries to that coast who brought with them the knowledge they had acquired in Greenland.




In 1804, the British and Foreign Bible Society was formed, with a daunting mandate to translate the Bible into all the languages of the world. Within a century, their publications were available in over 1,000 languages.
















In Labrador, the Inuit Moravian converts eagerly accepted the British and Foreign Bible Society’s publications of the Gospel, as translated by their missionaries, who usually worked by revising Greenlandic publications into their understanding of the local dialect.




Grateful Inuit wrote letters of thanks to the society. Brother Benjamin Kohlmeister sent some of these letters from Nain to Rev. C. J. Latrobe, who provided them to the society.




The Labrador Inuit, unprompted, decided to make a collection of seal blubber to send to the society to help in the costs of its work. They knew that blubber was a valuable trade commodity at the Moravian stores — the Moravians supported the costs of their missions through trade with the Inuit.




Kohlmeister wrote: “Some brought whole seals, others half a seal or pieces, as they could spare it. Some brought pieces of blubber in the name of their children, requesting that their poor gifts might be accepted.”




The Inuit had learned that the society’s work was supported through donations from pious people, who were often poor.
















They explained, through Kohlmeister: “We have indeed spoken together, and observed, that these many books, given to us without pay, must be very dear somewhere, but we never have known before now, that even poor people bring their money, out of pure love, that we may get these comfortable words of God. We are indeed poor, but we might bring now and then some blubber as a contribution.”




The blubber yielded 30 gallons of oil. Kohlmeister went on: “They now begged me to send this collection of blubber to those generous friends who printed the Bibles for them, that more heathen might be presented with that book.”




A careful reading makes it clear what the Inuit intended. They were not offering the blubber to pay for the books they had received “without pay.”




Rather, they were offering to support the society in its translations of the Bible into other languages far removed from the Moravian missions to the Inuit.




The Inuit in Labrador saw themselves as part of a worldwide community of Christians.




[Note: I owe the title to a scholarly paper by Hilary Mary Carey of the University of Bristol. It was too good a title to pass up.]




Taissumani is an occasional column that recalls events of historical interest. Kenn Harper is a historian and writer who lived in the Arctic for over 50 years. He is the author of 

Give Me Winter, Give Me Dogs: Knud Rasmussen and the Fifth Thule Expedition

, and 

Thou Shalt Do No Murder

, among other books. Feedback? Send your comments and questions to kennharper@hotmail.com.

author: rti_admin
title: Class Interests in Casteless Disguise: Can Caste Be Disowned Without Surrendering Property and Lineage?
content:
‘I don’t believe in caste. I have no caste. Let’s build a casteless society.’ One hears this all the time now, from people who call themselves progressive, rationalist, liberal. On the face of it, there’s nothing to argue with. Who could object to that?

But look at the Indian socio-economic structure honestly, and the slogan starts to look less like idealism and more like a sleight of hand. Because you can’t abandon caste in your speech while quietly holding on to the wealth and advantages caste handed you. That isn’t annihilation of caste. It’s a way of protecting the hierarchy while pretending to be above it.

Louis Althusser, in Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses (1970), made a point worth taking seriously here: ideology always exists in an apparatus, in practices—its existence is material. Caste is no different. It isn’t just a mental delusion people can shrug off. It has a material life, and in India that life runs through what we might call PPP: Property, Parents, Privileges.

Property means land, urban real estate, commercial capital—concentrated over generations in dominant-caste hands. Parents means lineage: hereditary prestige, ancestral standing, social capital kept carefully inside kin groups through endogamous marriage. Privileges means the leverage that comes from all of it—the networks that open doors in elite schools, boardrooms, professions, and commerce.

So when someone says they’ve “given up caste” because they dropped their surname, while still inheriting the family estate, the legacy networks, and the generational cultural capital—what exactly have they given up? You cannot disown caste while safeguarding the material lineage and property that caste produced. The two don’t come apart that easily.

Ambedkar: Annihilating Caste Means Annihilating Class

Ambedkar saw this clearly in Annihilation of Caste (1936). The caste order, he insisted, is not some innocent functional division of labour: “The Caste System is not merely division of labour. It is also a division of labourers.”

To the socialists of his day who thought economic reorganization alone would dismantle caste, he put the question squarely: can you have economic reform without first reforming the social order? If that order is graded by caste, what guarantee is there that Indian proletarians—divided into watertight caste compartments—will ever combine against their exploiters?

And on the myth of individual merit, he was blunt: those who benefit from birth, education, family name, business connections, and inherited wealth will win the race. But that isn’t a selection of the able. It’s a selection of the privileged. For Ambedkar, annihilation of caste was never about nominal changes in personal conduct. It demanded structural equality across economic, educational, political, and material life. Keeping the assets inside dominant groups while claiming caste is abolished runs directly against everything he argued.

The Biography of the “General Category”

Sociologist Satish Deshpande, in “Caste and Castelessness: Towards a Biography of the ‘General Category'” (2013), gave this rhetoric its proper name. Upper castes, he showed, have systematically laundered historical caste capital into the secular language of “merit” and individual competence. They shed the overt markers of caste, settle comfortably into the constitutionally unmarked “General Category,” and reinvent themselves as casteless modern citizens.

The burden of caste then gets shifted entirely onto SC, ST, and OBC communities—who are caricatured as “casteist” or backward for invoking affirmative action. Constitutional certificates become a badge of sectarian identity, while upper-caste generational capital passes as unmarked merit. That’s the strategy of the General Category, and Deshpande names it for what it is.

Lately there have been petitions before high courts—Telangana, Madras—asking for a “No Caste / Casteless” column in census forms, school transfer certificates, state applications. These deserve a closer look, because they tend to come in two flavours.

One is misguided cluelessness: well-meaning but politically naive people, from oppressed or liberal backgrounds, who imagine that leaving a box blank on a form dissolves structural violence. It doesn’t.

The other is more deliberate: an upper-caste design to escape structural accountability. If caste disappears from the census and public records, surveys can no longer measure how land, corporate wealth, and state power concentrate in dominant groups. And once it can’t be measured, constitutional claims to representation, reservations, and welfare quietly lose their footing.

For marginalized communities, a caste certificate is not a subsidy or a badge of backwardness. It is a tool for survival, statutory protection, and democratic entitlement. In an unequal society, petitioning to erase caste administratively only dismantles the legal foundations of social justice.

What Genuine Annihilation Would Require

It won’t come from rhetorical denial or blank forms. It requires redistributing material resources—land, productive wealth, educational access, and the employment monopolies built through caste networks. It requires treating affirmative action as restorative justice, not charity. And it requires exposing the performance of castelessness that runs in tandem with keeping Property, Parents, and Privileges intact.

Insisting on being called casteless while sitting on accumulated caste monopolies isn’t an emancipatory program. It’s a defence mechanism for the status quo.

Dr. B. Karthik Navayan is an Advocate and Human Rights Activist

author: Corey Larocque
title: Pirutsiagutiit ends Inuit Child First Initiative uncertainty
content:
It’s welcome news the federal government has finally ended the uncertainty around its Inuit Child First Initiative that has existed for two years. But there’s still a lot of work to be done to see how its $115-million-a-year replacement will work as Ottawa transfers responsibility to four Inuit treaty organizations.




On Wednesday, Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty and Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami president Natan Obed unveiled details about the new 

Pirutsiagutiit

 program the federal government unveiled in its recent budget.




The government created it to provide health, social and education products, services and supports to address what Obed called the “profound inequities” Inuit children face. It has been nearly a year since Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty pledged to 

retool the old program

.




The Liberals had stumbled along since 2025 when funding for the Inuit Child First Initiative dried up. Ottawa provided two temporary 

extensions

 to keep the program going while it worked on a long-term replacement.




Pirutsiagutiit, which means “resources for growing well” in Inuktut, hands the responsibility for managing the five-year, $575-million funding to Inuit treaty organizations — Nunavut Tunngavik Inc., Makivvik, Inuvialuit Regional Corp., and the Nunatsiavut government.




It’s rooted in the idea that community-based decisions are better than Ottawa-based decisions.




“Inuit are best-placed to understand the needs of our children,” Obed said.
















Many Nunavummiut will remember Inuit Child First Initiative as the program that funded universal food vouchers in most of the territory’s communities in 2024 and 2025. It helped feed 

15,000

 Inuit children over the two years it was in place.




In most communities, Inuit families were eligible for a $500 grocery store voucher for each child under the age of 18 and an additional $250 a month for each child under four.




But Ottawa ended that universal program, plunging thousands of families who had come to rely on the vouchers into 

financial uncertainty

. The government replaced it with a scheme that required families to make individual applications for money to pay for groceries.




A return to a universal food voucher program “is not the path we have chosen,” Gull-Masty said during Wednesday’s news conference. It will be up to each treaty organization to determine the terms and conditions for all the supports it will provide.




Pirutsiagutiit should provide more certainty about what supports will be eligible for funding. There had been what Obed called “real frustration” caused by the federal Indigenous Services Department’s changing terms and conditions about what was previously eligible.




Pirutsiagutiit will take effect on April 1, 2027 — the start of the government’s next fiscal year. Even then, the Inuit Child First Initiative will remain in place until each treaty organization works out terms and conditions of the new program with Ottawa.
















With each treaty organization responsible for making decisions about how to use its share of the money, it sounds like the supports that will be eligible for funding might vary from one part of Inuit Nunangat to another.




One of the problems with the Inuit Child First Initiative was the lack of clarity about what was eligible for funding. To make Pirutsiagutiit more effective in helping Inuit children, the important task will be to make it clear what health, education and social supports are eligible to be funded.

author: Binoy Kampark
title: Floods add to severe humanitarian crisis in Gaza
content:
Palestinians in the Gaza strip continue to live in precarious conditions, accommodated in makeshift, overcrowded shelters and tents brought about by a war waged with catastrophic consequences.

Israeli authorities are resisting efforts to improve living conditions in Gaza, even as they advance the demarcated Yellow Line that is shrinking the already diminished territory.

Heavy rainfall since November 6 has added to the misery for Gazans, 65% of whom live in tents or rudimentary shelters. Just under 1 million people live in areas prone to flooding, with 400,000 living in areas determined by the World Health Organisation (WHO) as “extremely high risk”.

Tens of thousands of tents housing displaced Palestinians have been flooded.

Instances of respiratory illnesses are on the rise. “The numbers already show the pressure,” Dr Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, WHO representative in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, said. “Acute respiratory infections are 33,000 cases higher than at the same time last year.”

According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), the rains “damaged displacement sites, shelter and humanitarian facilities, and disrupted services across all five governorates”.

The damage caused within 24 hours was formidable, affecting 26,000 households. (That number has since risen to 46,000.) More than 6000 family shelters were destroyed in that time, with 17,400 damaged. Damaged buildings have collapsed, and the rains have added to existing structural and environmental risks.

Adding to this are the problems of exposed ordnance buried under the debris or shifted to other areas, endangering the lives of residents and humanitarian personnel.

The November 13 humanitarian situation report from OCHA is evenly grim. Between November 3–9, Israeli airstrikes, shooting and shelling continued, killing 22 Palestinians and injuring 90.

This brought the total number of reported deaths since the October 2025 “ceasefire” agreement to 1613, with 5833 suffering injuries. The Ministry of Health in Gaza retroactively added 12 fatalities once their identification details were verified.

But there has not been a rise in humanitarian supplies to cope with the rain-borne crisis — rather the opposite. Between November 2–8, 228 of the 262 United Nations and partner trucks intended for entry into Gaza were offloaded on the Israeli side of Kerem Shalom; 128 from Ashdod, 25 from Egypt, 44 from Israel, 12 from the West Bank and 18 from Jordan.

The OCHA reported that the number of trucks offloaded constituted a fall of 42% from the previous week. Israel suspended the Egyptian corridor, citing concerns over smuggling. Between November 3–8, no trucks were offloaded.

The overall figures also fell due to, in the UN agency’s words, “reduced aid volumes available to partners amid funding constraints”.

The Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT), responsible for coordinating aid, says otherwise. The crisis is being addressed; poor sanitary conditions were being improved prior to the rain, an effort coordinated with international bodies. More than 93,000 tents and over 8600 trucks holding tarpaulin sheets, blankets and winter clothing have entered Gaza since the winterization plan was launched by the Board of Peace, UN agencies and NGOs.

But the Haaretz newspaper obtained data which revealed a growing decline in food deliveries to Gaza, to add to severe shortages of medical supplies, tents and materials to repair crippled infrastructure.

Under the ceasefire deal, Israel had pledged that it would permit 4200 vehicles carrying essential humanitarian aid and commercial items, including food, fuel, vital medical equipment and supplies, shelter materials and equipment for repairing essential infrastructure into Gaza each week.

COGAT’s own figures supplied to the US-led International Gaza Support Center (IGSC) show totals well short of the promised monthly rate of 18,200 vehicles allowed into the Strip: 4700 in March, 5300 in April and over 9600 in May.

In June, the number rose to 12,000, only to fall again to 10,000 for the months of July and August. September proved to be the high point with 13,000, while in October only 6500 vehicles were allowed in. (Seemingly caught out by this unusual affliction of verisimilitude, COGAT called its own figures “inaccurate”, saying that Israel had met and even exceeded its humanitarian commitments.)

COGAT’s mangled version of reality has not impressed some foreign ministries. In its November 14 statement, the Council of the European Union expressed concern that flooding and wintry conditions were “further aggravating the living conditions of an already exhausted population, exacerbating unsafe conditions and human suffering”.

The Council also noted the lethal strike on Nasser Hospital by the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) that killed six people, including a surgeon and a 13-year-old boy.

Israel was urged “to allow immediate, unimpeded access and sustained distribution of humanitarian assistance and early recovery support at scale, and to reopen all Gaza border crossings”.

A few days later, a joint statement from the foreign ministers of Australia, Canada, Italy and the United Kingdom warned that “as winter takes hold in Gaza, the humanitarian situation on the ground is dire”. It said 150,000 tents, along with other essential supplies were “being held at the border and prevented from entering Gaza. The situation is entirely reversible – and there is still time to act before the winter fully sets in.”

They called on Israel “to stop the delays now and allow immediate, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza”. The crossings had to be opened, and tents permitted to enter. “Dual-use items necessary for humanitarian operations and early recovery must be granted entry before it is too late.”

Van De Weerdt said of the crisis that promises to deteriorate: “It is shocking that just a few days of rain really showed us what the coming months will bring. And winter has not even fully set in. The worst really is yet to come.”

[Binoy Kampmark currently lectures at RMIT University.]

World Health Organization (WHO)

United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

author: taz
title: Jetzt noch schnell räumen lassen
content:
Alt­mie­te­r*in­nen der Rigaer94 haben schon länger den Widerstand gegen Räumungspläne aufgegeben. Rückt Mitte Dezember der Gerichtsvollzieher an?




„Rigaer94 verteidigen“, diese Parole findet sich seit Jahren auf vielen Plakaten und Transparenten. Doch zuletzt war es um das linke Hausprojekt im Friedrichshainer Nordkiez ruhiger geworden. Das könnte sich in den nächsten Wochen wieder ändern.




Für den 15. Dezember hat sich der Gerichtsvollzieher angekündigt. Er will mehrere Wohnungen im Seitenflügel und Hinterhaus der Rigaer Straße 94 räumen lassen. Die Bewohner*innen, von denen niemand mit Namen in der Zeitung stehen will, hatten damit gerechnet, waren aber trotzdem über den Zeitpunkt der Räumungsankündigung überrascht. Die Wohnungen waren nicht besetzt: Es gab Mietverträge, die noch in den 1990er Jahren abgeschlossen worden waren. Doch die Alt­mie­te­r*in­nen wohnen längst nicht mehr im Haus. Mehrere von ihnen hatten sich schon im Sommer 2024 mit dem Hauseigentümer verständigt, sich nicht weiter gegen Räumungsklagen wehren zu wollen. Dafür gab es unterschiedliche Gründe: Manche von ihnen wollten nicht mehr die juristischen Probleme tragen, zudem gab es politische Differenzen mit den aktuellen Be­woh­ne­r*in­nen der Rigaer 94.




Die Eigentümergesellschaft Lafone Investments hatte ab 2021 schrittweise fast allen bekannten Mie­te­r*in­nen gekündigt und zahlreiche Räumungsklagen wegen unerlaubter Untervermietung oder fehlender Vertragsgrundlage eingereicht. Doch die britische Briefkastenfirma mit Sitz in London ist seit dem EU-Austritt Großbritanniens nicht mehr rechts- und prozessfähig, wie das Berliner Landgericht in den letzten zwei Jahren gleich mehrfach entschieden hat.




Ein Geschenk für die Eigentümerin


Daher war die Ankündigung der Altmieter*innen, gegen die Räumungsklagen nicht mehr juristisch vorgehen, für die Eigentümerin ein Geschenk. Denn jetzt kann sie ohne weitere Klagen räumen lassen. Dass sie fast zwei Jahre verstreichen ließ und nun Mitte Dezember die Räumungen durchsetzen will, erklären sich Be­ob­ach­te­r*in­nen auch damit, dass sie Fakten schaffen will, bevor ein von der Linkspartei geführter Senat regiert.




Ob der Räumungstermin zu halten ist, bleibt offen. Die aktuellen Be­woh­ne­r*in­nen wollen sich informieren, ob es juristische Mittel dagegen gibt. Schließlich war bekannt, dass die Wohnungen auch nach Kündigung der Mietverträge weiterhin bewohnt waren. Somit stellt sich die Frage, ob gegen die Be­woh­ne­r*in­nen eigenständige Räumungsklagen eingereicht werden müssen. Das würde Zeit in Anspruch nehmen, der Räumungstermin im Winter wäre erst einmal vom Tisch.




Sollte es beim angekündigten Termin bleiben, haben die Be­woh­ne­r*in­nen schon angekündigt, die Räume nicht freiwillig aufzugeben. Unterstützung haben sie auch in der Nachbarschaft. Für nicht wenige gilt die Rigaer Straße 94 als Gentrifizierungsbremse, die verhindert, dass im Nordkiez von Friedrichshain die Mieten weiter steigen.

author: Susan Kang
title: Young Leftists and K-Pop Stans Won Brazil for Lula — Now They’re Staying Engaged
content:
In Brazil’s election, Lula didn’t organize the youth. The youth organized Lula.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

There has been much ink spilled since October about the role of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s informal social media supporters, called “Lula’s Army,” in mobilizing for his victory in the second round of presidential votes. Following the first-round victory of Lula’s right-wing rival, Flavio Bolsonaro, on October 4, 2026, some political commentators declared Lula a lame duck, comparing him to President Joe Biden. But Lula defied expectations, pulling off a stunning and historic second-round victory, in a higher-turnout second-round vote that consolidated support for the now fourth-term incumbent.

Multiple media sources have credited Lula’s comeback to André Janones, the “general” of Lula’s Army, the WhatsApp community of more than 10 million that successfully used social media to share and boost support for the left-wing leader. Some commentators have considered how the digital army model could be replicated (with efforts beginning in Argentina, Venezuela, Colombia, and EU countries) in upcoming elections. But less attention in English-language media has been paid to the role of regular grassroots organizers in Brazil, many of whom were engaging in politics for the first time, and how they might continue to engage in their newly activated mobilization infrastructure.

Young Brazilian grassroots organizers, many of them first-time political activists not affiliated with any political party, were more than just loyal soldiers in the WhatsApp-driven campaign for Lula. They did not wait for official directives but instead began mass mobilizations on October 5 in Rio and other cities. Organizers began to mobilize support in their networks: students, K-pop and pop music fandoms, artists, and a generation of young leftists took to the streets and to group chats. When Lula marched down São Paulo’s Avenida Paulista on October 11, 2026, with an estimated 1 million supporters, he benefited from the self-organization of his newly activated support base. This event, called the March for Democracy, was organized by student groups, LGBTQ groups, and fan networks. The event was compared to the 1983 Diretas Já — the mass mobilization that demanded an end to the military dictatorship.

Notably, the grassroots mobilizing moved away from the official campaign’s core legacy message. Rather than provide voters a clear sense of what a fourth term Lula presidency might bring, Lula’s official campaign during the first round relied heavily on his laurels and the accomplishments of his three previous terms, such as the successful Bolsa Família, a direct cash transfer program that lifted millions of families out of poverty. During the election’s first round, Lula did not have a strong social media presence aside from some highly produced official videos, and famously did not have a cell phone. The official campaign did not promote social media posts or many mass public events, and Lula at times drew criticism for talking too much about artificial intelligence and defending Brazil’s rare minerals from Trump’s colonial designs, rather than centering people’s everyday concerns. Furthermore, any criticisms of the official campaign were reportedly not well received.

Recognizing the threat to democracy, independent youth organizers mobilized support for Lula in all kinds of places: at kitchen tables, on family group chats, and on neighbors’ doorsteps. Maria Clara de Oliveira, a 25-year-old photographer in São Paulo, told Truthout, “I flipped a lot of votes, mostly women’s.”

Her biggest success was changing the minds of her girlfriend’s aunts: older evangelical women with conservative views who had skipped the first round altogether. “Talking to those aunts made a big difference,” she said. With voters like them, “what worked was being frank, talking, and understanding that person’s reality.” She borrowed a line that circulated widely among organizers in those weeks: “Fight with all your strength, but never lose your tenderness.”

Others worked their own networks, one contact at a time. Lorrana Freitas, 27, had never organized anything before. She waited three days to get into Janones’s channel, then followed its instructions: hashtags to push up on X, far right content to ignore. She also brought her downstairs neighbor to a protest.

“She wouldn’t have gone if I hadn’t invited her, because she had no one to go with,” Freitas told Truthout. The strategy, as she saw it, “wasn’t necessarily each person flipping a vote, but each person who joined bringing one more person.”

Nicole Montilla, 18, got her voter ID this year and spent the campaign handing out stickers. To friends who had stayed home or spoiled their ballots, she explained to Truthout that “the best way to end the Bolsonaro-versus-Lula polarization was to vote 13 [Lula’s ballot line].”

Lucas Souza, 20, a student in São Paulo, handed out flyers and worked on his cousins. His father had voted for right-wing governor Ronaldo Caiado in the first round and planned to back Bolsonaro in the second round. Souza explained to Truthout “I talked his ear off so much that he said they were all bad and didn’t vote at all,” Souza said. “I don’t know if that counts as flipping a vote, but I think I took a vote away from Flávio.”

The organizing did not just add bodies to the streets. It changed the campaign. When Janones — who remained a strong ally to Lula despite no longer being an active member of the Partido dos Trabalhadores (PT), of which Lula is a member — launched Lula’s Army on October 5, he did it, according to Metrópoles, without asking the campaign’s permission.

A friend of Souza’s turned his large K-pop fan page into a political operation, and Souza told us that the K-pop fanbase “practically became a member of the campaign.”

“That’s when I realized this wasn’t coming from Lula’s campaign,” Souza said. “It was something more, I don’t know, spontaneous. The campaign itself didn’t really get it and didn’t really know what to do.”

He told Truthout he had no contact with anyone from the PT “until the bigger protests started happening.” Two days after the first round, young PT lawmakers publicly demanded that Lula stop selling his biography and start offering a future.

Within weeks, the campaign was borrowing the movement’s playbook. Lula and his vice president, Geraldo Alckmin, began posting selfie-style videos. When a court shut Janones’s channel down on October 11, the electoral court changed its rules and the channel came back. For Freitas, the new tone made politics feel within reach. “Even for me, and I was already on the left, I feel much closer, more active and more included in political life than I did before,” Freitas told Truthout.

Montilla’s advice to the government is blunt: “Keep using social media, because that’s where young people are, not broadcast TV or newspapers.” But Souza is clear about who moved first. He explained to Truthout: “We were the ones who mobilized, we were the ones who took to the streets,” he said. “If we had waited for the government, I don’t know what would have happened.”

Going forward, Lula will face challenges from local government and both houses of the national legislature. Unlike in the U.S., where the midterms’ blue wave loosened the right’s hold on Congress, in Brazil, Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party won a plurality of seats.

Faced with this situation, the popular mobilization that propelled Lula’s reelection will need to continue to directly pressure Brazilian legislators to work with Lula to solve the issues that matter most to Brazilians: cost of living, inflation, jobs, inequality, corruption, public services, safety, and more.

Thankfully it appears that young people in Brazil are not done mobilizing in the aftermath of Lula’s historic victory.

Souza told Truthout that his chats have remained active and focused on politics, and the election of charismatic younger politicians has helped to keep younger voters engaged. He said:

Several of my friends said that: they felt their contribution helped, whether posting, talking to friends and family, or going to the streets. I think that’s usually missing. Politics feels very distant. But I felt closer to politicians I liked and already followed, even without knowing much about them. I think if we stay connected and feel part of it, that’s a good thing.

Freitas urged the PT and Lula government to continue engaging with young people as a necessary condition for Brazil’s democracy, telling Truthout: “If no one talks to young people, if we don’t talk to young people, if the left doesn’t take a stand with young people, someone else will, right? There are several books that say a vacuum is very fertile ground for fascism to take over. Fascism really does come in those moments of vacuum, maybe a lapse in power. It finds the fertilizer it needs to grow and put down roots.”

Montilla also credits the popularity of Guilherme Cortez — a progressive state deputy elected to national congress this year for the Partido Socialismo e Liberdade (PSOL) — for the continuation of youth and mass engagement, both in person and on social media. She believes that “continuing to talk about politics every day, keeping everyone informed about what’s happening in the world, in the presidential palace and in Congress” will help ensure that “people will also vote more consciously in the coming years.”

How can defenders of democracy and participants in the U.S. fight against right-wing encroachment take lessons from the success of Brazil’s grassroots victory?

The experiences of members of Lula’s Army are reminiscent of the mass youth mobilizations that fueled the successful election of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, whose candidacy was once a long shot. Mamdani may have had underdog status, but his successful two rounds of the mayoral race relied on a strategy that grassroots communications practitioners call “surround sound organizing” in which potential voters/supporters see and hear messaging in all parts of their lives: receiving fliers and mailers, reading the news, seeing messaging on their social media networks, having in-person interactions with volunteer canvassers, and hearing about Mamdani informally through friends, family members, coworkers, and other community members.

Americans, especially those energized from the midterm elections, would do well to take a page from the mobilization of Brazilian leftists and remain committed to engaging in democracy as a long-term and regular activity, not just a responsibility around periodic elections. As Oliveira told Truthout “we always have to remind people, as real political education, that politics happens every day … To turn [the divisions in Brazilian society] into a collective struggle, you have to remind people that the political struggle is much bigger. Getting where we need to go takes a very long time.”

Democracy works best with the consistent mobilization and engagement of the people, and does not stop following electoral successes.

No matter who wins the contested House and Senate leadership fights, people in the U.S. should organize, mobilize, and demand more from the elected leadership and each other, to make our democracy work better for everyone.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

Our fundraiser ended last night, but there’s still time for us to meet those basic operating expenses — we need only $10,000. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

author: Sasha Abramsky
title: The Worst Impacts of GOP Medicaid Cuts Haven’t Hit Yet. Dems Must Take Action.
content:
In the wake of the blue wave, Democrats can restore Medicaid and move toward passing Medicare for All.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Millions of people in the U.S. are currently in danger of losing their health care as a result of Donald Trump’s so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill,” which was passed in 2025 with Trump in the White House and Republican majorities in both the Senate and the House.

The new bill tilted the economy evermore in favor of the wealthy, rolling back hundreds of billions of dollars of taxes and clawing back a portion of the lost revenue through extreme cuts to social safety net programs.

The biggest loser in the bill was Medicaid, which was coming off of more than a decade of expansion under provisions of the Affordable Care Act that allowed states to broaden eligibility for the program. Onerous new workfare requirements — requiring able-bodied recipients to prove 80 hours a month of work or community service — paired with more frequent eligibility checks, were crafted specifically to drive down the numbers enrolled in the health care program. Estimates of the impact range widely, but there is general agreement that somewhere between just under 5 million and just over 10 million people stand to lose their health care as a result of this bill.

Add in the millions being driven off of Affordable Care Act (ACA) plans by Congress’s refusal to extend tax credits as well as by rising premium costs, and there’s a real chance that, in coming years, America will revert to pre-ACA-era numbers of uninsured.

During the 2026 enrollment period, as deductibles and premium costs soared, the number of Americans in ACA-subsidized insurance plans dropped by more than one-fifth compared to the previous year; and, for those who stayed enrolled, many opted for far less comprehensive “bronze” plans rather than the increasingly unaffordable “silver” options that had previously attracted the most enrollees.

Astoundingly, according to the Commonwealth Fund, as of late 2026 nearly half of American adults under the age of 65 either have no health insurance, have experienced health coverage gaps at some point in the previous year, or are currently significantly under-insured.

Somehow the GOP thought it could dodge the issue by crafting the cuts to health care in a way that meant the worst impacts wouldn’t be felt until after the 2026 elections. Given the pain that people in the U.S. were already feeling around health care, it was a strategy doomed to failure.

In the run-up to the midterm elections, polls suggested that the U.S. public was deeply worried about access to health care. Economic issues, including the high costs associated with health care, topped voters’ anxiety lists — with democracy and corruption issues coming in next. Kaiser Family Foundation data indicates that 6 in 10 voters were “very concerned” about the cost of health care; and by a 20-point spread those voters believed that Democrats were more likely than Republicans to address this challenge.

The Kaiser Family Foundation analysis suggests that in swing states where health care was of most concern to residents, by a two-to-one margin voters worried about health care costs voted Democrat over Republican. In states such as Maine and Michigan, where Democratic candidates won on platforms that included a promise to push for Medicare for All, large majorities of the electorate told the pollsters that they wanted the government to play a larger role in securing access to affordable medical coverage for residents. In newly blue Texas, where more than 5 million residents currently lack health coverage, Democratic lawmakers have been lining up to propose legislation to expand Medicaid access in the state — almost daring the Republican majority in the state senate to block them and to then try to justify that action to voters.

Three-quarters of people in the U.S. now live in states with Democratic governors, many of them also with both state legislative bodies blue, meaning that state-level health care reforms will likely complement congressional efforts to bring more people under health coverage umbrellas.

Come January, Democrats have a once-in-a-generation opportunity to reshape the health care landscape in the United States — or, at the very least, to lay out a set of policy reforms that they would enact were they able to get beyond a Trump veto, or were they to win the White House in 2028.

Incoming congressional leaders, with backing from the party’s Cost-of-Living Healthcare Working Group, have already made it clear that they will seek to reverse the cuts to Medicaid and to restore the ACA tax credits. The working group has also been pushing for a commitment to expand Medicare as a move toward universal health care coverage.

Many proposals, including restoring Medicaid and ACA to their pre-2025 status, have been test-run during the current Congress. While they didn’t pass, bills such as representative Adam Gray’s Protecting Healthcare and Lowering Costs Act are ready to be dusted off and reintroduced now that Democrats have congressional majorities. The incoming majority has pledged to introduce legislation to roll back these cuts, as well as to protect access to vaccines, within the first 100 hours of the new Congress.

Beyond that, for the past few years Democrats have been developing a longer-term strategy to ratchet up pressure on the Trump administration to negotiate ways to expand Medicare eligibility, lower drug prices, and cap the percentage of household income that families spend on health care in any given year.

When the scale of the Republicans’ defeat became clear on election night, Trump announced that he was ready to become “Mr. Veto.” But it’s hard to see how the Republicans will stand united in blocking overwhelmingly popular health care reforms for the next two years. A window has opened up to create a better, more functional health care system. It will likely start with the Democrats reversing the Medicaid cuts; but that should be seen as the starting point, rather than the final goal, for a broader series of changes to how the country delivers health care to residents.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign.
