author: Unknown
title: İHD, tutuklanan ÇHD'li avukatlar için serbest bırakma çağrısı yaptı
content:
İnsan Hakları Derneği (İHD), İzmir merkezli yürütülen bir soruşturma kapsamında 17 Kasım 2026 tarihinde ev baskınlarıyla gözaltına alınan ve 19 Kasım’da tutuklanan Çağdaş Hukukçular Derneği (ÇHD) üyesi dört avukata ilişkin yazılı bir açıklama yayımladı.



















İzmir'de gözaltına alınan 4 avukat tutuklandı




20 Kasım 2026










Açıklamada, dört avukatın derhal serbest bırakılması ve savunmaya yönelik baskıların sona erdirilmesi istendi.







SAVUNMA MAKAMINA YÖNELİK BASKILARA SON VERİLSİN, TUTUKLU AVUKATLAR DERHAL SERBEST BIRAKILSIN! İzmir merkezli soruşturma kapsamında 17 Kasım 2026 tarihinde ev baskınlarıyla gözaltına alınan Çağdaş Hukukçular Derneği üyesi Av. Veysi Çetin, Av. Yemen Cankan, Av. Erdoğan Akdoğdu ve Av. Bahattin Özdemir, 19 Kasım’da tutuklanmıştır. Aralarında derneğimiz üyelerinin de bulunduğu avukatların 24 saati aşkın süre müdafileriyle görüştürülmemesi ve mesleki faaliyetlerinde kullandıkları dijital materyallere el konulması, savunma hakkı ve avukatlık mesleğinin bağımsızlığı açısından ağır hukuki ihlal oluşturmaktadır. Ceza hukukunun temel ilkesi, kişilerin kimlikleri, düşünceleri veya mesleki faaliyetleri üzerinden değil, somut fiilleri ve hukuka uygun deliller temelinde yargılanmasıdır. Günther Jakobs’un kavramsallaştırdığı düşman ceza hukuku anlayışı, bireyin işlediği fiilden ziyade devlet tarafından tehlikeli olarak tanımlanmasını esas alarak hukuki güvencelerin daraltılmasını ifade eder. Avukatların mesleki faaliyetlerinin kriminalize edilmesi, bu anlayışın savunma makamına yönelmesi tehlikesini ortaya koymaktadır. Savunma faaliyetlerinin suçla ilişkilendirilmesi, ceza muhakemesini adaletin gerçekleştirilmesi amacından uzaklaştırarak bir baskı mekanizmasına dönüştürür. İnsan Hakları Derneği olarak, yargı makamlarını Anayasa’nın 19. maddesi ve tutuklamanın istisnailiği ilkesi doğrultusunda dört avukatın derhal serbest bırakılmasını sağlamaya çağırıyoruz. Savunma makamının bağımsızlığını hedef alan her türlü müdahalenin karşısında duracağımızı, Çağdaş Hukukçular Derneği ile tutuklanan avukatlarla ve savunma hakkını koruyan bütün hukukçularla dayanışma içinde olacağımızı kamuoyuna duyuruyoruz. Adalet, yalnızca bugün hakları ihlal edilenlerin değil, herkesin bir gün ihtiyaç duyacağı evrensel bir güvencedir. https://t.co/HDOfHtVibs


— İHD Genel Merkezi (@ihdgenelmerkez) 

November 21, 2026




Çalışma materyallerine el konuldu




Açıklamada, avukatların mesleki çalışmalarında kullandıkları dijital materyallere de el konulduğu belirtildi. İHD, bu durumun avukatlık mesleğinin bağımsızlığını zedelediğini belirtti.




İHD, avukatların mesleki faaliyetlerinin suç konusu yapılmasının savunma makamını hedef alan bir baskı anlayışını gösterdiğini söyledi.




Serbest bırakma çağrısı




İHD, tutuklanan avukatlar Veysi Çetin, Yemen Cankan, Erdoğan Akdoğdu ve Bahattin Özdemir'in derhal serbest bırakılmasını istedi. Dernek, bu talebini Anayasa'nın 19. maddesindeki kişi özgürlüğü güvencesine ve tutuklamanın istisnai bir tedbir olduğu ilkesine dayandırdı. Ayrıca Çağdaş Hukukçular Derneği (ÇHD) ve tutuklu avukatlarla dayanışma içinde olacaklarını açıkladı.







Ne olmuştu?




17 Kasım'da İzmir merkezli soruşturma kapsamında ev baskınlarıyla gözaltına alınan avukatlar, 19 Kasım'da tutuklandı. Dört avukat da ÇHD üyesi. İHD, açıklamasında avukatların serbest bırakılmasını istedi.







(FY)

author: Unknown
title: “I will always have more in common with oppressed group A than with oppressed group B because of…
content:
“I will always have more in common with oppressed group A than with oppressed group B because of these shared oppressed experiences”

… I don’t care?

I thought we were doing solidarity here, not sectarianism?

Like, I know this sentence is used a lot when people are grouped together according to AGAB or some frustratingly pointless shit like that, but we can just challenge the AGAB-grouping thing without making new teams of who is and isn’t in our community. 

Like, it’s fine to want to spend time with only people who experience roughly the same oppressive structures as you, but to take that as a guiding principle for your activism is a path to isolated irrelevance. 

I don’t need to have any shit in common with my comrades other than ‘let’s smash oppressive structures and build a better world’.

author: Kristopher Drummond
title: Therapy as Rite of Passage Pt. 2: Cultivating Secure Attachment to the Earth
content:
Photo courtesy of the author.




Therapy, in its crazy way, by emphasizing the inner soul and 

ignoring the outer soul, supports the decline of the actual world

. Yet therapy goes on blindly believing that it’s curing the outer world by making better people. We’ve had that for years and years: “If everybody went into therapy, we’d have better buildings, we’d have better people, we’d have more consciousness.” 

It’s not the case

.




—James Hillman




W

e know—

we know—

that the future our imaginations were promised is not the future that awaits us. This summer, more than any previous, is our evidence. As I write, fires rage across the American west, bombs drop on children, surveillance architecture is daily being constructed outside rural convenience stores. In our hearts, if we look, the knowing of where we really are is clear.




For many in the West, the future has long been a source of secure attachment. It has been our god, a shining destination justifying the sacrifices of generations. All the brutality of history has supposedly made sense through the lens of progress. 

We’re going somewhere amazing. 

Utopia has been just around the corner with every technological advance, asking for just a bit more patience, a bit more sacrifice, a bit more relinquishment of our humanity—just enough so that when the robots take our jobs, the foretold dawning of endless leisure will arrive as prophecy fulfilled.




For many, this enculturated fantasy of the future has been the bedrock of busy lives, unconsciously justifying cycles of overwork, burnout, and addiction. For a brief window in time, for some, it seemed true that children could build better lives than their parents and that technological advances did indeed improve the quality of life for a majority of the populace. However, here at the logical conclusion of an infinite growth paradigm, driven by technological development that has greatly outpaced our moral or spiritual development, we are left to contend with the starkness of reality.




Anytime you’re gonna grow, you’re gonna lose something. You’re losing what you’re hanging onto to keep safe. You’re losing habits that you’re comfortable with, you’re losing familiarity. That’s a big one, when you begin to move into the unfamiliar. You know, in the organic world when anything begins to grow it’s moving constantly into unfamiliar movements and unfamiliar things.




—James Hillman




As I discussed in 

part one of this essay

, we are at a collective threshold that in another cultural context would imply the need for a “rite of passage.” As Peter Kingsley describes in his book 

Catafalque: Carl Jung and the End of Humanity, 

the mythic energy fueling our collective stories has withdrawn—our society is like a ship at sea, moving forward without propulsion, carried only by its remaining inertia. Soon, the density of the water will have its way.




Rites of passage are about growing up. They are designed to activate our latent soul capacities, allowing us to rise to moments of change and loss, ultimately pointing back to the fundamental uncertainty of existence. These ceremonies intentionally confront us with the facts of life—birth, transformation, and death—with the aim of engendering our surrender to a larger order. True adulthood is marked by the capacity to live in ever deepening levels of complexity, holding nuance, paradox and change with open hands, neither resisting nor clinging to easy answers.




As eco-depth psychologist Bill Plotkin has expressed through his eco-centric developmental model (presented in his book 

Nature and the Human Soul

), mainstream western culture is an expression of arrested development at the adolescent level. Look around—the values of ego strength, material accumulation, competition, hubristic certainty, and tribalistic social organization dominate the discourse. It’s all about speed, growth, victory, dominance, knowledge, vitality. The developmental values of healthy adulthood—humility, community, cooperation, surrender, service, death literacy and wisdom—have not yet been embodied on a collective level. As a result, we cling to a future that only exists in the illusory linearity of our underdeveloped psyches. As the promised future and our capacity to attach to it falls away, we face the daunting task of discovering what remains, and where our security actually comes from.




Stubbornly insisting on life can result in its opposite. The frantic desire to ward off death can actually invite it. Conversely, if you wish for life you must be prepared to welcome death. If you demand life, you must accept that death is a part of life, its dark half, without which no life, no experience, no living meaning, no poetry, no love is possible.




—Andreas Weber




I spent many years in exile—from my body, my heart, my community, and earth herself. A traumatic psychedelic initiation at 19 ripped my hands from the security of my just-forming adolescent identity. In a single night, the future I thought I was moving toward disappeared. For nearly a decade, I moved in the world without a sense of ground beneath my feet, wandering through anxiety, depression, and addiction, desperately seeking some sense of belonging. While I was lucky to have a solid family and to have been raised with relatively secure attachment, I knew after such a rupturing experience that I couldn’t remain regressively clinging to their psychological structures or the identity I generated from them. I was terrified, but I understood that I had to let go. Forward was the only way.




This hellish chapter finally ended at age 28, when I mustered the courage to attend my first wilderness rites of passage program with the Animas Valley Institute. It was a crisp February morning in Joshua Tree National Park and the facilitator, Brian, had invited us to go “wander the land and let yourself be guided to a being that feels like a nurturing, generative adult,” and to “have a conversation with them.” Although I struggled to intellectually comprehend what he meant, some intuitive part of me knew.




Standing from my chair in the group circle, I turned my body in a circle, listening for the direction I was being called. As I came around to the west, I felt a tug in my belly from beyond the beige cactus-dotted hill I was facing. Instinctively, I started walking.




Photo courtesy of the author.




As I crested the hill and looked down the other side, the urgency in my belly expanded into a mixture of anxiety and excitement. Something was actually happening and my body recognized it. Dropping down the other side of the hill into a small valley, I noticed a dry arroyo and realized it was where I was being called. As I approached, my mind went silent. When I reached the arroyo, without knowing why, I knelt down and then prostrated, pushing my forehead into the dust and stretching my hands forward, palms up. Immediately, the grief arrived.




Like those first drops of a rainstorm, the tears dripped slowly, and as they hit the sand, the full force of the storm revealed itself. I wept and wept, saltwater pouring from my eyes into the long-parched earth. Initially, they were tears of grief for all the loneliness and trauma I’d been carrying, lament for the years of wandering without meaning or belonging. But at a certain point, they transitioned to tears of gratitude.




Words can’t convey it, but as I cried, I felt myself being truly welcomed home for the first time in my adult life. In that moment, I realized that my first and most primary belonging is and always had been with the earth. The arroyo kept taking me deeper, energetically opening itself to hold me in its wide embrace, communicating in some mysterious transpersonal way the truth of my irrevocable belonging to this wider body. I knew then that nothing could take this from me—that I am tied, like every other earth-bound being—to seasons and cycles of death and rebirth. I knew then that my decade-long winter was finally over.




When I am among the trees,


especially the willows and the honey locust,


equally the beech, the oaks and the pines,


they give off such hints of gladness.


I would almost say that they save me, and daily.




—Mary Oliver




In re-reading what I just wrote, I see that it sounds outlandish, even to me. That in itself is an indicator of how much of our intuitive, imaginative capacity we’ve lost. For the vast majority of humanity’s time on this earth, we lived in 

participatory relationship 

with the world. Visionary experience was so common as to be expected. Societies dictated their decisions based on dreams and prophetic events and variously accessed forms of trance, all of which emerged through and from the earth. In fact, these capacities are one of the most beautiful things about us; we have the ability to be in conversational, imaginal, somatic relationship with a four billion year old self-organizing system that leans toward sentience. Our current paradigm writes this off this “an accident.”




Before the advent of the written word, which incrementally moved our species toward a left-brained, analytical way of knowing, we lived largely in the holistic present, orienting to natural seasons and cycles with the reverence and attention we now pay to our Google Calendars. The mythologist Martin Shaw says that “our culture is three days deep, because it only takes three days in the wilderness for it to start washing away,” revealing the wholeness of our embodied selves beneath the noise of our minds. Through my personal experience and those of participants in the many wilderness retreats I’ve attended and guided, I know he’s correct.




There’s a lot of talk in therapy land about “attachment” these days. Instagram has gotten ahold of it, and it seems like everyone has a hot take on what to do with avoidant partners, how to create unshakable security with yourself, and the five easy steps to secure attachment in your relationship. What mainstream psychology (and Instagram) almost always miss is the fact that we are not the individuals we think we are, and our attachment needs run much deeper than our minds. There’s soil beneath our feet made of billions of decomposed trees providing more physical, emotional, and spiritual security than a lifetime of “self-regulation” ever could. We just need to remember how to access it.




Earth, isn’t this what you want? To arise in us, invisible?


Is it not your dream, to enter us so wholly


there’s nothing left outside us to see?


What, if not transformation


is your deepest purpose? Earth, my love,


I want it too. Believe me,


no more of your springtimes are needed


to win me over — even one flower


is more than enough. Before I was named


I belonged to you. I see no other law


but yours, and know I can trust


the death you will bring.




—Rilke




A lot can happen in a clinical setting. Simply having compassionate, attuned relationship with another human, as Carl Rogers pointed out, offers significant healing potential. However, there’s only so much connection and wholeness available within the 55 minute, highly boundaried, mostly indoors, often online medical model of healing. The tenderness and depth of our souls are shy and suspicious of speedy things, and as we know, the capitalistic engine of the insurance industry is oriented almost entirely to efficiency. In this setting, it’s difficult to access the slow and mysterious rhythms of the terrestrial psyche that come alive through earth connection.




And yet, the clinical paradigm is most of what we currently have. It’s what insurance pays for (for now) and where most of us turn when our lives aren’t working. Week by week, we open ourselves to a stranger doing their best to offer unconditional positive regard, a stranger who is asked to do this 5 – 7 times a day, 4 – 5 days a week. As one of those strangers myself, I like to think I have a lot of empathy available, that I am most often showing up in a “healing” way for my clients. Even so, the care and attunement I have to give are limited and fluctuate depending on what’s going on in my own life. Regardless, at the end of each work day, I am spent.




My work as a wilderness guide feels very different. At the end of a program, while still tired, I am often invigorated and enlivened, cracked open and tender, clear in my knowing and whole. There are several reasons for this, the most important being that we are outside for 4 – 12 days at a time, co-regulating with the natural world and each other.




Photo courtesy of the author.




For participants in these programs, much of the work happens in solitude, with many hours a day spent engaging contemplative practices out on the land. The invitations for these “wanders” differ, but they all involve placing the land at the center, slowing down, feeling their bodies, speaking the truth out loud, intuiting the responses they may receive. They are encouraged to listen, walk, and speak with all of their capacities, rather than just their minds. Sincerity, intention, and longing are the central ingredients, and when participants can focus on what is most real, most hurting, most in need of change, the earth, impossibly, responds. Many of them have never done this before, and some (like I was) are highly skeptical about “speaking to the land.” I have yet to meet a single participant whose skepticism survived the experience.




In engaging with wilderness rites of passage work for the past decade, I have come to recognize that the truth at the heart of the mystical experience—that Love is always available—is central to participating with the earth in this way. As a guide, my job is not to be a healer, but a mirror, reflecting the magnitude and magnificence I perceive in the stories the participants share in our circle after they’ve come back. Simply being expressed and witnessed, at the soul level, is the medicine. Souls are inherently whole and beautiful, and when the clouds of trauma and persona finally burn off in someone’s eyes, soul is there, obvious as the noonday sun.




the war of the worlds hangs here, right now, in the balance


it is a war for this world, to keep it


a vale of soul-making


the taste in all our mouths is the taste of power


and it is bitter as death


bring yourself home to yourself,


enter the garden.




—Diane di Prima




What I am proposing in this essay and this essay series feels audacious, especially for someone still holding a provisional license. And yet, these feelings have been growing in me for almost two decades, in which I’ve been in my own personal therapy most of the time. I’ve had the opportunity to do my inner work within the clinical setting (and have experienced major healing there) as well as outside it, in silent meditation retreats, men’s work, ancestral explorations and earth-based intensives and vision fasts. Becoming a therapist has actually only strengthened the convictions I had already formed.




Through all of it, I’ve gotten to pull therapists, teachers, gurus, and facilitators off the pedestals I had them on as their humanness, flaws, and quirks became apparent. The ultimate message I have come to, over and over, is that the truth we’re searching for can only ever be found within our own selves through the sincerity of our willingness to look. All the rest are just mirrors and soul friends, walking with us for a time until we’re again at the center of our own self, with our own next right step, which no other can truly know.




And so from my own place of sincere and humble incompletion, I’m going to audaciously claim that clinical therapy itself is in dire need of a rite of passage. The paradigm it was born of is dying, and the future that paradigm orients us toward is vanishing with it, revealed in its emptiness as a frantic and delusional flight from terrestrial reality.




The earth is an emergent being, constantly shapeshifting to meet changing conditions, dancing through the unfolding present to remake itself in every moment. We are that earth, and we have access to that nonlinear intelligence in every cell of our bodies. Our minds will never understand it, and that’s why it feels like grace when we make contact with it. An earth rooted therapy will, and does, depend on this grace more than any particular intervention. And that’s why it’s a major threat to the medical model—mystery laughs in the face of causality’s pretense.




The paradox from this perspective is, of course, that the more we let go of the false security of certainty, the more securely attached to life we actually become. May it be so.




The post 

Therapy as Rite of Passage Pt. 2: Cultivating Secure Attachment to the Earth

 appeared first on 

Mad In America

.

author: Brian Hioe
title: KMT Passes Cash Handouts, Leans into Attacks on Solar Energy Before Elections
content:
THE KMT PASSED a 20,000 NT cash handout to the general public yesterday in the legislature, shortly before elections. This would continue a familiar tactic of the party–to distribute cash handouts to the public in order to affect election outcomes. The TPP, unusually, broke from the KMT when it came to the cash handout at the last minute, but because insufficient DPP legislators were present in the legislature, it still passed.

Indeed, this has proven to be a useful electoral tactic in the past. While President Lai Ching-te called for opposition to the cash hand-outs, one notes that on other occasions the DPP first resisted cash hand-outs and then pivoted toward trying to take credit for the move after seeing that it was popular with the public. At other times, it has been the DPP itself that sought to move for cash hand-outs with the claim that this was distributing the dividends of Taiwan’s AI windfall to the public.

At the same time, one notes that, both last year and this year, the KMT pushed a drastic, far-reaching set of cuts to the government budget. This includes not only the defense budget but social services. While the KMT has claimed that such budgets were necessary for fiscal balance, the cuts it currently calls for would be at the expense of social services.

The KMT has historically leaned into vote buying to win elections, and this is perhaps no different. One notes that practices regarding vote buying continue, especially in rural areas of Taiwan, with young progressive candidates reporting that voters were paid 6,000 NT to vote for anyone but them.

In the meantime, the KMT is also leaning into what has increasingly been a recurrent theme for the party in past years–attacks on solar energy and an attempt to frame it as dangerous. Even as much of the world has sought to boost development in the renewable sector in order to offset the impact of climate change, the KMT has increasingly alleged that solar power is new, untested, and dangerous. By contrast, nuclear power is the only clean and safe alternative, and the DPP only advances solar energy projects because of corruption.

In the past, one has observed the circulation of AI-generated disinformation online claiming that solar panels are radioactive and showing birds seeming to die after drinking water near solar panels damaged by a typhoon–never mind that the species of bird depicted in the video does not exist in Taiwan.

As such, issues regarding solar panels have become contentious in several local races. In Tainan, KMT candidate Hsieh Lung-chieh has hit out at floating photovoltaic solar farms in the Wushantou Reservoir to suggest that chemicals used to clean the panels will be dangerous for the water supply.

Members of the Chiang mayoral administration have also hit out at suggestions to install solar panels on historic buildings such as the National Palace Museum, leading to an unusual spat between the Chiang mayoral administration and the National Palace Museum after Taipei Cultural Affairs division director Tsai Shih-ping published AI-generated images of solar panels being installed on the museum. The museum has since demanded a policy. Such controversies have also led Chiang to be criticized for not knowing his own mayoral administration’s policies, in that it was policies under his mayorship that have led solar panels to be installed on historic buildings such as the Longshan Temple in Wanhua.

Indeed, the KMT’s advocacy for nuclear energy was never rooted in science, but in historic nostalgia for a period in which the KMT was the sole ruling party of Taiwan, the economy was booming, and Taiwan was much more dependent on nuclear energy in its energy mix. The KMT, then, would be suggesting that the restoration of nuclear energy could bring back this period of greater order and economic prosperity. By contrast, any newer form of energy must be framed as potentially a threat to traditionalist reliance on nuclear energy. But it may be a sign of how the KMT has sought to mobilize its voters along traditional party issues to see this recent wave of attacks on the DPP over solar power.

title: After joining protests, Ayta leader faces military harassment
content:
An Ayta community leader in Zambales faced military interrogation and surveillance days after joining protests against the US-backed Pax Silica initiative, raising concerns over the harassment of Indigenous Peoples defending their ancestral lands.

Orlino Lahut, also known as Tiyong Nilo, was visited by a military personnel identifying himself as Jasper Dalit in the afternoon of November 19 at the residence of an Ayta community elder in Iram, Zambales.

According to statements from Indigenous Peoples’ and environmental organizations, Dalit questioned Lahut about the community’s recent trip to Manila, including who organized their participation in the protests, who provided their “Reject Pax Silica” shirts, and how they financed their transportation.

Lahut was also reportedly coerced into completing a form requiring his personal information and organizational affiliations. Dalit threatened to return with additional personnel to question other community members.

The incident followed reports that unidentified men in civilian clothing monitored Ayta delegates during their journey home from Manila.

Katribu Youth Katipunan, Amihan National Federation of Peasant Women, and Kalikasan People’s Network for the Environment condemned the incident, describing it as an attempt to intimidate Indigenous communities exercising their right to protest.

Lahut rejected claims that the Ayta were manipulated by outsiders, asserting that their participation in the demonstrations was based on their own decision and opposition to projects threatening their ancestral domains. “We are not fools,” he said.

For the Ayta communities in Central Luzon, opposition to Pax Silica is premised on the threat to their ancestral lands, livelihoods, and environment.

The initiative, alongside the Marcos Jr. administration’s Luzon Economic Corridor, includes proposed developments such as the Aboitiz solar power project in Olongapo and an artificial intelligence and semiconductor hub in New Clark City, Tarlac.

These developments threaten ancestral and agricultural lands, including areas containing Ayta burial grounds. Amihan also warned that affected communities could face relocation to areas without adequate livelihood opportunities and access to clean water.

The proposed data hub is projected to consume up to 1.8 billion gallons of water annually and operate around the clock, with noise levels potentially reaching 105 decibels, according to Amihan.

Zenaida Soriano, national chairperson of Amihan, said that the initiative would further expose the country’s natural resources to foreign exploitation at the expense of Indigenous communities and farmers. “Pax Silica is a project of wealthy countries that will only destroy our lands, waters, and Indigenous communities.”

She stressed that the developments also threaten national food security, particularly with the planned expansion of the Luzon Economic Corridor across major ports in Luzon.

The harassment of Lahut coincided with another attack against an environmental defender, Lumad youth activist Mawing Pangadas, coordinator of Panalipdan Youth Davao. He was pursued by 10 to 12 suspected state agents wearing black clothing and caps along Upper Madapo Hills in Barangay 8-A, Davao City.

Read: Groups decry abduction attempt on Lumad youth activist in Davao City

Kalikasan condemned both incidents, stressing that these are growing threats against environmental defenders who oppose destructive projects and protect their communities’ land and resources.

For 13 consecutive years, the Philippines has been Asia’s deadliest country for environmental defenders, according to environmental organizations.

Despite this record, the Marcos Jr. administration has proposed a P9.75-billion ($152 million) budget for the National Task Force to End Local Communist Armed Conflict (NTF-ELCAC) in 2027, nearly P2 billion ($31 million) higher than its previous allocation.

Kalikasan criticized the proposed allocation, saying it results in sustained red-tagging, surveillance, and militarization instead of addressing the needs of communities affected by land grabbing and environmental destruction.

Soriano also condemned the continued military presence in rural communities, saying intimidation would not stop farmers and Indigenous Peoples from defending their rights. “Marcos and the military serve their master Donald Trump rather than the Filipino people. They resort to violence and intimidation to seize land and sell it to foreign businesses.”

The organizations called for an investigation into the attempted abduction of Pangadas and the prosecution of those responsible. They also demanded an end to the surveillance and harassment of Lahut and other Ayta leaders, as well as the withdrawal of military personnel from their communities.

Amihan vowed to continue opposing the exploitation of the country’s natural resources and the militarization of rural communities. (AMU, DAA)

title: Guess who's back ! Le réseau Mutu de retour sur pieds après un important piratage
content:
Dans ce communiqué : explications après dix jours de maintenance, conseils après la fuite de vos données, et infos sur le retour de vos sites locaux

 

!




 

Sommaire

 

Les conséquences pour les auteurices et lecteurices des sites

 

Renforcer la sécurité collective, encore et toujours

 

Pour conclure







Le réseau Mutu (qui héberge notamment Paris Luttes Info) ressort d'une longue tempête de plusieurs semaines et d'une opération de maintenance qui aura duré une dizaine de jours. Comme vous avez peut-être pu le lire 

ailleurs chez Indymedia Nantes

, nous avons été victime d'une double attaque particulièrement importante, qui a atteint la «

 

machine hôte

 

» de nos services, impactant aussi ceux d'Indymedia. Ces portes dérobées, découvertes peu de temps après le 

précédent piratage

, nous ont plongé·x·es dans l'urgence de la réinstallation de cette dite machine hôte ainsi que de la «

 

refonte

 

» de toute notre infrastructure. Cela nous a contraint·x·es à une longue période de maintenance, fort heureusement raccourcie grâce à l'aide précieuse de nos camarades trop fortiches de Riseup, d'Infokiosques.net et d'Indymedia Nantes ❤️🖤




Les portes dérobées que nous avons découvertes étaient installées avec les privilèges les plus élevés sur la machine hôte en question. Par conséquent, toutes nos données ont potentiellement été compromises, voire corrompues. Nous avons donc procédé à une remise au propre de nos serveurs (web et mail), ce qui nous a permis de regagner un niveau de confiance suffisant dans nos services pour pouvoir les relancer. Cependant, pour toute information qui vous paraîtrait compromettante ou risquée à nous communiquer, nous vous recommandons toujours l'utilisation d'emails chiffrés. Notez aussi que nous avons à nouveau 

changé les adresses 

.onion

 des sites

.




La remise en ligne des sites du réseau s'est faite progressivement car nous avons rencontré des difficultés importantes de surcharge de nos serveurs. Peu de temps avant la découverte de ces piratages, vous étiez nombreuxses à faire remonter des ralentissements importants dans l'utilisation de nos sites, chose que nous avions tenté de limiter en ajoutant une page de chargement pour bloquer les robots 

IA

 qui aspirent et sur-sollicitent nos sites en permanence, mais avec une efficacité somme toute assez limitée. En fin de compte, ce sont des camarades administrateurices système d'autres sites qui nous ont éclairé·x·es de leurs lumières et nous ont aidé·x·es à résoudre ce fâcheux problème. (Merci encore, plein de cœurs et de paillettes sur vous, les copaines

 

!)




Enfin, ces attaques et la tempête dans laquelle nous avons été pris·x·es ne sont que l'illustration de l'hostilité grandissante qui règne actuellement sur les infrastructures numériques alternatives, autogérées ou militantes. Les failles et les mises à jour de sécurité critiques s'enchaînent les unes après les autres quotidiennement. L'importance de l'autonomie technique pour diffuser nos informations et nos luttes n'a probablement jamais été autant mise sous pression et s'avère d'autant plus cruciale à maintenir.




Les conséquences pour les auteurices et lecteurices des sites




Pour revenir aux conséquences concrètes pour toutes les personnes et collectifs utilisant nos sites, au risque de répéter des bouts de textes que nous avons déjà produits par le passé (c'est le jour de la marmotte) :




Parmi les données auxquelles les pirates avaient facilement accès (et dont on peut supposer qu'ielles les ont probablement récupérées) :




 les «

 

hachés

 

» des mots de passe

 [

1

]

, les adresses mail et les pseudos des auteurices inscrit·es sur les sites

 les adresses mail des personnes inscrit·es aux newsletters des sites

 les pseudos des auteurices des articles, si leurs pseudos sont restés associés aux articles en question (car il est aussi possible de se retirer d'un article en tant qu'auteurice)

 les messages de modération et les éventuels messages internes des sites

 les adresses 

IP

 utilisées par les visiteureuses et les auteurices pour accéder aux sites pendant toute la période où la porte dérobée était présente (et jusqu'à 15 jours avant)

 le contenu des boîtes mail hébergées sur nos serveurs, et en particulier celle de l'adresse contactmutu@mediaslibres.org : les emails reçus, envoyés, etc.




Aussi, nous ne savons pas s'ielles l'ont fait mais, au prix de quelques efforts supplémentaires, ielles étaient tout à fait en capacité :




 d'intercepter les mots de passe 

en clair

 des personnes qui se sont connecté·es aux sites durant cette période. Si ces mots de passe sont utilisés à d'autres endroits, il nous semble crucial de les changer au plus vite à ces autres endroits aussi.

 d'intercepter les emails envoyés aux adresses de contact des collectifs durant cette période, et de les lire s'ils n'étaient pas chiffrés.




Pour les lecteurices et visiteureuses des sites, l'adresse 

IP

 que vous utilisiez pour consulter les sites a pu être récupérée, mais les risques sont probablement assez réduits : la consultation des sites du réseau Mutu n'est pas répréhensible (pour l'instant tout du moins) et, si ça venait à être le cas, sauf si vous utilisez un 

VPN

 ou (encore mieux) le Navigateur Tor, votre fournisseur d'accès à Internet sait de toute façon que vous consultez des sites Mutu. Néanmoins, cela peut tout de même servir à alimenter les services de renseignements.




Pour les auteurices et contributeurices qui ont un compte sur ces sites, là aussi, votre adresse 

IP

 a pu être récupérée et associée aux articles auxquels vous êtes lié·es. C'est d'autant plus gênant si certains de ces articles étaient des appels ou des revendications d'actes illégaux (action, sabotage, incendie, etc.), ou même juste des contributions sensibles (type appel à manif non déclarée, conseils d'autodéfense, etc.) : si une enquête est ouverte et que les flics parviennent à mettre la main sur l'adresse 

IP

 de l'auteurice d'un tel article, ielles peuvent demander son identité à son fournisseur d'accès à Internet, à moins là encore d'avoir utilisé un 

VPN

 ou le Navigateur Tor pour masquer sa véritable adresse 

IP

 (voir les recommandations à ce sujet plus bas).




De même, si votre compte est toujours indiqué comme auteurice d'un article sensible, il est possible que cette information finisse par tomber entre les mains des flics. Nous recommandons alors d'arrêter au plus vite d'utiliser cette identité numérique (pseudo et adresse mail) afin d'éviter que les flics puissent collecter plus d'informations sur cette identité et risquer de vous retrouver.




Enfin, comme le mot de passe que vous utilisiez sur les sites a potentiellement été compromis, s'il s'agit d'un mot de passe que vous utilisez aussi pour d'autres choses (par exemple pour accéder à votre boîte mail), il est important de le changer là aussi et, si possible, d'utiliser des mots de passe différents à chaque fois.




Renforcer la sécurité collective, encore et toujours




Afin d'en faire un petit pense-bête à part entière, plus facile à partager et à mettre à jour, nous avons regroupé dans 

cet article

 quelques bonnes pratiques pour réduire les risques que nous prenons touxtes lorsque nous utilisons les outils informatiques, ceux du réseau Mutu comme les autres :




Avec plus de sécurité collective, on est plus fort·x·es

Pour conclure




Sans ses contributeurices, sans ses lecteurices, le réseau Mutu n'est rien. Nous vous sommes reconnaissant·x·es de la confiance que vous nous faites en consultant nos sites et en les utilisant pour relayer vos informations, vos actions, vos événements ou vos communiqués. Il est important pour nous d'honorer cette confiance en tâchant au mieux d'éviter de vous mettre en danger ou de vous exposer à la répression, qu'elle vienne des flics ou des fachos.




Nous espérons que ces piratages n'auront de conséquences fâcheuses pour personne. Nous espérons aussi que les quelques pistes évoquées plus haut nous permettront à touxtes, collectivement, de réduire les risques que nous prenons lorsque nous utilisons les outils informatiques, ceux du réseau Mutu comme les autres.




Au plaisir de vous retrouver sur nos sites,




La commission serveur du réseau Mutu










[

1

] 

Avant d'être stockés dans la base de données, les mots de passe sont passés dans une moulinette (une «

 

fonction de hachage

 

») qui les rend complètement illisibles et irrécupérables. Obtenir le haché d'un mot de passe ne permet donc pas de retrouver celui-ci directement. Par contre, une personne qui connaît le haché d'un mot de passe peut essayer de deviner celui-ci : à chaque essai, ielle prend un mot de passe possible, le passe à la même moulinette, compare avec le haché dont ielle dispose, et, si les hachés sont les mêmes, c'est qu'il s'agissait du bon mot de passe. Bien sûr, chaque essai prend un peu de temps, mais un ordinateur standard est déjà capable d'en faire plusieurs milliards par seconde. Donc si le mot de passe est «

 

faible

 

» (c'est-à-dire trop court, un mot du dictionnaire, un mot de passe déjà fréquemment utilisé par d'autres personnes, ou une variation de c3rt41ne5 let7r3s), il pourra finir par être retrouvé, nettement plus vite que si la personne essayait les mots de passe directement sur le site, en essayant de se connecter à chaque fois.

title: Vigil for ill prisoners: The right to life is not negotiable
content:
The protest, launched outside the Ministry of Justice following a call by the Federation of Associations for Legal Solidarity with the Families of Prisoners and Convicts (TUHAD-FED), the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) and the Association of Lawyers for Freedom (ÖHD), will enter its fifth day. 




The indefinite protest will continue every day at 14:00 outside the Ministry of Justice.




On Friday, the relatives of ill prisoners Ömer Güneri, Yakup Akman, Mehmet Ali Taşkın and Selim Çiftçi, Tuncer Sağlam, who died on 7 November in the hospital where he was receiving treatment, attended the protest.




During the demonstration, which was supported by representatives of organisations and members of the public, a banner bearing the names of seriously ill prisoners was unfurled. It read: “We are at the gates of justice; we will open the prison gates through resistance. Freedom for ill prisoners.”




‘Don't stay silent’




Deniz Topkan, a member of the Central Executive Board of the Health and Social Service Workers' Union (SES), called for support for the protest, saying that the vigil outside the Ministry of Justice must not be ignored.




Pointing out that numerous ill prisoners had lost their lives in prison after being denied access to healthcare, Topkan stressed that restricting someone's freedom does not mean their right to health and life can be taken away.




Stating that prisons had become places where illnesses deteriorate and deaths occur, Topkan said that isolation practices in Type S and other high-security prisons negatively affect prisoners' mental health.




Deniz Topkan noted that practices such as delays in hospital transfers, examinations conducted while prisoners are handcuffed, strip searches and intrusive oral cavity searches obstruct prisoners' right to treatment. She called for the release of seriously ill prisoners and guaranteed access to medical care to prevent further deaths.




Ercan Sağlam, a relative of Tuncer Sağlam, who died in the hospital where he was receiving treatment, said that delays in diagnosis and treatment had led to Sağlam's death. Explaining that Sağlam had been transferred from Wan to Ankara Etlik City Hospital and that, despite being unable to meet his own basic needs, there had been attempts to send him back to prison, Ercan Sağlam said:




“We have been experiencing this pain for years. But from now on, we will never accept another one of our comrades dying in prison.”




Noting that while deaths resulting from armed conflict had ceased during the Peace and Democratic Society Process, ill prisoners continued to lose their lives in prisons, Sağlam called for the immediate release of seriously ill prisoners.




‘Responsibility lies with the state’




Nurten Karagöz, co-chair of the Marmara Association for Solidarity and Mutual Assistance with the Families of Prisoners and Convicts (MA-TUHAYDER), emphasised that the right to health and the right to life are fundamental human rights.




Stating that the state is responsible for the lives and healthcare guarantees of all prisoners, Karagöz said: “The deaths of people held in the state's custody should not be this easy. From now on, no ill prisoner should lose their life in prison. The right to life is a sacred right. It cannot be negotiated. Prisoners' lives cannot be used as bargaining chips.”




Karagöz said that while people were speaking about the democratisation of society, it was unacceptable to remain silent as people continued to die in prison. She called for the right to life of ill prisoners to be protected.




‘Prisons must not be turned into places of execution’




Mahfuz Güleryüz, Deputy Co-Chair of the DEM Party, also condemned human rights violations taking place in prisons.




Güleryüz said: “Prisons must not be turned into places of ‘execution’. The state and the Ministry of Justice must immediately abandon these practices. We will continue to oppose this lawlessness, to resist it and to demand justice.”

title: Women artists: No peace or justice without women's freedom
content:
Actors Lale Mansur, Jülide Kural and Merve Asya Özgür spoke to ANF on the occasion of the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on 25 November.




The actors said that male dominance in the arts negatively affects women's creative work and visibility, while also drawing attention to television content that fuels violence. They said that men are emboldened by the failure of the justice system and stressed that there can be no justice, peace or democracy in a society where women are not free.




Lale Mansur: Male perpetrators are emboldened




Lale Mansur stressed that violence against women and femicide should be on the agenda not only on 25 November, but every day, even every moment. She said, "In Turkey, we need to talk about this five times a day. Turkey has become a slaughterhouse for women! We have reached this point because there is impunity. There is no rule of law, the law is not enforced, and there is no justice. Murderers walk among us. They search for the body of one woman and find the bodies of two more women in a well. How much worse can it get?"




Lale Mansur said that murders do not simply result in the loss of one life, but also devastate the lives of mothers, fathers and other relatives. She emphasised that the culture of impunity emboldens perpetrators, adding, "Male murderers are emboldened by impunity."




Lale Mansur also addressed the situation in the media and the shrinking space for opposition, saying that television programmes and series fuel violence: "The absence of any opposition, the disastrous state of television series... Truly disgraceful things are being produced on national television channels, including content that incites violence. They even made a television series about Abdullah Çatlı."




'Male dominance also prevails in television channels'




Lale Mansur said that male-dominated structures also prevail in the arts: "The owners and executives of television channels are mostly men. Male dominance exists there too. As for actors, many people have children to educate and support. With the high cost of living, they are forced to take part in such productions to earn money. Of course, there are very rare cases of people who refuse, saying, 'I'd rather sell lemons.' But when you have children or a family to support, you have little choice."




Lale Mansur said that impunity and the male-dominated mentality lie at the root of violence and femicide. She stressed that the problem cannot be resolved through criminal penalties alone, but requires a fundamental transformation of attitudes across society: "The biggest factor fuelling violence is impunity. They walk among us, and these people are murderers... This language, which targets and objectifies women, confronts us in every aspect of our lives. There is nothing we can tell women. You cannot say something like 'Don't let yourself be killed.' People say, 'Those men were raised by their mothers.' No, they were not raised by their mothers alone; they were raised by society. And society is now morally rotten."




Jülide Kural: There can be no democracy without women's freedom




Jülide Kural said, "25 November is a day of struggle and solidarity for women across the world against all forms of violence, discrimination and inequality. Violence is not directed only at the body. Discrediting a woman's character, disregarding her labour and will, and surrounding her with lies, insinuations and systematic attacks are also forms of violence."




Jülide Kural said that depriving women of their agency over their own lives, defining them through the existence of a man and attempting to confine them to a passive and dependent identity are among the most deeply rooted forms of violence produced by the male-dominated mentality. She emphasised that this violence is not perpetrated exclusively by men, adding, "Anyone who reproduces the male-dominated mentality and its discriminatory language can become part of this violence. Violence does not have a gender; it has a mentality that sustains it."




Jülide Kural stressed that no woman should have to prove her existence, worth or dignity through the judgements of others. She said, "25 November is not merely a day to condemn violence, but a day to confront the social and political order that produces it. In a society where women are not free, there can be no genuine democracy, justice or peace."




Jülide Kural declared that women would not remain silent, saying, "We will not be silent! We will strengthen solidarity and will not give up our right to have a say over our lives and our future. Because the struggle for women's freedom is the struggle for the freedom of humanity."




Merve Asya Özgür: From belittling our intelligence to harassment




Actor Merve Asya Özgür responded to our question about how courageously art challenges and transforms male-dominated language. Özgür said:  "What can the works we create and the encounters we experience, which freeze the ordinary flow of life and allow us to look at it from different perspectives, change in our lives? Perhaps that is one rather superficial way of describing art and its outcomes. Yet these encounters, or aestheticised confrontations, can certainly create awareness of gender and every identity crushed by gender roles, and open up a path towards confrontation and transformation. Indeed, that path is already open to such possibilities.




I am currently reading Cemil Meriç's Journal. At the very beginning of the book, he defines what he considers true art to be. He says that art means giving life to abstract and ghostlike imaginings, giving them blood, light and warmth. He describes how artists breathe life into these elusive dreams and abstract concepts by infusing them with a part of their own souls and lives. The experience of systematic violence and what it does to human beings inevitably finds its way into artists' work through their souls, including a spirit that resists and seeks change. The extent to which this happens is debatable, but even if nothing else remains, the traces of what a person has experienced can be seen in their eyes. However, I think the real key issue here is who presents artistic productions and how they are presented. I believe it would be more sensible to direct our attention towards that.




As for how courageous we are... In answering that question, I do not want to underestimate the achievements of the struggle. Nor do I want to paint an overly positive picture, as though everything were good enough and major transformations were taking place across society."




Merve Asya Özgür said that male dominance in the arts negatively affects women's creative work and visibility: "Exercising power, dominating, making women invisible or making them visible only according to your own aesthetic preferences... We could go on listing the destructive consequences, from belittling women's intelligence and failing to provide equal pay for equal work to dominating spaces of social and cultural production, harassment, violence and abuse.




Beyond all this, the achievements of the struggle are presented under the guise of patriarchal kindness and generosity, through expressions such as 'creating space for women', 'women artists' and 'supporting women artists'. It is a kind of celebrated tolerance, a supposed act of generosity intended to ensure that those considered 'lacking' are not left behind. You are repeatedly confronted, in every setting, with a superficial understanding that treats being a woman as though it were your only identity in life. It is truly infuriating."

title: Alfred de Zayas: Why should Kurds be denied the right to self-determination? - Part One
content:
The right of peoples to self-determination is one of the fundamental principles of international law. However, its implementation remains contested because of the political and economic interests of states. The international representation of the Kurdish people, who are divided among four countries and have no state of their own, and the protection of their political, cultural and linguistic rights remain among the unresolved issues of international law.




Alfred de Zayas, an expert in international law and human rights who served as the United Nations (UN) Independent Expert on the Promotion of a Democratic and Equitable International Order from 2012 to 2018, spoke to ANF about the Kurdish people's right to self-determination and autonomy, the possibilities of obtaining status within the UN, the treatment of stateless peoples and double standards in international law.




De Zayas said that the Kurdish people's right to self-determination has a strong foundation in international law, emphasising that the main obstacle to exercising this right is political rather than legal. He stressed that the UN has failed to fulfil its responsibilities towards the Kurdish people and said that Kurds should bring human rights violations before international mechanisms, explore interstate complaint procedures and build stronger networks of solidarity within the international community.




De Zayas also strongly criticised the European Union's approach to the Kurdish question, arguing that international law must be applied equally to all peoples. He asked, "If the right to self-determination has been granted to other peoples, why should it not be granted to the Kurdish people?"




ANF spoke to international law expert Alfred de Zayas.




Mr. de Zayas, you have worked for many years within the United Nations on international law, human rights and the right of peoples to self-determination. I would like to begin with a fundamental question. What does the right of a people to self-determination mean under international law? Does this right refer only to establishing an independent state, or can it also be exercised in other forms?




Of course, the right to self-determination can also be exercised internally. If there is a federal state and a people enjoys extensive autonomy, that system can work. But what happens when a state oppresses a people who have lived on their own land for thousands of years? The Kurds are not immigrants who recently arrived in the territories of Turkey, Syria, Iran or Iraq.




If we genuinely took the right to self-determination seriously, we would ask which people have the clearest claim to this right. I would say the Kurds. There are between 40 and 45 million Kurds, divided among four states. Yet they have no state of their own.




After the First World War, they could have had their own state if the Treaty of Sèvres had been implemented. However, Mustafa Kemal fought against the French and British forces at that time. Those forces were expelled from the territory of the new Turkey. The Treaty of Sèvres was subsequently replaced by the Treaty of Lausanne, which made no mention of the Kurdish or Armenian peoples.




What, then, are the legal foundations of the right to self-determination?




You can find them in Articles 1 and 55 of the United Nations Charter, as well as Chapters XI and XII. This right is also enshrined in the common Article 1 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. There is extensive literature on this subject, including my report A/69/272, which I submitted to the UN General Assembly in 2014. In that report, I examine the criteria determining which peoples may claim autonomy or independence.




Before continuing, I would like to mention a book that you may not know about because it has only recently been published. I supervised the doctoral thesis of a young Norwegian researcher, Blerim Mustafa, whose family originates from North Macedonia. He devoted his doctoral research to the right of secession, particularly the concept known in international law as "remedial secession".




His book is entitled Remedial Secession After the Cold War: Self-Determination and the Question of Secession. A substantial part of this work is devoted to the Kurds. The author examines three examples. The first is the people of East Timor, who were previously occupied, colonised and oppressed by Indonesia. The second is Kosovo, which is not recognised by all states and is not yet a UN member, but continues to exist as a state. The third is Iraqi Kurdistan, where a referendum produced an extremely clear result concerning self-determination.




'

International law must also apply to the Kurds'




What happens in these cases? The issue concerns perceptions and the application of different standards to different situations. As a professor of international law, there is one matter that has always particularly concerned me: the equal application of international law to everyone.




By definition, international law is international and universal. Therefore, you cannot say, "I will apply this law to Kosovo, but I will not apply it to Kurdistan." There is also a fundamental political dimension here, namely the recognition of a state by the international community, meaning other states.




Who, then, has the right to self-determination under international law? Without question, the Kurdish people do. The Kurds are a people, and they can rely on the UN Charter, the principles of international law developed through the process of decolonisation, and their right to preserve their identity, culture and language.




All these rights are protected by international human rights treaties and the jurisprudence of the International Court of Justice (ICJ). When we speak about territorial integrity, we must of course acknowledge that it is one of the fundamental principles of international law, just like state sovereignty. However, paragraph 80 of the ICJ's 2010 advisory opinion on Kosovo clearly states that the principle of territorial integrity applies to relations between states.




In other words, this principle protects a state's sovereignty against occupation, aggression or the seizure of its territory by another state. In my interpretation, it cannot be used to deny peoples their right to self-determination.




Therefore, in this context, the principle of territorial integrity does not apply to a state's internal relations. It concerns external relations between states. For example, State A cannot occupy or colonise the territory of State B or settle its own population there. However, when a conflict arises between a people's right to self-determination and a state's desire to preserve its existing borders, I believe that the right to self-determination should take precedence over the principle of territorial integrity.




You say that the right to self-determination is clearly recognised under international law. Nevertheless, serious obstacles prevent Kurds from exercising this right. Do you think the main reason is shortcomings in international law, or the political and economic interests of states?




What I have explained is the theoretical dimension of the issue. I address this subject in my book Building a Just World Order, which has also recently been published in Spanish. I devoted the fifth chapter to the theory and practice of the right to self-determination. However, there is a reality that we must understand, acknowledge and confront: this is an extremely political issue.




If international conditions are unfavourable and you cannot secure the support of sufficiently powerful states, exercising the right to self-determination becomes almost impossible, whether through autonomy or secession. In other words, it is a matter of power relations and the economic interests of states. For example, we must remember that Iraqi Kurdistan is a region rich in oil. There are significant resources, economic assets and interests there. Multinational corporations and other actors want to preserve the status quo and are concerned about Kurdistan's independence.




'

Kurdish rights are sacrificed to political and economic interests'




I believe that the people of Iraqi Kurdistan have a right to a remedy, particularly in view of the genocide committed in Halabja in 1988. In my opinion, that remedy should be independence, meaning secession.




What, then, can the Kurds do? International law is applied with double standards. Another people who have the right to self-determination and to establish their own state are the Palestinians. Every day, we see on television events that I consider to constitute genocide. We have extremely extensive information about Israel's oppression of the Palestinian people. What has the international community done to stop it? Nothing. There is the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement.




Has this movement achieved any progress? No. There is complicity on the part of European states, particularly the United States. The US, the United Kingdom and European Union countries have provided Israel with military, economic, political, diplomatic and media support. In my opinion, this makes them complicit in genocide.




'

Kurds have the right to resist occupation'




What is happening in the world? Nothing. Even UN Secretary-General António Guterres has not used the word "genocide". Not once. Similarly, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk can condemn crimes and human rights violations committed against Palestinians, but he has not dared to use the term "genocide".




You see, this is also a question of perception, and the media plays a role in it. In my opinion, the media has adopted a hostile attitude towards Palestinians. It has vilified them, portrayed them as terrorists and contributed to their demonisation. Yet the Palestinian people have the right to self-determination and the right to resist occupation, oppression and exploitation by a state such as Israel.




Of course, the right to resist also applies to the Kurds. According to my interpretation of international law, the Kurds also have the right to resist occupation and violations of their human rights. This principle is also addressed in Article 7 of UN General Assembly Resolution 33/14. However, I repeat that these are theoretical considerations.




You have said that the implementation of rights recognised under international law depends largely on political power relations. What path should the Kurds follow to bring their right to self-determination more prominently onto the international agenda and gain support? In particular, what should they do to mobilise international public opinion and different states?




In practice, economic interests determine the policies of the US, the United Kingdom and the European Union. At present, these powers have no interest in changing the situation in Turkey, Syria or Iraq. Of course, Israel and the US want regime change in Iran. We know this, and we can see it.




In my opinion, this is completely contrary to international law. However, we do not have sufficiently effective mechanisms to oppose it. So what can we do? What remains is public opinion, global public opinion.




'Kurds need to win the information war'




It is extremely important for the Kurds to find friends and allies among countries known as the "Global South" or the "Global Majority". However, to gain friends and allies, people must first know about your situation. If you mention the Treaty of Sèvres to someone here in Geneva or in New York today, they will probably look at you without understanding anything. Many people have no idea about this issue.




Similarly, when you mention the Kurdish people, some people may never have heard of them or may have learned almost nothing about their history. That is why the Kurds need to win the information war. You must ensure that people read about your situation, become informed and understand what you have experienced. As I told you, I deeply believe that the Kurds are among the peoples with the clearest and most fundamental right to self-determination. It is unbelievable that a people of 45 million should have no state of their own. It is absurd, absolutely absurd. But that is the reality. Nevertheless, very few people know about your situation.

author: Isaac Nellist
title: RAFFWU members locked out of work, rally against ‘union-busting’ Book Grocer
content:
Retail and Fast Food Workers’ Union (RAFFWU) members at the Book Grocer in Naarm/Melbourne rallied outside the Northcote store on November 21 to demand it end its lockout of workers.

The Book Grocer notified workers of the lockout at 8pm on November 20, shutting unionised workers out of their workplaces and stopping their pay at Bourke St, Spencer St, Northcote and its Tullamarine warehouse.

RAFFWU said in a media release that members had been bargaining since May for their first enterprise agreement, demanding a right to a safe workplace, protections from unfair treatment and options for permanent jobs. RAFFWU said the Book Grocer “rejected all their claims”.

RAFFWU members notified their employer on November 16 that they would be taking protected industrial action as part of their bargaining campaign, including handing out information flyers and wearing stickers to promote their campaign.

RAFFWU secretary Loukas Kakogiannis said the Book Grover had “crossed a line no retailer in Australian history has crossed”.

“Book Grocer has locked its own workers out in response to workers notifying that they would take action as small as wearing a sticker on their shirt while at work … “t has cut off their pay, just weeks out from Christmas, to starve them into giving up. That is a cowardly, vindictive attack on booksellers whose only crime is asking for fair treatment.”

Kakogiannis said this made The Book Grocer “the worst union-busting employer in the retail sector”.

“The Book Grocer would rather shut their stores and see their workers struggle to put food on the table than give them secure jobs.”

Book Grocer worker and RAFFWU delegate Fen Strangeways said the lockout would be difficult for workers. “Being locked out just weeks before Christmas is going to put real strain on our ability to pay rent and put food on the table.

“We’ve said from the start that we are open to compromise, we just want a safe workplace and to be treated fairly. Some of us have worked as casuals for ten years and just want to be made permanent.”

But workers are “not going to be intimidated”, Strangeways said. “We are sticking together.”

Retail and Fast Food Workers Union (RAFFWU)

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: ‘Predators-in-chief’ attack ICC
content:
Former United Nations (UN) Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial killing Agnès Callamard visited the Philippines after almost a decade of being barred from entering the country.

“It begins with Duterte, in a few weeks. But it doesn’t end there,” said Callamard, also Amnesty International’s secretary-general in a press conference on November 20. “This is bigger than him. It is about the Philippines. It’s about humanity.”

When she was UN Special Rapporteur, she called for investigations into the thousands of killings under Duterte’s anti-illegal drugs campaign. The immigration ban started in 2017 and Duterte ordered that she and any representatives of the International Criminal Court (ICC) be arrested and deported.

Callamard’s immigration ban was lifted in September 2026 after years of petitioning the Philippine authorities, with the support of Amnesty International Philippines and support from several lawmakers.

“The supposed war on drugs was a slaughter that destroyed lives and families. They have carried their grief with little hope for justice and nowhere else to turn for almost a decade,” Callamard said.

Duterte is charged with three counts of crimes against humanity by the ICC for extrajudicial killings during his term as Davao City mayor and President of the Philippines. His trial is set to begin on November 30.

Human rights organizations reported more than 30,000 extrajudicial killing victims from Duterte’s anti-illegal drugs campaign, significantly higher than the official government records of just over 6,000 victims. Only five cases resulted in conviction and some of them remain on appeal.

“We had conversations with the victims, survivors, and families in the past 48 hours [with Callamard]. It is still depressing. The families have accepted that there will be no justice at home and that they are depending on what will happen in The Hague. It is very ironic,” said Ritz Lee Santos III, section director of Amnesty International Philippines. “We have a justice system here at home. The government is claiming that they are working, but the victims’ families are saying that there is no hope. There is still a culture of impunity and a climate of fear.”

These structures, both of them said, are evident in the continuing drug-related extrajudicial killings, Duterte’s children remaining in power, and the widespread vilification of the victims and their families.

Read: Women human rights defenders face rising tech-assisted violence

The United States has imposed sanctions against the ICC, banning transactions with the court to paralyze its resources and ability to operate. The administration of US President Donald Trump previously sanctioned 13 prosecutors and judges of the ICC, three Palestinian human rights organizations, and the United Nations special rapporteur on human rights in the Occupied Palestinian Territory Francesca Albanese.

Read: US intensifies sanctions vs. ICC

The United States, China, and Russia issued a so-called “peace declaration” in their first trilateral summit on November 29, after Trump’s visit in Manila, Philippines. Particularly, the ICC garnered special attention in their declaration.

“The three heads of state recognized that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction,” the declaration read.

Part of the declaration is to “reform” the United Nations (UN) as permanent members of the United Nations Security Council (UNSC).

“They are the ‘predators-in-chief’ in our current system. This so-called peace treaty is about as worthless as who they are– predators,” said Callamard, highlighting their aggression in Venezuela, Iran, and Palestine. “They are attacking the ICC because international justice for them is a battle ground.”

“We are calling on the rest of the world to stand up to these predatory actions and threats. There are far more governments that ratified the Rome Statute. So in terms of the numbers, we are far more powerful than they are,” Callamard said.

In her international human rights work, Callamard said that there are less powerful governments living in fear of what the US, Russia, and China could do in their economy. “It is about economic characters being fearful of being kept out of the American market, Russian market, or the China market. And for those reasons, humanity is being thrown out. We’re being hanged, sold in fact. The soul of our work, of our humanity, is being sold so that some rich individuals can make a few bucks on those markets.”

She called on ICC member-states to push back against the sanctions. “They have the legal, political, and policy tools to push back. But they haven’t done that. The problem is not just the predators-in-chief, but also the cowards.”

During the press conference, she also led the launching of Walang Pahimakas (No Farewell: Anthology of Poems on the “War on Drugs”) published this year by Amnesty International Philippines. It is a collection of poems that brings stories of the victims and their families at the forefront of the search for justice, accountability, and truth.

“In a climate marked by fear and silencing critics, the written word becomes a means of restoring the truth. Walang Pahimakas is an act of remembering lives that were reduced to labels and statistics,” editor and poet Ron Atilano said. “Poetry cannot bring back those who were killed nor can it take away the trauma of losing a loved one in cold-blooded murder, but it refuses to let lives be forgotten. These poems remind us that behind every reported killing was a human being, and behind every victim was a family whose lives were forever changed.” (RTS, DAA)
