Note for readers: This is a transcript of Zimbabwean-American Zoé Samudzi’s panel titled “On A Black Feminist Anarchism” given at the Orange County Anarchist Bookfair on March 25th, 2017, in Anaheim, California. Despite the rougher audio quality from the video recording of the original panel, the folks associated in the production of “A Black Autonomy Reader” (Seditionist Distribution, 2024), a compilation of Black autonomist and anarchist texts throughout history, were able to transcribe a large amount of Zoé’s panel. While there was a Q&A section where Samudzi answered roughly 3-4 questions from the audience, much of the audience’s questions are garbled compared to Zoé’s clear answers picked up by their microphone. As such, this transcription is solely of what they said as part of her panel, not the answers they gave.

This updated transcription, done by myself, corrects nearly all omissions from the original, restores words that were left out, corrects misspelled names, and includes revisions to grammar and citations. Samudzi’s multiple “and’s” were omitted for readability. Public figures, book titles, and specific events mentioned have been footnoted, recognizing that readers may be unfamiliar with the histories and cultural contexts of what is being discussed. - AnarchoGuac

Hi everyone. I’m really excited to be here. I don’t like — I much prefer to have generative dialogue spaces than to talk at you. So I’m gonna try to keep it on the shorter side, and then we can have some more conversation on what I am trying to talk about.

In her 1983 literary work In Search Of Our Mothers’ Gardens, Alice Walker described a womanist as “a woman who loves another woman, sexually and/or non-sexually. She appreciates and prefers women’s culture, women’s emotional flexibility. She’s committed to the survival and the wholeness of an entire people. She’s not a separatist, except periodically for health. She loves the spirit, she loves struggle, she loves herself, regardless.”[1]

So I have a really complicated relationship with political theory, particularly as someone that studied political science as an undergraduate. My relationship to political theory, especially to the kind of horribly white supremacist enlightenment values of “rationality” and “objectivity” is generally, like, a knee-jerk reaction to the whiteness and the eurocentricity of it and of the canon. With regards to anarchism specifically, I often feel alienated from the theory because of the non-white and non-western globality of the politics of the ideology that have, all of a sudden, been turned into this white politic. Anarchistic values of horizontalism, of mutual aid, of voluntary participation, of non-extra or markably anti-state organization existed prior to Pierre-Joseph Proudhon’s self description of “anarchist” in the mid-1800s, or William Godwin’s framework laying work in the 1790s. I say this, you know, what I’m about to say, in the same vein that Russell Means of the American Indian Movement sought to resist; being “Europeanized.” He said that like capitalism, Marxism is right smack in the middle of European tradition, and the Hegelian dialectic is a secularizing theory that is even further despiritualized and despiritualizes humanity that we kinda end up also end up seeing in industrialization and Marx’s materialism.[2]

So, I want to share a confession that’s made me a bit unpopular in different anarchist communities that I’ve kind of tried to involve myself in. I don’t read canonical anarchist theory, and I have no intention to. I’ve read some of and I deeply value Emma Goldman’s development of anarcho-feminism, but I’ve never read Kropotkin, I’ve never read Bakunin, and I don’t plan to anytime soon. My most important and foundational left-politics have been derived from observing organizations and political formations themselves. The Black Panther Party taught me what it looked like to apply Maoism in the development of a racialized resistance politic for community self-determination. The Zapatista’s Zapatismo taught me about the synthesis of articulated Indigenous practices and sovereignty and socio-cultural organization with familiar principles and ideologies. African liberation leaders like Amílcar Cabral and Thomas Sankara taught me what a culturally relevant post-colonial formation and an agrarian revolution might look like on the continent, unfortunately before they were both assassinated. Brazil’s Landless Workers Movement & South Africa’s Abahlali baseMjondolo, which is a shack dwellers’ movement, and they’re about land reclamation and about widespread democratization processes beginning with the most poor and the most disenfranchised communities in the country— taught me what it meant to organize around reclaimed resources. Indigenous peoples and First Nations peoples of North America taught me what sovereignty meant. In addition to these global struggles, I’m deeply inspired by the myriad ways that Black people have resisted in the Americas and throughout the African diaspora. Boaventura de Sousa Santos— so I do read a ton of theory, I just don’t read white dudes— he developed a concept of “societal fascism,” which describes the mechanisms and logics of state formation wherein whole populations are excluded prior to or after the formation of a social contract.

Pre-contractual exclusion refers to populations that have never been part of and can never be a part of the social contract. So in the United States, think of Indigenous people or think of Black people. Post-contractual exclusion, or ejection from the contract, means that a given population could enjoy conditional access to the contract. Think of immigrants who had to appeal to a proximity to whiteness in order to become American citizens. Think of poor white people, who are part of the contract through the merit of their whiteness, but are excluded because of their working classes. Black people, obviously as I said, exist within the former realm of exclusion, because Black people are residents within a settler colony predicated upon both the genocide of Indigenous people and the enslavement of African peoples. Despite formal emancipation in 1865, Blackness can only be perpetually relegated to the afterlife of slavery as long as the settler project continues to exist.

Though we’re formally born [bound?] to the laws of the land, Black America can be understood as an extra-state entity because they are not a part of the social contract. Because of this location, I understand Blackness in so many ways to be anarchistic. African Americans, that is, the ethno-social identity of descendants of enslaved African people, have innovated new cultures and social organizations, much like anarchism would require us to do outside of the state structure in the event that the revolution happens tomorrow. Black radical formations are fundamentally anti-fascist despite often and generally functioning outside of conventional “antifa” spaces, and Black people have engaged in anarchistic resistances since our arrival in the Americas. From slave ship and plantation rebellions during enslavement, to post-emancipation labor and prison camp uprisings, to Harriet Tubman’s literal removal of enslaved people from the custody of their owners, to the creation of maroon societies in the South, to combatting the historic and present collusion between state law enforcement and white supremacist groups, assertions of Black personhood, humanity, and liberation have always called into question both the foundation and the legitimacy of the American state.

So given this particular positionality, and the historical and contemporary relationship that Black people do have to the state — I’m developing an analysis from this particular position as opposed to simply analysis of the position. That is, I’m kind of trying to develop a decolonized dialectic because I’m in midst of reading Decolonizing Dialectics, which I actually recommend reading.[3] Marx and Engels have provided us admittedly useful dialectical tools for understanding history, state formation, class, and these are tools that have been adopted and adapted by countless resistances to colonialism all around the world. But I find Cedric Robinson’s critique of Marxian shortcomings to be incredibly useful, particularly when he writes around the non-universal applicability of an orthodox western political thought, these processes of industrialization and proletarianization, and the failure to account for the inherently racial character of capitalism.[4]

In his 1997 article “Identity Politics and Class Struggle,” Robin D.G. Kelley writes that “class is lived through race and gender,”[5] highlighting both the inextricability of race and gender with class, and the necessity for an anti-capitalist identity politic— yes I said it, I’m a firm believer in identity politics— that instrumentalizes unique experiences and understandings from a particular social positionality in racial capitalist regimes. It’s not simply enough to center Blackness, right, to toss it into your analysis once you’ve created this grand theory of how oppression functions and how the state functions. But I specifically want to center Black womanhood because of the ways in which race is inextricably linked and co-constituted through gender. If anarchism is to be of any use to me, I must have an anarchism that speaks directly to my needs and vulnerabilities as a Black woman and to Black women of all stripes and all identities. If you’re unaware, there have been a spate of kidnappings of Black girls and disappearances of Black women across the country. There are ongoing bold murders of Black trans women. Why is this? Because Black women’s safety is a non-priority of the state and every predator knows this. We are being hunted, but this hunting season is grossly un-and-under addressed because of the degendering of anti-racist politics. Because of the way that Black womanhood is made invisible through diversity language around “women” and “people of color” that overlooks the intersections of race and gender. Because of the erasure of Black womanhood though “women of color,” and because of the understandings of the ways that state violence against Black bodies tends to focus on the humiliation and emasculation and almost sole targeting of cisgendered Black Men — and so I hope to speak to a Black feminist anarchism, an identity politic, a dialectic, and an analytical framework that specifically addresses these urgent material needs.

So first, womanism. Womanism is the social theory based on the race and gender oppression of Black women that is rooted in materiality, lived experience, and embodied knowledge. Womanist theologian Dolores Williams describes this embodied activism as being associated with traditions and resistances that are formed from different conditions, events, socio-cultural, and contextual meaning and all of the different values that these things have within Blackness. Womanism offers two things for me in particular. It offers the opportunity to break from traditional definitions of womanhood, where cis Black womanhood is othered and Black trans womanhood is doubly othered in the way that it presents a threat to gender hegemony and to the gendered anxiety of us as cis women. The second thing that it presents to me is the emphasis of kinship and community over individuality. Womanism seeks to reconcile Black women’s relationships with one another and with nature, most notably our deeply commodified and violated bodies, over which we have historically had very little agency, our physical environment, and our spirituality.

Now, Black feminism says that sexism and misogyny, gender identity, class depression [oppression?], and racism are inextricably linked in a mutually constitutive web of, to quote Patricia Hill Collins, and I’m sure as you’ve all heard, “interlocking systems of oppression,” and within this tradition, of course, is Kimberlé Crenshaw’s “intersectionality,” which builds off of the Combahee River Collective’s “simultaneity,” and even 19th century Black feminist works like that of Anna Julia Cooper. Black Feminism too seeks to ground political understandings and anti-capitalist critiques in embodied knowledges and in lived experiences and also present a non-essentialized and non-biologized critique of Black womanhood’s identity and position within history; a useful historical revisionism that highlights racial capitalism’s critical subjugation and Black nationalism’s exclusion of Black women. It presents a response to the racist exclusion of Black women from women’s issues, issues around safety, deservingness, agency, autonomy, and class oppression. In understanding Black women’s unique subjugation by the state means understanding race and gendered labor extraction within capitalism, most incisively, the ways Black feminism is a modality for understanding how the anti-Black settler state is a fundamentally illegitimate construction. Unlike what Jacobin and their class fetishizing ilk of all sectarian stripes might tell you, intersectionality does not undermine Marxism, or anything. It doesn’t.

What does it mean to properly understand Black women’s subjugation? It means to understand the ways in which Black women’s labor was central to the development of the capitalist state and to the American slaveocracy. Sarah Haley’s book No Mercy Here outlines the myriad ways in which gendered anti-Blackness forms the construction of the Jim Crow system.[6] [This] paves the way for the contemporary systems of mass incarceration and school to prison pipelining that we see today. Haley’s book makes direct comparison between the hyper-imprisonability of Black women’s gender deviance and the redeemability of white femininity, and the ways in which these constructs were made oppositional and reified through judicial sentencing that enforced Black women’s objection.

Black women were thought to be “as strong as men” and were frequently used for all kinds of labor, whereas white women were only employed in fields as punishment for particularly bad behavior. Where Black men were 1.4 times more likely than white men to be arrested, Black women were 6.4 times more likely than white women to get arrested. It becomes evident that white women’s normativity is made more and more concrete through the tripled labor: the domestic, industrial, and sexual (euphemistically called “social reproductive”) labor, as Black women became playthings for prison guards and male approximate punishment. White women ultimately became exempted from chain gang labor— there was literally legislation saying that white women were not allowed to work on chain gangs. They were the only demographic to be protected from carceral punishment in this way, and this codifies the race/gender normativity and highlights the ways in which carcerality and punishment operate in service of white womanhood and how carceral gendering enforced both white women’s superiority and Black women’s distance from innocence.

So then when we look at contemporary anti-racist politics, right, we look at the ways that Black humanity and personhood continues to be evaluated through the impossible-to-obtain lens of innocence within the white liberal imagination. In "Against Innocence: Race, Gender and the Politics of Safety," Jackie Wang makes a constructive framework for Black personhood and victimization that resonates really deeply with me and sits at the bedrock of all of what I’m talking about.[7] She writes on this phenomenon saying that “innocence becomes the precondition for launching antiracist campaigns,” campaigns where empathy can only be established if and when Black people are able to pass rigorous tests of moral purity. So for example, we can agree for the most part, that Tamir Rice was egregiously victimized because he was a child, and also because we saw that video, but that’s a different story.[8] Empathy was a product of his youthfulness, and that’s the same with Aiyana Jones[9], but Mike Brown[10] was not enough of a victim because he may or may not have committed strongarm robbery, and Darren Wilson’s testimony[11] added to the process of what Frank Wilderson refers to as “niggerization,” we now know that Mike Brown did not commit strongarm robbery, but whether or not he did should not affect whether or not you believe that extrajudicial assassination is suddenly a reasonable punishment for robbing a convenience store.

We didn’t however see this overwhelming outpouring of empathy and support for CeCe McDonald, a Black transwoman who was convicted of second-degree manslaughter after killing an attacker that violently confronted her with first racist and transmysoginistic language and then smashed a drink against her face. She accepted a plea bargain of 41 months in prison in June, 2012, served 19 months in two different men’s facilities (which is another story) prior to her release in 2014. Now, given the epidemic murders of Black trans women, is her defensive violence not warranted? Is she not innocent enough? What makes her less innocent, and we’re not using these juridical measures of guilt and innocence that the state kinda arbitrarily lays out, but what makes her less innocent is than say Marissa Alexander who fired a warning shot in the air after her husband attacked and threatened to kill her? There was far more outcry about the gendered implications of women invoking stand-your-ground laws then there was about the perfectly reasonable use of any form of violence in response to the assault on Black trans women’s personhood. Perhaps, because in the case of Alexander, white liberals, particularly white feminists, were able to apply their carceral logics of “protecting the world from scary Brown men” that sits at the root of so many anti-domestic and intimate partner violence interventions.

Where there were so many anti-racist logics, even ones that emerged from radical spaces appeal to innocence, we continue to rely on the logics of the white imaginary and draw upon exceptional cases to buttress our arguments. But ultimately in doing so, we affirm illegitimate modes of governance and social regulation in an illegitimate state. Reliance upon empathy fails to produce a politics that unequivocally affirms Black humanity. Enduring out our own judgements of who we perceive to be innocent and who we perceive to not be innocent enough fails to actually articulate the state’s relationship to and production of Blackness. So to return to Frank Wilderson, if one were to ask the police why they shot a Black person, they would say “I shot you because you were Black, you are Black because I shot you.” We are Blackened, we are made Black by the logics of violence that are born out chattel enslavement in the Americas [and] colonial subjugation in the continent. Innocence defenses can only ever be flawed because the disciplinary and extractive systems erected around us, the ghetto, the plantation, the prison, the colony, can only ever define us solely through our criminality, our deviance, our ongoing existence as both capital and a heavily subsidized labor force for the state. We can never be innocent, and the issue is not the brutalized and slain Black individuals we decide to immortalize through hashtags after death, but rather our fundamentally criminal subject position. The state does not produce anti-Black socialities, the state is anti-Black sociality.

If it isn’t yet obvious, my almost singleminded focus within a Black feminist anarchism is that of safety. We should be able to rely on mainstream feminism because we’re women, but we’re precluded from white supremacist notions of womanhood, an exclusion that’s doubly compounded for trans women. White women are only virtuous and worth [protecting] because Black women are not. Protecting white women includes a regulation of public space and criminalization of personhood that still victimizes Black women. We’re unable to rely upon popular criticism of police misconduct that fail to understand that violence and murder of Black people is not an indiscretion and bad behavior on the behalf of police officers. It’s not something that can be trained away by diversity training. But it’s rather the output of white supremacist settler colonial machinations. It can never not happen again as long as the state continues to exist. Nevermind that the African American Policy Forum, which Kimberlé Crenshaw is a member, had to coin the “SayHerName” hashtag in February, 2015 because of Black women’s exclusion from these narratives and memorializations of victims of police violence.[12] Because how can you indict the state for violence against Black bodies when, in a post-Daniel Holtzclaw’s conviction world, we’re still failing to highlight the racialized gendered violence that has characterized it since its inception, and that the state has imposed, and the means by which the state has imposed it’s violence against Black women’s bodies?[13]

Furthermore, how do we have the audacity as anti-capitalists, or anarchists, or however we self-define it, to name anti-Blackness while failing to have Black people in organizing spaces? How do we entertain these lazy rejections of identity politics when our politicized way of knowing and resisting and understanding are a product of the embodied knowledges that come from our marginalized identities?

Wang discusses the ideas of these “zones of intelligibility,” that is spaces of being, and habitation, and navigation that are understandable to white people.[14] She highlights the fact that perhaps there was so much support that was mobilized for Trayvon Martin[15] and for Oscar Grant[16] because both were murdered in places that were intelligible and understandable to white imaginations. Trayvon Martin was killed in a gated community and Oscar Grant was murdered in a public transportation station. Still, she writes, there are violences that occur and have occurred in alternative universes, like the slave ship, the hood, the prison, at the hands of the state. But what happens when you’re unable to articulate the violence of and from your subject position because you possess an unintelligible identity, as is possessed by Black people, hence the need to constantly perform the dehumanizing mental gymnastics of appealing to an innocence that we can never attain? What happens when the violence is simply a logical extension of the politics you either knowingly or unknowingly enable and perpetuate?

When white liberals favor order over justice, they by extension support segregatory policy and ghetto policing because that’s what order is. Perhaps part of our silence about the murders of Black trans women, both by Black and non-Black cis communities, is because the violence and abuse they experience is the logical extension of the cisnormativity that materializes our very identities as cisgendered people. Because as with cis Black people killed by the state, we name and exceptionalize and count and deadname the murdered transgendered women, but we fail to interrogate the way that cisnormativity and gender regulation are central to white supremacist state-making.

You need only look at the way that CeCe and Chelsea Manning[17] and nearly every other transwoman is placed into male facilities, or in administrative segregation, for their own protection which is tantamount to torture. So we’ve got to reject this innocence in favor of a politic of Black women’s deservingness of safety in a world where Black womanhood is unviolable and unrapeable. Even in childhood, we’re still hypersexual-baby-jezebel-fast-tailed girls, and innocence is impossible for us to attain.

So that’s all I have, because I want us to have a conversation.

[1] In Search of Our Mothers' Gardens: Womanist Prose (1983) by Alice Walker.

[2] https://www.filmsforaction.org/news/revolution-and-american-indians-marxism-is-as-alien-to-my-culture-as-capitalism/

[3] Decolonizing Dialectics (2017) by George Ciccariello-Maher.

[4] Possibly a reference to Black Marxism: The Making of the Black Radical Tradition (1983) by Cedric Robinson.

[5] Kelley, Robin D. G. “Identity Politics and Class Struggle.” 1997, p. 5. Internet Archive, https://archive.org/details/identitypoliticsandclassstr/page/n5/mode/2up

[6] No Mercy Here: Gender, Punishment, and the Making of Jim Crow Modernity (2016) by Sarah Haley.

[7] “Against Innocence: Race, Gender, and the Politics of Safety,” by Jackie Wang, originally in LIES: A Journal of Materialist Feminism. https://theanarchistlibrary.org/library/jackie-wang-against-innocence-race-gender-and-the-politics-of-safety

[8] Tamir Rice was a 12-year-old boy fatally shot by a Cleveland police officer on November 22, 2014, while carrying a replica airsoft gun at a recreation center.

[9] Aiyana Stanley-Jones was a 7-year-old girl fatally shot during a Detroit police raid in May, 2010.

[10] Michael Brown, an 18-year-old Black teenager, was fatally shot by Ferguson police officer Darren Wilson on August 9, 2014, sparking the Ferguson uprising, which were days of protests and unrest in Ferguson, Missouri, that drew national attention to issues of police violence and racial injustice.

[11] Darren Wilson was the police officer who fatally shot 18-year-old Michael Brown on August 9, 2014 in Ferguson, Missouri.

[12] #SayHerName is a campaign Kimberlé Crenshaw and the African American Policy Forum launched in 2014 to bring attention to Black women and girls affected by police violence, working to counter their exclusion from wider conversations about racial justice.

[13] Daniel Holtzclaw, a former Oklahoma City police officer, was convicted in 2015 of eighteen sex-crime counts involving eight Black women and sentenced to 263 years in prison. Holtzclaw abused his position as an officer by running background checks to find information that could be used to coerce his victims into sex.

[14] “Against Innocence: Race, Gender, and the Politics of Safety,” by Jackie Wang, originally in LIES: A Journal of Materialist Feminism. https://theanarchistlibrary.org/library/jackie-wang-against-innocence-race-gender-and-the-politics-of-safety

[15] Trayvon Martin was a 17-year-old from Miami Gardens, Florida, who was fatally shot by 28-year-old George Zimmerman in Sanford, Florida, on February 26, 2012. Zimmerman was acquitted. After the shooting, Zimmerman painted the Confederate flag, mockingly posting images of Trayvon Martin's body, and sold the gun he used to kill Martin for $250,000.

[16] Oscar Grant was a 22-year-old man from Hayward, California, who was shot and killed on January 1, 2009 at the Fruitvale BART Station in Oakland. The shooting was carried out by BART police officer Johannes Mehserle, and video of the incident helped spark widespread protests.

[17] Chelsea Manning is a transgender woman and former U.S. Army intelligence analyst and whistleblower who disclosed hundreds of thousands of military and diplomatic documents to WikiLeaks. Sentenced to 35 years in prison in 2013, she was released in 2017 after President Barack Obama commuted most of her sentence.

Oggi dalle piazze italiane è passato un messaggio chiaro: lo sciopero è del popolo. L’accordo “sindacati-imprese” sigilla un tradimento non nuovo di chi dovrebbe rappresentare gli interessi dei lavoratori e lavoratrici – perlomeno quelli che hanno un contratto, un salario, delle condizioni minimamente garantite – e invece tutela quelli del padrone. E oggi le piazze in Italia hanno sottolineato questa realtà delle cose con la serenità di chi sa che non ha più niente da perdere ma tutto da prendere. 




foto di Marioluca Barona 




L’inimicizia, per usare un eufemismo, nei confronti di un sindacato come la Cgil non ha però dissuaso dal fare sciopero, anzi. Ha fatto sì che il popolo scendesse in piazza, sfruttando l’ultima delle garanzie che sopravvivono a stento in questo Paese, ossia sottrarsi dall’espropriazione del proprio lavoro, per continuare a manifestare con forza la propria contrarietà al riarmo e, quindi, al carovita. Le piazze di oggi non sono state della Cgil, sono state del popolo che dice basta. 




Oltre la metà degli italiani è contrario, secondo un 

sondaggio

, all’invio di armi all’Ucraina e al sostegno della guerra. Questo è quanto emerge dai sondaggi ma ad avere occhi per guardare è ciò che viene di fatto richiesto dalle mobilitazioni di questi mesi. In fondo ciò che sta accadendo in Francia, in Italia, in Albania, in Serbia, è la riappropriazione dell’ultimo baluardo di ciò che ci rimane, ossia la possibilità di aggregarsi intorno a un’idea-forza quale il proprio territorio “nazionale” – e le bandiere italiane, la marsigliese cantata dagli studenti di periferia, la bandiera albanese ne sono il simbolo – come elemento di potere per difendere i propri interessi collettivi, di popolo. Un’identificazione che non è da leggersi nei termini “reazionari” del becero sovranismo che i Vannacci di casa nostra vorrebbero rappresentare pur facendosi finanziare dagli Stati Uniti, ma nei termini di una sorta di nuovo patriottismo, o meglio, di nuovo sentimento collettivo che respira aria internazionalista. Questo è possibile oggi grazie alla Palestina, come orizzonte dal quale apprendere il significato di emancipazione. Diventa quindi evidente, anche in queste piazze, ulteriore passaggio di mobilitazione che si iscrive in un ciclo mobilitazione diffusa, che l’unica via per difendere un interesse comune non passa dall’alimentare una guerra come quella Ucraina, tritacarne per giovani ucraini e russi, in funzione degli interessi degli Stati Uniti. Non c’è da difendersi dalla fantomatica guerra della Russia, ma c’è da difendersi da una cricca di mentecatti pronti a tutto solo per salvaguardare la poltrona. C’è da difendersi da una élite europea pronta a tutto pur di far mangiare le proprie lobby di armi e di speculazione e garantirsi il proprio pezzo della torta. Questi sono stati i messaggi di questa giornata di sciopero. 




Lo si vede a partire dal fatto che in tutte le città si sono sviluppati cortei che, o hanno preso le distanze dal principio dalla chiamata della Cgil, o hanno pensato di occupare quello spazio perché era naturale essere in piazza con i temi all’ordine del giorno per il Paese. Così è stato a Torino, dove lo spezzone sociale ha raccolto 20 mila persone che, dopo una prima parte di corteo, hanno deciso di deviare raggiungendo l’ingresso dell’autostrada per poi riconvocarsi la sera stessa per un corteo giovane e vivace che ha tentato di attraversare il centro a più riprese senza arrestarsi a fronte di cariche, lacrimogeni e idranti. Così a Roma, dove 50 mila persone sono scese in piazza e gli studenti universitari hanno sanzionato il Ministero dell’Istruzione e del Merito. Così a Modena, dove un determinato spezzone di giovani (ma non solo) è riuscito a deviare dal corteo sindacale e per poi prendere il palco della Cgil, arrivando prima della testa. Così a Cosenza, dove lo spezzone studentesco e sociale non ha concluso il corteo con la Cgil ma ha proseguito fino all’ufficio scolastico regionale. Così a Bologna, dove un corteo partecipato da decine di migliaia di persone ha raggiunto la sede di Confindustria, difesa dalla polizia che ha risposto al tentativo di avvicinarsi con cariche. Così a Padova, dove il corteo studentesco ha occupato la tangenziale, ma anche a Venezia, Trento e Vicenza dove migliaia di persone sono scese in piazza per contestare le scelte vigliacche del sindacato e contestare i responsabili del carovita. A Milano 50mila hanno sfilato per le vie della città per poi attuare una riappropriazione di uno spazio nel quadro di rispondere alle esigenze dei giovani che oggi si mobilitano. A Pisa tantissime hanno scioperato e, sulla scia delle riappropriazioni, la residenza Fascetti di proprietà del DSU è stata presa perché chiusa da anni lasciando senza posti studenti e studentesse che ne avrebbero bisogno. Cortei anche a Napoli, Pavia, Palermo, Lucca e in quasi tutte le città italiane, anche di provincia. 




Il governo si stringe sulle sue posizioni, firma una finanziaria che regala soldi alle industrie belliche, dà il via libera sui territori a progetti completamente dannosi per la salute che li svendono a big tech americane, fa pagare ai poveri il conto dei ricchi quando si tratta di energia, spesa, servizi essenziali, accesso alla sanità. Non ha alcun interesse a dare qualche briciola alla componente giovane di questo Paese di vecchi. Il punto non sono le dimissioni di Meloni, per quanto ambite dalle piazze di queste settimane, il punto è che chi non siede al governo oggi sa già che continuerà il lavoro domani, se verrà eletto. Dunque, la questione è semplice: non c’è governo che tenga a fronte di un profondo e necessario stravolgimento delle basi stesse dell’organizzazione di questa società, dei rapporti di produzione e di consumo e della riproduzione sociale. Il seme della possibilità del domani per una società che si fondi su altri principi viene gettato oggi, nel marciare insieme e nello scontro senza paura con la rappresentazione plastica degli interessi nemici del popolo. Il 12 dicembre sarà l’occasione di esprimere l’autonomia e la forza del movimento nato in questi mesi, con un grande corteo nazionale a Roma per assediare il governo e le sue politiche.

author: David Swanson
title: Muslims Are Not a Security Threat. Western Governments Are.
content:
By Zobidah Yousif Elamin and Joseph Essertier, 

Dissident Voice

, November 20, 2026




Sudan is a country where 

9 million people

 have been driven from their homes; 

34 million are in need of assistance

; 

19.5 million people

 do not have enough to eat; and drones killed more than 

300 civilians

 in three weeks in October alone, many of them in crowded markets.




The United Nations calls it the “

world’s largest humanitarian crisis

.” Yet if you asked your neighbors what is happening in Sudan, few could tell you anything. Here we explain in plain language what this war is about, why so few people have heard of it, and who is making money while Sudanese people die.




What is happening in Sudan?




Sudan is a large country in northeast Africa, on the Red Sea, with a population of about 50 million people. In 2019, after months of peaceful street protests, Sudanese people overthrew the dictator 

Omar al-Bashir

, who had ruled for 30 years. Subsequently, a transitional government was formed, in which the generals shared power with a small group of civilian leaders.




That government did not last. In October 2021, two generals seized power together in a coup d’état. One was 

Abdel Fattah al-Burhan

, the head of the “

Sudanese Armed Forces

” or “SAF.” The other was 

Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo

, whose 

nom de guerre

 is “Hemedti,” the head of a paramilitary force called the “

Rapid Support Forces

” (or “RSF”). The RSF grew out of the 

Janjaweed militias

 that committed mass atrocities in Darfur between 2003 and 2008.




The two generals fell out over the question of who would control the guns. On 15 April 2023, fighting broke out in the capital Khartoum and spread across the country—not a war between “Muslims” and non-Muslims, or a war of ideas, but a war between two armed groups fighting for power, land, and money, with civilians caught in the middle.




Today the country is split into two territories. The 

SAF holds Khartoum

, the north, and the east, including Port Sudan on the Red Sea. The RSF holds almost all of Darfur in the west and runs a rival government there. The heaviest fighting is now in Kordofan, near central Sudan, and in the 

state of Blue Nile

, in the southeast.




A meeting of mediators in Geneva ended on the 21st of October 

without a ceasefire

.




Why the 2019 transition failed




After al-Bashir’s fall, there was no democratic transition in any real sense. What happened instead was a political deal between the SAF and the RSF, the two forces actually in control on the ground, and a small group of leaders from revolutionary organizations, including the 

Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-Revolutionary Democratic Front

 (SPLM-RDF), whom the military accepted as representatives of the civilian side. In other words, this period cannot be called democratic. It was a power-sharing arrangement between the two sides.




The group that represented the civilian side, the 

Central Council of the Forces of Freedom and Change

 (CCFFC), kept political representation to itself. It extended the transitional period more than once. It never created the 

Transitional Legislative Council

 required by the transitional constitution, even though that Council was meant to give the revolutionaries a voice and keep the transition in check. Over time, disputes grew between those who had climbed into civilian power and the revolutionaries on the street, and also between the CCFFC and the prime minister 

Abdalla Hamdok

. In 2021, Hamdok’s government also stayed silent while 

protesters were attacked and killed

, most notably at the first anniversary of the sit-in, in front of the prime minister’s office. As a result, the government, and Hamdok himself, became cut off from the revolution happening on the street.




There was also an unspoken dispute between Hamdok and some CCFFC leaders over who had the power to appoint people to senior posts, which deepened the rift between them. While these divisions grew, the SAF and the RSF watched and waited, until the coup came. Some have said that there was an indirect understanding between Hamdok and the military because he believed the revolutionaries would support him once the CCFFC was pushed aside.




After the staged arrest and his return as the prime minister appointed by the military, the revolutionaries on the street did not stand with him. Protests continued, and dozens of revolutionaries were killed. He then resigned and left for the United Arab Emirates (UAE).




It is also worth noting that some military leaders have stated that certain members of the CCFFC who led the revolution asked the military to extend their partnership for 15 years without elections, on the grounds that this was needed to dismantle the old regime. This shows that calling these leaders democratic is inaccurate. What resulted from their rule was not a democratic system but a failed transition, undermined by both sides: the civilians who took the lead and the military who kept the real power.




The human cost




Nobody knows how many people have died. The conflict monitor ACLED (the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project) had recorded 

about 56,000

 deaths by June 2026

 and 

calls that number “conservative

.” Some estimates reach 

as high as 150,000

. The former U.S. envoy Tom Perriello has put the death toll 

above 400,000

. Since many hospitals are 

closed or destroyed

 many deaths are never counted.




What we do know is shocking. Besides the problems of displacement and hunger mentioned above, there are the health problems and the lack of aid. Around 

40 percent of health facilities

 are not functioning and 17 million people lack safe drinking water. 

Cholera and measles

 are spreading. By April 2026, only 20 percent of the 

UN’s aid plan

 for Sudan had been funded.




The worst single atrocity came in October 2025, when the RSF captured El Fasher, the last army-held city in Darfur, after an 18-month siege. The UN human rights office 

documented more than 6,000 killings in just three days

, and says the real number is much higher. In February 2026, UN investigators concluded that the RSF’s campaign against non-Arab peoples there, especially the 

Zaghawa and Fur

, 

bears the hallmarks of genocide

.




The SAF (i.e., “the army”) is not innocent either. Its air strikes and drones have hit markets and villages, and in 2025 the United States 

determined that it used chemical weapons

 

(chlorine)

 in 2024, although they deny using such weapons. UN investigators say both sides commit serious crimes against civilians. To stand with the Sudanese people means standing with civilians, not with either general.




Why is the world not watching?




Sudan is called a “

forgotten war

.” But it was not forgotten. It was ignored.




The numbers are clear. During one year, the 

New York Times

 

ran almost ten times as many articles about Gaza as about Sudan

, and more than thirteen times the number of articles about Ukraine. 

A recent university study of the Swedish press

 found that, in a month when all three wars were raging, Gaza and Ukraine filled 98 percent of the war coverage. Sudan appeared in just five articles, 1.5 percent.




Of course, Gaza and Ukraine deserve attention. The question is why Sudanese lives seem to count for so little. Part of the answer is racism. Western media too often treat suffering in Africa as normal, as “just another day in Africa.” One wonders how many Western journalists actually believe that Africans deserve to live in peace?




The other part of the answer is politics. Western newsrooms follow their governments. The war in Ukraine and the genocide in Gaza are situations in which Washington and Europe openly arm one side, so they are treated as “our” story. In Sudan, the main foreign backer of the RSF is the UAE, a close Western ally and a country that buys huge amounts of Western weapons. Looking closely at Sudan would mean asking uncomfortable questions about the West’s own friends. Silence is easier.




Silence also has a cost. Crises that get no coverage get no money and no political pressure. When the cameras are absent, the killers feel free to do whatever they want.




America’s role




The United States likes to present itself as a peacemaker in Sudan. Its record tells a different story.







Punishing ordinary people.

 From 1997 to 2017, Washington kept Sudan 

under sweeping economic sanctions

, and from 1993 to 2020 listed Sudan as a “state sponsor of terrorism.” These measures hurt hospitals, students and businesses far more than they hurt the dictator. Even after the 2019 revolution, the new civilian government had to pay U.S.$335 million in compensation and had to agree to normalize relations with Israel before Sudan was removed from the list. Many Sudanese saw this as blackmail, at the very moment when their democracy most needed help.




Bombing.

 In August 1998, U.S. cruise missiles destroyed the 

al-Shifa factory

 in Khartoum, claiming it made chemical weapons. It actually produced over half of Sudan’s pharmaceuticals. The U.S. has not apologized.




Shutting the door.

 Sudan was on President Trump’s 

travel ban list

 in 2017 and again 

in 2025

, closing America to people fleeing this war.




Arming the arms supplier.

 This is the most serious issue today. Members of the U.S. Congress from both parties 

say there is credible evidence that the UAE is arming the RSF

. Yet in May 2025 the Trump administration 

bypassed a congressional hold

 on arms sales and approved a U.S.$1.4 billion arms sale to the UAE, including helicopter and F-16 parts. In August 2026, senators again asked the Secretary of State to 

pause arms sales

 to the UAE. However, the sales continue.







To be fair, Washington has also taken some action to reduce the violence. In January 2025 it declared that the RSF had committed genocide and sanctioned both Hemedti and Burhan. But sanctions on two generals mean little when billions of dollars in weapons keep flowing to the RSF’s main foreign backer. The UAE even sits beside the United States in 

the “Quad” group

 (the U.S., Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Egypt) that is supposed to mediate peace.




Who gets rich from Sudan’s war?




Sudan is not a poor country. It is one of Africa’s biggest gold producers, has fertile farmland, and sits on one of the world’s most important shipping routes, the Red Sea. This war continues largely because people outside Sudan are profiting from it.







Gold traders in the UAE.

 The RSF controls most of Sudan’s gold mines, especially in Darfur. Much of that gold is flown to Dubai, enters the world market, and pays for more weapons, which are used to capture more mines. The UAE’s own trade ministry says it 

imported U.S.$1.97 billion

 of Sudanese gold in 2024. Hemedti’s family and associates 

run gold companies

, some registered in Dubai. The army 

also sells gold

 in order to fund its own violence.




Arms suppliers.

 In September 2026, 

a UN fact-finding mission found

 that a network of people and companies linked to the UAE, with routes through Chad, Libya and Somalia, supplied the RSF with weapons, drones and training. The UAE denies this. The same mission found that the SAF uses foreign-supplied drones, such as Turkish-made 

Bayraktar Akinci drones

, in strikes that harmed civilians.




Mercenaries.

 UN investigators documented up to 

2,000 former Colombian soldiers

, recruited through private firms, who operated drones and artillery for the RSF, including during the attack on El Fasher.




Western weapons manufacturers

.

 Every arms sale to a country that fuels this war is profit for the companies that make the weapons, and jobs and influence for the governments that approve the sales.







In short: Sudanese gold leaves the country, foreign weapons come in, and Sudanese civilians pay with their lives. As long as the war continues, military generals and their foreign partners will grow richer and richer.




What can ordinary people do?




Sudan’s war can feel far away and impossible to fix. But outside support for each side is exactly what keeps it going, and that means outside pressure can help end it.







Learn and share.

 Read Sudanese voices, such as 

Radio Dabanga

 and 

Sudan Tribune

, and talk about Sudan. Silence is what the profiteers want.




Press your government.

 Ask your representatives to stop arms sales to any country arming either side, and to support extending the 

UN arms embargo

 from Darfur to all of Sudan.




Ask questions about gold.

 Ask jewelers and companies where their gold comes from.




Give directly.

 Sudanese volunteer groups called 

Emergency Response Rooms

 run community kitchens and clinics, often reaching people that big agencies cannot. Donate directly to these organizations when you can.







The people of Sudan showed the world in 2019 that they could 

bring down a dictator peacefully

. They did not choose this war. Two generals and their foreign backers chose it for them. The least the rest of us can do is look, speak, and refuse to let our governments profit from their suffering.










The post 

Muslims Are Not a Security Threat. Western Governments Are.

 appeared first on 

World BEYOND War

.

title: OG FFM: Aufenthaltsverbote nach den GenZ-Protesten in Frankfurt am Main
content:
OG FFM: Aufenthaltsverbote nach den GenZ-Protesten in Frankfurt am Main




Das Resümee auf Seiten der Teilnehmer*innen an den Protesten gegen soziale Ungleichheit, steigende Lebenshaltungskosten, Kürzungen im Bildungsbereich und die Wehrpflicht ist erschütternd. Viele, gerade junge Menschen, erlebten während und nach der Demonstration brutale Polizeigewalt. 

„Im Nachgang der Demonstration meldeten sich viele Betroffene bei uns und anderen Organisationen und berichteten von Verletzungen, die durch den Polizeieinsatz entstanden sind. Neben zahlreichen Augenverletzungen durch den massiven Einsatz von Pfefferspray gab es auch schwere Gehirnerschütterungen, Rippenbrüche und Knochenbrüchen“, so Anna Kaiser von der Roten Hilfe Ortsgruppe Frankfurt. 

Auch in Sozialen Medien ist einerseits das rücksichtslose Vorgehen der Polizei gegen alle Teilnehmenden der Proteste dokumentiert. Andererseits zeugen Berichte von den unbeholfenen und widersprüchlichen Polizeitaktiken vor Ort. Teilnehmende, welche den Protestzug verlassen wollten, wurden von der Polizei teilweise gewaltsam daran verhindert und kollektiv in der Frankfurter Innenstadt eingekesselt.

Einige der Protestierende erhielten in den letzten Tagen Post durch das Polizeipräsidium Frankfurt, genauer die 

SOKO

 3110. Ihnen wurde ein Aufenthaltsverbot für die Frankfurter Innenstadt angedroht. 

„Nach wochenlanger medialer wie stadtpolitischer Hetze gegen die Proteste schien es Aufgabe der Polizei zu sein, Bilder der Eskalation mindestens hinzunehmen, oder sogar mit zu produzieren“, so Anna Kaiser. „Die nun folgenden Grundrechtseinschränkungen dienen dazu, die rassistische und autoritäre Hetze zu untermauern.“ Viele der Verbote sollen willkürlich bis Januar 2027 ausgesprochen werden.

Die Gewalt und die jetzigen Versuche, die geplanten Proteste gegen die Wehrpflicht am 20. November zu kriminalisieren, zeugen davon, dass die Polizei kein neutraler Akteur ist. Die Rote Hilfe empfiehlt, nicht mit der Polizei zu kooperieren, gegen Auflagen und Aufenthaltsverbote Widerspruch einzulegen und sich juristisch und politisch dagegen zu wehren.

Rote Hilfe – Ortsgruppe Frankfurt am Main




Ezra




21.11.2026 - 00:46







Pressemitteilung













Während der GenZ-Regelt-Proteste in Frankfurt am Main am 31.10.2026 erlitten dutzende, meist junge Menschen durch den brutalen Einsatz der Polizei schwere Verletzungen – vom Rippenbrüchen bis zur schweren Gehirnerschütterungen. Darüber hinaus erhielten einige Protestierende in den letzten Tagen eine schriftliche Androhung eines Aufenthaltsverbots für die Frankfurter Innenstadt. Teilweise bis Januar 2027. Die medialen Szenen, welche die Polizei mitzutragen hat, dienen nun für weitreichende repressive Grundrechtseinschränkungen.

author: Keelan Jacobs
title: ‘They don’t see us as humans’: Indigenous youth call for national day of action
content:
For Ramon Kataquapit of Attawapiskat First Nation, the experience inside a special House of Commons committee reviewing Bill C-39 was troubling.




As lawmakers debated the proposed 

Building Canada Strong Act

, Kataquapit said he watched Indigenous consultation become a subject of parliamentary discussion, while Indigenous voices were largely absent from the proceedings.




He said he and fellow youth leader Jeronimo Kataquapit were invited by Gazan to observe the committee’s clause-by-clause deliberations.




“I want to speak about our experience we had yesterday. We were invited in to the committee with Leah (NDP MP Leah Gazan) to watch Bill C-39 be debated clause by clause and within this debate they were talking about Indigenous consultation but yet they had Indigenous people sitting on the sidelines; meanwhile, our only Indigenous representation in that room Leah Gazan was constantly being interrupted,”  Ramon Kataquapit said. 




“When she was fighting for us in there, watching the smirks on the Liberals’ faces, it really dawned on me that they don’t see us as humans, especially when it comes to debating Bill C-39.” 




His account came Friday as First Nation youth leaders announced plans for a national day of action against the proposed legislation on Dec. 8, in Ottawa, coinciding with the Assembly of First Nations’ winter gathering. 




Ramon Kataquapit said the demonstration is intended to bring First Nations people together to challenge what he described as the federal government’s attempt to advance legislation affecting Indigenous rights without adequate consultation.




Ramon Kataquapit speaking during a press conference with MP Leah Gazan on Parliament Hill (November 20, 2026). Photo: Keelan Jacobs/APTN







“I want to continue to fully express our opposition to Bill C-39 and how it’s being pushed through, without due consultation with First Nations,” he said.




The proposed legislation, known as the Building Canada Strong Act, is a sweeping “omnibus” bill that would change how major infrastructure, energy and resource projects are assessed and approved.




Introduced in September 2026, Bill C-39 proposes amendments to several federal laws, including the environmental statutes including Impact Assessment Act, Fisheries Act, and the Species at Risk Act, and the Labour Act. 




Among its measures are provisions intended to accelerate federal project reviews, coordinate regulatory approvals and Indigenous consultations, and establish pathways for certain projects in designated regions of national interest.




Jeronimo Kataquapit echoed those concerns, describing the committee experience as deeply troubling and questioning the federal government’s commitment to reconciliation.




“I stand here today to not only reaffirm our opposition to Bill C-39 but to talk about what myself and Ramon witnessed in the clause-by-clause committee on Bill C-39. It’s so inhumane,” he said. “They’re trying their hardest and fastest to rush this through into law. As we were sitting there, as Ramon was saying, we never saw Indigenous people so objectified as we have seen in that room.”




He said the experience was especially difficult to reconcile with the federal government’s repeated commitments to reconciliation and economic reconciliation.




“It’s disappointing to see that from the federal government that always talks about reconciliation, in this case economic reconciliation.”




Gazan said the government is moving quickly to advance the legislation, despite growing opposition.




“As you know, this government is attempting to fast-track Bill C-39 in committee; we have been sitting long days, in fact, 15 hours a day. We know that there is a lot of pushback that is emerging rapidly from around the country,” she said.




The committee will also sit all day Saturday and Sunday. 




The government has framed the legislation as a way to improve regulatory efficiency, reduce duplication and accelerate projects considered important to Canada’s economic interests.




However, the legislation raises fundamental questions about the relationship between economic development, Indigenous jurisdiction and the Crown’s constitutional obligations to First Nations.




The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, passed in 2021, further commits the federal government to aligning Canadian laws with the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.




For First Nations, the central concern is not necessarily whether major economic development should proceed, but who has the authority to make decisions about their territories, what meaningful participation looks like, and whether Indigenous rights will be respected when economic priorities are established.




Critics of Bill C-39 argue that accelerated approval timelines risk placing commercial and political priorities ahead of meaningful consultation, particularly when First Nations require time and resources to assess the potential impacts of projects on their lands, waters and communities.




For Ramon Kataquapit, those concerns extend beyond the legislative language itself.




He said the Dec. 8 demonstration is hoping to build a sustained presence on Parliament Hill.




“I also want to mention the support we have from Idle No More and Onion Lake First Nation. As we gather together here on Dec. 8, we will continue to show that presence to those that are passing and ramming through this legislation in this building, that we won’t be easily put aside and that you will continue to see our sustained presence in these rooms.”







Read More:




AFN warns Ottawa not to rush Bill C-39 or West Coast pipeline




Climate advocates say Bill C-39 is a new version of an old issue







He said the movement is about ensuring Indigenous people are not reduced to political talking points or treated as obstacles to economic development.




“We won’t be legislated away, we’re more than just words on a piece of paper, we’re more than just a debate, we’re more than just a political issue or red tape, we’re are people.”

‘They don’t see us as humans’: Indigenous youth call for national day of action

APTN News

author: Kodao Productions
title: Our undeniable victories and Marcos Jr.’s perpetual shame
content:
By 

Renato Reyes Jr.

 / President, Bagong Alyansang Makabayan







The Marcos Jr. regime is a certified US-puppet regime that will break laws, suppress the people, and sell out the Philippines to imperialist interests. Marcos Jr. “can’t keep the US president waiting” even if Trump made everyone wait because of his lateness to the ASEAN events. Yet for all his pining for his US master, Marcos Jr. failed to get the Pax Silica framework pact signed.




Pax Silica has generated broad resistance from the Filipino people in just seven months since the Philippine signing of the declaration. Our biggest victory is the high public awareness, the nationwide and international mass mobilizations, and the organizing work around the issues of imperialism, environment, indigenous rights, and genuine development.




The PNP and DILG are ignorant or simply do not care about laws and human rights and have demonstrated utter contempt for the people’s right to protest. The people, however, will not be denied, and no terror tactics can suppress an awakened people. The people will always find a way to make their voices heard. The nationwide protests amid police brutality affirm this.




The Marcos Jr. regime underestimated the public pushback on the Imeldific beautification of Metro Manila and the massive public spending on the preparations while poverty remains unresolved. The people saw no real benefits to Marcos Jr.’s vanity project, while Malacañang took pains to explain why spending P22 billion for the hosting is good for the people.




Marcos Jr., with his fascism and puppetry, has opened the eyes of a new generation of Filipinos in the same way that corruption and bureaucrat capitalism did last year at the height of the anti-corruption protests. There are moments when years become months and months become days, as a wave of protests spreads throughout the country. The days of disquiet of November taught the youth what kind of society they stand to inherit and why they should fight to change it.




Thus the challenge remains: we need to wage collective struggle to change the system dominated by imperialism, feudalism, and bureaucrat capitalism. We cannot expect real change from a puppet regime, from corrupt political dynasties, fascist police and military, and the big compradors and landlords. Our hope lies in the people—in the workers, farmers, indigenous peoples, youth and students, and all oppressed sectors fighting for national democracy. #

Our undeniable victories and Marcos Jr.’s perpetual shame

Kodao Productions
