author: Marianne Dhenin
title: Authors Sue LA Library Over Anti-Palestinian Discrimination After Talk Cancelled
content:
Even institutions meant to be dedicated to free speech and inclusion are censoring Palestinian writers.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Two authors have filed a lawsuit against the City of Los Angeles, alleging that the Los Angeles Public Library engaged in anti-Palestinian discrimination and violated their free speech rights after the library’s leadership canceled an online event last December where the two were slated to speak to teens about their books, which feature Palestinian characters. This lawsuit against one of the largest public library systems in the nation comes at a time when anti-Palestinian racism and censorship are growing more entrenched across the country, now more than three years into the U.S.-backed genocide in Gaza.

“The stakes are really high, and it’s about so much more than the rights of the authors or even the rights of the readers,” Nora Lester Murad, one of the authors and plaintiffs in the case, told Truthout. “If kids and adults can’t be exposed to representation of Palestinians that’s diverse and nuanced and human and complex and multifaceted, [that erasure] converges with the anti-Palestinian and anti-Muslim narratives that are being used to justify genocide.”

Murad and Palestinian American author Jenan Matari filed the lawsuit in the Superior Court of Los Angeles in late September to demand accountability for the Los Angeles Public Library’s cancellation of their event and to draw attention to anti-Palestinian censorship in the arts.

Matari is the author of the picture book Everything Grows in Jiddo’s Garden, about a young Palestinian girl and her grandfather. Murad was slated to discuss Ida in the Middle, her young adult novel about a 13-year-old Palestinian American girl. The two were scheduled to speak at an online event on December 6, 2025, as part of Read Palestine Week, a global weeklong program highlighting Palestinian authors and stories celebrated in late November and early December each year.

The Los Angeles Public Library’s teen council, a youth volunteer group, voted to host a Read Palestine Week event, and the library’s Middle Eastern North African Affinity Group invited Murad and Matari and acted as liaisons between the authors and library administration in the lead-up to the scheduled event, according to the legal complaint.

But just three days before the event was scheduled to take place, the group notified Murad and Matari that the library administration had canceled it. The notice provided no further explanation for the cancellation, according to the legal complaint.

Records obtained by Los Angeles Public Press in a public records request and cited in the legal complaint later revealed that a staff librarian had emailed library leadership in mid-November 2025, accusing Murad and Matari of having “strong terrorist ties and virulently antisemitic views.” The email said it was sent on behalf of a group of Jewish library staffers and referenced an article from the right-wing Washington Free Beacon and profiles of the authors on Canary Mission, a pro-Israel doxxing platform. It also accused the Middle Eastern North African Affinity Group of having “deeply antisemitic views” and showing “racist behavior to me and others in our Heritage group.”

“This attack was not from outside but from inside the library.”

Later in December 2025, City Librarian John Szabo sent an internal email to staff claiming Murad and Matari’s event had been canceled because the library “has a responsibility to remain nonpartisan and apolitical” and that doing so was “necessary to uphold the Library’s commitment to an inclusive environment free of hate, discrimination, and harassment,” according to a copy of that email obtained by The LA Reporter in a public records request.

Szabo did not respond to Truthout’s request for comment before deadline. A member of the library’s public relations team told Truthout that the library cannot comment on pending litigation.

Murad told Truthout the accusations and cancellation follow a familiar pattern in which criticism of Israel is conflated with antisemitism in order to silence Palestinian speakers like Matari, anti-Zionist Jewish speakers like Murad, or others who speak out to criticize Israel or in support of Palestinian liberation. But, she added, the Los Angeles Public Library case is also unique because the pressure to censor Palestine-related speech came not from outside pro-Israel pressure groups but from inside an institution mandated to oppose censorship.

“People assume that when an institution like a library caves into anti-Palestinian racism that the attack was from outside, and this attack was not from outside but from inside the library,” Murad told Truthout. “You have to address those things differently. One is you’re telling the library, ‘Please don’t cave into external pressure,’ and the other one is ‘Hey, Library, you are the censor.’”

Neither Murad nor Matari is unfamiliar with anti-Palestinian censorship. Murad has published about the silencing of Palestinian narratives in libraries and children’s books. Matari has had events canceled before: Two private bookshops had already canceled planned readings with her before the Los Angeles Public Library event, and she told The Guardianthat a New York library canceled a scheduled event with her after the Los Angeles news broke last year.

After the cancellation of Murad and Matari’s scheduled talk last December, more than 100 Los Angeles Public Library workers signed a letter condemning the move and emphasizing the library’s mission to oppose censorship. “Restrictions placed upon Palestinian voices are in direct opposition to the mission of the library,” the letter read. “It is the mission and the mandate of the Library to collect stories and protect them from censorship.”

The American Civil Liberties Union of Southern California and the National Coalition Against Censorship also called on the library to reschedule Murad and Matari’s talk in a joint letter in February 2026. That letter argued that the library “likely violated the First Amendment” when it canceled the event. It also criticized Szabo’s assertion that the library should remain “nonpartisan and apolitical,” calling it “absurd.” “If the library were to interpret its mission … to require it not to invite any author who has expressed strong political opinions, it would be hard pressed to find a single author to participate in its programming,” it read.

An Action Network campaign has since also resulted in more than 7,300 protest letters being sent to the Los Angeles Public Library from concerned patrons and community members. “The cancellation of an event that the youth of Los Angeles put the time and effort into putting on feels particularly antithetical to the mission of their library, both in their stated mission as well as the social function of the library as a space that fosters learning and exploring for youth,” Summer, a Los Angeles–based Palestinian artist and library patron who joined that campaign, told Truthout. “The library must be accountable to both the artists that they invited as well as the patrons who do not agree with that cancellation.”

“I don’t want to see any more authors experience the racism and discrimination I have faced at the LA Public Library, simply because I’m Palestinian and have continued to speak out against an ongoing genocide.”

Murad told Truthout that after such an outpouring of support failed to move library administrators, and after several unsuccessful attempts to engage them in conflict resolution talks, she and Matari felt they had little choice but to file a lawsuit. Their case alleges free speech violations, discrimination, and breach of contract, and seeks compensatory damages and an injunction that would require the library to reschedule the canceled event.

“When a library communicates through their actions that certain books and people are dangerous, so dangerous we can’t even let them come to the library and talk to us, it puts the weight of a public institution, so the government, behind a dangerous and racist message — it’s not just that our rights are being violated,” Murad told Truthout. “For Palestinians and for everyone’s right to learn from Palestinians and learn about Palestinians, we felt that we were doing a lawsuit for more than just us.”

Matari, in a press release announcing the lawsuit, said: “We need to hold public institutions accountable in order to protect free speech for all people, including the right to speak out for Palestinian freedom … I don’t want to see any more authors experience the racism and discrimination I have faced at the LA Public Library, simply because I’m Palestinian and have continued to speak out against an ongoing genocide.”

The city attorney’s office told Truthout it could not comment on pending litigation.

While it will take time before a resolution is reached in Murad and Matari’s case against the City of Los Angeles, Murad said she hopes the filing will send a message to other institutions that discrimination and silencing of Palestinian and other marginalized authors and narratives have consequences. “This isn’t just happening to us; Palestinians are being targeted by anti-Palestinian racism, and it’s affecting readers, and institutions have to be held accountable,” she said.

As Read Palestine Week approaches again, beginning November 29 this year, Summer told Truthout she hopes other arts institutions will reject the example set by the Los Angeles Public Library and that community members will advocate for those institutions to uplift Palestinian voices. “One of the ways people can support the blossoming of Palestinian art within public libraries is by requesting books and events by Palestinians,” she said. “All it takes is letting your desire to learn from them and read with them be known to your library branch.”

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

Our fundraiser ended last night, but there’s still time for us to meet those basic operating expenses — we need only $10,000. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

author: Amy Goodman
title: COP31 Declared a Failure as Declaration Text Excludes Mention of Fossil Fuels
content:
“I do not bear good news,” Panama’s environment minister said. “We are being held hostage by the petroleum mafia.”

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

In our closing broadcast from Antalya, Turkey, the site of the 31st annual U.N. climate change summit, we take a look at what has — and hasn’t — been accomplished at this latest attempt to reach an international framework to stem the impacts of climate change.

“This COP was being touted as a COP of implementation, but what it has become is a COP of betrayal and a COP of distraction,” laments environmental justice advocate Harjeet Singh, the founding director of India’s Satat Sampada Climate Foundation. He’s joined on Democracy Now! by Meena Raman of Friends of the Earth Malaysia and Nafkote Dabi of Oxfam International as a number of NGOs announce their rejection of the conference’s final declaration text, which contains no mentions of fossil fuels or clear financial commitments from polluter countries.

“At the heart of the negotiations right now lies money,” says Dabi. “What rich countries, especially the EU, [are] saying is, ‘There is no money at home.’ But we know there’s money. They can tax the richest. They can tax the excess profit of fossil fuel companies. They can tax private jets. They can tax extreme wealth and raise the funds that’s needed to support communities.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman. We’re broadcasting from Turkey on the final scheduled day of the global U.N. climate summit, known as COP31.

Climate advocacy groups and Indigenous organizations from across the world have slammed this gathering as the “worst COP ever” and rejected the latest draft text as a “disaster,” urging developing countries to reject the latest draft text.

Meanwhile, at a news conference just before our broadcast, Panama’s Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro has threatened to block any final agreement if it doesn’t include a cap on oil production. Earlier this week, he spoke out forcefully against the role of what he described as the “petroleum mafia.”

JUAN CARLOS NAVARRO: I do not bear good news. We are being held hostage by the petroleum mafia.

AMY GOODMAN: And this is Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama’s environment minister, speaking just before we went to air, flanked by representatives from Finland and Vanuatu, Belgium, Ivory Coast, France, Guatemala and other countries.

JUAN CARLOS NAVARRO: We have come together because we feel that the COP can still be saved if we focus on six key issues for our final declaration that clarifies for the world where we must go.

The first is that science must be the foundation. Everything we do must be based on science.

Second, we need a clear transition away from fossil fuels. It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover document that does not even mention fossil fuels, and we simply will not put up with it. We need to tell the truth and to speak clearly. We must transition away from fossil fuels in an orderly manner, if we are to confront climate change.

The third point for us, which is very important, is that fair contributions to climate finance must come from those with greatest responsibility. You pollute, you pay. It’s actually rather simple. You cause the problem, you must help to fix it. If you are the biggest emitter of CO2, if you are the biggest producers or consumers of petroleum, then you must contribute to solve this problem and these issues.

AMY GOODMAN: Earlier today, in a packed room for the press, the Climate Action Network, which encompasses over 2,500 civil society groups worldwide, as speakers detailed the failures of the COP, there were activists in the room, journalists and many others representing this COP31. The activists on the stage called out the European Union and other developed nations for their obstruction. The room repeatedly broke out into chants of “shame.” The moderator of CAN called the draft text a “disgrace” and introduced speakers.

DANNI TAAFFE: Tasneem Essop, executive director of Climate Action Network International.

TASNEEM ESSOP: There is nothing on the table that protects people or addresses the priorities of the Global South. In fact, the opposite is true. … This COP has had the highest number of lobbyists — fossil fuel lobbyists, AI lobbyists, CCUS lobbyists, CDR lobbyists. So, what we’re leaving this COP with is decisions made to actually promote the interests of those culprits.

DANNI TAAFFE: Avantika Goswami from CSE India.

AVANTIKA GOSWAMI: The European Union have, in a way, taken on the mantle that the U.S. has left the vacuum of, the blocker that the U.S. was. Unfortunately, we expected them to be leaders, but they have disappointed us. … And these are the parties that posture the most in the media. They say they are committed to climate multilateralism, and they are concerned about 1.5°C and the breach of the Paris Agreement goals. … So, we want to let them know that we see them and the games they’ve played, and we will not stand for it.

DANNI TAAFFE: Anabella Rosemberg from CAN International.

ANABELLA ROSEMBERG: The COP is not dying. The COP is being killed, not because it’s bloated, not because it’s inefficient or useless. It’s being killed because it’s the last space where civil society, where developing countries can hold developed countries accountable. … We are now asked to accept more empty words. We say no. We will fight back. And we say thank you for nothing. … So, this is also an appeal for all of us, for all the movements, to keep working together and change the faces of who’s representing developed countries in this place.

DANNI TAAFFE: And Mohamed Adow from Power Shift Africa.

MOHAMED ADOW: I can tell you, without any doubt, that this has been the worst COP ever.

MOHAMED ADOW: Communities living in drought, floods and failed harvest were promised action. They cannot survive on an annual renewal of promises. We’re effectively pushing poor, vulnerable countries into further debt to protect themselves from a crisis they did little to cause.

TASNEEM ESSOP: I want to just say two things. One, when you come into a COP and a commissioner of a very important regional bloc says, “We’re not coming with any finance. Finance is dead in the water,” think about that, “dead in the water.” For us in the Global South, dead in the water is very literal. So it’s a shameful way to come to a COP where we are going to be fighting for adaptation finance to protect people from being dead in the water.

Secondly, the pledges that they brought to this COP for adaptation finance, you would have seen totaled around $50 million, which we said in our ECO is half the cost of an F-35 Lightning fighter jet.

TASNEEM ESSOP: And we’re not even going to measure that $50 million in relation to the $3 trillion that rich nations are spending on wars, a genocide and conflicts across the world. Put that into perspective.

AMY GOODMAN: That was Tasneem Essop, the executive director of CAN, Climate Action Network International, and others speaking at a news conference earlier today. She is from South Africa.

For more, we’re joined by several leading environmental justice advocates.

Harjeet Singh is strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative and founding director of the Satat Sampada Climate Foundation, a social justice organization, also global convener of the Fill the Fund campaign.

Nafkote Dabi is the change policy lead for Oxfam International, where she works at the intersection of climate and inequality. She’s from Ethiopia, where the next COP, COP32, will be held, in Addis.

And Meena Raman is with us, head of programs at Third World Network and president of Friends of the Earth Malaysia.

We thank you all for being with us. We’re going to start with Harjeet. You, as well as Nafkote, were holding up a sign behind the speakers that said, ”ECO. End the Genocide,” with big letters, ”SHAME!” There was rage in this room. It was the most packed news conference I had seen, packed with activists. Talk about where we are at on this last scheduled day, though it’s clear it’s going to go further.

HARJEET SINGH: Well, it is a matter of shame, Amy. This COP was being touted as a COP of implementation, but what it has become is a COP of betrayal and a COP of distraction. We have spent more time on talking about electrification, without any details whether it’s going to be green or is going to be accessible to people. We have removed the reference to —

AMY GOODMAN: Wait. Just to explain that, “electrification” is sort of the watchword here.

AMY GOODMAN: And the idea was renewable electrification.

AMY GOODMAN: But that seems to be — “renewable” — being dropped.

HARJEET SINGH: Absolutely. And otherwise, why are we talking about electrification in this space, if it is not green? That’s the question we should be asking. We do not see any reference to fossil fuel phaseout. Now, only the words are not enough, and I can explain that later, but that being dropped from the previous draft is just not acceptable. Adaptation finance, there was a clear agreement to scale it to $120 billion annually for developing countries.

AMY GOODMAN: No one knows what “adaptation finance” means.

HARJEET SINGH: OK. So, adaptation means helping communities prepare to deal with climate impacts. It’s about retrofitting their homes. It’s about building dikes. It’s about making sure that their agriculture is resilient and we are food-secure. And if you do not provide money — let’s take the example of Nepal. The reason they faced such a catastrophic disaster, because they were not prepared. When we see people in Ethiopia —

AMY GOODMAN: More than seven — what? About 7,000 people dead or missing?

HARJEET SINGH: Exactly. That’s the number.

AMY GOODMAN: Because of a glacier that melted?

HARJEET SINGH: Absolutely. So, it was a glacial lake outburst floods. And the numbers are important. They lost — the destruction was to the tune of $2.6 billion, and they will need now $5 billion for recovery and rehabilitation, which is 10% of their GDP. Imagine.

AMY GOODMAN: Why should the wealthy countries give it to them?

HARJEET SINGH: Because glaciers melted because of the burning of fossil fuels, and they did not provide money to Nepal for adaptation, and they are facing now loss and damage. So, Nepal, we should see it as a report card of the climate inaction that we have seen over the last 30 years. We did not phase out fossil fuels in time. That resulted in melting of glaciers. And we did not even have a plan or support to Nepal to deal with these climate impacts. And it shows that how we are failing to deal with climate impacts. And that’s why we say “shame.”

AMY GOODMAN: Meena Raman, you are head of programs at Third World Network, head of Friends of the Earth Malaysia. You have been to so many of these conferences. You, too, have expressed rage on each panel you are at. What do you want to see happen here?

MEENA RAMAN: Well, at this particular point in time, it’s relatively empty. The most important aspect of the COP is money, whether it’s for emission reductions, whether it’s for adaptation, whether it’s for loss and damage. The developing world came together, and they said, “We need money on the table of provision of finance.” What the developing countries demanded was actually to ensure that we talk about this. It was about talking about how the developed world is going to do that.

But all we came here as, you know, the EU commissioner was saying anything about finance is dead in the water. Now, that is horror, because we just came out of Nepal, as we know, and you say, “dead in the water.” People are literally dying due to the historical —

MEENA RAMAN: “Dead in the water.” That’s what Hoekstra said. It was — it was for us —

AMY GOODMAN: The EU negotiator.

MEENA RAMAN: The EU commissioner. The EU commissioner. So, even before this COP, he said it. So, when you go to the negotiating halls, what you saw was finance was dead in the water, nothing on finance. So there’s no point talking about having higher ambition in terms of emission reductions or developing countries having to do fossil fuel phaseout or having more targets on electrification. They’re not going to be able to do this, if what they say is the means to implement that is not available. So, this is where this COP always becomes a problem.

AMY GOODMAN: You are wearing a sign — you are wearing a sticker, Nafkote Dabi, on the back of your ID here that says “Make rich polluters pay.” You have said — you’ve talked about inequality. Oxfam International is known for their report, “Disaster Divide.” The richest 0.1%, or 8 million people, have more emissions than the bottom 3.5 billion people, and that their carbon emissions contribute to the increase of climate disasters such as floods, fires, droughts and food crises. Can you explain how you feel this can be remedied? And how close to a tipping point are we?

NAFKOTE DABI: So, at the heart of the negotiations right now lies money, because, ultimately, you know, to support communities to adapt to the climate crisis, they need finance. And what rich countries, especially the EU, is saying is, ‘There is no money at home.’ But we know there’s money. They can tax the richest. They can tax the excess profit of fossil fuel companies. They can tax private jets. They can tax extreme wealth and raise the funds that’s needed to support communities. You know, just private jets alone, you can raise $45 billion a year. From the excess of profit of fossil fuel companies, you can raise $400 billion. So, this money is available, and you can support communities at home, whether in Europe or the U.S. And then you can commit to your international climate finance obligation and support communities in the Global South, especially, you know, in Africa, that are faced with droughts, floods, displacement and death.

AMY GOODMAN: You know, we just had a headline on a vote on war in the U.S. Senate, and the amount — the billions of dollars that are being spent on the war in Iran, which has also led the entire world to understand how dependent we are on fossil fuels.

NAFKOTE DABI: Exactly. You know, emissions from military is about 5%. This is something that we’re not talking about. There’s huge money, as you said, Amy, going towards militarization, when communities around the world are actually literally dying from escalating extreme weather events. For the first time, by the way, Amy, I’m feeling really desperate, because we’re being told next year is going to be the hottest year on record. It’s going to go up to 1.7. Right now as we’re speaking, communities around the world are faced with the worst El Niño on record, and there is no support. These are communities that have done the least to cause the climate crisis, but they’re being left alone to deal with this situation. So, it’s a very shameful COP.

AMY GOODMAN: Now, what are the NGOs going to do? We just have two minutes before we end with an 8-year-old child who spoke out. A few years ago, it was Greta Thunberg, when she was 15 years old. Now we’re going to Little Miss Environment Kenya, who is 8, who has something to teach her elders. But one last statement. Harjeet, where we go from here? Are the NGOs going to reject the text? And what does it matter? What role do you play?

HARJEET SINGH: So, we have already rejected the current text. And what we would like to see: the developing countries really standing up and reject this text. And we keep saying developing countries are here to represent their own citizens. They can’t accept a text which will not enable them to implement climate action back home because there is no money on the table. And that’s exactly the reason developing countries have now — need to be very loud and clear in saying this COP outcome is not going to help us, unless developed countries open their pockets. It’s all about money.

AMY GOODMAN: Meena, how can it be this is the largest COP, and you’re talking about it being the greatest failure? Pick up that mic.

MEENA RAMAN: Yeah. The problem is that when you have the developed world come here and say that they don’t have national budgets to put on the table, and they talk about leadership, I think it is really imperative that we work with our Global North to actually put the pressure on the developed countries. We can’t have COP after COP backsliding. We let alone scaling up our resources. The U.K. has cut its pledge to the Green Climate Fund. The Global Environment Facility, the worst replenishment ever. So, when they are backsliding, here we are asking for more top up.

AMY GOODMAN: And finally, Nafkote, if you can talk about next year? We’re going to Ethiopia for COP32. What is the point of these COPs?

NAFKOTE DABI: You know, Ethiopia is faced — is at the frontline of the climate crisis. Ethiopians know what it means to face drought. Ethiopians are the most resilient people. They have been through many droughts, droughts after droughts. Right now, as I said, we’re faced with El Niño. Next year, the Ethiopian COP presidency needs to deliver justice for communities at the frontline of the climate crisis.

AMY GOODMAN: We have to leave it there, Nafkote Dabi of Oxfam International, Harjeet Singh of Fossil Food Treaty Initiative, Meena Raman of Third World Network.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

Our fundraiser ended last night, but there’s still time for us to meet those basic operating expenses — we need only $10,000. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

author: Jaharra Anglin Stubbs
title: Family Caregivers Month: The Economic Burden of Unpaid Care
content:
Every November, National Family Caregivers Month recognizes the millions of Americans who provide care to their loved ones. Caregivers are adult children, spouses, partners, and other loved ones who complete daily tasks and maintain their quality of life. While caregiving is often an expression of love and family responsibility, it also comes with high financial, physical, and emotional costs that frequently go unrecognized.

More than 63 million Americans provide ongoing care for adults or children with complex medical conditions or disabilities. Of these, 59 million care for adults. Around 10% of U.S. adults are caregivers for parents aged 65 or older, while another 3% care for an aging spouse or partner.

The financial burden is particularly pronounced among lower-income households. Among adults with an aging parent, spouse, or partner, 39% of those with lower incomes identify as caregivers, compared with 23% of middle-income adults and 16% of upper-income adults. For caregivers whose household income is less than $40,000, nearly one-third of their income goes toward out-of-pocket expenses related to their loved ones’ needs.

The financial demands of caregiving can be substantial. Every year, $1 trillion in family caregiving services goes unpaid. Housing and household needs account for the largest share of expenses, at 42%, with home modifications for safety making up 29%, and 37% going to insurance premiums, co-pays, and other medical expenses not covered by insurance.

Yet 65% of working caregivers experience work-related disruptions. These can include needing time off and finding extra work to cover these expenses. These disparities also vary dramatically across racial and ethnic minority groups and by region.

These financial burdens are not distributed equally across racial and ethnic groups. AAPI caregivers report an average cost of $16,716. Black caregivers spend a high share of their household income, averaging 52%, while Hispanic and Latinx communities report the greatest financial strain among the racial and ethnic groups surveyed by AARP. By comparison, White caregivers spend about 24% of their household income on caregiving.

Regionally, caregivers in the Mid-Atlantic spend twice as much on average as caregivers in the West North Central region, reflecting the cost-of-living crisis. However, costs are not the only issue to consider as we reflect on the holistic effort of caregiving.

Beyond these financial costs, caregiving remains a deeply gendered responsibility. Women are more likely than men to identify as caregivers. In the U.S., 28% of women with aging parents or spouses or partners consider themselves caregivers, compared with only 23% of men. Forty-seven percent of women, versus 30% of men, experience a negative impact on their emotional well-being, and 38% of women experience negative impacts on their health while serving as caregivers for their loved ones. Outside formal caregiving, women provide most informal caregiving, often becoming hands-on health providers, care managers, care advocates, companions, and decision-makers.

As we recognize National Family Caregivers Month, it is important to acknowledge not only the dedication of caregivers but also the financial sacrifices and inequalities they face. Caregiving is rooted in love, but it is also sacrificial. If you or anyone you know is serving as a caregiver, show them a little more love this month so they know they are cared for.

author: Bianca Blell
title: Trump Administration Proposes Cuts to Pregnancy-Related Work Protections
content:
The Trump administration is preparing to narrow federal workplace protections for pregnant workers, potentially limiting access to accommodations for a range of reproductive health conditions.

On November 2nd , the New York Times reported that the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) is considering revisions to regulations implementing the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA), spearheaded by President Donald Trump. The PWFA was passed by Congress in 2022, initially implemented during the Biden administration.

The original law was meant to fill a gap in disability and discrimination protections that employees are guaranteed in the workplace. Under current regulations, employees are generally required to make reasonable adjustments for qualified employees experiencing pregnancy-related limitations. Examples of such accommodations include additional bathroom breaks, schedule changes, lighter duties, temporary reassignment, and time off for prenatal appointments, including more.

The proposed revisions aim to narrow workplace protections under the PWFA, potentially shrinking the types of accommodations employers are required to provide. One of the changes being considered is a modification to how the EEOC interprets the phrase “pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions.” This agency, under the President’s advisory, could present reversals that affect accommodations related to abortion and fertility treatments.

The potential rollback extends beyond abortion access. Under the current regulations, employers may be required to provide accommodations for employees seeking abortion, including time off for the procedure and related travel. While voluntary abortions have already been removed from this scope by a 2025 federal court ruling, medically necessary procedures currently remain covered.

The potential rollback extends beyond abortion access. Employees undergoing fertility treatments may need time off for medical appointments, medication schedules, or procedures. Workers experiencing miscarriages or postpartum depression may also require temporary adjustments to their schedules or responsibilities. Without clear federal protections, employees could face greater difficulty securing accommodations for these conditions, particularly in workplaces where employers are unwilling to provide flexibility.

Research also demonstrates the importance of workplace accommodations for maternal health. A 2025 study found that the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act was associated with a 3.2% increase in births in states newly covered by the law. The original 2022 law has contributed to a nearly 10% decrease in miscarriages.

The current administration strives for a pro-natalist agenda, encouraging American women to marry and increase births per family. In May 2026, the White House announced new initiatives aimed at expanding fertility benefits and supporting mothers. Yet the administration’s consideration of narrower workplace protections could make it more difficult for workers to access the reproductive health care and employment accommodations that help them build and support families.

The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act was an important bipartisan achievement that recognized workers should not have to choose between maintaining their employment and protecting their health. Although the law itself remains in effect, weakening its implementing regulations could leave workers with fewer protections during some of the most vulnerable periods of their lives. The federal government should strengthen protections, not undermine the progress that workers and advocates fought to achieve.

author: Jaharra Anglin Stubbs
title: Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders Unionize After Years of Fighting for Fair Pay
content:
On October 23, 2026, the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders Association was formally and voluntarily recognized as the official collective bargaining representative for the team’s cheer squad. For the first time in the NFL since the Buffalo Jills, an NFL cheer squad successfully unionized, highlighting the need for better protections for cheer team members.

For decades, the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders have been among the most recognizable cheerleading squads in professional sports. Despite their prominence and contributions to the team’s brand, members have historically received low wages for demanding work. Before a 400% pay increase for the 2025 season, some veteran cheerleaders reported earning just $15 per hour, in addition to flat fees for games and appearances. Even after the raise, questions about benefits and workplace protections remain.

The pay disparity became particularly visible in 2018, in afederal fair-wage lawsuit filed by Erica Wilkins, a former cheerleader. Wilkins claimed she earned no more than $16,516 in any year of her employment, while the team’s male mascot, Rowdy, earned approximately $65,000 annually. She also alleged that cheerleaders were not compensated for all hours worked, including rehearsals, training, and promotional activities. The lawsuit highlighted the significant pay disparities and lack of labor protections facing women in professional sports.

Although the Cowboys arevalued at $17B, making them the most valuable NFL brand, they were evidently more comfortable paying their male athletes fairly until recently. As Kelli Fingall, the cheer squad director, said, the raise to $75 was “60-plus years long overdue,” given the cheer team’s proven athleticism, ethics, and overall value to the brand and the NFL franchise, especially since it remains “one of the most talented dancers worldwide.”

Even though the Dallas Cowboys cheer team is a successful example of change, we must acknowledge that toxic, systemic gender inequity across the broader NFL cheer teams has long shaped cheerleading’s professional place in the NFL. In 1995, after the National Labor Relations Board ruled that the cheer team, the Buffalo Jills, could unionize, the squad was disbanded in 2014 due to severe wage violations, sexual misconduct, mistreatment, and other heinous violations.

Beyond the attempt to unionize, individual members across NFL cheer squads, such as Lacy Thibodeaux,sued their employers for violating numerous state labor and minimum wage laws. These instances of injustice show that cheerleading talent has been reduced to a casual skill rather than to dedicated competitive professional athleticism that deserves compensation.

Like all women, NFL cheerleaders deserve fair compensation for their work and should not be asked to work long hours without healthcare or enough to meet a standard of living. Although the Cowboys have acknowledged the cheer team’s unionization, the decision did not come from the goodness of their hearts; rather, it was a reaction to theNetflix documentary and the team’s threats to strike, which revealed injustices behind the curtain.

Union recognition is an important step toward that goal, but the NFL and its franchises must do more to ensure that fair treatment is standard across professional cheerleading.

author: Sofia Little
title: Protests Across the Pond: Gen-Z and the Fight for Affordability in Europe
content:
Across Europe, rising living costs, unaffordable housing, low wages and underfunded public services have fueled a growing wave of protests. Since mid-September, more than 1,700 cost-of-living demonstrations have taken place in 31 European countries. The protests have brought students, workers, and community members into the streets, with young people playing a visible role in organizing and demanding change.

In France, a country with a centuries-long history of protest, the demonstrations began with students demanding more resources for underfunded schools. Students raised concerns about overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages, and crumbling infrastructure. The demonstrations grew into a broader movement, drawing in labor unions and other activists who called out the rising cost of living and declining public services. On October 17th, an estimated 550,000 to 800,00 people protested nationwide.

Other countries began following suit. Since mid-September, demonstrations over high living costs, low wages, and lack of public services have broken out all across Europe. From Spain and Portugal to Germany and Albania, these protests have largely been led by Gen Z. In Spain and Portugal, protesters established encampments in public squares across major cities, demanding stronger laws to protect renters following the eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid.

In Italy, the “Italia in Piazza”, or Italy in the Streets movement, brought thousands of protesters to the streets. Demonstrators called for better employment, healthcare, education, access to housing, and better wages. Major demonstrations have also taken place in Albania, Belgium, the Czech Republic, Germany, and Serbia.

While the majority of demonstrations have been peaceful, some have escalated into riots involving looting, fires, and property destruction. Only 20% of the recorded events involved riots. However, the police response has been overwhelmingly severe, regardless of whether these protests have been peaceful or violent. French authorities have deployed military-style tactics to antagonize peaceful demonstrations, tactics that have long since drawn condemnation from international human rights monitors.

It is clear that all over the continent—all over the world— Gen Z is tired of waiting for promises to be delivered. They are demanding more than promises from political leaders. They want a future in which they can build secure lives. Young people are confronting economic and social challenges while remaining underrepresented in many of the institutions responsible for addressing them. Their participation in these movements shows that they are not willing to remain on the sidelines while decisions about their futures are made without them.

Across the world, communities are struggling to make rent, afford groceries, and childcare. We must demand more for ourselves, our communities and our future. And so, the fight for affordability continues.

author: Unknown
title: Илья Шакурский и «Цена свободы»
content:
«Цену свободы» фигурант пыточного «дела Сети» Илья Шакурский написал в сентябре 2025 года. Это текст о том, что на самом деле стоит за сухими строчками обвинения: пыльные обочины трасс, панк-гиги, споры о будущем, тишина зимнего леса и внутренняя свобода, которую невозможно запереть в бетонной клетушке.

Это место называется «следственные кабинеты». Я бываю здесь довольно часто.

Сижу в клетушке посередине комнаты, рисую что-нибудь на железном столике перед собой или просто смотрю в окно. Как правило, всегда в ожидании адвокатов, следователей, оперов или психологов. По большей части мне не нравится ходить сюда, особенно в кабинеты, находящиеся на левой стороне.

Окна здесь выходят не на волю, а на старый корпус СИЗО. Видны лишь арестанты в форточках, забирающие «дорогу» (верёвку с привязанным носком), мелькающие телевизоры в камерах и часть прогулочных двориков. Грустно… К тому же в кабинеты на левой стороне почти не пускают защитников. Здесь я могу встретить только местное начальство, приезжих оперов или казённые комиссии. Я никогда не знаю, кто сейчас войдёт в кабинет, но всегда испытываю волнение, так как ничего хорошего от моего присутствия на этой стороне следственных кабинетов не ожидаю.

В этот раз зашёл совершенно незнакомый мне человек. Рубашка, ветровка, брюки, аккуратная стрижка, красивые часы, чёрная кожаная папка. Всё ясно — следователь. Что ж, начинается игра. Он пришёл провести опрос по поводу моего заявления о применении ко мне пыток током. Его задача — минимизировать подробности, запугать опрашиваемого, скрыть факты за ненужными обстоятельствами, максимально постараться уличить заявителя во лжи. Моя — дополнять, исправлять, требовать записывать дословно и убирать то, чего я не говорил. Такое противостояние. Нюансы подобных встреч познаёшь лишь с опытом, но чаще всего такие юридические противоборства заканчиваются не в пользу опрашиваемого. В эти моменты особенно осознаёшь своё одиночество в борьбе с бетонной системой, которая нагло и лицемерно защищает себя от воздействия правды.

За всё время нашей встречи следователь, кажется, ни разу не посмотрел мне в глаза. Он уткнулся в заполняемый бланк и монотонно задавал вопросы, лишь нервно вздыхая при моих уточнениях и замечаниях. И только в самом конце встречи передо мной вдруг появился человек. Я увидел перед собой живое лицо, а не должностного робота. Я поймал на себе взгляд человека, способного видеть во мне живое существо, которое тоже может мыслить, чувствовать и говорить не только под запись. Меня ошарашил его вопрос:

Этого вопроса нет в перечне его документов — это личный интерес, вызванный его собственными мотивами.

Какими? Может, он просто хочет пополнить свою копилку историей с работы, чтобы за ужином было что рассказать жене на вопрос: «Дорогой, как дела на работе?» Или же он искренне пытался понять мой выбор — то, что движет мной и даёт смелости в подробностях рассказывать ему о чекистских методах пыток? Но от его вопроса веяло какой-то предсмертностью. Казалось, будто он уже знал, что я обречён, и перед моей участью решил узнать у меня о чём-то неофициальном, ценностно-философском. «Стоило ли оно того?» — вопрос, знаменующий некий финал, конец истории, где главному герою предстоит осознать ценность пройденного пути.

В кинематографе существует сюжетный приём, когда история начинается с финальной сцены. Итог известен, но что-то заставляет нас вернуться обратно, ибо только в развитии всей истории можно найти ответы.

«Стоило ли оно того?» — вопрос повисает в кабинетной тишине. Камера застывает крупным планом на лице главного героя, и из темноты погасшего экрана плавно всплывает основная часть истории, которая и привела его в это помещение.

«Когда одинокий рассвет нагло лезет в окно — не гони его…»

Интенсивный панк-рок играет в наушниках. Солнце на закате выплёскивает свои последние яркие лучи. Свет из щелей облаков обливает собой стены лесов. Впереди — неизвестность. Под ногами пыльный путь бесконечных обочин. Легковушки, фуры, «газели» и автобусы. Уроды сигналят и тычут в меня средний палец, выглядывая из-за руля. Девчонки улыбаются, но боятся остановиться. На примятой придорожной пылью траве валяются груды мусора.

Меняются цифры на электронных стендах с ценами на бензин у заправок. От маленьких кафе пахнет шашлыком и выпечкой. За спиной большой рюкзак. Музыка придаёт сил и бодрости. Большой палец поднят вверх. Пролетающие машины обдают ветерком. Я знаю, что скоро кто-то остановится. Так бывает всегда. Под Нижним Новгородом у старой кирпичной остановки прогуливается красивая молодая проститутка в вызывающих клетчатых колготках. Прохожу мимо. Мы встречаемся взглядами. Она подмигивает. Я смущённо улыбаюсь. Мне очень жалко её красоты. Отгоняю от себя мысли о её клиентах в подъезжающих фурах.

Ночь. За окошком пойманной попутки мелькают огни фонарей. За рулём — разговорчивый, добродушный пожилой армянин: — Илья-джан, сэйчас заедем в кафе. Там знакомая. У него лучший (характерный жест рукой со сжатыми пальцами для подчёркивания особой оценки) кофэ, что ты пробовал в жизни.

Уютные деревянные столики. Хохотушка и грубиянка в фартуке сама принимает заказы дальнобойщиков и ночных водил. Маленькая чашечка горького кофе торкает меня настолько сильно, что я сразу же ловлю волну веселья и неутомительных обсуждений с попутчиком. К утру мы приедем в назначенный город.

«Согласно материалам дела, участники организации передвигались в другие регионы, соблюдая меры конспирации, посредством автостопа».

На окраинах Рязани, под мостом, опоры которого разрисованы граффити, шумят генераторы и разливается пиво. Отдельные гурманы угощают присутствующих самогоном. Лысые головы, ирокезы, дреды и челси. В круговерти жестоких танцев летят куски земли и капли крови с разбитых губ. «Ой! Ой! Ой! Ой!» Вокалист отдаёт микрофон в толпу. Происходящее под мостом напоминает смесь русских народных танцев с кулачным боем. Бунтари с Поволжья, как во времена Стёпки Разина, снова дошли до Рязани.

Вольница уличного подполья. Объятия и разговоры с надрывом голоса. Шипящий ритм панк-рока будет стоять в ушах всю ночь. Музыканты садятся в арендованную «газель» и отправляются в другой регион по маршруту своего тура. Наши стаи разбредаются по впискам. Знакомства, водка, споры на грани драки, секс в чьей-то ванной и прохладный ночной воздух на балконе. Обжигающие лучи утреннего солнца заставляют открыть глаза и встать с пола. Перешагивая через ещё не пробудившихся ребят, ищу свой телефон и рюкзак. Умываюсь прохладной водой из-под крана. Нужно выехать до обеда. Путешествие продолжается…

«В ходе следствия установлено, что фигуранты дела знакомились на концертах и тренировках по смешанным единоборствам».

Хаос в квартире подчёркивает постоянную текучку её обитателей. С кухни пахнет жареным соевым мясом. Группа молодых людей удобно располагается в середине комнаты: на креслах, на диване, на полу. Обсуждаются серьёзные темы о будущем и настоящем. Поэты, курьеры, бродяги, стартаперы и работяги с заводов говорят о неугасаемых вещах со времён «Союза спасения» и «Народной воли». Каждый рассуждает строго по очереди, не перебивая и уважая чужое мнение, но споров избежать всё-таки сложно. Много мыслей и предложений, скептицизма и максимализма — и горевший в веках вопрос всех мечтателей и радикалов: «Что делать?» У каждого есть свой абстрактный ответ, у кого-то имеется и письменное руководство, но сложнее всего добиться консенсуса без единого лидера и поводыря. Наша методичка общения — книга «Консенсус» Гелдерлооса. Мы действительно верим в собственную способность повлиять на изменения в мире, и эта вера несёт в себе силу, которую ещё не каждый из нас осознал. Нам пока ещё не страшно, и многие готовы на риск, но никто ещё не знает — на какой. Время пролетает незаметно. Кто-то принёс ароматный сапатистский кофе. Из рюкзака достаётся пачка веганского печенья «Орео». Подобных встреч было неисчисляемое количество, и лишь меньшая часть из них приводила к реальным действиям. Входная дверь забаррикадирована множеством замков. Наше присутствие здесь — тоже часть активистской деятельности по защите жилья от чёрных риэлторов. Там, где нет закона, существует самоорганизация. Каждый стук в дверь будоражит в нас готовность к бою.

Все солидарно поднимают вверх вращающиеся ладони — это знак достижения общего плана действий. За окном стемнело.

«В ходе расследования уголовного дела установлено, что члены организации и неустановленные лица встречались на общих собраниях для принятия решений по реализации преступной деятельности».

Мелкие снежинки, освещённые светом ярко-жёлтой луны, плавно кружатся над нами. По маршруту накатанной лыжни мы прошли вглубь леса, чтобы установить ряд импровизированных целей у ближайших деревьев.

Я вижу, как на её щеке тает крошечная снежинка. Её худые пальцы дрожаще снимают предохранитель. Поправляю приклад у её плеча. Свет фонарика направлен в сторону деревьев. Под ногами похрустывает снег. Она прицеливается. Не нужно прислонять щеку слишком близко. Учитывай силу отдачи. Небольшая заминка с перезарядкой. Необходимо применить усилие. Упорная стойка. Выстрел! Эхо хлопка разносится по окрестностям леса и утопает в глуши. Мы здесь одни.

— Теперь попробуй в сидячем положении, меняй стойки по два-три выстрела. Чередуй цели. Меняй магазин.

Из-под облаков за нами подглядывает луна. Я собираю остатки гильз. В городе праздник. Шумят первые салюты, один за другим с разных сторон. Чуть проваливаясь в снег, мы возвращаемся к машине. Согреваем руки горячим термосом, разливая чай. Ключ в зажигании. Начинает играть музыка. Дворники очищают снег с лобового стекла. Фары освещают голые деревья и наши следы, уходящие в заснеженную глубь леса. Мы смотрим друг на друга и улыбаемся. Она целует меня.

«Обвинение гласит, что фигуранты проходили тренировки с целью получения навыков стрельбы и выживания в дикой природе».

Мы окружены громкими лозунгами. Путь огромному потоку людей перекрыли люди со щитами. Студенты и школьники лезут на столбы и уличные возвышенности. Толпа пытается просочиться сквозь кордон силовиков. В небо взлетают бумажные салюты листовок. Я набираюсь решимости, набираю полную грудь городского жаркого воздуха и освобождаю из себя голос гражданского протеста. Мой крик подхватывается окружающими людьми и волной проносится по одной из улиц центра столицы. Я ловлю на себе внимание нахмуренных глаз молодого омоновца. Он видит во мне зачинщика, он видит во мне врага. Я внимательно смотрю на него и чувствую крепкое, почти до боли, сжатие её руки.

Она старается увести меня от его взгляда, от эпицентра событий, ведь мы так давно не виделись, и ей не хочется, чтобы этот день снова закончился в ОВД. Огромное шествие гуляет по столице, и с каждым часом антиправительственные лозунги становятся агрессивнее. Позже столичные чиновники заявят, что мы испортили праздник москвичам. Провожаем закат за столиком веранды «Макдоналдса». Город вернулся к привычной шумной суете. В наших стаканчиках кола размешана с алкоголем. Это было наше последнее лето. Задержаний тогда было немного.

«Из показаний свидетелей обвинения известно, что группа должна была защищать от сотрудников правоохранительных органов народные массы, защищать свои интересы с помощью оружия и не давать подавить митинги и восстания».

Воспоминания рассеивались на фоне бежевой стены и сетчатой рабицы тесной клетушки. Я ухмыльнулся в готовности дать уверенный ответ на вопрос следователя, но уже никого не увидел перед собой. Я остался один в помещении. Один на один со своим ответом. Впереди меня ждали допросы, обвинения, ознакомления и суды, но уже без каких-либо сомнений в том, стоил ли мой путь выпавших испытаний. Цена за свободу уже была оплачена.

«Делай что должно, и будь что будет! Делай что должно, и будь что будет! Безумцы землю ногами крутят. Безумцы землю ногами крутят!» — тихо напеваю я, возвращаясь в камеру из следственных кабинетов.

Редакция Автономного действия напоминает, что вы можете подержать Илью Шакурского.

author: CMI Argentina
title: Fiyi: El niño, la crisis hídrica y el negocio millonario del agua
content:
Fiyi está siendo golpeada por una gran sequía asociada al fenómeno de El Niño y vuelve a poner en emergencia a miles de ciudadanos de este archipiélago del Pacífico. Pero mientras 6 de cada 10 habitantes no tienen acceso al agua potable, la empresa Fiji Water explota una fuente subterránea de aguas, considerada entre las más puras del mundo. El objetivo: abastecer mercados internacionales.







Por Adrián Flores para Red Eco




Este conjunto de Islas suelen aparecer en las postales turísticas como un paraíso de playas y aguas transparentes. Sin embargo, lejos de esa imagen, miles de personas atraviesan una situación muy diferente: conseguir agua segura se ha convertido en un problema cotidiano.




La sequía que afecta al archipiélago, está llevando al límite al precario sistema de abastecimiento. Los datos permiten ver la magnitud el problema. Según UNICEF y la Organización Mundial de la Salud, en 2022 solamente el 42 % de la población de Fiyi tenía acceso a servicios de agua potable gestionados de manera segura. Esto significa que casi seis de cada diez habitantes no alcanzaban ese estándar. Aunque una proporción mucho mayor contaba con algún servicio básico, eso no necesariamente garantizaba agua segura y sin contaminación.




Los informes difundidos durante noviembre muestran la gravedad del actual escenario. El periódico The Fiji Times, publicó el 1 de noviembre que 19 de las 44 fuentes de abastecimiento monitoreadas por la Autoridad del Agua de Fiyi se encontraban en niveles críticos.




El Gobierno realiza operativos de emergencia con camiones, plantas de tratamiento y embarcaciones para abastecer a las comunidades insulares. Los pronósticos tampoco son alentadores: si continúa la falta de lluvias, hasta el 82 % de las fuentes monitoreadas podría alcanzar niveles críticos.




La crisis ya golpea la salud. En la isla de Batiki se registró un aumento de casos de diarrea que motivó la intervención del Ministerio de Salud. Los productores agrícolas enfrentan pérdidas de cultivos y dificultades para mantener el ganado.




La crisis climática golpea sobre una estructura que no estaba preparada para responder. Y mientras miles de familias dependen de operativos de emergencia para acceder al agua, en el mismo territorio funciona una industria que convirtió ese recurso en un producto de exportación.




Fiji Water, el gran exportador de agua para las élites del mundo




En el valle de Yaqara, sobre la isla de Viti Levu, se encuentra la planta de Fiji Water. Desde allí se extrae agua que luego es embotellada y comercializada en distintos países.




La empresa pertenece a The Wonderful. Su negocio se construyó alrededor de una característica que funciona como argumento comercial: el origen natural del agua y su procedencia de un acuífero de Fiyi.




No hay elementos para atribuirle a Fiji Water la responsabilidad directa por toda la crisis hídrica del país. Los problemas de infraestructura, la desigualdad en el abastecimiento y las condiciones climáticas tienen una historia propia. Pero resulta inevitable preguntarse por las prioridades que establece el modelo capitalista donde una actividad industrial puede expandirse para abastecer mercados internacionales mientras una parte de la población sigue sin contar con agua segura.




Desfinanciamiento mas sequía




Las dificultades del sistema público no se explican únicamente por la sequía. Según datos del Departamento de Comercio de Estados Unidos, alrededor del 47 % del agua se pierde por filtraciones en las redes de distribución antes de llegar a los hogares, en un país donde miles de personas padecen interrupciones del servicio.




En este contexto, la información sobre las regalías de Fiji Water resulta particularmente significativa. La empresa matriz declaró en 2025 que sus operaciones en Fiyi, junto con las de su compañía hermana de transporte marítimo, aportaban anualmente en regalías al Estado, el equivalente a unos 43 millones de dólares estadounidenses. Esto representa un tercio de lo que el Estado destina al mantenimiento de la red pública de agua.




La comparación permite observar – y no de manera caprichosa – que el negocio privado aprovecha un recurso natural del territorio y obtiene ingresos de su comercialización internacional de centenares de millones (aproximadamente 500 millones de dólares en el 2023) mientras que paga regalías en una suma que ni siquiera sirve para mantener la precaria red de distribución.




Cuando la escasez abre negocios




La apropiación comercial del agua tiene otra dimensión que va más allá de las empresas embotelladoras. En diciembre de 2020, la Bolsa de Chicago comenzó a operar contratos a futuro vinculados al precio del agua en California. No se trata de comprar y vender físicamente el agua disponible, sino de negociar instrumentos financieros cuyo valor depende de las variaciones de determinados precios de referencia.




Es un paso importante en la financiarización de un recurso indispensable para la vida. Y es así como las expectativas de escasez pueden convertirse en oportunidades de especulación.




Esta expansión tiene relación con una necesidad permanente del capitalismo de encontrar nuevas fuentes de rentabilidad. La competencia entre empresas y la presión sobre los márgenes de ganancia impulsan al capital a buscar nuevos espacios de acumulación. La apropiación de fuentes de agua, su explotación comercial y su incorporación a los mercados financieros forman parte de ese proceso, que también debe entenderse en el marco de la tendencia decreciente de la tasa de ganancia.




El mecanismo lo conocemos bien en Argentina donde las empresas se apropian de los beneficios, pero no necesariamente asumen todos los costos de su actividad. Siempre que una explotación agota acuíferos, contamina fuentes o deteriora los sistemas naturales, los gastos de recuperación y las consecuencias sanitarias terminan en manos del Estado y de las comunidades. Los pasivos ambientales se socializan mientras la rentabilidad permanece en el ámbito privado. Incluso la reparación de los daños puede abrir nuevos mercados y convertirse en otra actividad lucrativa.




Así, el agua puede generar ganancias en su extracción, en su comercialización y también con sus escases a través de la especulación bursátil. Mientras tanto, quienes necesitan ese recurso para vivir quedan expuestos a la falta de infraestructura, la contaminación y la escasez.




Una disputa que va más allá de Fiyi




Lo que sucede en Fiyi no es un fenómeno aislado. En distintos países del mundo, la presión sobre las fuentes de agua se combina con el deterioro climático, la contaminación y la concentración de los recursos en manos privadas.




El Niño puede explicar la intensidad de la sequía, pero no por qué tantas comunidades llegan a una emergencia con sistemas de abastecimiento precarios. Tampoco explica que un recurso indispensable para la población pueda convertirse en una mercancía de lujo para consumidores de otros países.




En Fiyi, como en tantos otros países la emergencia vuelve visible una disputa que atraviesa cada vez más territorios: de un lado, el agua como derecho y condición para la vida; del otro, su apropiación como fuente de negocios, rentabilidad y especulación.




La discusión no puede ceñirse a cómo conseguir más camiones cisterna o cómo enfrentar las próximas sequías. También exige discutir quién controla las fuentes y bajo qué condiciones se permite su explotación.




Porque el problema no es solamente que falte agua. Es que, en un mundo donde el agua se vuelve una mercancía cada vez más valiosa, tenerla cerca no garantiza que los pueblos puedan disponer de ella.

author: CMI Argentina
title: El Congreso aprobó los desalojos exprés en plena crisis habitacional y caída del empleo formal
content:
Mientras miles de familias se endeudan para pagar el alquiler, el Senado aprobó una ley que permite solicitar la restitución anticipada de inmuebles con juicios sumarísimos. Inquilinos Agrupados advirtió sobre sus consecuencias.







En plena crisis habitacional y caída del empleo formal, el Gobierno acelera la asfixia a los millones de argentinos que alquilan a partir de la habilitación de los desalojos exprés. Los cambios impulsados por el gobierno de Javier Milei con la flamante Ley de Inviolabilidad de la Propiedad Privada permiten que el dueño de una vivienda, terreno o campo pida su desocupación inmediata por falta de pago o vencimiento del contrato, antes de que haya una sentencia firme.




Para esto, la nueva norma promovida por la Casa Rosada y sancionada este jueves por el Senado, introduce profundas reformas al Código Procesal Civil y Comercial de la Nación al modificar artículos clave como el 679, 680, 684 bis y 686 bis, entre otros. A partir de ahora, la ley establece que, antes de iniciar una demanda, el dueño debe intimar al ocupante y darle al menos diez días corridos de plazo. También permite que la orden judicial de desalojo autorice el uso de la fuerza pública, el allanamiento y la apertura de cerraduras.




Tras la votación, la organización Inquilinos Agrupados denunció públicamente la medida al sostener que habilita el “desalojo masivo sin juicio previo de inquilinos urbanos y comunidades rurales”, al tiempo que compartió una foto con los legisladores que respaldaron la medida.







Estos son los senadores que acaban de votar el desalojo masivo sin juicio previo de inquilinos urbanos y comunidades rurales. https://t.co/7PKD6aYEJG




— Inquilinos Agrupados (@InquilinosAgrup) 

November 20, 2026







El impacto de la crisis económica y los indicadores habitacionales




La aprobación de este régimen de desocupación rápida se produce en un escenario socioeconómico marcado por el deterioro del poder adquisitivo y el incremento de la precariedad en el acceso a la vivienda. De acuerdo con la Encuesta Nacional Inquilina realizada en junio de 2026, el 29,7% de los hogares inquilinos se encuentra en situación de emergencia habitacional, al acumular en forma simultánea sobrecarga del costo del alquiler, deudas y riesgo de mudanza.







El relevamiento señala que el 48,5% de las familias locatarias destina la mitad o más de sus ingresos salariales al pago del alquiler, situación que derivó en que un 20% debiera afrontar mudanzas forzosas por imposibilidad financiera. El sobreesfuerzo económico impactó severamente en los niveles de endeudamiento:







El 72,9% de los hogares inquilinos tiene deudas activas.




El 55,3% de esos hogares se endeudó para comprar alimentos.




El 47,4% de los encuestados recurre a más de un empleo para poder pagar el alquiler.







Por su parte, los datos oficiales del Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censos (INDEC) correspondientes al primer semestre de 2026 muestran la enorme porción de la población a la que afecta esta medida, ya que reflejan que, sobre un universo de 31 aglomerados urbanos, el 20,9% de los hogares revista en condición de inquilino o arrendatario, lo que representa a 2.144.000 hogares y 5.522.000 personas.




La desprotección de este grupo social converge con una pronunciada contracción de la actividad productiva y el empleo formal. Según un informe del centro de estudios Fundar, entre noviembre de 2023 y agosto de 2026 el país registró una pérdida neta de 32.429 empresas empleadoras, lo que equivale a una caída del 6,3% en el total de firmas. Se trata de la reducción porcentual más elevada para los primeros 33 meses de un mandato presidencial desde que existen registros comparables en 1996.




Patentes: aval del Senado y alerta por los medicamentos




Durante la misma sesión legislativa, el Senado aprobó por 47 votos a favor y 22 en contra la adhesión de la Argentina al Tratado de Cooperación en Materia de Patentes (PCT), norma solicitada por el gobierno de los Estados Unidos. En el debate, los legisladores del oficialismo argumentaron que la ratificación implica que “la Argentina abraza la previsibilidad jurídica” y promueve la economía del conocimiento, sectores de la oposición objetaron la medida.




Mientras que, por su parte, el senador del peronismo José Mayans sostuvo que “esto es un tratado de libre comercio donde la Argentina le levanta aranceles a 233 productos de Estados Unidos” y advirtió sobre el perjuicio para la producción local de medicamentos genéricos, al tiempo que el senador del mismo espacio Jorge Capitanich remarcó su preocupación por el “aumento estrepitoso del precio de los medicamentos” en el marco de la crisis sanitaria y económica de las familias.

author: CMI Argentina
title: El Senado sancionó por unanimidad la Ley de Discapacidad
content:
El Senado dio sanción definitiva a la ley de discapacidad con 71 votos a favor y ninguno en contra y a 40 días del vencimiento de la ley de emergencia que rige hasta el 31 de diciembre.







El texto acordado en Diputados y aprobado sin cambios en Senadores mantiene en forma permanente varios puntos de esa ley. Amplía la posibilidad de acceder a pensiones a las personas imposibilitadas de trabajar, fija que las pensiones por discapacidad serán compatibles con un trabajo formal aunque no se podrán tener ingresos superiores a dos salarios mínimos teniendo en cuenta el ingreso individual y no del grupo familiar. Además se mantiene el arancel único universal de prestaciones que será actualizado por el índice de movilidad jubilatoria.




La nueva ley también obliga a la Agencia Nacional de Discapacidad a pagar las deudas con prestadores en un plazo máximo de 90 días.




La senadora de Unión por la Patria, Florencia López, dijo que se logró porque se le pudo torcer el brazo al gobierno.




“Una plaza llena de familias y de personas con discapacidad, bastones blancos, sillas de rueda, con medicación, le torció el brazo al gobierno nacional”, remarcó. Y agregó: fue como David y Goliath, los más débiles, los más humildes, los más vulnerables, le torcieron el brazo al gobierno.




El debate en el Senado fue acompañado afuera del Congreso por una movilización de familiares, organizaciones y prestadores.




“Esta ley va a permitir dar los instrumentos, los elementos para que realmente podamos avanzar en las respuestas que las personas con discapacidad necesitan” dijo Pablo Molero, coordinador del Foro Permanente de Discapacidad.




Además agregó: “Ahora viene otra lucha, que es la del presupuesto 2027, que la semana que viene se va a tratar en diputados”.




Molero remarcó que es muy necesario que haya partidas presupuestarias para dar respuestas a los reclamos del sector sin que el Ejecutivo defina el futuro de las prestaciones.




El Senado también sancionó la denominada Ley de Inviolabilidad de la Propiedad Privada manteniendo los límites a la extranjerización fijados en la Ley de Tierras y el capítulo que facilita los desalojos de inquilinos y de comunidades indígenas y campesinas.




También se aprobó que se trate la semana que viene la prórroga del Estatuto del Periodista reclamada por los gremios de prensa de todo el país y que se reúna un plenario de comisiones para avanzar con el proyecto de ley de Prevención de Ludopatía y Regulación de las Apuestas Online que tiene media sanción de Diputados.

author: Unknown
title: 12 jours, 4 manifs, 2 occup' (et plein de blocus)
content:
L'occupation de la Bourse du Travail 




Le jeudi 5 novembre, après 

la manif

, l'Assemblée Générale de Cultures en lutte 69 pond un communiqué pour annoncer l'occupation de la salle Albert Thomas de la Bourse du Travail.




Depuis ce jour, l'Assemblée Générale de Cultures en lutte 69 (mouvement des étudiant·es et travailleur·ses de la Culture de Lyon) occupe la salle Albert Thomas de la Bourse du Travail de Lyon pour donner écho aux revendications de notre secteur et à celles de toutes les personnes en lutte (lycéen·nes, étudiant·es, travailleur·ses et retraité·es). 

 Les Bourses du Travail sont des lieux d'organisation des travailleur•ses arrachées aux municipalités par les ouvrier•es à la fin du 19

e

 siècle. En novembre 1966, il y a soixante ans, Louis Pradel, alors Maire de Lyon, a fait voter à son conseil municipal la transformation de la salle Albert Thomas en salle uniquement dédiée aux spectacles plutôt qu'en lieu d'organisation des luttes du monde du travail. Nous récupérons aujourd'hui le lieu qui nous est dû, pour lui redonner sa fonction première.




Pendant 9 jours, la Bourse est donc occupée et devient le cœur névralgique de la mobilisation : AGs à gogo (interfac, interpro, occupation, culture, autonome, travailleur·euses de l'hôtellerie-café-restauration...)

 

; after manif

 

; projections

 

; crêpes <3 ...
















 







Après de sombres histoires de concert, de producteurs énervés, de négociation avec la Mairie, de tags, de toilettes et d'alarme incendie... la salle Albert Thomas finit par être expulsée sous menace policière le samedi 14 novembre matin.




Lycéen·nes et étdudiant·es en lutte




Toute la semaine dernière (9/11) et cette semaine (16/11), les lycéen·nes et étudiant·es ont continué à se mobiliser, même si les relais médiatiques se sont fait moins nombreux... à part quand il s'est agit de pleurer sur l'impact des blocus sur la santé mentale des jeunes.




Côté lycées, la lutte a continué sous diverses formes et confrontée à un véritable durcissement de la répression, tant policière et judiciaire, que disciplinaire à l'intérieur des établissements. —> 

Lire le bilan publié sur Rebellyon

.




Côté facs, Lyon 2 a continué sur sa lancé, et inauguré les blocus festifs sur le campus Porte des Alpes : pochoirs, chamboule tout tête de fafs, conférences, 

AG

, frites, musique... au rendez-vous. Le Campus de La Doua (Lyon 1) a été partiellement bloqué à plusieurs reprises également, mais aussi Centrale Lyon. Les beaux arts ont perpétué leur université populaire, et des 

AG

 ont continué à se tenir dans les établissements (Lyon 2, Lyon 1, 

IEP

, 

ENS

, Centrale...).




Manif du mardi 10 novembre 




À l'appel de l'intersyndicale de l'éducation, peu encline d'attendre le prochain gros appel de l'intersyndicale, une manif festive et joyeuse a eu lieu le mardi 10/11. Le parcours : Jean Macé - Guichard, la Préfecture ayant refusé l'accès à la Presqu'île et à Bellecour. Des jeunes motivés et deter, la police est restée à distance, et une mini sauvage en fin de manif pour finir en beauté, mais rapidement gazée et dispersée.
















 




Soutien et antirep




Plusieurs rassemblements de soutien, aux camarades interpelés en manif, ou aux camarades lycéens sur les blocus, se sont tenus ces 12 derniers jours. Une formation antirep a été organisée par Extinction Rebellion, et une autre à l'Amicale du futur le samedi 14, avec une permanence juridique exceptionnelle et un atelier contestation d'amendes. 


On peut également mentionner des distribuations alimentaires gratuites à Lyon 3. 


Enfin, côté Place de Milan, des piquets ant-expulsion se sont tenus tous les jours, alors que le collectif solidarité entre femmes à la rue explique être menacé d'expulsion par la Métropole.




Acte V : manif du samedi 14 novembre




Le 14 a commencé avec un péage gratuit sur le périph' Nord de Lyon (le 4

e

 depuis le début du mouvement

 

!).




Toujours privé de Bellecour par la Préfecture, le cortège a défilé entre la Manufacture et Jean Macé en passant par le cours Garibaldi. On retient : le concert de l'orchestre en Luth à la Manu, une manif rapide, des sit ins et danses tout le long du cortège, une barricade de enflammée photogénique sur Berthelot, les journalistes de 

BFM

 chassés, et des œuvres de qualité.
















 







En soirée, quelques cortèges sauvages ont pu se promener jusque dans le 3

e

, mais une nasse et des interpellations ont été déplorées à Saxe.
















 



















 




Manif du mardi 17 novembre




Une manif historique puisque, en dernière minute et sur décision du tribunal, elle s'est élancée à 11h pour un parcours Manufacture... Bellecour

 

!




On retient : des camions syndicaux et un cortège de tête sympathique animé par un chef d'orchestre au pistolet à eau astucieusement perché sur un cadis, une arrivée sous le soleil à Bellecour...
















 







... des retrouvailles émues avec la rue de la Barre et l'Hôtel Dieu...
















 



















 



















 







... et que tout le monde a hâte de l'acte 

VI

 ce samedi 21/11...
















 
















 
















 







... et une arrivée à Bellecour sous le soleil

 

!
















 
















 
















 




L'occupation éclair du Palais de la Mutualité




Ce mardi 17/11, on annonce une occupation du Palais de la Mutualité, promis quelques jours avant par la Mairie, arraché sans préavis par des camarades ce jour de mobilisation. Une 

AG

 aura eu le temps de s'y tenir, malheureusement la Mairie a envoyé les keufs dès mercredi matin aux aurores, expulsant l'occupation, contrôlant et arrêtant pour vérification d'identité les camarades qui y dormaient.
