title: Baroya Amedê: Divê zarok bi zimanê dayîkê bê perwerdekirin
content:
Navenda Mafên Zarokan a Baroya Amedê, bi boneya 20ê Mijdarê Roja Mafên Zarokan a Cîhanê li avahiya baroyê daxuyaniyek da.




Li gorî nûçeya Ajansa Welat Serokê Baroyê Sertaç Buluttekîn û gelek parêzer tev li daxuyaniyê bûn. Daxuyanî ji aliyê Seroka Navenda Mafên Zarokan Nursel Sariogluyê ve hat xwendin.



















Ji Egîtîm Senê banga 20ê Mijdarê: Ji bo her zarokekî mafê perwerdehiya bi zimanê dayîkê




20 Mijdar 2026










Nursel Sariogluyê bi bîr xist ku parastina mafên zarokan erka bingehîn a dewletê ye û bal kişand binpêkirinên mafên zarokan û ev daxwaz rêz kirin:







* Perwerdeya bi zimanê dayikê: Divê Tirkiye şerhên li ser xalên 17, 29 û 30î yên Peymana Mafên Zarokan rake û mafê jiyan û perwerdeya bi zimanê dayikê mîsoger bike.




* Karkeriya zarokan û xizanî: Divê dawî li kedxwariya di bin navê MESEMê de were anîn û li dibistanan ji bo hemû zarokan xwarineke belaş a rojane were dayîn.




* Zarokên di pêvajoya dadweriyê de: Em li dijî zêdekirina cezayan in; divê polîtîkayên parastin û piştgiriyê zarokan dikin werin pêşxistin.




* Ewlehiya dibistanan û dîjîtal: Divê dibistan ji tundiyê werin paqijkirin û zarok ji platformên dîjîtal werin parastin.




* Aştiya mayînde: Şerên li cîhanê, di serî de li Xezeyê, herî zêde zirarê didin zarokan; divê ji bo zarokan aştiyeke mayînde were avakirin.”






















Rêxistina Parastina Zarokan: 589 milyon zarok li herêmên şer dijîn




20 Mijdar 2026










Nursel Sariogluyê di dawiya axaftina xwe de bang li rayedaran kir û got: “Em bang li hemû saziyên peywendîdar dikin ku çavên xwe ji binpêkirinan re negirin û erka xwe ya berpirsyariyê bi cih bînin.”

author: Maverick Avila
title: Scientists call for conservation of horseshoe crabs found in Tawi-Tawi
content:
Researchers with a horseshoe crab in the coastal waters in Tawi-Tawi. Photo courtesy of Quesie T. Omnos and Dr. Pedrosa-Gerasmio.

Residents have confirmed to Mindanao scientists the presence of horseshoe crabs in the waters of the southern Philippine island province of Tawi-Tawi. Previously, the arthropods were only found in Palawan province, but a recent study documented fishers and coastal residents accounts of two distinct horseshoe crab species with features resembling those of the tri-spine horseshoe crab (Tachypleus tridentatus) and the mangrove horseshoe crab (Carcinoscorpius rotundicauda) in the waters of Tawi-Tawi.

The tri-spine horseshoe crab is listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List, while the mangrove horseshoe crab is listed as data deficient, meaning not much is known about its conservation status.

Ivane Pedrosa-Gerasmio, the corresponding author of the study and an associate professor in marine sciences at the Mindanao State University (MSU) – Iligan Institute of Technology, said that on her visit in a market in Bongao, the capital of Tawi-Tawi, in December 2023, locals claimed of seeing horseshoe crabs.

Pedrosa-Gerasmio told Mongabay she shared the news with her student Quesie Tolero Omnos, and together they decided to investigate further with the MSU Tawi-Tawi College of Technology and Oceanography.

“I saw an opportunity to establish baseline information that could support future research and science-based conservation initiatives for horseshoe crab species,” Omnos told Mongabay.

Pedrosa-Gerasmio, Osmos and their colleagues decided to rely on the people who best know the coastal areas. The scientists talked with 142 residents across four municipalities in Tawi-Tawi about where they had seen horseshoe crabs, how frequently, what they thought of the crabs’ population changes, and how they collected and consumed the crabs. Horseshoe crabs are called “bangkas” by the locals, due to their boat-like shape.

Those interviewed had observed horseshoe crabs turn up on sandy beaches, in mangroves, among rocky coral and seagrass, and in waters 10-15 meters (32.8-49.2 feet) deep in Bongao and other coastal towns such as Simunul, Sitangkai and Panglima Sugala.

Residents and fishers told the researchers that locals capture horseshoe crabs to use in medicine to cure asthma and other illnesses, and in rituals for people possessed by bad spirits. More than half of those interviewed also thought that horseshoe crab numbers were declining, possibly due to collection for medicinal purposes, climate change and industrial pollution.

Horseshoe crabs are often referred to as “living fossils,” because they have existed for 450 million years, outlasting dinosaurs. There are just four known species of these crabs; three are found in Asia. All Asian horseshoe crab populations are declining due to threats including habitat loss in Japan, bycatch and beach litter in Indonesia, and overharvesting, pollution and coastal reclamation in China.

Omnos said conserving the two horseshoe crab species they’ve potentially documented in Tawi-Tawi is important because of their ecological significance, possible pharmaceutical applications and cultural value to the communities.

“I believe conservation should begin with sufficient scientific evidence on their occurrence, distribution, population status, and threats, which can guide local government units in developing science-based management plans,” she said. Reposted by Bulatlat

Disclosure: This article was first published by Mongabay on October 27, 2026, and is republished here under a Creative Commons license. It was produced as part of the Southeast Asia Ocean Reporting Fellowship, for which the author is the Philippines fellow.

title: Ji Egîtîm Senê banga 20ê Mijdarê: Ji bo her zarokekî mafê perwerdehiya bi zimanê dayîkê
content:
Sendîkaya Kedkarên Perwerde û Zanistê (Egîtîm Sen), di daxuyaniya xwe ya bi boneya 20ê Mijdarê Roja Mafên Zarokan a Cîhanî de diyar kir ku li Tirkiyeyê mafên jiyan, perwerde, tenduristî û parastina civakî yên zarokan tên binpêkirin.




Sendîkayê aşkere kir ku karkeriya zarokan bi rêya Navendên Perwerdehiya Pîşeyî (MESEM) tê berbelavkirin û da zanîn ku li gorî daneyên Wezareta Perwerdehiya Neteweyî (MEB), 37 zarokên ku di vê çarçoveyê de dixebitîn jiyana xwe ji dest dane.



















Rêxistina Parastina Zarokan: 589 milyon zarok li herêmên şer dijîn




20 Mijdar 2026










Egîtîm Senê xwest ku zarok ji tundkarî, îstîsmar û kedxwariyê bên parastin, li dibistanan xwarina bêpere bê dayîn û mafê perwerdehiya bi zimanê dayîkê bê misogerkirin.




"Karkeriya zarokan di bin navê perwerdehiya pîşeyî de tê rewakirin"




Sendîkayê diyar kir ku MESEM û dibistanên navîn ên pîşeyî zarokan ber bi wê ve dibin ku piraniya hefteyê bi mûçeyên kêm bixebitin û teqez kir ku mafê perwerdehiyê tê paşguhkirin.




Egîtîm Senê bal kişand ser wê yekê ku zarokên di çarçoveya MESEMê de di karên bêkontrol û metirsîdar de tên xebitandin û da zanîn ku li gorî daneyên MEBê 37 zarokan dema dixebitîn jiyana xwe ji dest dane û bi sedan zarok jî rastî qezayên kar hatine. Sendîkayê destnîşan kir ku ji ber ku hemû qeza nayên tomarkirin, dane tabloya rastîn nîşan nadin.



















Yekem rêzefîlma anîmasyonî ya kurdî: "Pirsên Azad" wê di Zarok TVyê de dest pê bike




14 Cotmeh 2026










Egîtîm Senê diyar kir ku daneyên Meclisa Tenduristiya Karkeran û Ewlehiya Karî (İSİG) jî zêdebûna kuştinên zarokan ên li kar radixin pêş çavan û bang kir: "Divê demildest dev ji vê sepanê bê berdan ku tê wateya rewakirina karkeriya zarokan bi destê dewletê."




Daxwaza xwarina bêpere li dibistanan




Egîtîm Senê destnîşan kir ku hejariya zêde û buhayên bilind ên xwarinê rê li ber têrxwarina zarokan digirin û teqez kir ku xwarina bitendurist ne alîkariyeke civakî ye, mafekî bingehîn e ku dewlet bi dabînkirina wê berpirsyar e.




Sendîkayê bal kişand ser wê yekê ku kêmxwarinî dikare bibe sedema pirsgirêkên pêşketina fîzîkî û derûnî, têlçûna balê û zehmetiyên fêrbûnê ya zarokan. Her weha xwest ku ji bo pêkanîna wekheviya di perwerdehiyê de li dibistanan xwarineke tendurist a bêpere û ava paqij bên dayîn.



















FİSA: Di sê mehan de 239 zarok mirine




29 Îlon 2026










Bal kişand ser mafê perwerdehiya bi zimanê dayîkê




Egîtîm Senê anî ziman ku şerhên Tirkiyeyê yên li ser xalên 17, 29 û 30î yên Peymana Mafên Zarokan a Neteweyên Yekbûyî, mafên perwerdehî û nasnameya çandî yên zarokên ku xwedî zimanên dayîkê yên cuda ne sînordar dikin.




Sendîkayê diyar kir ku zarokên penaber û xwendekarên ku xwedî nasnameyên çandî yên cuda ne di perwerdehiyê de rastî cudakariyê tên û got ku dûrketina ji prensîbên perwerdehiya zanistî û laîk jî bandoreke neyînî li gihîştina perwerdehiya bikalîte dike.



















2025: Zarokan di bianet kurdiyê de çawa cih girtiye?




31 Kanûn 2025










Egîtîm Senê bal kişand ser wê yekê ku zewacên bi darê zorê yên di temenê zarokatiyê de, îstîsmara zayendî, karkeriya zarokan û girtinên li dijî zarokan didomin û xwest ku Tirkiye şerhên xwe yên li ser peymanê rake û polîtîkayên giştî yên ku prensîba "berjewendiya bilind a zarokî" esas digirin bixe meriyetê.

title: #…oh #how do I stop?
content:
queeranarchism

:

caspercryptid

:

I feel like not enough people realize that people under enormous strain act really really fucking Weird 

things humans are known to do when stressed:

-hallucinate

-cry over what seems to be small things

-become furiously angry over what seems to be small things

-hit a self destruct button over and over again

-lose all sense of reality

-becoming straight up unable to communicate

-view every situation as life or death

-experience delusions/become vulnerable to irrational worldviews

-perceive hostility where none exists

-become extremely nauseous and/or throw up

-stop engaging in sleeping/eating/basic hygiene

-stop processing sensory input

-process way too much sensory input all at once

-lash out at others/themselves

-and more!

being able to recognize when a human (ie. you or another person) is so stressed out they cannot think clearly is VERY important for conflict resolution and diffusing emotional crisis. highly recommend trying to train yourself at being able to recognize that state of panic- there is a point in which logic and rationality is useless and you have to address the underlying emotional issue first. knowing that saves everyone a lot of pain and struggle.

It’s also good to understand that all of these reactions are USEFUL. They’re all part of our survival system, telling us we need to be able to fight better, flight better, freeze better, fawn better. 

-hallucinate > some experiences are too difficult for our brain to process all at once. To avoid complete overwhelm, the mind seeks distraction and escape or translates invisible stress into visble metaphors. 

-cry over what seems to be small things > Crying releases tension. Our body needs it. If we don’t cry over the Big Stress, we will cry over the small things to regulate.

-become furiously angry over what seems to be small things > Rage also releases tension. Our body needs it. If we don’t rage over the Big Stress, we will rage over the small things to regulate.

-hit a self destruct button over and over again > Our survival instinct does not accept powerlessness. When we lose all sense of control over reality, we do whatever makes us feel in control again. If the only control we can have is self-destructive, that is the control we will reach for.

-lose all sense of reality > again, some experiences are too difficult for our brain to process all at once. To avoid complete overwhelm, the mind seeks distraction and escape or translates invisible stress into visible metaphors. 

-becoming straight up unable to communicate > Too much stress is really bad for us, not just mentally but also for our heart, our blood pressure, our digestion, etc. Our biology has a fail safe system: if the stress is too much, shut parts of the brain down. Block the input until the stress is lowered, so that at least we don’t overload complete.y 

-view every situation as life or death > When we go into survival mode, our body is pumped full of stress hormones and they linger (both because your body needs time to process them and because we’ve evolved around predators that might linger in an area, so we’ve evolved to stay on guard long after a danger). Our body keeps us in survival mode - ready to fight/flight/freeze/fawn to keep us alive. 

-experience delusions/become vulnerable to irrational worldviews > again, some experiences are too difficult for our brain to process all at once. To avoid complete overwhelm, the mind seeks distraction and escape or translates invisible stress into visble metaphors. 

-perceive hostility where none exists > again, when we go into survival more we stay there a while - ready to fight/flight/freeze/fawn to keep us alive. 

-become extremely nauseous and/or throw up > when we go into survival mode, our body puts all its energy into the organs that we need to fight/flight/freeze/fawn. Digestion is suppressed. It can wait. (This is also why stress constipation is a thing). If what’s currently in the stomach can not stay there and wait, best to get rid of it so the body doesn’t waste vital energy on digestion. 

-stop engaging in sleeping/eating/basic hygiene > Again, when we go into survival mode, our body is pumped full of stress hormones and they linger. They keep us awake. They suppress feelings of hunger, thirst etc. to make us better survivors in the moment of danger. 

-stop processing sensory input > again,  if the stress is too much, our system shuts parts of the brain down. Block the input until the stress is lowered, so that at least we don’t overload completely. 

-process way too much sensory input all at once > part of that survival mode again, this is here to keep us safe

-lash out at others/themselves> part of that survival mode again, 

-and more!

These are all processes designed to keep us alive, to keep us safe. Experiencing them isn’t just normal, it’s useful. We would be much worse off if our body-brain-system didn’t have all these safety valves to regulate us during and after experiences that are too intense to process without such safety valves. Yay to all our useful weirdness! 




#…oh #how do I stop?

Good question! Since all of these are 

some form of ‘stuck in survival mode’, and 

functional 

Trying to stop the behavior generally does not work and is likely to make things worse, because suppressing survival mode mechanisms tends to just give you more stress. 

The only real answer

 

is:

 reduce the causes of stress

Depending on your situation, that can be very difficult, but it’s the only way to really get out of constant survival mode. 

Next: 

give your body some recovery. 

Sleep, food, warmth. Plenty of it. 

And 

give your brain some stability

. Routines, traditions, familiar places, family recipes, showers. Things that push your 'i feel safe here’ buttons. 

When you are feeling a little less constantly in danger, next steps:

Connect to the world around you. 

Have dinner with friends. Take a walk outside. Touch grass. Hug a dog. Talk to someone you love. 

Connect to your sense of control and capableness.

 Stress feels helpless and out of control, so do small things that do the opposite: fix a flat tire, learn a new song on your guitar, complete a puzzle. 

Connect to your sense of meaning

. Stress can make everything feel pointless. Connect to what gives your life meaning. Is it friends? family? social justice? religion? great sex? It’s your life, there are no wrong answers here. You don’t have to do any meaningful things for now, the point is to rediscover what motivates you. 

Finally:

Take your time. 

It takes a long time to get your survival mode to switch off. Recovering from a short period of very high stress generally takes about 6 weeks. Recovering from a long, intense period of stress can take much longer. Recovering from a full burn out can take years. Don’t give up just because you experience a relapse. Notice whether the waves of bad things are getting less bad over time. 

Work through guilt and shame. 

Guilt and shame will keep you back in survival mode, as will any believe that you do not deserve to feel better. If you notice these things in your head, tackle them. You responded to stress the way all humans do. Your behavior was not weak, weird, broken, etc. Your survival mode was doing what it’s supposed to do. As long as you’re still here, it worked.

author: Authors and Editor
title: Seeds and Seedbeds: Two Venezuelan Initiatives for Science for Life
content:
A group of farmers runs a potato-seed laboratory in Mucuchíes, in the Venezuelan state of Mérida, 3,600 metres above sea level. The Ministry of Science and Technology (Mincyt) describes this laboratory, the Biotechnology Centre for Training in Agamic Seed Production (Cebisa), as the most advanced of its kind in the country. In April 2025, the government formally handed over expanded training facilities to Cebisa, which has operated since 2009.

[1]




A few weeks later, on 2 May, more than 250 children and young people from ten municipalities in Zulia presented 100 robotics projects designed to solve problems in their local communities.

[2]




Initiatives of this kind exist in other Global South countries. What sets these apart is their context: the Venezuelan state has incorporated them into a national project, and that project stems from a question posed by Hugo Chávez: what is the purpose of each technology?

[3]




For Chávez, that question could not be answered within the confines of laboratories. A national development project could not succeed, he argued, unless it conceived, designed, and built its own scientific and technological approach. In Venezuela, this project took on institutional form in 1999, when Chávez came to power. The Scientific-Peasant Alliance and the National Scientific Seedbeds Programme (Semilleros) are two of its manifestations: one sows seeds, the other sows vocations. By bringing farmers and young people into scientific work, these initiatives also raise another question: who is recognised as a producer of knowledge, and who decides?




What Kind of Science? For What Purpose, and Who Produces It?




In June 2007, speaking to a group of grassroots inventors, Hugo Chávez acknowledged that Venezuela needed technological mastery for reasons of sovereignty and security. However, recalling the Argentine scientist Oscar Varsavsky, he added that the primary problem was not ‘know-how’ but ‘know-what’. Technology, he argued, should be neither an end in itself nor a commodity, but a means to meet needs. He concluded: ‘we have an obligation to understand the purpose of every technology’.

[4]




Varsavsky (1920–1976) devoted much of his work to a question that was uncomfortable for his profession: who decides what is researched and for what purpose? In 

Science, Politics and Scientism

, he argued that the science of his time was not neutral but adapted to the social system that funded and organised it. He described ‘scientism’ as the attitude of researchers who adapted to this scientific market, ceased to concern themselves with the social significance of their work, and adopted the norms and values of the major international centres. For him, the decisive task was to set the research topics, assign priorities, and organise the work around the needs of social change.

[5]




In 

Towards a National Science Policy

 (1972), he extended the argument to the realm of public policy. If a country framed its scientific development as ‘closing the gap’ with advanced nations, he warned, it effectively smuggled in the essence of their way of life. Every societal project, by contrast, required its own scientific and technological approach.

[6]




What Varsavsky termed ‘scientism’ has a longer history. Modern science took shape alongside capitalism and Europe’s colonial expansion from the 16th century onwards, with methods, values, and perspectives that this expansion imposed on the world as universal. It rested on a division between two planes of knowledge: that which distinguishes the true from the false, and that which distinguishes right from wrong. The former was taken to be objective knowledge and became science. The latter was assigned to the subjective realm of ethics.




Modern science was thus constructed in isolation from ethics. It declared itself objective and neutral, and proclaimed itself the only valid form of knowledge. It has undoubtedly brought great advances for humanity. Yet, alongside unprecedented scientific and technological development, humanity’s major problems – inequality, poverty, hunger, disease, and environmental crisis – persist, and the way science is put to use has helped deepen some of them.




This contradiction is rooted in the economic and political relations within which science develops. Under capitalism, the accumulation of capital shapes research priorities, funding, the ownership of results, and the direction of innovation. Knowledge becomes a commodity, produced for expected profit rather than collective need.




The starkest example is that of weapons. On 28 February 2026, the United States and Israel went to war against Iran and, on the very first day, an attack on a girls’ primary school in Minab killed more than 160 people, most of them children. Behind attacks such as this stand scientists and engineers trained at universities and research centres, working for military establishments and the corporations that supply them, and increasingly using artificial intelligence systems. Discussing the wider role of AI in military targeting, Bappa Sinha describes how Palantir’s Maven system aggregates satellite imagery, drone footage, and signals intelligence to prioritise targets and recommend weaponry. With the Pentagon’s own mantra that ‘speed wins’, he argues, the time taken to verify whether a building is a school or a barracks tends towards zero.

[7]




Technical capability does not explain itself: it depends on who organises it and what agenda it serves. That is the distinction Chávez drew: technological mastery for reasons of sovereignty and security is one thing; technology placed at the service of a superpower’s agenda over other peoples is quite another. As he said in 2006, ‘there is no such thing as neutral science’. He argued that anyone who conducts research and claims not to be involved in politics is, in fact, involved in politics, because their work may strengthen the dominant system.

[8]




The first question is ‘what for?’: which problems should science address, and for whose benefit? Answering it also requires asking who sets research priorities and controls the resources. The direction of science is not fixed: it can be contested and transformed, and with it, science policy.




The other question is who produces knowledge and who recognises it as valid. The presentation to Mincyt’s 2025 collection of Chávez’s speeches asks: is modern science ‘above peasant knowledge, ancestral knowledge, or popular knowledge’? How can we ensure that ‘the frameworks of knowledge of the wretched of the world and of history’ are upheld and respected? The answer is a science that is ‘community-based, participatory, diverse, and in solidarity with the oppressed’, a ‘science of the people – that is, of subalternity’ – rooted in life or, in Chávez’s words, ‘for life, for happiness’. The presentation also warns against ‘the academic trap’: declaring a different kind of science does not eliminate the geopolitics of knowledge, which is ‘a real struggle’.

[9]




The science that is needed does not abandon rigour, nor does it have different laws of nature: those have no nationality. What changes is who asks the questions and what the answers are used for. Chávez described it as a dialectical process whose synthesis is the interaction of popular knowledge with academic knowledge.

[10]

 The in vitro laboratory does not compete with the memory of those who preserve native potatoes in the páramo, the high Andean grassland above the tree line; they need one another. This does not mean setting modern science aside. It means taking seriously what peasants and Indigenous peoples have learned over generations about seeds, soils, and plants – knowledge that colonial rule dismissed as backward and that capital has often appropriated – and testing it with the same rigour as any other claim.




Science and the National Project




Varsavsky argued that a society’s scientific and technological ‘style’ should grow out of its national project. That style would guide the organisation of research and the choice of technologies, providing the basis for specific technological strategies.

[11]




Chávez likewise linked technological choices to the society Venezuela sought to build. In April 2008, he rejected the idea of bridging the technological gap, arguing that this ambition meant adopting the ‘Northern project’, which he accused of putting science at the service of inequality and exploitation between countries. Venezuela had to build, not imitate. ‘It is not a question of bridging any gap; it is a question of building, of inventing’ a ‘highly dynamic, highly diverse’ style. That style, he specified, must come ‘from our very core, from our history, our culture, our traditions’ and be driven ‘by our needs’.

[12]




He also set out the needs this style should serve. ‘We need a scientific-technological style to achieve our food security and sovereignty, and holistic human development’ – that is to say, education, health, housing, and ‘meeting the fundamental needs of the people’.

[13]




But a distinctive style depends on the political choice about the society to be built. Varsavsky saw scientific autonomy as both a prerequisite for developing and carrying out a country’s own national project and a consequence of that process.

[14]

 In Venezuela, political change made it possible to turn this approach to science into public policy.




Venezuela: Two Sowings




When Hugo Chávez took office, Venezuela’s public science sector depended on the National Council for Scientific and Technological Research (Conicit), which funded research projects. Chávez described the situation before 1999 in two sentences: science ‘was reserved for an elite’ and science and technology ‘were hijacked’. What had to change, in his words, was what science and technology were for: they ‘must be formidable instruments, not for the domination of minorities over majorities but, above all, for the liberation of majorities through knowledge, through scientific and technological research and its application to the social battle, to social development’.

[15]




The institutional change was swift. In the first year of government, the Ministry of Science and Technology was established. The Constitution approved by a referendum in December 1999 incorporated science, technology, and innovation for the first time as matters of public interest (art. 110) and required the state to guarantee the ethical principles governing research.

[16]




In 2000, a programme of productive cooperation networks – later renamed productive innovation networks – was launched to link rural producers with the research capacity of universities and specialist centres. In 2001, the Organic Law on Science, Technology, and Innovation (LOCTI), issued by decree, repealed the 1984 Conicit Act and transformed Conicit into the National Fund for Science, Technology, and Innovation (Fonacit). The law has since been reformed four times, in 2005, 2010, 2014, and 2022.

[17]




Following the enactment of the LOCTI, research priorities shifted from individual disciplines, such as physics, chemistry, and biology, towards problems concerning food, health, energy, the environment, and education. A style of science was promoted that sought to generate knowledge to construct a socially, politically, economically, and culturally just, equitable, and sustainable society. This reflected Varsavsky’s argument that science must develop from its own roots to overcome its peripheral position.




Beginning with its first version in 2001 and developing through successive reforms, the law recognised traditional, ancestral, and popular knowledge and progressively broadened participation in scientific work to include communes and organised popular power.

[18]

 Support extended beyond academic activity to projects arising from popular power, such as the Socialist Networks for Productive Innovation. Through these networks, organised groups of producers tested innovations to increase the production of food, goods, or services.




Particular emphasis was placed on networks linking different stages of research, disciplines, and institutions. Antivenom research illustrates this approach: studies of snake distribution were linked to research into venom properties, the development of antivenoms, and their production. A single network brought together taxonomy, biochemistry, immunology, and drug development and production. In 2021, researchers at the Institute for Advanced Studies Foundation (IDEA) and the Francisco de Miranda University were developing antivenoms for snake and scorpion bites.

[19]

 These connections show how planning and cooperation can direct scientific work towards public needs, treating knowledge as the heritage of the people rather than a commodity.




Since 2003, the government has also turned to the ‘missions’, programmes operating alongside traditional institutions to address urgent needs in health, literacy, and university education. In 2006, the Science Mission was launched to integrate social and institutional actors into networks to generate and disseminate knowledge. In 2011, the Great Agro-Venezuela Mission set out to strengthen national food production with scientific and technological support. The Science Mission was the precursor to the ‘Dr Humberto Fernández-Morán’ Great Mission for Science, Technology and Innovation, which President Nicolás Maduro presented on 10 April 2024. Its five pillars included developing and preserving national scientific talent, and applying science, technology, and innovation for production.




The Scientific-Peasant Alliance formed part of science policy supporting food production, while the Semilleros fell under the first pillar. Food sovereignty was one of the areas where the Alliance put this approach to science into practice.




The Seed: The Scientific-Peasant Alliance




According to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the world produces enough food to feed everyone. Hunger therefore raises questions about what is produced, using which technologies, and how it is distributed.

[20]

 The companies that promoted the Green Revolution through commercial seeds, fertilisers, and pesticides gained influence over what and how much to sow, how to distribute the harvests, and whom to finance. Seed patents and genetically modified organisms (GMOs) later became part of this system of corporate control. Within this framework, food is a commodity: it is worth whatever it can be exchanged for.




The foundations laid since 1999 enabled Venezuela to respond to the food crisis caused by the unilateral coercive measures imposed on the country. Mincyt and the Corporation for Scientific and Technological Development (Codecyt) could bring universities together and fund their work, drawing on the experience of socio-productive networks. In 2013, Codecyt joined the Association of Integrated Producers of the Páramo (Proinpa), a group of producers from Mérida, to scale up the socio-productive networks. Mincyt’s 2025 publication, 

Alianza Científico-Campesina

, records a 2014 decision to stop importing potato seed to strengthen national production. According to the publication, the subsequent intensification of the blockade prevented purchases on the international market, exposing the vulnerability of a food system reliant on imports and increasing the urgency of domestic seed production. The 2015 Seeds Act, which recognised the strategic importance of seeds for agricultural production, strengthened the legal framework for this work.

[21]




When seed imports became impossible, the Alliance could draw on that work to produce pre-basic seed of different varieties. By January 2016, both organisations were publicly using the name ‘Scientific-Peasant Alliance’. The Alliance grew out of earlier ministry work on socio-productive networks, among which Proinpa and others had made significant progress in organising producers and developing specific productive projects. Without these laws, institutions, and networks, a group of producers from the páramo region would hardly have had access to the laboratory facilities, resources, and recognition needed to produce seed on a national scale.

[22]




Through seed banks, in vitro cultivation, agroecology, and networks linking communities and universities, the Alliance brings together their knowledge and resources for production. Cebisa, the laboratory in Mucuchíes, is its most visible manifestation.




The Mincyt book that systematises the Alliance’s experience highlights cases such as that of Bernabé Torres, a 64-year-old farmer who takes part in the Alliance and whom it calls the guardian of native potatoes. He recounted how the Alliance and the University of Los Andes had supported the rescue and propagation of local and native seeds, and said that without science they would be nothing, because those who did not use it were filling the land with chemicals. For Torres, the work he and his fellow farmers were doing there was ‘the future of this country’.

[23]

 Recognition has also come from abroad: in 2026, the FAO named María Cantalicia Torres, a rural leader and seed guardian from the Venezuelan Andes, one of its 100 heroes in agrifood systems for her work recovering native potato varieties.




According to the account of the experience that Mincyt has published, by 2024, the Alliance had planted more than 30,000 hectares in accordance with its guidelines across all its crop sectors (potatoes, cocoa, coffee, maize, and others), involving more than 3,500 families in 18 states. The same account, in its epilogue, adds that the Alliance now propagates more than 150 varieties of potato seed, nearly 80 of them native to the Andes, and that its locally produced seed supports potato cultivation in more than 80% of the country’s federal entities. It also reports that Cebisa saves the country more than US$460 million a year in imports.

[24]




The Alliance builds partnerships between farmers and scientists to advance food sovereignty, and farmers’ knowledge helps determine which seeds are propagated. Families collect and select the seeds with the greatest potential from their own territories and send them to laboratories for classification and improvement before they are returned. In practice, this is the synthesis of popular wisdom and academic knowledge that Chávez proposed. Community assemblies and conversations in the field, where producers who have worked with the Alliance share their experience, are one of the ways the approach reaches other farming families.

[25]

 The aim is to put the country’s talent and capabilities to work on needs found in the countryside, recognising traditional and ancestral knowledge and placing the advances of academic science at the service of the people.




One interviewee in the Mincyt book identifies new demands arising from the Alliance’s expansion: strengthening its seed nuclei in each region, giving farming families comprehensive technical support, and ensuring that knowledge is effectively transferred. The interviewee also considers bringing new talent into research centres key to generating solutions suited to producers’ needs. In these challenges lies an opportunity to deepen the Alliance’s impact and establish it as a reference for linking scientific research and peasant production.

[26]




The Semilleros: The National Scientific Seedbeds Programme




While the Alliance addresses the needs of the present, the Semilleros address the nation’s future. The programme, which the Ministry of Science and Technology has run since 2019, reflects an idea central to Chávez’s developmental model: the Bolivarian Revolution could not take ‘a leap forward without science and technology’.

[27]

 Sustaining that model also means encouraging children and young people to pursue science and giving them opportunities to generate knowledge and solve problems. The first pillar of the Great Mission reflects this aim: sowing and preserving national scientific talent.




The two programmes are not separate worlds. Even before the formal launch of the Semilleros, the Alliance had forged links with schools in Mérida, where pupils and teachers were showing an interest in agriculture, ecosystems, and seeds, and had organised educational activities in the countryside. Alicia Cáceres, a biologist and researcher and professor at the Central University of Venezuela, is quoted in the Mincyt book on the Alliance describing the children who visit its laboratories: ‘They ask questions, they take you along and tell you: “But I have a hypothesis”. Everything is impressive!’ Living alongside them, she adds, is something ‘we hadn’t had before, and now we do’. The programme also invites girls to take up science, so that they become the scientists of tomorrow.

[28]




The National Scientific Seedbeds Programme, promoted by Mincyt, seeks to identify, train, and protect the scientific and technological talents of the future, guide early career choices, and strengthen science education amongst children and teenagers. Among its five components are ‘productive science pathways’, which bring students into contact with settings where science is directly linked to production, and educational robotics, with centres equipped with electronics and IT laboratories.




The programme, which has been running since 2019, offers several avenues for participation, including Olympiads, practical workshops, and school outreach. Outreach sessions involve entire secondary school year groups. In November 2026, 265 first-year secondary school pupils in the state of Sucre took part in activities involving microscopy, chemistry, physics, robotics, and astronomy. Another 655 pupils from the states of Portuguesa and Trujillo took part in practical workshops in June 2026.

[29]

 According to Mincyt, the programme had already reached 562,695 children and young people in 2025.

[30]




At the regional stage of the Creative Robotics Olympiad in Zulia state, one young participant presented an automated system for the initial processing of cocoa pods. The project was designed to support the Zulia Institute of Technological Research (INZIT) in the production of nutritious flours. Another participant designed a robot to monitor data from a manufacturing plant in real time.

[31]

 These projects showed young people taking ownership of scientific knowledge and technological tools to address local needs. Here, robotics went beyond programming and building machines: it became a way to explore solutions to problems in food production and manufacturing.




Training new generations of scientists, engineers, and technologists also raises a question of values. Creativity, rigour, and the capacity for innovation are indispensable, but they must go hand in hand with social responsibility, dialogue, and reflection on the consequences of technological applications. Preparing people to develop sophisticated technologies must be accompanied by a public discussion of purposes and limits. It is essential to nurture a population capable of participating in these decisions regarding their use, thereby sustaining the nation’s project.




The challenge is to turn participation into a career path. It is essential to ensure that those who have followed scientific pathways and attended robotics clubs go on to work in laboratories, factories, and the countryside, and that schools support this vocation through high-quality education.




Another Subject, Another Purpose




In Minab, a war imposed by the US and Israel killed scores of schoolchildren. In Mérida and Zulia, technical skills – measuring, cultivating, and programming – are directed towards producing seeds and training those who will continue to generate knowledge. Chávez called the producers, innovators, and scientists ‘the seeds of the new homeland’.

[32]

 The Alliance and the Semilleros are two ways of sowing them. In October 2026, the Alliance brought together more than 300 women producers from Mérida, Táchira, and Trujillo at a regional meeting in Mucuchíes.

[33]

 Through the Semilleros, children and young people from ten municipalities in Zulia developed robotics projects to address local needs.




Political change made both programmes possible, and in 2026 they continue to operate. Their continuity depends on that framework being institutionalised through legislation, the budget, and popular power. The challenge is to secure those conditions over the long term.




Neither initiative alone solves the problems facing science. Together, however, they show how public policy can expand scientific capacities, recognise new producers of knowledge, and direct innovation towards collective needs when it begins by asking what science is for.




What other contexts can learn from this is not the scale or the conditions, but the approach: asking ‘what for?’ first, recognising those who produce knowledge outside the university, and training from an early stage those who will sustain the effort. For the Global South, the task is not to secure a seat at the table where the scientific ‘centre’ sets the agenda, but to set its own priorities.




In an era marked by artificial intelligence and large language models, the question of who directs technology and whom it serves is even more urgent. As Sinha points out, artificial intelligence has enormous potential in healthcare, climate science, and planning for human needs; the problem is when its development and use are subordinated to the war machine.

[34]

 The ability to process information and automate tasks does not, in itself, determine which uses should be prioritised or who will benefit from them. Such decisions require public debate and participation in setting priorities.




A science for life is not a less rigorous or less advanced science. It is a science whose organisation, priorities, and applications address the question of its social purposes. Its direction and future are determined by what is researched, by who conducts the research, and by the national vision that underpins it. The decisive question is never what technology can do. It is who makes technology, and for whom.

, p. 237 (‘reserved for an elite’); Chávez, installation of the Infocentro of Propatria, Caracas, 21 November 2003, in

Authors

Guillermo Barreto

 is a Venezuelan biologist and a retired professor specialising in conservation and management of biological diversity. His areas of interest and research include reparations for slavery and colonisation, the environmental question, ecosocialism, and civilisational crisis.

title: La Bonaerense al banquillo: arranca el juicio por el crimen de Alejandro Martínez en la comisaría de San Clemente del Tuyú
content:
Alejandro Martínez es retirado del Hotel Fontainebleau | Captura de video




En noviembre de 2021 el hombre de 35 años fue detenido en el hotel donde se hospedaba. Dos horas después yacía muerto en un calabozo de la Comisaría Tercera. Sergio Berni lo culpó de su propio deceso. Kicillof bancó a su ministro y a su policía. El martes en Dolores arranca el juicio contra tres de los asesinos. “Están todas las pruebas, tienen que ser condenados a perpetua”, dice la familia querellante. El juicio comenzará el martes 24 y tiene fecha de finalización pautada para el 4 de diciembre. Las audiencias se harán en el Edificio Central de los Tribunales de Dolores, de Alberdi 137. La causa lleva el número 903-9719. A cargo del Tribunal Oral Criminal 2 está el juez Juan Martín Enzagaray. 

Por Daniel Satur (La Izquierda Diario).







La madrugada del 18 de noviembre de 2021 

Alejandro Martínez

, trabajador de 35 años oriundo de Brandsen, 

murió a golpes

 dentro de la 

Comisaría Tercera de San Clemente del Tuyú

, Partido de la Costa. Hasta allí había sido trasladado por una patota de efectivos de la 

Policía Bonaerense

, después de que desde el 

Hotel Fontainebleau

 

llamaran al 911 por “ruidos molestos” en la habitación 

707

, donde se hospedaba.




El 

Fontainebleau

 

está en Costanera y calle 3 de esa ciudad balnearia. La noche anterior 

Martínez

 se había alojado en esa habitación del séptimo piso. Llevaba pocas ropas, sus lentes (sin los que prácticamente no veía) y una mochila con bastante dinero. Esa plata, producto de una indemnización laboral, él se la iba a transferir al día siguiente a 

Laura Lagana Santillán

, la madre de su pequeño hijo.




Según la reconstrucción de los hechos, tras el llamado telefónico llegaron al hotel 

dos patrulleros

 de la 

Comisaría Tercera

. Los efectivos de 

La Bonaerense

 subieron y encontraron a 

Martínez

 fuera de su habitación, 

sentado

 en la escalera del pasillo. Poco después, según muestra el video de seguridad del hotel, 

se lo llevaron caminando

. Él iba 

con las manos atrás

, 

descalzo

 y 

sin sus indispensables anteojos

. No se le veía herido ni quejándose.




Tras la detención, el personal del hotel juró que en la habitación 

no había quedado nada de Martínez

. Pero la 

Policía

 nunca informó, al menos formalmente, que entre los elementos del detenido se había incautado una 

importante suma de dinero

. Difícil saber si esa plata tiene que ver con el móvil del crimen, pero lo cierto es que

 a Martínez le robaron

 esa indemnización. Y los policías tienen todos los boletos.




Menos de dos horas después de ser sacado vivo del hotel, 

el cuerpo inerte de Martínez

 yacía en uno de los calabozos de la seccional ubicada en San Martín entre 7 y 8. A su alrededor, la patota discutía nerviosa qué hacer con él. Y empezaron los llamados desesperados buscando “instrucciones”.




Martínez murió por 

asfixia mecánica

. Tenía varias 

costillas rotas

, 

golpes 

y 

heridas 

en todo el cuerpo. Otro detenido, desde un calabozo contiguo, escuchó la secuencia. Afirmó que varios policías tiraron al piso a 

Alejandro

 y 

le dieron una feroz paliza

. Los oficiales 

José Pereyra

, 

Christian Rohr 

y 

Maximiliano Munche

 estuvieron al frente de las acciones. Sus “camaradas” 

Laura Chiarullo

, 

Evelyn Garófalo

, 

Jaqueline Mansilla

, 

Carla Cantarella

, 

Sandro Mujica

 y 

Miguel Boulos

, de una u otra manera, participaron.




En 2022 se cerró la instrucción y la causa contra los nueve fue elevada a juicio. El próximo martes 24, más de cuatro años después, comenzará la primera parte del proceso. 

Pereyra

, 

Rohr 

y 

Munche 

se sentarán en el banquillo, acusados de ser coautores de “

homicidio triplemente agravado

 por 

alevosía y ensañamiento

 por el concurso premeditado de 

más de dos personas

, por haber sido cometido por 

miembros integrantes de una fuerza de seguridad

, 

abusando 

de sus funciones o cargos”.




Según el artículo 80 del Código Penal, la expectativa de pena por ese delito es de 

reclusión perpetua

. Sin embargo, los tres acusados gozan del beneficio de la 

prisión domiciliaria

 y llegarán al juicio habiendo estado poco tiempo tras las rejas. Por elección de los imputados, el juicio será por 

jurado popular

 y las audiencias estarán presididas por 

Tribunal Oral Criminal 2 de Dolores

.




Axel Kicillof, Sergio Berni y la Policía Bonaerense | Foto Prensa PBA




El rol de Berni, el aval de Kicillof




Cuando el hallazgo del cuerpo en la 

Comisaría Tercera

 se hizo noticia en los medios nacionales, el entonces ministro de Seguridad bonaerense 

Sergio Berni

 sintió un impulso irrefrenable y salió a dar entrevistas con el objetivo de 

defender personalmente a los policías

. Y lo hizo con el patético, pero no por ello inusual, recurso de crear 

una versión retorcida de los hechos

 para terminar 

culpando a la víctima

.




Además de la pulsión encubridora, en 

Berni

 también pareció operar cierto 

oportunismo político

. El día anterior al crimen de 

Martínez

, la 

Policía de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires

 había asesinado a tiros a 

Lucas González

, un pibe de 16 años que salía de entrenar en el club 

Barracas

. Por unas horas, el ministro bonaerense usó el caso para la puja entre su gobierno y el del PRO. Le duró poco. Menos de un mes después del crimen en San Clemente, otros policías bonarenses mataron a 

Luciano Olivera

 en Miramar. Tenía 16 años, como 

Lucas

.




Sin mostrar pruebas, el funcionario de 

Axel Kicillof

 salió a decir a quien le pusiera un micrófono delante que 

Martínez

 ya había sido detenido varias veces, que estaba 

“totalmente drogado”

, que había intentado 

“robar una casa”

 y que las heridas eran 

“autolesiones”

 provocadas por un supuesto 

brote psicótico

 en el hotel. Pero nada de eso se pudo comprobarse.




A su vez, 

Berni callaba

 ante lo que denunciaba la familia de 

Alejandro

. Primero la Policía les dijo que había muerto 

“en la vía pública”

. Después cambiaron la versión y dijeron que sí había muerto en la comisaría, pero no por golpes sino 

“por una sobredosis”

. Sin embargo, nunca llamaron a una ambulancia ni lo llevaron a un centro de salud.




Mientras el ministro, la cúpula de La Bonaerense y los 

abogados defensores

 (bien pagos por el propio Ministerio) forzaban un relato para salvar a los implicados, 

el gobernador parecía no tener registro del tema

, pese a que en sus discursos cada tanto hablaba de “derechos humanos”.




Kicillof

 tuvo la misma actitud que desplegó ante cada caso de 

gatillo fácil

, 

torturas

 y 

muertes

 en cárceles y comisarías ocurridas en su gestión. De hecho, en diciembre de 2023 despidió con honores a 

Berni

 de su cargo (se mudó a una banca del Senado provincial) y le dio la bienvenida a su “discípulo” 

Javier Alonso

. Es curioso, pero pocas veces un gobernador “progresista” bancó tanto a sus ministros de Seguridad pese a que estos cumplieron un rol clave en el encubrimiento y la impunidad de crímenes atroces.




“Desde que mataron a 

Alejandro 

no cambió nada, sigue todo igual, 

hubo un montón de casos más

. Creo que después de este juicio tanto 

Berni

 como la 

plana mayor de la Policía

 deberían ser imputados y juzgados por todo lo que hicieron”, dice desde La Plata 

Laura Lagana Santillán

 en diálogo con 

La Izquierda Diario

. Razones para acusar no le faltan.




Foto Facebook «Justicia por Alejandro Nicolas Martínez»




“El caso de Alejandro no les significó nada a las autoridades”




La expareja de 

Martínez

, madre del niño de casi nueve años, ultima detalles para afrontar el juicio. Se reúne con los abogados de la 

Comisión Provincial por la Memoria 

que la patrocinarán en la querella. Vuelve a recordar, una vez más, todo lo que pasó hace cinco años. No quiere fallarle a la memoria del padre de su hijo, por eso analiza cada recuerdo para 

no dejar ni un trozo de verdad sin exponer

 cuando le toque atestiguar ante fiscales, jueces y jurado. En medio de todo eso, se toma un tiempo para hablar con 

La Izquierda Diario.




– La espera va terminando, estamos a las puertas del primer juicio por Alejandro. ¿Qué sensaciones, pensamientos, emociones te cruzan?




–

 Fueron cinco años de una espera terrible. Hoy la sensación es de angustia, de dolor, pero también de 

esperanza en esta búsqueda de justicia

. Que se obtenga una condena para los tres asesinos de 

Alejandro

 sería un poco eso. No es fácil de explicar lo que se siente. En estos últimos tiempos, al acercarse la fecha, en cada charla que tengo es como que revivo todo lo que pasamos, es una sensación extraña.




– ¿Cómo llegás en lo personal a esta instancia?




–

 Fue durísimo. Más que nada por el nene, que todos los días extraña a su papá. Fue un corte abrupto, de un día para el otro dejar de comunicarse, pero a la vez empezar a ver su foto en la televisión y no comprender por qué no lo llamaba más. Durante años pidió ver a su papá “aunque sea por última vez”. Por eso en casa intentábamos nombrar lo menos posible a Alejandro, para no herirlo más. No fue fácil. Ahora lo toma de otra manera, con menos angustia. Pero para mí sigue siendo duro, porque no quiero que sufra. Por suerte tengo un gran sostén en mi mamá, en mi familia, en mis amigas y amigos. Y agradezco el apoyo terapéutico de la psicóloga, la psiquiatra y quienes trabajan en el 

Centro Ulloa

 de asistencia a víctimas de violencia institucional. Lamentablemente en los últimos años hubo recortes y achicamiento en el Centro, que depende de Nación, y me quedé sólo con una psicóloga.




– ¿Cómo está hoy tu hijo? ¿Sabe algo de lo que va a pasar?




–

 Al principio, con cinco años, no le podíamos decir lo que había pasado. A medida que pasó el tiempo y él fue preguntando, acompañada por mi psicóloga llegamos a contarle que unos hombres malos le hicieron cosas malas a su papá y él murió. Sabe que ahora habrá unas personas que van a juzgar a esos hombres, para que paguen por lo que hicieron. Él dice que quiere que vayan a la cárcel. Sabe que son policías, que eran nueve y ahora se va a juzgar a tres. Hoy también superó aquella angustia y nombra a su papá con cariño, recordándolo a su manera. El otro día hizo un dibujo de la familia e incorporó naturalmente a su papá. Alejandro está muy presente en su vida.




– ¿Qué expectativas tenés sobre el juicio?




–

 Confieso que el hecho de que sea un juicio por jurado me da un poco de temor. Tengo miedo de que el jurado le tenga miedo a la Policía, que se sientan presionados y no resuelvan como tienen que resolver. Y tampoco descarto que puedan haber ciertas influencias políticas o amiguismos. Las pruebas están, todas, así que creo que por sentido común se debería hacer justicia. ¿Qué más quieren? Quienes tenían que “cuidarlo” lo torturaron hasta morir.




– En estos años vimos a las familias de los policías muy activas, revictimizando a Alejandro, haciendo campaña contra vos y hasta marchando al grito de “son todos inocentes”. ¿Qué pensás de eso?




–

 Yo terminé con custodia por las amenazas que recibí. Me llamaban continuamente, tanto a mi celular como al teléfono de mi casa, que no sé cómo lo consiguieron, y al de mi mamá, que es quien llamó primero a la comisaría. Fue una constante en estos cinco años. Si salgo en alguna entrevista periodística, lo comparten en grupos y redes atacándome, acusándome de mentirosa, estigmatizando a Alejandro diciendo que era un drogadicto al que la familia lo abandonó. Todo tipo de cosas. Hasta llegaron a decir “un falopero menos”. Pero de lo que pasó en la comisaría no dicen nada. Porque saben que lo mataron.




– A 

La izquierda Diario

 

también le mandaron algunos de esos mensajes, porque desde el principio difundimos tu denuncia y contamos la verdad del caso.




–

 Sí, son así. Es como que te dicen “tené cuidado, te estoy mirando”. Actúan con agresividad e impunidad.




– ¿Creés que desde que murió Alejandro cambió algo en la Policía? ¿Pensás que hubo alguna política diferente para, al menos, prevenir casos así?




–

 No, no cambió nada. Sigue todo igual. Los casos siguen sucediendo y nada cambia. Desde que pasó lo de Alejandro me llagaron un montón de casos nuevos, de gente que se contacta para contarme sus historias, una más dolorosa que la otra, siempre con la Policía involucrada. Me he reunido con compañeras y compañeros que se organizan. Recuerdo los casos de 

Lolo Regueiro

 y de 

Daiana Abregú

, pero hay montones de los que la gente ni se entera. 

La violencia institucional es permanente

. Está claro que 

el caso de Alejandro no les significó nada a las autoridades

.




– Suponiendo que Pereyra, Rohr y Munche terminarán condenados, ¿cómo esperás que siga el caso y hasta dónde creés que debería llegarse para decir que hubo algo parecido a la Justicia?




–

 Yo espero la mayor condena, la perpetua, por haberle quitado la vida a una persona. Y que el segundo juicio se haga como se debe, a los otros seis partícipes que encubrieron a los asesinos, por acción u omisión. Que sean juicios transparentes.




– A nivel institucional, del Estado en general, ¿esperás que cambie algo a partir de una condena como la que decís?




–

 Yo creo que 

Sergio Berni debería ser imputado

 y juzgado por todo lo que hizo. Lo mismo 

la plana mayor de la Policía Bonaerense

 que actuó en ese momento. Los seis partícipes secundarios siguen trabajando mientras esperan el juicio, eso no puede ser. La propia Policía fue la que nos impidió reconocer el cuerpo. ¿Qué ocultaban? ¿Quién se va a hacer responsable de todo eso? Después, creo que estaría bien que se ponga una placa en la comisaría diciendo que el 18 de noviembre de 2021 allí se torturó y mató a Alejandro Martínez, con nombre y apellido de quienes lo hicieron. Muchas cosas deberían ser diferentes. Quiero que no sucedan más casos como el éste. Hoy uno lo ve por televisión y cree que nunca le va a tocar, pero un día quizás le toca. Yo no le deseo a nadie que un familiar suyo sufra violencia institucional.




El juicio comenzará el martes 24 y tiene fecha de finalización pautada para el 4 de diciembre. Las audiencias se harán en el 

Edificio Central de los Tribunales de Dolores

, de Alberdi 137. La causa lleva el número 903-9719. A cargo del 

Tribunal Oral Criminal 2

 está el juez 

Juan Martín Enzagaray

title: Yazidi women forced to relive trauma to access their rights
content:
Years have passed since the genocide that remains etched in the memory of the Kurdish people. Yet for Yazidi (Êzîdî) women, the darkness that began on 3 August 2014 has not ended. Many of the women abducted from Shengal are still missing, while their families continue to wait for news of their whereabouts and what happened to them. Some hope for a mass grave to be opened, others await DNA test results, while others still hope that a loved one who has not returned home for years will one day come back.




Massacres, abductions and captivity




ISIS carried out a systematic genocide against the Yazidi community when it attacked Shengal on 3 August 2014. Men and boys were separated from their families and massacred, while women and girls were abducted, sold in slave markets, forced into marriage and subjected to rape. Women's bodies became a target of ISIS's campaign to destroy Yazidi identity and the community's very existence.




2,474 women still missing




During the genocide, 6,417 Yazidi women were abducted. Of these, 3,647 regained their freedom, while the fate of 2,474 remains unknown. Among those registered as missing, 269 were confirmed dead, and their remains were returned to their families. The abducted women were first taken to Mosul, then to Tal Afar, Raqqa, Deir ez-Zor and Baghouz. Women and children were moved between different cities, separated from one another and cut off from their families.




For women, captivity was not limited to a single act of abduction. Some were transferred between captors, sold to different individuals and forcibly displaced within ISIS-controlled territories, leaving their whereabouts unknown for years. Some women managed to escape, while others reached different countries. The fate of thousands remains uncertain.




Those who sought refuge in Europe




For Yazidi women who escaped ISIS captivity, the struggle to rebuild their lives extended far beyond Shengal. Some survivors were forced to settle in different countries to access medical treatment, rehabilitation and safe living conditions.




Following the genocide, Germany launched a special humanitarian resettlement programme for Yazidi women and children. Under the programme implemented by the state of Baden-Württemberg in 2015 and 2016, approximately 1,100 women and children, the vast majority of them Yazidis, were brought to Germany. They were provided with accommodation, healthcare, psychological support and educational opportunities. Canada also implemented admission and family reunification programmes for ISIS survivors, including Yazidi women and children. In 2023, the Canadian government announced that it had enabled more than 1,400 survivors to build new lives in the country.




However, establishing a safe life in another country did not erase the absence of missing loved ones or the pain of families torn apart. Some women who settled in Europe are still trying to discover the fate of their relatives in Iraq, while survivors forced to live far from their homeland have encountered new obstacles in seeking their rights. The rupture caused by the genocide has therefore continued to shape women's lives not only in Shengal but also in the countries where they have been forced to settle.




The path to freedom in Rojava




Following the liberation of Shengal in November 2015, Rojava played an important role in reuniting women and children rescued from ISIS with their families. Those freed through the efforts of the Women's Protection Units (YPJ) and the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) were reunited with their families through the work of the Yazidi Women's Freedom Movement (TAJÊ) and the Shengal Autonomous Administration.




Women rebuilt their lives




The struggle of Yazidi women did not end with their liberation from captivity. Following the genocide, women began organising to prevent similar attacks and gain control over their own lives. Women established self-defence forces within the Shengal Women's Units (Yekîneyên Jinên Şengalê, YJŞ), playing a major role in the defence and liberation of Shengal. The women's organising efforts that began in 2015 gained an institutional structure in September 2016 with the establishment of TAJÊ.




This process also brought significant changes to women's position in society. Previously largely confined to family and traditional social roles, women began taking responsibility not only for self-defence but also in education, politics, diplomacy and community organising. Through women's councils and organisations, Yazidi women sought solutions to their own problems and participated in decision-making processes within the committees and institutions of the Shengal Autonomous Administration. Women whose will ISIS had sought to break thus began struggling to shape the reconstruction of their society through their own collective will.




Thousands remain displaced




Despite women's struggle for liberation and organisation, the demographic and social devastation inflicted on the Yazidi community by the genocide continues. A significant proportion of those uprooted from Shengal have been unable to return to their homeland despite the years that have passed. Currently, 36,500 people have refugee status, while 200,750 live in Iraq and 150,000 in other countries.




ISIS attacks also targeted the Yazidi faith and cultural heritage, destroying 68 sacred sites. In addition, 2,753 children were left without one or both parents during the attacks, which separated thousands of children from their families. Displacement, family separation and the destruction of sacred sites remain among the main obstacles preventing the community from rebuilding life in its homeland.




Waiting beside the mass graves




One of the most serious obstacles to establishing the fate of missing women today is the existence of mass graves. Numerous sites in and around Shengal contain the remains of Yazidis massacred by ISIS. Exhuming these graves, identifying the remains and returning them to families is essential to determining what happened to the missing.




In Shengal, 77 mass graves have been opened, while 19 remain unopened. Of the remains of 857 people recovered from the excavated graves, 296 have been identified and returned to their families. The remains of another 561 people, whose identities have yet to be established, are being held at a forensic institution in Baghdad for DNA analysis.




A further 91 mass grave cases have been investigated, including 67 in Xanesor and the surrounding area and 24 in Shengal. However, the exhumation of graves and identification of remains are not progressing at the pace families of the missing have been waiting for. The need to collect DNA samples from relatives living in other countries, coordinate between institutions and conduct forensic examinations has prolonged the process. Unopened graves and unidentified remains mean that families seeking to learn the fate of their loved ones continue to wait.




The law exists, but implementation remains inadequate




The Iraqi Parliament adopted Law No. 8, known as the Yazidi Female Survivors Law, on 1 March 2021. The law recognises ISIS crimes against Yazidis, as well as Turkmen, Christian and Shabak communities, as genocide and crimes against humanity. It grants survivors rights including monthly pensions, rehabilitation, healthcare and educational support, land allocation and participation in social life. It also places responsibility on the relevant institutions to locate abducted women, men and children, exhume mass graves and return remains to their families.




However, the rights recognised under the law face new obstacles in practice. In particular, the requirement to file a criminal complaint to obtain compensation and other benefits makes it difficult for genocide survivors to access their rights. Women seeking justice after experiencing grave violations are expected to file criminal complaints and recount their experiences before official authorities as part of the application process. As a result, a significant gap remains between the legal recognition of these rights and survivors' ability to exercise them in practice.

title: Kurdish young man faces trial in Iran on charges carrying death penalty
content:
A young Kurdish man, Mehdî Roşanî, who was detained and arrested following protests held in the city of Melîkşah (Malekshah), in Iran’s Îlam province, between December 2025 and January 2026, appeared before a court in Îlam on 18 November. He is facing several charges, including “enmity against God” and “spreading corruption on earth.”




The Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN) reported that Roşanî and his defence lawyers attended the hearing before the First Branch of the Revolutionary Court in Îlam. Roşanî denied all the charges against him.




Roşanî was first arrested on 16 January during protests in his hometown of Melîkşah. After spending approximately three months in prison, he was released on bail. The Revolutionary Court in Îlam subsequently sentenced him to three years in prison, a sentence that was later reduced to nine months.




Roşanî was arrested again by regime forces on 18 July and transferred to Îlam Central Prison.




Following his re-arrest, the Sixth Branch of the Investigation Department of the Public and Revolutionary Prosecutor's Office in Îlam opened a new case against him. The charges of “enmity against God” and “spreading corruption on earth” brought against Roşanî are offences under Iranian law that can carry the death penalty.

title: DFG pays tribute to newspaper distributors murdered in the 1990s
content:
In a written statement, the Dicle Fırat Journalists Association (DFG) paid tribute to newspaper distributors who were murdered while taking part in the struggle for a free press during the 1990s. The statement recalled that Adil Başkan was murdered in Nusaybin on 9 November 1993; Yalçın Yaşa in Amed on 10 November 1993; Kadir Ipeksürer in Riha (Urfa) on 19 November 1993; Halil Adanır in Êlih (Batman) on 21 November 1992; Adnan Işık in Wan (Van) on 27 November 1993; and Nihat Yakut in Amed on 27 November 1998.




The statement noted that, despite the harsh conditions, threats and pressure of the time, the newspaper distributors struggled to deliver newspapers to the public. It said: “Risking their lives to bring the truth to the public under the most difficult conditions of the time, newspaper distributors stood on the front lines of the struggle for a free press.”




Emphasising that the distributors carried not only newspapers but also the public’s right to access information and the truth, the statement noted that they were known as Apê Musa’s “Little Generals”. It added that the struggle of the 17 newspaper distributors who were murdered, from Halil Adanır to Kadri Bağdu, remains an unforgettable part of the history of the free press.




The DFG concluded its statement with the following words: “We commemorate with respect and longing all newspaper distributors who lost their lives bringing the truth to the public. We once again reaffirm our commitment to keeping their memories alive and continuing the struggle for a free press.”
