Either you are zero-rated, standard-rated, or exempt — or a rate which is neither standard nor zero, like petroleum at 8 percent VAT, somewhere in between. But when you look at the excise duty regime, it’s different, because it’s looking at specific goods, and then there’s a specific tax rate for each of them. Traditionally these were sin taxes, but now it’s been widened.

Section two of the Excise Duty Act seeks to add antique, vintage, or classic vehicles, so there’s a definition for that. That means that further down the line, there’s a specific tax rate applicable to these vehicles. That was the notable amendment to section two — to define what these vehicles are.

Now, this is a hot one. There’s a new section, section 6A: imposition of excise duty on locally purchased or imported telephones upon activation. Interesting. Some have made noise about it, because right now, in the context of excise duty, it’s typically upon importation — as you import goods, that’s the point where excise duty or VAT is applicable. But now we’re seeing that upon activation of a phone, locally purchased or imported, the point at which you’re activating it is where you’re paying this particular excise. That’s a new section 6A of the Excise Duty Act being introduced.

Further down, section 36 of the Excise Duty Act: payment of excise duty on cellular phones. So section 6A is saying that there will be an imposition of excise duty — from July 1, if this passes through, there’ll be duty upon activation of a phone that is either locally purchased or imported — and then section 36 speaks to the payment of excise duty on cellular phones. It’s an additional provision: Section 36 speaks about what is subject to excise duty, so it basically says there’ll be a payment of excise duty on cellular phones, bringing alive this new section 6A. Then if you go to the First Schedule, it says that 25 percent excise duty on imported cellular phones will be applicable. This particular clause takes effect from January 2027.

There are a number of other amendments too — the various rates of excise duty for antique, vintage, or classic vehicles. It’ll be 50 percent of the excisable value. So if you have an antique car — say a 1950s car — with an excisable value of KSh 1 million (about $7,700), the proposed law says you have to pay excise duty of 50 percent of that: KSh 500,000 (about $3,900) on that vintage.

So we go to the next broad proposal, the Tax Procedures Act. So far, those were the explicit taxes, but now we get to the procedures, because there are procedures for how you pay taxes, and there’s a specific law that tackles those procedures. That’s the Tax Procedures Act, and various amendments have been brought into play. Section two speaks about the deletion of “certificate of origin” and the insertion of “virtual asset service provider.” Sometime last year, we saw the Virtual Asset Service Providers Bill being passed, so it’s now an act of Parliament. Basically, it brings to the fore the fact that virtual assets are quite significant in the economy: Bitcoin, forex, digital lending within the virtual asset space, and all that. So there’s a definition of virtual asset service provider in line with that act of Parliament that was passed last year.

Then there’s a new section 6C, which still touches on virtual asset service providers — how they file information returns. They’ve assessed that Kenya is becoming more of a digital economy with all these virtual assets, so now that we have the virtual asset service providers, this is how they need to go about filing information returns. There’s also section 6D, which speaks about agreements for the automatic exchange of information with other countries on virtual asset transactions. Some transactions in the virtual asset space cut across borders, so this proposal says Kenya can now share information with other countries that have implemented this framework, to assess transactions within the virtual asset space. That’s tied to recognizing that there’s a Virtual Asset Service Providers Act in place, and trying to fine-tune how they can better target that space.

There’s the section 10 amendment on deregistration. If for one reason or another you are deregistered in terms of your PIN — you have a PIN, but you’re deregistered — then in the event that you re-register, you can still get back the same PIN, because everyone has a unique PIN number. At least it enhances continuity, because they have your records. It’s easier than having two different PINs, one up until the point you were deregistered and another new one. It ensures continuity of your tax records if you re-register after deregistration.

There’s another one, section 12 of the Tax Procedures Act. I’m within that space, in the investment bank. Right now, one of the requirements for non-residents is that they need to have a PIN as one of the know-your-customer (KYC) documentation requirements. But the Finance Bill is saying that investment banks will no longer require them to have a PIN. It’s reducing compliance costs, because it’s quite lengthy to get a PIN — I’d experienced it previously, with some foreign investors coming in to acquire a PIN; it’s a lengthy process. This one is giving a reprieve, to spur foreign investors coming into the Nairobi Securities Exchange.

Tax avoidance schemes: As we said, this was in section 66 of the VAT Act, but now there’s a new section 18A of the Tax Procedures Act that brings alive these tax avoidance schemes. So they repeal section 66 of the VAT Act and bring in a new clause under the Tax Procedures Act.

There’s another new one, quite interesting: a new section 29A, whereby the KRA — in this case the commissioner — can issue its own assessment. Right now, section 29 of the Tax Procedures Act gives a person the leeway to self-assess. But this new proposal says that over and above you as an individual conducting your self-assessment, the KRA can now come in and issue an assessment independently. There’s some concern that they’ll be overstepping their mandate, going over and above what they are required to do. That’s quite concerning, but we’ll see. We’ve had lots of noise around that.

The other aspect, which is quite an interesting one, is the tax amnesty. In the event that, for one reason or another, you’ve not paid your taxes, there’s normally some interest and some fines that you’re supposed to pay over and above the tax.

Tax amnesty basically waives all those fines and penalties — just pay the tax you’re supposed to pay. The last tax amnesty, which ran through June last year, was on the tax for the year of income ending December 2023. Now this has been extended up to last year, and you have until the end of December to pay the outstanding tax you did not pay for last year, without incurring the penalties and fees. That’s the tax amnesty. As we mentioned earlier, this tax amnesty is expected to yield KSh 30 billion (about $230 million); the last one yielded KSh 50 billion (about $390 million). It brings about an issue of moral hazard: as a taxpayer, I know that at some point the KRA or the National Treasury will come with a tax amnesty, so why should I pay the tax right now? A year or two down the line, I can benefit from a tax amnesty without incurring penalties or fines. That’s an issue coming up with this proposal to extend the tax amnesty.

There are a number of other proposals here. Section 75: The KRA may use the electronic tax system to generate pre-populated tax returns. Going forward, they’ll be able to introduce pre-populated returns in the self-assessment system, so if the KRA brings in this IT system, you’ll be able to generate pre-populated returns, and the assessment is then just going through them and confirming whether they make sense.

There’s also the repeal of the certificate of origin. One of the things we spoke about at the beginning was the definition of certificate of origin being entirely shelved, because the focus on the certificate of origin will no longer be within the Tax Procedures Act but within the East African Community Customs Management Act. That’s the whole point of repealing the definition in section two, and then section 44A repeals the certificate of origin itself. Pretty much a cleanup, to ensure that anything to do with certificates of origin is handled from a customs perspective. There are others — section 86 being replaced with a new section dealing with failure to comply with the electronic tax system, a whole host of things — but by and large, we’re pretty much done with the Tax Procedures Act.

Next we move to miscellaneous fees and levies — two or three proposals here. The first is the reduction of fees paid into the fund from 20 percent to 10 percent. There’s the import declaration fee, and a portion of it ends up in a fund, the Import Declaration Fee Fund. Initially, the portion of the fees that went into this fund was 20 percent, but the proposal is to reduce it to 10 percent. Then section nine deals with the East African Community Customs Management Act. Initially, the import declaration fee, the railway development levy, and the export levy were within the ambit of the EAC Customs Management Act, but now the proposal is to delete that reference. It means that the other levies, which did not eventually end up within the context of the East African Community, will now be included, because initially they had restricted it to just the import declaration fee, the railway development levy, and the export levy. With the deletion, whatever levies are collected will now eventually end up within the context of customs.

Coming to the tail end is the stamp duty. As we mentioned earlier with real estate investment trusts: You have a property you want to transfer, and under the income tax proposals the capital gains tax on that was exempted.

So section 96A now specifically includes instruments that transfer interest in property to a real estate investment trust. If you have a property and you want to transfer it to a REIT, that instrument will now be included within the context of stamp duty — I think just to spur the transfers we’re seeing. If you have a property and you want it included within a REIT, a stamp duty proposal is coming in to redefine it.

Lastly, the road maintenance levy, which is collected through the purchase of petroleum products, petrol and diesel. A bit of it goes into the roads annuity fund. Right now, we are paying 25 shillings (about 19 US cents) per liter as road maintenance levy, and three shillings (about 2 cents) of that goes into the roads annuity fund. The proposal is to reduce what goes to the roads annuity fund from three shillings to one shilling and 50 cents (about 1 US cent). Largely, this is what you call appropriations-in-aid, so it doesn’t have a bearing on the tax revenue we spoke about.

That’s a snapshot of the Finance Bill — quite lengthy, quite detailed. I hope I’ve done it justice in slightly over an hour. It’s my first time just giving a lecture like this, quite an interesting one. Anyway, you can now submit your written memorandum to the Clerk of the National Assembly; there’s an email there that you can see. You can also submit to the Finance Committee of the National Assembly; there’s an email there too. The deadline is next Monday, May 25, by 5 p.m. East Africa Time. There’s no extension, for sure — Kenyans, I know you with extensions. There’s no extension. By 5 p.m. you need to submit your memorandum on the bill. Thanks.

Keith Ang'ana

Thank you very much, Mr. Churchill. That was an amazing presentation, and it has been very enlightening, because the thing about the Finance Bill is that it’s a very tough document to go through, especially because you need to compare it with the previous acts — the Income Tax Act, the VAT Act — and it’s a very tedious thing. But you have been able to break it down for us, and we’ve been able to understand it. So first of all, thank you very much for that. You made it look easy.

Before we release you, there are a couple of questions that have come out of the discussion, and we’d like to put them to you so that you can shed some clarity, so that we understand as we go ahead to make our public participation submissions.

First of all, just a general question, an overview. Do you have an opinion on how this bill compares to last year’s Finance Bill? Is it fair to the citizens, or does it lean more toward the government in terms of collecting more revenue?

Churchill Ogutu

An apples-to-apples comparison will be slightly hard — I may not do it justice. If you look at what was targeted to be collected last year, I think it was KSh 35 billion (about $270 million) in the initial Finance Bill proposal. This time we have KSh 54 billion (about $420 million) that is targeted to be collected, and there’s another KSh 30 billion (about $230 million) from the tax amnesty. So the proposal this time around seems to be quite aggressive. And there are other aspects on the procedures — for instance, the filing, which we now need to front-load, rather than filing by June 30 the way we know it, bringing it two months earlier to April 30. Ostensibly, from what you hear, that gives the KRA some time to do reconciliations and all that, but obviously it will increase compliance costs, if you think about how people will try to implement this. Those are some of the things that stood out for me in the bill.

Keith Ang'ana

Okay. And just generally, as an economist, do you think that the more taxes are increased, the less the government possibly collects? Because from the Finance Bill 2024, there was this issue of the Laffer curve, whereby the government is trying to be more aggressive and increase regulations, but in the end, when the quarterly reports come out, the KRA usually misses its target. So do you think it’ll possibly be the same now, with the introduction of these many amendments on taxes?

Churchill Ogutu

If you look at it from where I started, the tax revenue target, if you compare where we are right now, the supplementary budget, with what is being targeted in the next financial year, there’s an increase of KSh 258 billion (about $2 billion), of which KSh 120 billion (about $930 million) is coming from this Finance Bill and the EAC tax amendments, which are also part of the Finance Bill. The balance, they say, will come either from tightening administrative measures, or they’re just banking on the economy continuing to boom, so that revenue will continue. Remember that you still have the existing tax laws as they are. The Finance Bill, the 57 clauses, is just seeing avenues for other revenue measures.

Out of these KSh 258 billion (about $2 billion), KSh 120 billion (about $930 million) is coming from these new measures. So they’re also hoping that what they collected this financial year, ending in June — however little it is — continues. But already, looking at the numbers up to April and comparing them to where they ideally should be, it points to the fact that they might miss the target. There’s another aspect, what you call tax buoyancy: You look at the percentage growth in tax revenue against the percentage growth in nominal GDP. If the growth in revenues is more than the growth in GDP, that means they can meet their revenue target. But the numbers for the next financial year show that number is below one — it’s 0.7 — so the assumption is that the economy is growing faster than they can collect revenue.

A number of things feed into that. You’re largely looking at the formal sector. On the individual side, you’ve seen that disposable income has pretty much shrunk. On the corporate side, the analysis even in the Economic Survey shows that, as much as profits from businesses are quite significant, they’re not growing as fast as they used to. So the taxes expected from income taxes, whether individual or corporate — or even if you look at consumption, because disposable income has shrunk, you’re not consuming as much as you used to. This feeds into the negative revenue performance we’ve seen, and it challenges the point in your question: We are doing all these tax proposals, yet we know we may not even hit the target, so why do it? It’s still a debatable issue. But ultimately, you may find they are caught in a catch-22.

Step back: We had the medium-term revenue strategy, being implemented in two phases. The first phase started in July 2024 and is supposed to end by June 2027. They’re looking at it in terms of tax revenue to GDP. When they wanted to start it off, it was 14.3 percent tax revenue to GDP; the goal was to increase it to 20 percent. That’s what they were looking at in July 2024. There were some measures in that medium-term revenue strategy which potentially could have benefited people: They were looking at reducing VAT from 16 percent gradually, possibly to 14 percent; the corporate tax rate from 30 percent to 25 percent; the PAYE top band from 35 percent to 25 percent. But we missed the boat — June 2024 happened, and it went back. So even now, they still haven’t reached there. You can pity the government that they want to reach 20 percent, but even looking at the numbers for the next financial year, we are still at 14 percent.

We haven’t even moved, even within the context of implementing this medium-term revenue strategy. So you can pity them, but you also have to be alive to the economy — the economy probably is not solid enough to support higher taxes, or these tax proposals.

Keith Ang'ana

Yes, thank you. I think that sheds more light on it. On that note, I wanted to ask some questions about the specific amendments. This is something you’ve mentioned already, but some clarity was needed on the particular point of section 6A of the Excise Duty Act, imposing a 25 percent tax on mobile phones at the time of activation. The question that’s been asked is: At what particular point in time can we say a phone is activated? Is it when it’s been imported, or when it’s turned on? How will this work?

Churchill Ogutu

I think more of the latter, at the point where you turn it on, rather than at the point of importation. Ideally this stuff happens at the point of importation, whereby as you import these goods, you have the import declaration forms and all the requisite taxes and levies you have to pay. But this time, from the look of things — or the intent of this, if it sails through — you don’t pay them at that point, but at the point of activation. And that raises legitimate concerns: What is activation?

Keith Ang'ana

And is it levied on the importer and then transferred to the buyer, or directly on the buyer? It seems like — 

Churchill Ogutu

It seems like it’s on the buyer, at the point of activation of the phone, because the buyer is the one who has to activate it. So it means that even the purchase price will have to go up by 25 percent, because that’s the excise duty being slapped on at the point of activation. So it’s on the buyer — the consumer, ultimately.

Keith Ang'ana

Okay. The next question, because this is something that has generated a lot of heat on Twitter: There’s section 24 of the Income Tax Act, which provides the KRA with powers to tax companies on their retained profits — something about if a company does not pay out at least 60 percent of its profits as dividends, the KRA will treat part of the remaining profit as deemed dividends and go ahead and tax it. So first of all, have you seen that part? And the question being asked is whether this would choke businesses and make them lose the incentive for which they carry out their operations, because now the KRA will also be taxing more of the profits that haven’t been paid out as dividends. So the question is: What has been the practice with the KRA and dividends, and what does that section actually mean?

Churchill Ogutu

This section brings a different interpretation of what a deemed dividend is. Initially, the wording was that they considered a portion of the income. The example I gave: You have revenues of, say, KSh 1 million (about $7,700); expenses of KSh 600,000 (about $4,600); so you have profit of, say, KSh 400,000 (about $3,100), assuming you don’t have anything other than that. Part of it you can say is retained earnings; part of it could be taken through. But the assumption here is that there’s tax avoidance, in a way, by not distributing dividends. They need to look at why you are not making dividend payments — there could be a myriad of reasons behind that — whereas the lens being used, as it is, is that whatever profit you have, you have to be paying a portion of it as dividends. The underlying assumption is that at least 60 percent of what you did not distribute is now deemed to be the dividend paid to your shareholders. But it assumes a number of things. It assumes you just have money there that ideally you should be distributing as dividends — but potentially you could be retaining it; you could be trying to expand the business, or timing investment decisions for the future. So it’s not that you have to distribute it as dividends, but the requirement, as it is in the proposal, is that you should be distributing it as dividends. Other than that, they just assume at least 60 percent of it should be treated as if it’s been distributed — which might not necessarily be the case. That’s what’s problematic about this particular proposal.

Keith Ang'ana

So when the proposal says at least 60 percent, does it mean the baseline is 60 percent and the KRA can go up, if they want, to a particular percentage?

Churchill Ogutu

Yeah, that’s the thing, because it speaks about at least 60 percent. So in the assessment they may say: We’ve looked at you, and probably it’s 100 percent that you disbursed as dividends, and you have to pay tax on that distributed dividend — as it is, because it’s a deemed dividend. Ultimately, the KRA is the one coming in and saying 100 percent is what you distributed to your shareholders, when probably you didn’t even distribute to shareholders. But that’s the assumption this particular proposal is hinging on.

Keith Ang'ana

Just based on that: There’s the problem of how the KRA has been given more interventionary powers to audit people’s accounts, including their banks and their M-Pesa, to demand tax, and to punish non-compliance with fines. Do you think it’s advisable to give the tax body these powers?

Churchill Ogutu

I think, by and large, the KRA already has the necessary tools to conduct whatever audit they might want on a taxpayer. I think this particular proposal is the one that speaks about how, over and above the self-assessment, they can independently conduct their own assessment. At least it has to be within the current framework; it shouldn’t infringe on your privacy. The moment it goes into that, it negates data protection — because time and again, finance bills bring up this issue around data protection, with the KRA coming in and infringing on the data protection laws we enjoy as Kenyans. Ultimately it has to be within a certain framework. I believe they can’t assess unless they come up with some tools — I don’t know what tools they’re looking at to do assessments. But I think they might be targeting some of these other professionals, in my view, who are not within this ambit, because time and again they’ve been saying that the formally employed are the ones under personal income tax. We have other professionals — doctors, lawyers, professionals who don’t fit, who don’t get the salaries subject to this kind of personal income tax regime. So unless they want to widen the tax bracket to home in on some of these — ultimately, it has to be within a proper framework, not infringing on privacy, and within the context of data protection laws.

Keith Ang'ana

Okay, great. The next question touches on section 12 of the Tax Procedures Act, which basically states that a foreigner shall be exempt from the requirement of having a KRA PIN when opening an account with an investment bank. The question being asked is: What might be the motive for this, and might it by any chance increase the chances of fraud?

Churchill Ogutu

Ah, well, that’s at the heart of my bread and butter, because I’m an investment banker. Typically, as part of KYC, any local who opens an account with an investment bank has KYC documents required of them: a national ID, a PIN, not necessarily a bank statement, those kinds of things. Some of those also apply to foreign investors who want to invest in the Nairobi Securities Exchange — they’re required to have their passports, and they’re also required to have a PIN for the purposes of taxation. But now this is being removed. As I mentioned earlier, it tends to be a lengthy process for a foreigner to acquire a PIN in the country, so they’re just removing this compliance burden, which is part of the KYC documentation. I think it’s quite good. The motive is probably to stimulate foreign investment — or rather, foreign equity portfolio flows. Investors who invest in the Nairobi Securities Exchange are called portfolio investors, not foreign direct investors. So they want to stimulate that activity. It could be beneficial, as I said, within the investment bank — it’s something that’s quite welcome to us.

Keith Ang'ana

Something that you deal in. Okay, so it seems like we’re not done with section 24, because people still have more questions on it. The issue is that dividend distribution tax is already captured under corporate tax, meaning the income is already taxed. So does the introduction of this mean the KRA is placing a tax on top of another tax?

Churchill Ogutu

Quite an interesting one. You look at it to the extent of the businesses. I was just assuming a simple business where you have your profits, and then you can declare dividends — the same way Safaricom, for instance, recently declared a dividend on part of its profit. That dividend is paid from the profits. But before you get to the profits, there are the other expenses that have already been paid, which may typically exclude the payment of dividends. So in this scenario, it’s now the deemed dividend — the one they just assume you were supposed to have paid but did not pay out to your shareholders. I think that’s pretty much where they’re coming from with this proposal: this income — why haven’t you paid it as dividends? But it raises another conversation around how they’re sort of chaperoning all businesses into paying dividends as a must. Like, you have to pay dividends as a must, or the counter is that if you don’t pay dividends, it’s at the discretion of the KRA — at least 60 percent of whatever remains is now deemed as a dividend that was paid. I think that’s the heart of it.

Keith Ang'ana

Yeah, and I think you’ve just touched on this with your last statement. But the question being asked, which I think is a very tough question, is how this new change affects alignment with the Companies Act regarding dividend policy autonomy.

Churchill Ogutu

Those are the issues that come to the fore as you start implementing some of these proposals, and I think, by and large, we’ll keep hearing them in the context of the ongoing public participation, because they bring other angles that the framers of the bill potentially had not considered in the first instance. That’s why we have to give our submissions by next week Monday, to bring out some of these issues. But that’s a legitimate issue, because now you’re interfering with the dividend policy of a company.

Keith Ang'ana

Okay. We already saw a drop in the money being transacted through M-Pesa in the latest Kenya National Bureau of Statistics report. Now this Finance Bill actually proposes taxing mobile money more. Please elaborate on that section of the bill and maybe touch on its effect on people and the economy — since of course there’s a lot of digital money penetration, and we as a country are known for M-Pesa.

Churchill Ogutu

That speaks to the aspect of interchange fees — the inclusion of interchange fees, cards, and a whole array of payment platforms within the ambit of withholding tax. I think we first need to get better clarity on what the intention was, because on one hand, if you hear from the National Treasury, it’s like they’re targeting the providers of payment cards; that’s what they were keenly pursuing. Yet at the same time, mobile money payment is also part of payments — you can also make payments through virtual cards, or through mobile. So clarity needs to be sought on who is being pursued by this particular proposal. But obviously, if you look at it in the context of mobile money, assuming that will be within this ambit and subject to this withholding tax, it will definitely increase transaction costs — which I don’t think is the intention, looking at the Economic Survey data showing that transactions have somehow slowed down in the economy. As you increase transaction costs, obviously it will dampen the mobile money transactions we’re seeing in the economy.

Keith Ang'ana

The other question being asked is that Mbadi, and also President Ruto, had promised to look at the tax bands and lower PAYE — and, of course, you mentioned this within the medium-term revenue strategy — where the current top PAYE rate of 35 percent is higher than the 30 percent corporate rate, contrary to the national tax policy, which recommends that individuals should not be taxed more than companies. Is it feasible to just reduce PAYE?

Churchill Ogutu

Is it feasible to reduce PAYE? That was contained in the medium-term revenue strategy and the national tax policy: harmonizing the corporate tax, which was to be lowered from 30 percent to 25 percent, and also ensuring that the individual tax rate — the top band of PAYE — comes down from 35 percent to 25 percent. Because as it is right now, you’d rather pay the corporate tax rate, because it’s lower than the top band at 35 percent, depending on the income band you’re in. Remember this is graduated: Currently the first KSh 24,000 (about $185) is at 10 percent; the next KSh 8,333 (about $64) is at 25 percent; and then from KSh 32,333 (about $250) all the way to KSh 500,000 (about $3,900) at 30 percent, and so on. So I think they might have to do some simulations, not just look at reducing PAYE and whether it’s feasible. Because if you reduce it, it will lead to money being returned to people’s pockets, and then they’ll be able to consume more. So you’re reducing this, but you can see VAT going higher as a result. The last time, the National Treasury mentioned there are simulations ongoing.

Tied to that, speaking of zero-rating: That proposal came in around February, when we had CS Mbadi saying that the first KSh 30,000 (about $230) will be zero-rated. Remember, we don’t have a zero rate — the first KSh 24,000 (about $185) is at 10 percent; there’s no 0 percent, but we have a personal tax relief; everyone gets KSh 2,400 (about $19) in relief. So the way to think about this zero-rating: Is it that people who earn below KSh 30,000 (about $230) on a monthly basis get 0 percent? Also remember it’s a graduated scale, so if you’re earning KSh 200,000 (about $1,500), your first KSh 30,000 in this framework would be 0 percent — will it be applicable to everyone, because of the graduated scale as we know it, or will it be limited to people at or below KSh 30,000 shillings, so that they get 0 percent? And then the next band, between KSh 30,000 and KSh 50,000 (about $390), will reduce from 30 percent to 25 percent. So technically you’re jumping from 0 percent to 25 percent. And does it mean that, assuming the corporate tax rate comes down to 25 percent, everyone else. . . . ? There are a few things still up in the air; we need clarity around that.

In addition, we’ve been hearing — and I also mentioned this earlier — that they want to introduce PAYE even to some professionals who currently are not salaried employees, in consultancy or otherwise; they want to bring them within the PAYE regime. Is it that, as they do this for low-income employees — because I think the target is everyone below 50,000 (about $390), who one way or another are getting some form of relief — they now want to offset it with these professionals coming on board? Those are some of the things being worked out right now, from my sense.

But now the question is: We’ve seen the Finance Bill, and people are now doing public participation on the Finance Bill as it is. If they want to introduce this and have it passed by June 30, it means they will introduce an amendment well after the public participation stage has come and passed. We’ve been telling people they need to give their submissions by next week Monday. That closes. And then much later — because typically there’s the first reading of the bill, which is literally a first reading: This is the Finance Bill 2026, it proposes to make amendments, blah blah blah. Then it goes to the second reading stage, where there’s a report by the Departmental Committee on Finance and National Planning. This report also incorporates the public participation, and then Parliament debates the report — the merits of the current 57 proposals.

But then at the same time, it introduces some amendments before it goes to the third stage. So if this particular proposal is introduced, we’re looking at it being introduced well after the public participation has been conducted. Potentially, as I said, will they go for zero-rating, or will they — I don’t know — increase? I don’t know what modalities they’ll use. Some of them may be prohibitive, but people won’t get a chance to weigh in on them, because it will be well after the public participation. Those are the things that are still mind-boggling — how they’ll go about it. Or does it mean that, if this Finance Bill window closes, they introduce a tax amendment bill further down the line? That would be around six months from now, December thereabouts. So it’s still up in the air at this point.

Keith Ang'ana

Okay, and I think that’s a great point on which to finish up. It’s been an amazing session. Thank you very much once again. Just as we end, I want to ask you to remind us how to make our views known to Parliament. If you can take us through the submission process one last time.

Churchill Ogutu

You can submit your written memorandum — you can actually write it. I know I’m speaking to. . . .  there’s normally this debate about the millennials and the Gen Zs. So for the millennials, and those who are Gen X and all that, you can hand-deliver it to the Office of the Clerk, first floor, Main Parliament Buildings, Nairobi. You know where it is. I don’t know whether this will be applicable to other people, because this is not just a Nairobi affair; it’s also for people in other parts of the country. If you’re not able to hand-deliver your written or printed submission to the Office of the Clerk, you can send an email to the Clerk of the National Assembly, which you can see on the screen, cna@parliament.go.ke, and also to the Finance Committee, chaired by the Honorable Kuria Kimani, at financecommitteena@parliament.go.ke. The deadline is 5 p.m. next Monday, May 25 — East Africa Time. There’s no extension. By the way, that will be the day after a team in North London lifts the league. Remember: You lift the league first on Sunday, and then on Monday you submit. Whichever sequencing you want — lift the league first and then submit, or submit and then lift the league — you have to submit by next week Monday, 5 p.m. East Africa Time [Submissions have since closed. The email addresses above are given as they were shared during the lecture.].

Keith Ang'ana

Yeah, and they should look out for any public hearings that will be happening.

Churchill Ogutu

Yeah.

Keith Ang'ana

Yes, thank you very much, and I think we have come to the end of this. 

Shukran sana

.

Churchill Ogutu

Thank you for having me.

author: CMI Argentina
title: Neuquén: piden la renuncia de Carlos Quintriqueo a la CTA por su alianza electoral con Sobisch
content:
La conformación de una lista electoral entre el ex gobernador Jorge Sobisch y el actual secretario general de la Central de Trabajadores de la Argentina (CTA) Neuquén, Carlos Quintriqueo, generó el rechazo de distintos sindicatos de la provincia. Las organizaciones cuestionan que Quintriqueo haya puesto el sello de su partido a disposición de Sobisch para competir por la gobernación.










Escuchar el reporte de Fm Pocahullo de San Martín de los Andes




El repudio se centra tanto en la reaparición política de Sobisch, quien fue gobernador de Neuquén en tres oportunidades y responsable político del operativo represivo en el que fue asesinado el docente Carlos Fuentealba, como en el acompañamiento de Quintriqueo a esa candidatura.




Ante esta decisión, sindicatos como el gremio judicial, ATEN y otras organizaciones docentes, junto con la CTERA y distintas entidades gremiales, reclamaron la renuncia de Quintriqueo a la conducción de la CTA.




Carolina de Benedetti, secretaria local del gremio docente, expresó el rechazo a la alianza y cuestionó el regreso de Sobisch a la política provincial. “Nosotros seguimos sosteniendo, a pesar de que la Justicia dice lo contrario, que Sobich es el asesino de nuestro compañero Carlos Fuentealba y seguimos exigiendo justicia en ese sentido”, manifestó.




De Benedetti sostuvo que quienes conducen la CTA deben representar los intereses de las organizaciones y de la clase trabajadora. Por eso, consideró urgente que Quintriqueo y quienes acompañen la alianza den un paso al costado.




“Hay un acto de traición con la clase trabajadora, con los otros sindicatos que acompañaron ese proceso de unidad para la conformación de la lista y la presentación de elecciones”, afirmó. También señaló que la decisión de llevar a Sobisch como candidato no representa los intereses de los sectores trabajadores.







Fuente: 

https://agencia.farco.org.ar/2026/11/19/neuquen-piden-la-renuncia-de-carlos-quintriqueo-a-la-cta-por-su-alianza-electoral-con-sobisch/




La entrada 

Neuquén: piden la renuncia de Carlos Quintriqueo a la CTA por su alianza electoral con Sobisch

 se publicó primero en 

Indymedia Argentina Centro de Medios Independientes (( i ))

.

author: Gustavo Faleiros
title: Quase todas as cidades já sofrem com eventos extremos. O que farão os prefeitos?
content:
Quer receber os textos desta coluna em primeira mão no seu e-mail? Assine a newsletter Ligando os pontos, enviada toda quinta-feira. Para receber as próximas edições, 

inscreva-se aqui

.







Mal terminou a eleição presidencial e arrisco dizer que a política climática vai ocupar um espaço inédito daqui até as próximas eleições. Enquanto os temas econômicos e em especial o ajuste fiscal domina a agenda de Brasília, a dura realidade das mudanças climáticas vai se impondo em nosso cotidiano. São inúmeros episódios de cidades isoladas pela seca na Amazônia e tempestades deixando prejuízos no Sul e no Sudeste. Sem falar nas lavouras de soja e milho penando no Centro-Oeste.




Essa percepção de que a escolha para prefeitos e vereadores vai ditar os rumos da política é reforçada com a publicação dos 

resultados da última pesquisa de informações básicas municipais do IBGE

, a Munic.  

O levantamento mostra um crescimento no número de municípios afetados por eventos extremos climáticos. Já chega a 49,5% a quantidade de cidades brasileiras impactadas por alagamentos entre 2021 e 2024, sendo que na pesquisa anterior essa porcentagem era de 35%. Quando falamos de secas, é ainda pior: 59% dos municípios relataram falta de água.




No resultado agregado, é impressionante ver que apenas 385 dos 5,5 mil municípios brasileiros responderam não ter sofrido qualquer tipo de evento climático extremo.  

Isso significa que 

93% tiveram problemas

 nos últimos anos.

 Me pergunto como estão, neste momento, os prefeitos preparando-se para enfrentar a pior fase do Super El Niño. Provavelmente não estão. Será que os cortes de gastos federais esperados com o ajuste fiscal poderão afetar a capacidade dos municípios de adaptação aos efeitos das mudanças climáticas?




Estamos às portas do verão. É o verão que se segue ao mais quente já ocorrido na Europa. Os dados sobre o impacto das ondas de calor que passaram por lá são impressionantes: uma primeira estimativa indica que 

o calor extremo causou a morte de 50 mil pessoas

 nos países da União Europeia. Há uma trágica previsão de que 13,3 mil brasileiros, especialmente do Norte e Nordeste, podem morrer por conta do calor extremo causado pelo Super El Niño, de acordo com relatório do Laboratório de Impacto Climático da Universidade de Chicago, 

divulgado em setembro

.




Se ondas de calor se repetirem por aqui, a infra-estrutura das cidades precisa estar pronta para lidar com a realidade de um influxo de pessoas aos postos de saúde. Vejam que já tem sido um desafio lidar com o impacto da poluição por queimadas este ano em grandes cidades da Amazônia, como Manaus e Santarém. Crianças e idosos sempre são os mais afetados.




Há algumas semanas, também foram 

publicadas avaliações inéditas

 sobre o impacto do calor e dos eventos extremos na saúde das mulheres.  

Em muitos países, são as mulheres que estão nas funções mais expostas ao calor extremo, seja na agricultura ou em subempregos sem qualidade alguma e sem qualquer direito ao descanso.

 Além disso, o aumento da temperatura tem impacto direto na saúde das mulheres grávidas e das mães. Afetadas pela instabilidade causada pelos eventos extremos, eles são vítimas de mais violência, mais desigualdade.




Mais calor também representa mais casos de gravidez de risco, com abortos espontâneos e nascimentos premataturos. É alentador saber que já existe no mundo uma rede formada por profissionais de saúde para se preparam para as mudanças climáticas. Recentemente, fiquei impressionado ao conhecer a iniciativa HERA, totalmente dedicada a apoiar mulheres impactadas pelo calor extremo. Um dos instrumentos que utiliza é 

prover um seguro gratuito para mães de baixa renda

. Algo que lhes permite sobreviver a impactos como perda de emprego e quebra de safra.




Precisamos de respostas concretas




Como se vê, os eventos extremos climáticos levam a política ao nível mais básico, exigindo respostas concretas. A mudança climática já é e será ainda mais debatida como uma questão de justiça social. Sabemos que, nos momentos de crise, como foi durante a pandemia da Covid-19, são os mais pobres que sofrem as piores consequências. Agora, quando vemos a urgente necessidade de adaptação às mudanças climáticas, a desigualdade também fica em evidência. Há gente rica comprando terra com nascentes de água e planejando autossuficiência, em alarmante sinal de racismo ambiental. Precisamos de um poder público que nos proteja contra a sanha privatista.




Me chamou a atenção uma postagem nas redes sociais da deputada federal Erika Hilton (PSOL-SP), que usou a falta de ação frente aos eventos extremos para expor seus oponentes políticos. Em um vídeo no Instagram, vemos declarações do prefeito de São Paulo, Ricardo Nunes (PMDB), e de outros expoentes da extrema direita, como os deputados Nikolas Ferreira (PL-MG) e Julia Zanatta (PL-SC), sobre as ameaças de uma fantasiosa “ideologia de gênero”, em contraste com imagens de inundações nas cidades que representam. O post termina com uma pergunta pertinente: “Seu político está preocupado com você ou com uma pessoa trans fazendo xixi?”




A política municipal e as eleições para prefeitos e vereadores têm que ir além da guerra cultural que tem dominado as disputas eleitorais. A matriz econômica de cada candidato, se mais ou menos liberal, não faz sentido em uma era na qual as comunidades dependem de uma concertação pública para defender a sobrevivência em um mundo alterado pelo clima extremo.  

O gestor público, em última instância, tem que lidar com a realidade ambiental em que todos estamos inseridos: há momentos com pouca água e outros com muita água. Parece simples, mas é o ciclo natural que determina a presença de vetores de doenças, como o mosquito da dengue, e o preço da energia elétrica que consumimos.




Um dos livros publicados na última década que melhor expõe esta tensão entre o delírio da direita e a necessidade de uma nova política climática foi escrito pelo sociólogo francês, Bruno Latour. 

“Onde Aterrar”, originalmente publicado em 2017

 sob o impacto da primeira eleição de Donald Trump, e depois lançado no Brasil em 2020 pela editora Bazar do Tempo, discorre sobre o apelo do negacionismo climático em um mundo em que as classes trabalhadoras do Norte Global foram privadas do sentido de comunidade. O desmantelamento dos sindicatos, a desindustrialização e a globalização econômica foram terreno fértil para os populistas de direita.




Em mundo sem perspectivas, apontar o dedo para “ideologias de gênero” ou “terroristas ambientais” é uma forma bastante efetiva de angariar votos. A promessa de que tudo voltará a ser como antes, o 

Make

 

America Great Again

 ou os “bons tempos da ditadura militar” são convites tentadores. Por isso, Bruno Latour, que sempre foi um crítico preciso do movimento ambientalista, sugere que o caminho é descer ao nível do chão, das comunidades, das cidades. Os eventos extremos climáticos representam exatamente essa conexão entre os fenômenos globais e a política local. Ameaçados pelas secas e alagamentos, nós vamos precisar discutir a nação a partir do nosso quintal.

author: S.C.
title: Haldol First, Questions Later: My Psychiatric Detention
content:
T

his is not a post I wanted to write. I wanted to be able to go through my psychiatric admission patient file and affirm that healthcare providers definitively met their duty to the standard of care, and hewed as closely as possible to their Hippocratic oaths — within reason, of course. I wanted to be able to affirm that any initial feelings I had of betrayal and victimization were likely just figments of an overactive imagination, and potentially even evocative of a budding persecutory delusional disorder, and I should do my best to banish the thought.




But I can’t.




As the documents slowly trickled in from my family physician (because the hospital never provided any to me directly, despite my pleas), those feelings only deepened. Something monstrous really did happen to me in April of 2026. Doctors didn’t just breach the standard of care, but brazenly, maliciously, perhaps even gleefully continued to traumatize me, time and time again. This was not care. This was its evil twin: harm.







My first inkling that something might be amiss with my patient record was when I lay half-dead on the floor of a cold room, having been freshly injected with what I now understand to be a powerful antipsychotic drug, and my Form 42 (which informs a patient in writing that they are being detained at a psychiatric facility for a mandatory assessment) was carelessly tossed in by the doctor like some throwaway, rubber-stamp formality to be dispensed with without explanation




He checked two boxes where he indicated that he believed I was suffering from a mental disorder, and that I had:




1) shown a lack of competence to care for myself, and




2) this lack of competence would likely result in serious physical impairment of me.




That’s very odd, I thought. I had a good job, a lovely wife, two amazing daughters I saw off to school that morning, and I drove myself down to the emergency room asking for a sick note for work. Was I really among what the French call “les incompetents”?




And who exactly was he to judge, anyway? He never physically examined me. Actually, come to think of it, he never once 

spoke

 to me. So, all of a sudden, I am being deprived of my freedom and drugged against my will because a physician who never once entered the same room as me believes I’m in such a degenerative mental state that I can’t eat, dress myself, or tend to my own wounds? No. That didn’t sound right. There must be some misunderstanding.




It’s worth noting that in the entire lead-up to my being hauled out of the psych room by six security guards and then administered Haldol on an emergency basis, no one once told me what particular ailment they believed I was suffering from. Sure, a mental health social worker shoved a pill in my face and told me to take it, but since she didn’t tell me what it was or what it did, I refused. It only became clear much later, when I reviewed my records, why everyone I encountered seemed so scared of me. I was deemed to be in “psychosis” (which apparently a lot of people seem to associate erroneously with the term “psycho” — thanks, Hitchcock).




I really didn’t understand how the physician made this assessment, so I resolved to get the ER consult note. When it eventually came from my GP (again), rather than being clear and elucidating, I found that note to drip with scorn, derision, and vague non-descriptive psychobabble that made it seem as if he had actually made a real investigation into my condition, when he clearly had not.




The title of his ER note? “Chief Complaint: Bizarre.” Okay. That’s a pretty good title… for a work of medical fiction. That’s supposed to be a space where the doctor writes what the patient was complaining about on that day — not a space to cheekily slander the patient’s presentation. I told triage that I was simply looking for a sick note for work. Once again, I found the doctor inverting the typical power dynamic that I had come to expect in the Canadian healthcare experience.




This had all started a few months earlier when I shared with my family doctor some traits of mine that I thought might be consistent with ADHD: traits like executive dysfunction, forgetfulness, and binge eating were just some of the classic indicators I felt underscored the need for more focus in my life. She largely agreed with the self-assessment, but instead of sending me to an occupational therapist or psychotherapist, she started me straight away on Vyvanse, 30 mg. For a while, it was great: I was more focused at work, and became a more attentive father to my children. But things took a turn for the worse when I went away for a work trip in the days leading up to the event.




While on this trip, I came across several startling signs that something was seriously amiss in the provincial government’s regulation of the highway transportation industry. I won’t go more into it than that, but let’s just say that the level of corruption I personally witnessed jeopardized thousands of lives on my province’s roadways, and I resolved to try and stop it. I also discovered several new tax loopholes that people involved in this corruption were exploiting, and I was determined to try to interdict them as well. Two days later, I’d be involuntarily admitted to a provincial psych ward.




When I returned to the office, I found out that the unit I was assigned to would be severely diminished in its capacities. Instead of increasing scrutiny of certain tax records, a top-down edict had been declared that our unit would effectively do the opposite, and cease serious scrutiny of the various schemes we were looking at. I immediately thought about becoming a whistleblower regarding this upside-down approach, and was also thinking about going to my member of provincial parliament to address the highway transportation issues. But first, I needed some real time and space to think about what I was going to do, and plan my next moves. And so my idea to obtain a work sick note from my local ER was born. Big mistake.




Back to the ER note: what comes after the title is not much better. Incredibly vague terms are bandied about like “disordered thinking,” “ideas of reference with people watching,” and “paranoid thoughts” — things I never told the doctor, nor anyone else for that matter. And yet the ER note made it seem as if he himself had made those investigations. He also did a bit of CYA, saying that I had refused a physical examination.




I reject that statement in the strongest possible terms. That doctor avoided me like the plague, and never once made any attempt at conversation. It was as if he knew what he was going to do from the moment I walked in. With him, it was Haldol first, questions later.




In fact, the doctor made no real effort to abide by the terms of the Health Care Consent Act either — he certainly didn’t ever tell me what he was injecting me with, nor did he make any effort to gain consent from my would-be “secondary decision-maker,” my spouse, whom they were keeping in a separate room (probably so as not to traumatize us together). I had brought my wife and then called my mother-in-law to come to the ER because I had a sense of foreboding that something awful might happen to me, and that I needed them to keep me safe. Ultimately, however, when my wife started to feel a little dizzy, they led them both out of the room, leaving me alone.




The first time I knew what drug I was “administered with security assistance,” it was two months later upon consulting my ER note. On the day of the event, I had no idea what was in that syringe. It could have been anything. I thought I was going to die. This kind of cowboy behaviour doesn’t just show clinician ignorance, it evinces real intent to harm. Mens Rea. Malice aforethought.




So I kept pushing for the documentation that authorized my detention to see if some good reason had been articulated to so brazenly abrogate my Charter rights (the fundamental protections guaranteed by Canada’s constitution).




And when I finally received it, six months later (once again through my GP), I was not impressed with what I saw: seven words of extremely vague psychobabble symptomology without reference to any facts or events — just rank aspersions cast about my character and condition. Under his own observations, the doctor simply wrote “disorganized thinking,” and under facts relayed to him by others, “grandiose delusions” and “ideas of reference.”




I’ve since been able to ascertain that a well-executed Form 1 should relay real facts and answer a lot of the same basic 5W1H questions (who, what, where, when, why, how), in a way that’s similar to an indictment. Examples can include “patient screaming and attempting to punch orderly” or “patient yelling at nurse and running after her down the hall.” Mine contained no such details. Only the vaguest possible psychiatric terms, potentially describing a rationale for ascribing a ‘psychosis.’ I still have no idea where he got “disorganized thinking” from — particularly since he never spoke to me or examined me, nor did my loved ones ever relay to him that I was suffering from “grandiose delusions” or “ideas of reference.” They explicitly reject both those terms and really anything on that form. As far as I know, the doctor just decided to pluck those terms out of thin air.




All of this wouldn’t be so bad if it weren’t for the fact that after being psychiatrically processed, and CT scanned, and subjected to all manner of Geneva Convention mistreatment under drug duress, a resident psychiatrist did confirm the existence of a ‘psychosis’ and put me on a path for powerful, lifelong antipsychotic drugging. This wasn’t based on any auditory or visual hallucinations, or really any kind of thinking that was tremendously disorganized. No, it was because I told them that through my work, I had uncovered some far-ranging tax avoidance schemes that could potentially destabilize the nation’s tax base. This was apparently the extent of my delusional thinking and sufficient grounds to confirm a psychosis.




Would they say this about a lawyer’s case? Or a police officer’s investigation? No. But for some reason, “thinking tax stuff might be important” is enough to certify a delusional disorder and continue psychiatric drug therapy, maybe forever.




Later, the same resident would also invent fabrications in my patient file that I was “full of energy” and “needing a lot less sleep” — things I really don’t ever remember telling them. I now know that these fabrications are the classic indicators of bipolar disorder.




This is relevant because an outpatient psychiatrist would later diagnose bipolar disorder on the strength of these fabrications, as a justification for continued antipsychotic treatment.




This is not a trivial matter. Antipsychotic drugging comes with serious risks and side effects. I felt drowsy, had anhedonia, gained a lot of weight, and generally couldn’t concentrate at work.




After talking with my family physician I am now off of the antipsychotics, but the PTSD and trauma disorder remain. Some days I wake up extremely angry, other days sad, still others I get concerned that these doctors are still doing this stuff to other people like Nicholas Jordan Wagter (the Canadian biophysics researcher who gained viral attention in May 2026 after being involuntarily detained under British Columbia’s Mental Health Act). I’m just lucky I was able to break free. If I didn’t have my family behind me, I’m quite sure I would be pacing an asylum solitary cell for the next 20 years, otherwise.




Some days, I really feel as though I was the victim of bona fide crimes. Fraud (fabricating medical records), battery, administration of a noxious substance, false imprisonment… serious stuff that if these doctors didn’t have the cover of a white coat, they wouldn’t get away with. I have been advised that it wouldn’t be wise to legally pursue this, because cops will just default to “the patient is clearly crazy” and I might actually get a ticket back to the hospital (police can issue mental health forms too).




I have a reason to think that at least one of the doctors involved has a certain level of support in these efforts, which means it might be more systemic in nature than just targeting my own person. Unlike 99.9% of ER doctors in town, he has no patient reviews available, which raises suspicions that he’s having his online image massaged and curated by outside parties.




This flip side of this is that the one Facebook post of him through the hospital’s foundation site has literally dozens of generic “great doctor” and “well deserved” comments (some anonymous person made a donation in his honour to the university hospital’s foundation — not normally an accolade that deserves that level of plaudits).




The combination of these two indicia is fairly compelling evidence that his online image is being massaged by someone. Who that is, I have no idea but they probably are not local.




In the end that’s what bothers me the most about my experience. How “through the looking glass” foreign it all was to me. “Sentence first!” the Queen of Hearts bellowed to Alice….




As a student of history I know for a fact that this is exactly how political psychiatry works in dictatorships. Wouldn’t it be nice to have your critics summarily locked up without jury trial, away from lawyers, because their thoughts have been deemed sick, “disorganized,” delusional?




I am confident my doctors completely and totally abandoned their Hippocratic Oaths, and their behaviours that day were more in line with certain terror states than the Canadian healthcare system.




I am terrified that I won’t be the last patient to get subjected to this treatment — and I fear that perhaps the second time, I won’t be so lucky as to be released after three and a half days of “swearing never to have delusional thinking regarding tax schemes.”




As much as I try, I will never be free from this experience.

Mad In America

.

author: admin
title: Indigenous Environmental Network urges Congress to reject the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.
content:
On Wednesday, in a shocking attack against Tribal sovereignty, Senate Democrats voted to move forward with the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) (S. 5653), a bill steeped in environmental racism that would legally ensure the rapid buildout of fossil fuel infrastructure and AI data centers, while stripping away the federal-Tribal consultation process.

Senators Martin Heinrich (D-NM) and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI) are leading the effort, alongside far-right Republican colleagues Mike Lee (R-UT) and Shelley Capito (R-WV), to enact an aggressive attack on the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) Section 106 Tribal consultation process. In addition to undermining Tribal consultation, the BAAJA erases protections under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), Clean Water Act (CWA), and Endangered Species Act (ESA), paving the way to bring hyperscale data centers and natural gas projects online without critical guardrails for the land, water, and animals.

The Senate voted Wednesday 65-31 to invoke a cloture vote, which is a procedural vote that formally ends debate and allows the bill to move forward. Consideration of amendments is expected to begin Thursday, after which the bill will move into a final vote on passage before moving to the House. Despite the BAAJA being vastly opposed among climate justice groups, Tribal Nations, and Indigenous organizations, 14 Democrats voted to move forward with the bill; Chris Coons (DE), John Fetterman (PA), Ruben Gallego (AZ), Kirsten Gillibrand (NY), Martin Heinrich (NM), John Hickenlooper (CO), Jack Reed (RI), Jacky Rosen (NV), Brian Schatz (HI), Chuck Schumer (NY), Elissa Slotkin (MI), Mark Warner (VA), Raphael Warnock (GA), and Sheldon Whitehouse (RI) all voted yes.

In perhaps the most egregious betrayal of all, the majority of the Senate Indian Affairs Committee–those Congress members charged with the highest responsibility to uphold the federal Treaty and Trust obligations–have continued to support stripping away Tribal consultation in the BAAJA. This includes Chairman Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) and Vice Chairman Brian Schatz (D-HI), as well as John Hoeven (R-ND), Steve Daines (R-MT), Jerry Moran (R-KS), and Alan Armstrong (R-OK).

Meanwhile, key Congressional environmental leaders and Tribal allies have strongly opposed the BAAJA and uplifted the concerns of Tribes and communities, including Sen. Ed Markey (D-MA), Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-OR), Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D-AZ), and Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-MI).

As an Indigenous organization representing grassroots Indigenous land protectors, the Indigenous Environmental Network stands with the hundreds of Tribal Nations, climate justice organizations, and community members strongly opposing this disaster bill. We encourage everyone to call your senators and representatives today to urge them to vote no on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act to preserve our land and sovereignty for future generations.

The BAAJA is a violation of the federal Treaty and Trust obligations.

The BAAJA proposes sweeping changes to the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) Section 106 Tribal consultation process that could effectively cut out Indigenous voices when determining whether a historically significant, sacred, or cultural site is worth protecting.

Congress and the federal government have a legally enforceable fiduciary obligation to protect Tribal Treaty rights, lands, assets, and resources, as contained in the framework of federal Indian law and legally binding Treaty-making. The Tribal consultation process is the basic function of this Treaty and Trust obligation, which has been codified since 1966 in the NHPA Section 106.

Under the BAAJA Sec. 2301, opportunities for Tribal input in permitting will be reduced and restricted in a way that reflects termination-era policy. Mandatory Section 106 Tribal consultation becomes optional, and agencies will no longer need to notify Tribal Nations before decisions are made that could impact sacred sites. The definitions of what agency actions require consultation and which cultural or historic properties qualify for protection is narrowed in such a way that cuts out a Tribe’s ability to define what is protected as sacred. Tribal Historic Preservation Officers (THPOs), often a Tribe’s greatest tool in preserving historic and cultural sites, will be under strict federal oversight with the risk of federal takeover. Along with State Historic Preservation Officers (SHPOs), THPOs could be subject to total takeover by the Secretary of the Interior if they fail to meet strict federal timelines and guidelines. The opportunity for Tribes to legally challenge decisions would be so restrictive that it would make it extremely difficult for a Tribe to legally enforce their rights. Claims would be subject to a “punitively short 150 day” limitation and strict criteria for who is even allowed to file suit.

Section 106 is the only codified standard for Tribal consultation in federal law, and the proposed changes are akin to a termination-era policy that seeks to diminish the Tribal-federal relationship and exclude Tribal voices rather than respecting the autonomy and self-governance of Tribes. Although the bill’s authors proposed some minor manager’s amendments to Sec. 2301 and 2302, the amendments do not meaningfully address the violations of Tribal consultation standards. Tribal Nations still strongly oppose the BAAJA in its entirety. The bill authors and Senate leaders will determine whether to allow an amendment to be heard, proposed by Sen. Adam Schiff (D-CA), to completely strike the NHPA section and preserve the Section 106 Tribal consultation process.

The BAAJA paves the way for more fossil fuels and AI data centers.

Far from being a “renewable energy bill” – this bill is designed to accelerate pipeline and natural gas projects, as well as data center expansion.

There is a reason the American Petroleum Institute, along with the CEOs of Enbridge, BP, Chevron, Exxon Mobil, ConocoPhillips, Devon Energy, EQT, Halliburton, Marathon Petroleum, Plains All American Pipeline, Shell, TC Energy, Williams, Woodside Energy, and Caturus, have fully endorsed and made passing the BAAJA a top legislative priority. The BAAJA creates vast categorical exemptions for gas pipeline expansions that will no longer be subject to environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). Many of these gas expansions are requested to bring hyperscale data centers online.

The proposed changes to the Clean Water Act (CWA) would make it easier for pipelines to damage waterways. The BAAJA would significantly reduce the authority of states and Tribal Nations under CWA Section 401, especially their ability to enforce their own water protections. By increasing the burden of proof, shortening review periods, and favoring certain energy projects, the bill would lead to more water pollution, habitat destruction, and damage to waterways with less government oversight. States and Tribes would have less power to deny permits or require protections for waterways affected by pollution, runoff, erosion, and sedimentation. Section 1204 would limit the Army Corps of Engineers’ review of projects, making it harder to consider impacts such as habitat destruction, flooding, and harm to fish and wildlife. It would also automatically classify damage to less than two acres of water as having minimal environmental effects. For example, a pipeline could cross dozens of small streams, each affecting less than two acres, but collectively cause serious damage to an entire watershed.

The bill’s changes to federal environmental laws would also make it easier to approve data center projects on public lands with fewer delays and legal challenges. Under Executive Order 14318, the Trump administration has been considering at least 12 data center projects covering 17,600 acres of Bureau of Land Management (BLM) property in Arizona, Idaho, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, and Wyoming. Although the BLM approved the 88.5-acre Townsite Data Center in Nevada, construction is currently paused due to ongoing litigation. However, BAAJA’s proposed changes to NEPA would make challenges like these more difficult in the future. Other proposed developments include the 9,000-acre Project Beehive in Utah and the 3,200-acre Rhea Data Center in Idaho. These changes would also lead to an expansion of ICE detention centers on public lands.

The BAAJA rescinds bedrock environmental regulations.

This bill would restrict public participation and legal challenges under NEPA, the NHPA, and the CWA, while imposing a 150-day deadline for filing lawsuits. These restrictions make it considerably more difficult for affected communities, particularly Indigenous Peoples and communities of color, to challenge projects that threaten their land, resources, habitat, and health.

The BAAJA strips courts of the authority to halt an ongoing project, generally preventing them from vacating or enjoining project authorizations, even when a court determines that a permit was issued in violation of NEPA. Rather than allowing courts to invalidate an unlawful approval or halt a project through an injunction, the bill would require them to remand the decision to the responsible agency for reconsideration while the existing authorization remains in effect.

Additionally, the BAAJA would reduce the Fish and Wildlife Service’s ability to conduct inter-agency consultation, reducing the consultation period under the Endangered Species Act (ESA) from 90 days to 60 days, leaving less time to evaluate potential threats to endangered species. Certain projects could also be exempted from federal ESA reviews, with states assuming responsibility for the consultation process.

The BAAJA creates an open door for mills and mining waste disposal on public lands.

This bill would substantially expand the ability of mining companies to use public lands for industrial development by removing longstanding limits on the number and total acreage of mill sites used for processing, waste disposal, roads, pipelines, and other mining infrastructure. The BAAJA would allow companies to establish unlimited mill sites and potentially claim hundreds or thousands of acres of public land for mining waste disposal and storage.

Section 2215 would also undermine the court decision that blocked the Rosemont copper mine in Arizona from dumping toxic waste that threatened Hohokam burial grounds sacred to the Tohono O’odham Nation, Pascua Yaqui Tribe, and Hopi Tribe.

The BAAJA does not guarantee more renewable energy.

But it does guarantee more fossil fuels. Under Section 1401, the “project certainty” provision would make it difficult for future administrations to modify or revoke existing federal permits, even in response to new environmental information, health concerns, or policy changes. Section 1402 allows developers to sue federal agencies for “disparate treatment” – patterns of discriminatory permit delays or denials across specified energy industries, including renewable energy, fossil fuels, and mining. This is likely to result in locking in fossil fuel projects, as Trump has declared that his administration will not approve renewable projects, and companies will be permitted to default to the Trump administration’s favorable treatment towards fossil fuels.

In this heartless giveaway to fossil fuel companies, Senators Heinrich and Whitehouse are granting polluter corporations rights against “disparate treatment” that were originally reserved under the 1964 Civil Rights Act for protections against racial discrimination in the workplace, while simultaneously stripping Black and Indigenous communities and Tribal nations of their rights to challenge corporations threatening their health and livelihoods, resulting from cumulative impacts and disproportionate burdens.

Yet, even with generous predictions, the modeling only shows anywhere from a 0 to 4% reduction in emissions from the BAAJA–with some showing a risk that emissions would increase. It is simply not worth sacrificing Indigenous Peoples yet again, especially for such poor returns.

The “blue wave” will not save us if Democrats won’t stand up.

With the Democrats celebrating a sweeping win in the midterm elections and securing the majority in both houses of Congress, voters sent a clear message that Americans do not want more data centers or fossil fuels. It begs the question as to why those 14 Democrats would capitulate all of that power to Republican demands and big oil giveaways? Why would Democrats choose this moment to terminate the Tribal consultation process? Does the “blue wave” hit a brick wall when it comes to Indigenous sovereignty and Black and Brown communities? We need those 14 Senators to stand up for frontline communities and fulfill their Treaty and Trust obligations to Tribal Nations by having the courage to vote no on the BAAJA.

title: Russian Indigenous Activist Daria Egereva Remains Jailed; Arrested After 2025 U.N. Climate Talks
content:
Human rights and climate groups are calling on Russia to release two prominent activists, Daria Egereva and Natalia Leongardt, who have been held in pretrial detention in Moscow for nearly a year, since December 2025. Egereva, a leading Indigenous rights activist in Russia, was arrested shortly after attending the COP30 United Nations climate summit in Belém, Brazil, where she served as co-chair of the International Indigenous Peoples Forum on Climate Change. Leongardt has worked for decades to support Indigenous rights.




“Right now all we are demanding is the release of Daria and Natalia, because they shouldn’t be in prison. You shouldn’t be arrested for activism,” says Viktor Suliandziga-Bagat, an Indigenous rights activist and representative of the Udege people from the Russian Far East. He is living in exile due to the risk against activists. “I don’t think I can come back to Russia,” he says.
