title: Enquête élevage de cochons E.Leclerc
content:
L214 publie sa onzième enquête sur les conditions de vie désastreuses des cochons élevés pour E.Leclerc. Les images proviennent d’un élevage intensif de cochons situé sur la commune de Poullaouen, dans le Finistère (Bretagne). Elles témoignent des infractions répétées et des pratiques sources de souffrance pour les animaux : porcelets castrés à vif, coupe des queues de tous les porcelets et sans anesthésie, meulage des dents systématique...

L214 demande à E.Leclerc de s’engager à respecter la réglementation et à interdire les cages dans les élevages qui l'approvisionnent. L’association se mobilise devant les 16 centrales d'achats de E.Leclerc et porte plainte contre l’élevage et E.Leclerc pour sévices graves et mauvais traitements sur les animaux.

Depuis 2024, l’association L214 a rendu publiques des images issues de onze élevages de cochons approvisionnant les magasins E.Leclerc. Les pratiques qui y ont été constatées sont cruelles et, pour certaines, illégales :

Les truies passent la moitié de leur vie enfermées dans des cages où elles ne peuvent même pas se retourner ;

Les queues des porcelets sont coupées à vif de façon systématique ;

Les porcelets subissent d’autres mutilations, comme le meulage des dents et la castration, souvent sans anesthésie ;

Les cochons sont détenus sur caillebotis, au-dessus de leurs déjections, sans matériaux manipulables (paille, etc.) pour satisfaire leurs besoins essentiels.

En votre qualité de présidents de centrales d’achats (SCA), vous siégez au comité stratégique de E.Leclerc, ce qui vous confère un rôle important dans l’élaboration du consensus interne de l’enseigne. Vous avez la responsabilité de porter au sein de cette instance un engagement contre les pires pratiques d'élevage pour les cochons

Nous, signataires de cette pétition, demandons à E.Leclerc de mettre fin à l’enfermement des truies en cage et de respecter la réglementation, afin d’épargner aux cochons les souffrances les plus extrêmes.

title: Διεθνείς ημέρες δράσης ενάντια στον πόλεμο και τον μιλιταρισμό 20-22/11
content:
FIGHT FOR OUR FUTURE, NOT THEIR WARS!




20 Νοέμβρη 2026: πανευρωπαϊκή φοιτητική απεργία ενάντια στη στρατιωτικοποίηση.




20-22 Νοέμβρη: διεθνείς ημέρες δράσης ενάντια στον μιλιταρισμό και τον πόλεμο.




Από τις 20 ως τις 22 Νοεμβρίου 2026 διοργανώνονται συντονισμένες αντιμιλιταριστικές διαμαρτυρίες και πορείες σε περισσότερες από 20 ευρωπαϊκές χώρες.




Η αρχική πρωτοβουλία προήλθε από τη 

Διεθνή Απεργία Νεολαίας

 (

International Youth Strike

 – “Fight for Our Future, Not Their Wars” = «Στη Μάχη για το Μέλλον μας, Όχι για τους Πολέμους τους») και σύντομα υιοθετήθηκε από τον συνασπισμό 

Stop ReArm Europe

 (

Stop ReArm Europe

 coalition – “Welfare, not Warfare”).




Δημοσιεύουμε το αρχικό κάλεσμα του International Youth Strike:




ΣΤΗ ΜΑΧΗ ΓΙΑ ΤΟ ΜΕΛΛΟΝ ΜΑΣ, ΟΧΙ ΓΙΑ ΤΟΥΣ ΠΟΛΕΜΟΥΣ ΤΟΥΣ!




Ο κόσμος φλέγεται




Ο κόσμος στον οποίο μεγαλώνουμε διαμορφώνεται από ένα σύστημα που αδιαφορεί για τις ανάγκες των ανθρώπων. Η εκμετάλλευση των εργαζομένων, η κλιματική αλλαγή και ο πόλεμος δεν είναι αστοχίες του συστήματος, αλλά η ουσία του καπιταλισμού. Η αύξηση της στρατιωτικοποίησης, ο αυταρχισμός και η διάλυση του κράτους πρόνοιας δεν είναι ξεχωριστά προβλήματα, αλλά συναποτελούν συμπτώματα της κρίσης του παγκόσμιου καπιταλισμού.




Οι στρατιωτικές δαπάνες φτάνουν σε ιστορικά υψηλά, ενώ η εκπαίδευση, η υγειονομική περίθαλψη, η στέγαση και οι δημόσιες υπηρεσίες θυσιάζονται για τη χρηματοδότηση των επανεξοπλισμών. Προγράμματα όπως το ReArm Europe (το οποίο στοχεύει να επενδύσει 800 δισεκατομμύρια ευρώ), η επέκταση στρατιωτικών συμμαχιών όπως το ΝΑΤΟ και οι αυξανόμενες εκκλήσεις για υποχρεωτική στρατιωτική θητεία προετοιμάζουν τη γενιά μας για πόλεμο αντί να εγγυώνται το μέλλον μας. Το ΝΑΤΟ δεν υπερασπίζεται την ειρήνη. Έχει επανειλημμένα προωθήσει τα ιμπεριαλιστικά συμφέροντα μέσω στρατιωτικών επεμβάσεων, κλιμάκωσης και προστασίας της γεωπολιτικής και οικονομικής ισχύος – και γι’ αυτό πρέπει να διαλυθεί.




Ο δυτικός ιμπεριαλισμός, με επικεφαλής την κυβέρνηση Τραμπ στις ΗΠΑ, επιβάλλει σχέδια επανεξοπλισμών που επικροτούνται φανατικά από την ευρωπαϊκή άρχουσα τάξη και υποστηρίζονται από συντηρητικές και ακροδεξιές κυβερνήσεις στην Ευρώπη και σε όλο τον κόσμο.




Αλλά δεν υποστηρίζονται μόνο από αντιδραστικές πολιτικές δυνάμεις. Η δίνη του μιλιταρισμού έχει επίσης συναντήσει ενθουσιώδη υποστήριξη από διάφορες σοσιαλδημοκρατικές κυβερνήσεις που έχουν εγκρίνει στρατιωτικούς προϋπολογισμούς ρεκόρ.




Από την Παλαιστίνη μέχρι το Σουδάν, από τον Λίβανο μέχρι το Ιράν, από τη Βενεζουέλα μέχρι την Κούβα, λαοί σε όλο τον κόσμο συνεχίζουν να υποφέρουν από ιμπεριαλιστικές επιθέσεις – κατοχές, στρατιωτικές επεμβάσεις, κυρώσεις, αποικιακή κυριαρχία και γενοκτονία που διαπράττονται στο όνομα γεωπολιτικών και οικονομικών συμφερόντων.




 

Η νεολαία και η εργατική τάξη πληρώνουν το τίμημα




Είμαστε οι άνθρωποι που θα αναγκαστούν να πεθάνουν και να σκοτώσουν στους πολέμους τους για τα συμφέροντά τους. Η στρατιωτικοποίηση εισέρχεται στα σχολεία και τα πανεπιστήμιά μας μέσω της εργασίας για τον στρατό και της στρατολόγησης, μέσω ερευνών που χρηματοδοτούνται από βιομηχανίες όπλων και συνεργασιών με ιδρύματα που συνεργάζονται σε πολέμους και γενοκτονίες. Η στρατιωτικοποίηση κανονικοποιεί τη βία, ενισχύει τις πατριαρχικές δομές και ενδυναμώνει την ακροδεξιά, ενώ οι κυβερνήσεις επιμένουν ότι δεν υπάρχει εναλλακτική και μας πουλάνε ως δικαιολογία το παραμύθι της «άμυνας». Αλλά ξέρουμε καλά ότι ο επανεξοπλισμός δεν αποτρέπει, αλλά αντιθέτως κλιμακώνει τις συγκρούσεις.




Απορρίπτουμε αυτό το μέλλον.




Αγωνιζόμαστε για εκπαίδευση απαλλαγμένη από στρατιωτικά συμφέροντα. Αγωνιζόμαστε για την κατάργηση τόσο της εθελοντικής όσο και της υποχρεωτικής στρατιωτικής θητείας.




Αγωνιζόμαστε για δημόσιες επενδύσεις σε σχολεία, υγειονομική περίθαλψη, στέγαση και κλιματική δικαιοσύνη αντί για όπλα και πόλεμο. Αγωνιζόμαστε για μια γρήγορη και δίκαιη [οικολογική] μετάβαση πέρα από τα ορυκτά καύσιμα, με γνώμονα τις ανάγκες των εργαζομένων, όπου καμία, κανείς, κανένα δεν θα μείνει πίσω· για διεθνή αλληλεγγύη αντί για ιμπεριαλιστική κυριαρχία, και για το δικαίωμα κάθε λαού να καθορίζει το μέλλον του απαλλαγμένο από την κατοχή και την αποικιοκρατία.




Ο αγώνας κατά της στρατιωτικοποίησης είναι άρρηκτα συνδεδεμένος με τον αγώνα κατά του οικονομικού συστήματος που τη συντηρεί. Ο ανταγωνισμός για πετρέλαιο, το φυσικό αέριο και στρατηγικούς πόρους συνεχίζει να οδηγεί σε πολέμους, στρατιωτική κατοχή και αποικιακή βία, ενώ οι εταιρείες ορυκτών καυσίμων, οι εταιρείες όπλων και τα χρηματοπιστωτικά ιδρύματα επωφελούνται από την καταστροφή και τον εκτοπισμό.




Αυτή η λογική της ατελείωτης εξόρυξης δεν τροφοδοτεί μόνο τον πόλεμο. Οδηγεί επίσης στην κλιματική κατάρρευση. Καθώς οι κυβερνήσεις συνεχίζουν να αυξάνουν τη χρήση ορυκτών καυσίμων και τις στρατιωτικές δαπάνες, κοινότητες σε όλο τον κόσμο αντιμετωπίζουν θανατηφόρους καύσωνες, πλημμύρες, πυρκαγιές και πείνα. Η κλιματική κατάρρευση δεν είναι ατύχημα, αλλά αποτέλεσμα πολιτικών επιλογών, όπως ακριβώς και η στρατιωτικοποίηση. Αυτές οι προτεραιότητες δεν είναι τυχαίες. Είναι επιλογές που γίνονται σε διεθνή φόρουμ όπου οι πολιτικές και οικονομικές ελίτ επιλέγουν την προστασία των στρατοκρατικών συμφερόντων καθώς και των συμφερόντων εταιρειών ορυκτών καυσίμων, παρουσιάζοντας την επιλογή αυτή ως αναπόφευκτη. Είτε μέσω στρατιωτικών συνόδων κορυφής και της G7 είτε μέσω διαπραγματεύσεων για το κλίμα, όπως η COP, η οποία έχει αποτελέσει μέσο για το «πράσινο ξέπλυμα» του ορυκτού κεφαλαίου, συνεχίζουν να θυσιάζουν το μέλλον μας για τα κέρδη και τη γεωπολιτική ισχύ.




Θα αντεπιτεθούμε




Ο αγώνας μας είναι διεθνής επειδή το σύστημα που απειλεί το μέλλον μας, μας εκμεταλλεύεται και μας καταπιέζει είναι διεθνές. Οι βιομηχανίες όπλων, οι στρατιωτικές συμμαχίες, τα χρηματοπιστωτικά ιδρύματα και οι εταιρείες ορυκτών καυσίμων λειτουργούν πέρα από τα σύνορα. Η αντίστασή μας πρέπει να κάνει το ίδιο.




Οι φοιτήτριες/τές και οι νέες/οι έπαιζαν πάντα καθοριστικό ρόλο στην αλλαγή του ρου της ιστορίας, παίρνοντας θέση στο πλευρό της εργατικής τάξης και της επαναστατικής της δύναμης. Από τους αντιαποικιακούς αγώνες μέχρι τα κινήματα κατά του πολέμου και των δικτατοριών, γενιές πριν από εμάς μας έδειξαν ότι όταν οι φοιτητ(ρι)ές και η νεολαία οργανώνονται και αγωνίζονται, η κοινωνία κινείται. Τον τελευταίο χρόνο, φοιτήτριες και φοιτητές σε όλη την Ευρώπη και πέρα από αυτήν οργάνωσαν πορείες, απεργίες και συντονισμένες δράσεις κατά της γενοκτονίας, της στρατιωτικοποίησης, της υποχρεωτικής στρατιωτικής θητείας και του ιμπεριαλισμού των ορυκτών καυσίμων.




Το μέλλον μας δεν θα μας το χαρίσουν. Τώρα είναι η ώρα για κλιμάκωση των αγώνων.




Στις 20 Νοεμβρίου, φοιτήτριες/ές/ά και νεολαία σε όλη την Ευρώπη θα απεργήσουμε. Θα εγκαταλείψουμε τις τάξεις μας, θα οργανώσουμε συνελεύσεις, πορείες, δράσεις και διαδηλώσεις.




Καλούμε τις 

φοιτητικές και νεανικές οργανώσεις 

σε όλη την Ευρώπη να συμμετάσχουν σε αυτήν την απεργία. Καλούμε τα

 συνδικάτα και τα κοινωνικά κινήματα

 να σταθούν στο πλευρό μας και να κινητοποιηθούν από τις 20 έως τις 22 Νοεμβρίου.




Απεργούμε και κινητοποιούμαστε για να κερδίσουμε το μέλλον μας.

 Μαχόμαστε για το μέλλον μας μέσα από αυτά τα κοινά αιτήματα:







Τέλος στη στρατιωτικοποίηση, τον επανεξοπλισμό και τη λιτότητα που επιβάλλονται στο όνομα του πολέμου. Επενδύσεις στην κοινωνική πρόνοια, τη δημόσια εκπαίδευση, την υγειονομική περίθαλψη και τη νεολαία αντί για τα όπλα και τους στρατούς.




Κατάργηση όλων των μορφών υποχρεωτικής θητείας. Τα σχολεία και τα πανεπιστήμια πρέπει να είναι χώροι κριτικής σκέψης και απελευθέρωσης, όχι χώροι στρατολόγησης ή υποχείρια της πολεμικής βιομηχανίας.




Ελευθερία, δικαιοσύνη και αλληλεγγύη για όλους τους καταπιεσμένους λαούς. Τέλος στον ιμπεριαλισμό, την αποικιοκρατία, την κατοχή, το απαρτχάιντ και τη γενοκτονία, καθώς και στη συνενοχή των κυβερνήσεών μας σε αυτά, ξεκινώντας με τη διακοπή όλων των δεσμών με κράτη που έχουν διαπράξει γενοκτονία (όπως το Ισραήλ).




Κλιματική και κοινωνική δικαιοσύνη για όλους. Τέλος στον καπιταλισμό των ορυκτών καυσίμων, στον εξορυκτικό ρατσισμό, στην καταστροφή του κλίματος και του περιβάλλοντος.




Ριζοσπαστική αλλαγή συστήματος ενάντια στον αυταρχισμό και την καταστολή, και για την υπεράσπιση των δημοκρατικών μας δικαιωμάτων. Για το τέλος του ρατσισμού και της πατριαρχίας, και για την ήττα της ακροδεξιάς σε όλες τις χώρες.







Η ιστορία δεν άλλαξε ποτέ επειδή αυτοί που βρίσκονται στην εξουσία επέλεξαν τη δικαιοσύνη. Άλλαξε επειδή οι άνθρωποι οργανώθηκαν και αγωνίστηκαν γι’ αυτήν. Τώρα είναι η δική μας σειρά να το κάνουμε!




Στις 20 Νοεμβρίου, ας κάνουμε τα πρώτα βήματα προς την οικοδόμηση ενός διεθνούς φοιτητικού και αντιμιλιταριστικού κινήματος νεολαίας. Αγωνιζόμαστε για το μέλλον μας, όχι για τους πολέμους τους!

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Trump Has Turned SEC Into “Subservient Lapdog” for Corporations, Watchdog Says
content:
There are at least a dozen high level officials in the agency with potential conflicts of interest, a new report finds.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

One of the U.S.’s top financial regulators has been reduced to nothing but a “subservient lapdog” for corporate interests under the Trump administration, a government watchdog warns in a new report identifying at least a dozen high level officials in the agency with ties to the very firms they’re tasked with overseeing.

Under Paul Atkins, a Donald Trump appointee, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is being run by a swath of officials who have formerly done work on behalf of major private equity firms, fossil fuel corporations, crypto companies, military contractors, and more — including figures who previously served as defense attorneys for firms when they were being investigated by the agency, finds the report released Wednesday by Public Citizen.

The SEC was created in response to the Great Depression as a safeguard against the types of corruption and conflicts of interest that led to the economic disaster. Under Atkins, the group warns, conflicts of interest appear to be a selling point for leadership appointments.

“Under Paul Atkins, the SEC has radically transformed from a muscular investor watchdog into a drooling, subservient lapdog that does nothing but serve the very corporate interests it’s supposed to be keeping in check,” said Jon Golinger, democracy advocate for Public Citizen, in a statement.

Among the questionable actions since Atkins was confirmed by the Senate last year has been the SEC’s dropping of several of its cases against Atkins’s former clients. Atkins also seemingly has conflicts of interest related to work with several firms and companies, including his past leadership for three crypto companies and ownership of crypto assets.

Numerous other senior SEC officials similarly have deep ties to companies they’re supposed to regulate. One senior adviser to the Crypto Task Force, for instance, was a crypto lobbyist for a prominent crypto nonprofit known as the Coin Center up until he was appointed in February 2025.

The SEC’s Division of Enforcement, which is supposed to enforce laws, has been filled with figures who have represented the other side, serving as defense attorneys for companies and firms investigated by the SEC, Public Citizen found.

This includes the director of the division, David Woodcock — a former in-house counsel for ExxonMobil and leader in major law firm Gibson Dunn, where he headed the firm’s Securities Enforcement Practice Group. There, he represented numerous major companies, like AT&T, ExxonMobil, SpaceX, UPS, the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company, and more.

As the report finds, Woodcock was twice named on the list of the “Enforcement Elite” by legal hub Securities Docket — a distinction described as “the kind of defensive specialists critical to have on speed-dial should the SEC’s Division of Enforcement come calling.”

The detailed report finds numerous other potential conflicts of interest across other parts of the agency, including the SEC’s Division of Corporate Finance, its public relations head, and the Office of General Counsel, the latter of which is led by a former managing director for BlackRock and general counsel for major firm Focus Financial Partners.

Even the inspector general — the figure who is supposed to lead internal investigations into wrongdoing inside the agency — has potential conflicts of interest, the report found. SEC Inspector General Kevin Muhlendorf was formerly a criminal defense attorney for those accused by the SEC of violating financial regulations and laws, and also faced accusations of conflict of interest when he became the acting inspector general for the D.C. metro operator, Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority (WMATA).

“There are cases where criminal defense attorneys have transitioned to the IG community, but it certainly merits a pause to consider how adequately and aggressively someone who once defended alleged criminals and is now in charge of the office tasked with identifying and pursuing individuals who may have violated the law will be in their newfound role as an inspector general,” the report said.

The report also notes that the extent of potential conflicts of interest within the agency is not known because Muhlendorf and another official each declined to disclose 22 former clients in forms, citing confidentiality requirements.

“Trump has surrounded himself with people like Atkins, who view government service and political power as a means to bestow favors on their friends and associates and amass ever greater personal wealth,” said Public Citizen co-president Lisa Gilbert. “And once again, the millions of Americans whose retirement funds and life savings depend on a fair securities marketplace are left out to dry.”

The report may fuel further scrutiny of the SEC. Lawmakers, most prominently Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts), have previously called out the SEC for effectively abdicating its mission of enforcing the law, ushering in what Warren calls a “Golden Age of Fraud.”

Indeed, the agency’s latest report on its actions in fiscal year 2026 show that its enforcement actions are plummeting. In the past year, the SEC’s enforcement penalties fell to an 18-year low, decreasing by nearly 24 percent over the previous fiscal year.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $19,000 in the next 24 hours. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

author: Mitch Perry
title: Florida Will Break Its Own Death Penalty Record With 20th Execution on Thursday
content:
Thomas M. Overton’s attorneys and Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty say Overton is innocent of murder.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Death row prisoner Thomas M. Overton is scheduled to be executed at 6 p.m. Thursday at Florida State Prison. His would be the 20th conducted by the state this year, breaking the record 19 that took place in 2025.

More are coming: Gov. Ron DeSantis has signed death warrants for Ricardo Gonzalez and that execution is set Dec. 1, and for Willie Seth Crain Jr. for Dec. 10.

Overton was sentenced in 1999 for the 1991 murders of a Monroe County couple and their unborn child. At the time of her death, the woman was eight months pregnant, and Overton was also convicted in the death of their unborn son.

Overton has always maintained that he is innocent.

“Executing Overton would violate his right to Due Process and be a manifest injustice because there remains a great deal of untested evidence and inconclusive evidence that must be retested,” his attorneys claimed in a motion to vacate his conviction and death sentence filed in the circuit court in Monroe County on Oct. 28. “Further, there remains information that was never disclosed to Overton regarding potential third-party guilt. This evidence would independently support Overton’s actual innocence claim.”

The group Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty says the new motion documents “extraordinary failures” in the original investigation of the murders.

“Thomas Overton’s case sounds outrageous, but the reality is that Florida routinely sends people to death row based on unreliable evidence and deeply flawed investigation,’ said Grace Hanna, executive director of the organization.

Overton’s attorneys have also filed for a stay of execution with the U.S. Supreme Court. They contend DeSantis’ refusal to grant clemency to anyone convicted of murder violates the due process rights of those on death row seeking a final act of mercy.

More than half of all the public executions in the United States have taken place in Florida this year. If Overton’s execution takes place as scheduled, it would be the 38th in the country in 2026. It would also be the 39th execution to take place in Florida in the past two years.

The death penalty is legal in 27 states, but only 14 states have executed anyone since the start of 2019, according to the State Court Report.

author: Petala Ironcloud
title: Native American Candidates Won on Platforms Around Land, Water, and Data Centers
content:
National wins among Native politicians could augur change at the state level.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

The 2026 midterms didn’t only swell the ranks of progressives and green economic populists in Congress — they also ushered in a stunning number of Native American leaders in down-ballot races across the country. Among the state legislative races involving Indigenous candidates that have been called so far, Native American candidates won 83 percent of the time, according to ICT.

Montana led the way: 12 of 13 Indigenous candidates there, all Democrats, won legislative seats, including Natalie Weeks-O’Neal (Fort Peck Assiniboine and Sioux) in House District 31 and Katie Fire Thunder (Oglala Lakota) in House District 59.

In Nevada, Brian Wadsworth, a former Pyramid Lake Paiute Tribal Council member, won a seat on the Washoe County Commission representing the county’s rural north, becoming the first tribal member from any of the county’s tribal nations to serve on it, Wadsworth told Truthout. Native Republicans won too, including Emily McIntire (Muscogee) in Oregon and Heather Ellison (Navajo) in New Mexico.

In Alaska, Mary Peltola defeated the incumbent to became the first Native person to represent the state in the U.S. Senate.

Many of these candidates spoke to voters’ concerns on the campaign trail about the affordability of groceries and health care. In Northern Nevada, voters also raised concerns about water, land, and unchecked growth. And the offices these candidates won are increasingly in locales where fights over land, water, and AI data centers get decided, as the federal government weakens its obligation to consult tribes. “We have about 120 proposed hyperscale data centers for Indian Country,” said Krystal Two Bulls, executive director of environmental advocacy group Honor the Earth.

Locally, “these fights are currently being fought and won,” Two Bulls told Truthout. A U.S. Senate permitting bill, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, despite its name, focuses on narrowing environmental review processes and threatens tribal consultation on projects affecting tribal water, land, and cultural sites. “That’s pretty much going to gut any kind of protections or legs that tribes can stand on to push back against these corporations,” said Two Bulls. The bill passed a preliminary vote on November 9 but has yet to clear the next hurdle in the Senate.

National wins among Native politicians could augur change at the state level, especially in states with multiple Indigenous candidate victories. Montana’s wins were historic: “It’s not lost on us that we’re making history, being the largest American Indian caucus in the United States at the state level,” said Weeks-O’Neal, adding that the state’s main media has yet to cover this fact.

Two Bulls expressed hope that the Indigenous bloc will be able to exert real leverage, saying: “They can actually throw a lot of wrenches into the fast tracking that’s currently happening.”

Despite Two Bulls’ forward-looking ambitions for the new class of Native politicians, especially around AI, Weeks-O’Neal faces extant costs to her district: The Zortman mines, which extracted gold from the Little Rocky Mountains in the 1980s and ’90s, contaminated Montana’s water and still cost $3 million a year to treat. “The water is devastated. It is tainted in perpetuity. That means forever,” she said. “Whatever profit was made from the mine, I mean, I can’t imagine.” The site has been re-listed for $52.5 million with geologists estimating “that only 20% of the gold and silver [was] harvested, leaving plenty of reserves for investors or operators,” the listing states.

House District 31 includes much of the Fort Peck Reservation, whose median age is 30 and median household income is roughly $53,000, far below the national median of around $87,000. It’s no surprise then that voters’ primary concern is affordability, especially groceries. “They were struggling to even feed their families,” said Weeks-O’Neal. Trump’s administration has moved to slash the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, which could cut off access for 6.3 million people nationally.

Meanwhile Katie Fire Thunder’s constituents in South Bozeman, which is one of the wealthiest areas in the state, are also worried about affordability: Rising property taxes, driven by soaring land values, are creating a crisis for retirees on fixed incomes who are being priced out of homes they’d expected to keep for life. “That tax burden is being shifted on to residential and property owners,” she said, joining the call alongside Weeks-O’Neal.

Rep. Thedis Crowe (Blackfeet), reelected in House District 15, which borders Canada and includes part of the Blackfeet Reservation, said protecting the water compacts negotiated by the Blackfeet Nation and the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes is a top priority, because both are “headwaters tribes.” He said data center bills expected in the coming session will force lawmakers to weigh impacts on rural and tribal communities, and on water quality.

Weeks-O’Neal said too many of those decisions in Montana have been left to counties, which she said “is just way too much power given to county entities,” and that it was part of why she ran for the Montana House of Representatives.

In northern Nevada, that county power is exactly what Brian Wadsworth just won. Wadsworth lives in Nixon, on the Pyramid Lake Paiute Reservation, about an hour from Reno. Rush-hour traffic along I-80 by the area’s industrial center was once quite rare, he said. Now, “it’s literally a daily occurrence,” something “that we haven’t seen in our lifetimes.”

Wadsworth told Truthout that voters are fed up with unchecked growth and have been asking cities to examine the area’s economic growth and really grapple with infrastructure issues.

“We definitely have a lack of adequate roads here in Washoe County,” said Wadsworth. Growth has far outpaced infrastructure, and that issue drove all the commissioner candidates in his election. The county’s tech boom is blamed by water experts, residents, and the Pyramid Lake Paiute for negative impacts on public roads and the doubling of home costs from roughly $280,000 in 2015, to an estimated $550,000 in 2026, according to The Nevada Independent.

Wadsworth was also outraised by 5 to 1, drumming up only $27,000. When asked how he won despite being outraised, Wadsworth credits his win to showing up instead. He drove an hour to attend meetings in Gerlach. He also held events in communities where, he said, people told him they’d “never had someone… come out and talk to us.” That’s why, he said, he didn’t have to raise hundreds of thousands of dollars to run a campaign: “It doesn’t take a lot of resources to drive out to a community and talk to people… it takes a lot of time.”

“I think the communities are looking to someone that is going to really listen to the concerns and issues of the county, and not just be pro-development, you know, approving developments at no matter what cost,” he said.

Many of Washoe County’s development concerns hinge on water. “We’re at the terminus endpoint of the Truckee River,” he said, adding that “we’re always concerned about growth and development with the upstream users.”

Pyramid Lake sits downstream of the Tahoe-Reno Industrial Center, where data centers are going up alongside Tesla and a Walmart distribution center. “We’re greatly concerned about not only water quantity issues but also water quality issues,” Wadsworth said.

Right now, Wadsworth said, data centers can be built “under the guise of a warehouse,” with no guardrails on water, energy, or land use. He said he would “vehemently oppose” any project that uses excessive water in a region that is “always going to be in a constant state of drought.” For Pyramid Lake, at the end of the Truckee River, that is not at all abstract.

“Jurisdiction lines don’t matter,” Wadsworth said. “You know, the water is going to flow where the water is going to flow.”

In Arizona, Clara Pratte (Diné) made a percussive win, taking a seat on the Arizona Corporation Commission (an independent state regulatory body established by the Arizona Constitution), alongside fellow Democrat Jonathon Hill. Pratte and Hill’s election disrupted the GOP’s stranglehold on what had previously been an all-Republican commission.

“It’s these offices, these down-ballot offices, like planning and zoning, public utilities commissions, corporation commission,” Pratte told Truthout, that “really do play a vital role in how all of those things actually happen or don’t happen.” Her primary priority, she said, is investigating whether ratepayers are subsidizing infrastructure for large energy users like data centers. “Right now, the commission has no credibility with the public,” she told Truthout.

Not every race went that way. “We should not mistake these victories for having closed the representation gap,” Chrissie Castro, executive director of the California Native Vote Project, said in a written statement, noting that there are “communities where Native candidates faced truly significant barriers.”

In Montana, Angeline Cheek (Hunkpapa and Oglala Lakota) lost her bid for the Public Service Commission, 65 to 35 percent. Had she won, Two Bulls said, “it would have been a huge deal,” because utility regulators “make so many decisions that impact everyday folks.”

Shannon Wingfield finished fourth in the June primary for California State Assembly to represent District 68, including conservative-haven Orange County. In a state and year when tech billionaires are pouring more money than ever before into California’s elections, Wingfield felt the paucity in her campaign pocketbook. “It 100 percent would have been money,” she said. The two Democrats, David Penaloza and Jessie Lopez, went on to wage the most expensive legislative contest in California this year, with $5.6 million in spending, according to CalMatters.

Wingfield, who is tribal secretary for the Juaneño Band of Mission Indians, Acjachemen Nation, ran and lost in the state with 109 tribes, the largest number of tribes of any state. She said nearby tribes waited until the general election to back anyone Native, perhaps worried about electability. Wingfield told Truthout that an internal poll of about 7,000 likely voters by her campaign found only 23 percent support for a first Native woman legislator.

At the county level, though, Native candidates in California had a much stronger night.

In a written statement provided to Truthout, Castro noted that Native candidates in California won races including Inyo and Lake County supervisor seats but warned against mistaking these victories “for having closed the representation gap.” And while big decisions about tribal lands and water are often made on the local level, she said, “local representation cannot replace the federal government’s legal and trust responsibilities to tribal nations.”

Two Bulls is generally skeptical about elected officials’ ability — whether at the federal, state, or local level — to deliver for Native communities. “I don’t have a lot of hope as it is,” she said. But she says she has higher expectations of the new Indigenous legislators, saying, “I definitely do hold them more accountable.”

What Two Bulls expects of the new class is simple: Protect “land, air, and water.”

Weeks-O’Neal, meanwhile, frames the stakes in larger terms. Tribal communities, she said, have been stewards of the land for generations, “way beyond just the two terms of an elected official like myself.”

author: J. David McSwane
title: Trump’s DOJ Is Hiring Inexperienced Attorneys to Fill Purged or Vacated Ranks
content:
“It’s a good time to be a white-collar criminal,” said a former federal prosecutor.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

In early October, a recent law school graduate shared a post on LinkedIn that would have been unheard of before the second Trump administration.

After passing the bar exam, 29-year-old Preston Bigley wrote, “With this milestone complete, I will begin serving as an Assistant United States Attorney in the Criminal Division of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Texas.”

It was a remarkable achievement, considering Bigley had graduated from Texas A&M’s law school in May and had been hired by the Justice Department in August to be, as his resume notes, an “incoming” assistant U.S. attorney. That unusual title was followed by an unusual caveat: “pending bar admission.” Once officially licensed to practice the law, he updated his profile to show he had become a bona fide federal criminal prosecutor.

Bigley is one of a growing cohort of inexperienced attorneys, many of them fresh out of law school, who are being fast-tracked to fill the shoes of seasoned career prosecutors who fled or were purged from the DOJ in President Donald Trump’s second term. That brain drain, amounting to thousands of years of experience, comes as prosecutions of fraud and drugs have fallen in key districts to make way for Trump’s immigration agenda, ProPublica found.

Across the country, ProPublica identified more than 50 new assistant U.S. attorneys with less than three years of experience who traditionally wouldn’t have been considered for such vital positions, legal experts said. Some were hired with the intent to anoint them as prosecutors — once they pass the bar exam, public disclosures show.

That figure is likely a fraction of the actual total, as a comprehensive analysis is impossible because DOJ staff identities are redacted in government personnel data. But of those ProPublica identified through bar membership records and social media, about 20 passed the bar within the last year. At least seven were in the same May graduating class as Bigley, from a range of schools.

“The fact that the DOJ is hiring, and indeed actively recruiting, right out of law school — it’s an astounding break with past practice,” said Juliet Sorensen, a Loyola University Chicago law professor and former assistant U.S. attorney. “It reflects a lowering of standards for a job that is important and requires lawyers who are meticulous, committed to doing the right thing, and bring with them experience beyond just law school.”

To understand how Trump transformed the DOJ, ProPublica examined federal court data and records, federal workforce and state bar information, and social media accounts. We also interviewed more than two dozen former assistant U.S. attorneys.

More than half of those who left the Justice Department in Trump’s first 18 months boasted nine-plus years of legal experience. Those who left had spent, on average, more than 13 years working for the government, the analysis shows. Those more experienced attorneys were the ones most likely to take on complex cases, such as money laundering, organized crime and drug trafficking, legal experts say and court dockets show.

ProPublica shared its analysis and detailed questions with the DOJ; the department did not respond. Previously, the DOJ said it “remains committed to investigating and prosecuting all types of crime.”

The DOJ has long hired recent graduates through its Honors Program, which places graduates into rigorous training through the main office in Washington, but experts say the program was small and not meant to replace prosecutors.

Before Trump’s second term, the DOJ typically would not hire new prosecutors unless they had a minimum of three to five years of legal experience, former officials and law professors said. That standard is gone. Earlier this year, Bloomberg Law reported, the DOJ waived a policy requiring at least one year of experience.

While private law firms routinely hire promising graduates before they pass the bar exam, typically to begin their training, the DOJ’s hiring of new grads is a striking departure from its once-rigorous hiring process, said University of Michigan law professor Barbara McQuade, a former U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Michigan.

“The people who I hired came to us as partners in law firms,” said McQuade, who was appointed by President Barack Obama. “These were superstars who had been very successful at large law firms or in state court prosecutors’ offices.”

Trump’s creation of a less experienced DOJ will have longstanding consequences, McQuade said.

“It means that some very serious crimes will go unpunished,” she said. “It takes experienced prosecutors at the federal level to bring down corporate fraud, transnational gangs and corrupt public officials.”

While experts expressed concern, some of those benefiting from the law school-to-federal prosecutor pathway have voiced excitement on LinkedIn. “I look forward to beginning my DOJ career by serving the Del Rio Division,” wrote Jacquelyn Kilcommons, who graduated from Pace University’s law school in May. “Upon receiving my bar exam results, I will transition into an Assistant United States Attorney (AUSA) position.”

As he announced his new role in the district of Washington, D.C., newly graduated assistant U.S. attorney Ellis O’Donnell wrote, “In the past few months I have had the honor to graduate from Vanderbilt University Law School and to sit for and pass the Wisconsin Bar Exam.” None of the recent law school graduates responded to requests for comment.

The departure of assistant U.S. attorneys in Trump’s second administration marks the largest number of exits two years into a presidential term in at least two decades.

Beyond the personnel turnover, the administration’s priorities have shifted since Trump retook the White House, an analysis of Federal Judicial Center data shows.

As immigration cases shot up nationwide, felony fraud prosecutions fell sharply in key districts. Amid an exodus of prosecutors in the Western District of Virginia, for instance, fraud cases fell 66%. Those cases dropped 14% in the Southern District of Florida, a hotbed for white-collar crime, where many prosecutors have left in protest of Trump’s retribution campaign against people deemed political enemies. Nationally, drug prosecutions have fallen about 10% in Trump’s first 18 months and fraud cases are flat.

Meanwhile, the number of people facing immigration-related charges skyrocketed by almost 50%, clogging the courts and depleting resources at U.S. attorneys’ offices nationwide. Even in border districts where immigration proceedings can dominate the caseload, prosecutions have risen dramatically. For instance, New Mexico and the Southern District of California saw 300% and 125% increases in immigration cases, respectively, the ProPublica analysis shows. In the Western District of Texas, where Bigley and at least two other recent graduates just became prosecutors, immigration cases have surged at least 36%.

The immigration caseload, including tens of thousands of unlawful-detention cases filed in civil court, has strained the department so severely that the DOJ has drafted hundreds of attorneys from other federal agencies and the military to keep up, former officials said.

Those cases coincided with violent deportation sweeps led by masked immigration agents, who killed U.S. citizens, and the nationwide protests that sprouted up in response. Many of the cases Trump’s DOJ brought against people protesting immigration authorities’ actions fell apart, a ProPublica analysis showed. The news organization also reported how the truthfulness of Trump’s prosecutors has come under question in courts across the country. The DOJ previously said its attorneys “represent the United States with integrity.”

Amid the unrest, ProPublica has tracked nearly 100,000 habeas corpus petitions filed by immigrants arguing that their detentions were unjust. In each case, an assistant U.S. attorney must defend the government’s position, a task that had some U.S. attorneys reassigning veteran lawyers — experts in financial crimes, civil rights and human trafficking — to immigration. In Washington state, an acting U.S. attorney said he’s so overbooked with unlawful-detention petitions, his office cannot handle every case.

In South Florida, where an exodus of veteran lawyers presaged a drop in fraud and financial crime cases, one former white-collar crimes prosecutor said he and his colleagues could not decline an immigration case without permission from U.S. Attorney Jason Reding Quiñones, who abruptly resigned this month. Before his resignation, Quiñones had led the “grand conspiracy” investigation targeting former officials Trump alleged were part of a “deep state” plot against him.

“Every case takes time, and you want to put in effort, and now you’re wasting your time on cases you don’t believe in or think are unjust,” said the former prosecutor, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because he hopes to return to the Justice Department after Trump leaves office. “It affects morale.”

In recent months, the DOJ has ramped up efforts to recruit lawyers to replace the lost expertise, government data and the department’s recruiting materials show.

While Justice Department personnel data is kept secret, assistant U.S. attorneys are paid on a unique pay scale set by the attorney general, a quirk that dates to the 1950s and distinguishes them from other civil servants. By tracking the number of people compensated this way, it is possible to obtain broad data on the numbers of assistant U.S. attorneys.

As of January 2025, the department employed about 6,200 assistant U.S. attorneys, the data shows. Then Trump’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency took a hatchet to the Justice Department and other federal agencies. Led by the world’s richest man, Elon Musk, DOGE offered employees financial packages to resign from the federal government by September 2025. About 1 in 10 of all assistant U.S. attorney departures were part of that offer, the data suggests.

The ranks shrank much faster than the department anticipated, former officials said, and it was unable to hire sufficient replacements. By the end of January 2026, the DOJ lost over 1,300 assistant U.S. attorneys and replaced only about 470 of those attorneys.

The DOJ began turning to novice attorneys to fill the empty desks.

In early 2026, a former White House official shared a post on X, the social media platform owned by Musk, that hinted at the DOJ’s growing desperation to find new hires.

“If you are a lawyer, are interested in being an AUSA, and support President Trump and anti-crime agenda, DM me,” wrote Chad Mizelle, who had recently left his DOJ role as chief of staff to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi. Mizelle did not respond to a request for comment.

In March, the department hit its lowest numbers since 2014. A month later, the University of Miami hosted an event titled “Lunch & Learn: Entry Level Opportunities with The U.S. Attorney’s Office.” The invite, targeted toward third-year law students, promised a new pathway to become a criminal prosecutor in one of the country’s busiest districts.

“The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Florida is now recruiting 3Ls for entry-level positions beginning immediately after graduation — an exciting expansion of opportunities for Miami Law students interested in federal prosecution,” the invitation said.

To lure new hires, the DOJ is offering signing bonuses. As of August, due in part to the hiring spree focused on greener attorneys, the department lifted its ranks to about 5,600, still a 10% drop from the end of the Biden administration.

U.S. Rep. Jamie Raskin, the ranking member on the House Judiciary Committee and the presumed chair once Democrats take charge, told ProPublica that the shift toward inexperience is showing in courtrooms across the country.

“They’ve sacked some of the finest lawyers in America, by tradition, and replaced them with a large group of inexperienced lawyers,” said Raskin, himself an attorney.

In his home state of Maryland, fraud cases fell 31% and drug cases nearly 16%, while immigration charges nearly doubled. “Those numbers are jaw-dropping,” he said.

Jim Fang was among the veteran prosecutors who left.

Fang’s road to becoming a criminal prosecutor was winding. After working in tech for about a decade, he switched careers, and in 2009 graduated from Georgetown Law. He worked in private practice, focusing on intellectual property law, but couldn’t shake a feeling that what he really wanted was “to take down bad guys.”

In April 2020, he got his dream job and was named a federal criminal prosecutor in the District of Nevada. He moved to Las Vegas and, aided by his 11 years handling complex areas of the law, took on tough white-collar crime cases.

After the election, Trump picked Sigal Chattah, a former Republican political candidate, to run the Nevada U.S. Attorney’s Office.

Through court records and sources, ProPublica confirmed that more than 30 staff have left under Chattah’s tenure. The Nevada district is so depleted that for months it didn’t have prosecutors in its Reno office, about 450 miles away. Las Vegas prosecutors were asked to fly there for court appearances, sources said. Chattah disputed the 30 figure but acknowledged that Las Vegas-based staff flew to Reno “to ensure that our federal and local partners had competent and aggressive prosecutors.”

The office dropped cases it had been building as Chattah pushed immigration and politically motivated prosecutions. To ease the caseload, Chattah ordered her civil defense unit, charged with fighting lawsuits demanding cash from taxpayers, to pay out all cases that could be settled for $250,000 or less, multiple sources said. “We were ordered to settle those cases even if they didn’t have merit,” one former assistant U.S. attorney said. “It was just throwing money at a problem.”

Chattah called the allegations that she issued such a directive “patently false” and pushed back on her former employees’ characterizations of her tenure.

“There were attorneys that failed to meet the expectations of competent workmanship with the Department of Justice, and chose to leave or retire, some were terminated,” she wrote. “Former AUSAs who failed to handle an expected case load were replaced with aggressive prosecutors who will keep our state safe.”

In September 2025, Fang took the DOGE offer and went back into private practice as a defense attorney. He suspects the department’s loss of financial crime experts like him will result in fewer successful prosecutions.

“It’s a good time to be a white-collar criminal,” Fang said.

Now facing off against his former colleagues, he’s mostly busy representing clients who’ve filed habeas petitions. He was recently surprised to learn that one of the new hires brought into his former office had just passed the bar. “They’re taking a gamble on them,” he said.

Fang says they may well end up being fine attorneys but added, “There’s no way I could have taken that job and done it well right out of law school.”

title: Riflessioni di alcunə giovani italianə sullo sciopero generale dell’11 di novembre a Barcellona
content:
Riceviamo e pubblichiamo un racconto sulla giornata di sciopero a Barcellona da parte di alcune compagne che vivono lì.




Mezzanotte dell’11 di novembre, qualche secondo dopo l’inizio dello sciopero generale per la casa. Nel cielo di Barcellona compaiono fuochi d’artificio da vari punti della città, seguiti da cori e canti, per festeggiare l’inizio della giornata. 

La libertá è quando comincia l’alba in una giornata di sciopero generale

 dice una strofa di una poesia di Joan Margarit, che circola nei giorni precedenti.  Qualche ora dopo, verso le 3.30/4, escono di casa lə primə compagnə per raggiungere a piedi i primi blocchi stradali delle principali arterie viarie della Catalogna. 

A Barcellona i principali obiettivi sono le varie 

ronde

, tangenziali con una funzione simile al raccordo anulare romano, che abbracciano tutta la cittá. Il livello di tensione con lə conduttricə di moto e macchine, determinatə a raggiungere i propri posti di lavoro, sono delle piú variegate. Nella 

ronda del mig

 a Lesseps tutto procede senza particolari problemi; ad uno dei tagli della 

ronda litoral

lə manifestantə, bardatə, si stendono sull’asfalto per dormire e recuperare le poche ore di sonno. In vari punti della Catalogna le macchine investono lə scioperanti procurando feritə; molte sono lə manifestantə che, visto il grande numero di persone, si autogesticono e separano per bloccare altre uscite o entrate della stessa arteria. Le reazioni sono delle piú diverse, tra chi tira fuori la sdraio felice di non andare a lavorare a chi ha un crollo psicotico quasi gritando tra le lacrime: “E il mio diritto di andare a lavorare dov’è? Io muoio se non vado a lavorare!”. Rispettando una buona tradizione catalana, quella de 

elfoc i la rauxa

, i primi fuochi della giornata riempono l’aria periferica barcellonina, bloccando persino l’entrata di zone logistiche strategiche come quella di Mercabarna e del porto di Barcellona.




L’adesione allo sciopero è storica, l’84% secondo le principali sigle sindacali. In Spagna non si vedeva uno sciopero generale cosí da almeno quattordici anni. 

Nonostante il tempo passato, si nota la tradizione 

vaguista

 della città con un programma giá ben collaudato: blocchi stradali a prime ore dell’alba, poi, mentre alcuni di questi si mantengono fino all’ora di pranzo come a Lesseps, iniziano i picchetti informativi (e meno informativi) per i vari quartieri. È evidente una differenza molto grande tra gli scioperi italiani e quelli di Barcellona. Qui la storia sindacale è molto differente. Mentre in Italia una delle tradizioni politiche piú forti, quelle dell’autonomia, nasce propriamente come movimento extraparlamentare e contro i principali sindacati (basta pensare alla ben nota cacciata di Lama alla Sapienza), qui sindacati come la CNT hanno avuto un ruolo centrale giá dalla resistenza antifranchista nel ‘36 . Oggi rilevante è soprattutto il ruolo della CGT, nata da una scissione della CNT, che mantiene viva la tradizione di sindacalismo anarchico e combattivo.




Se negli scioperi di dimensioni minori, come quelli per la Palestina, l’obiettivo dei 

cercavila

 di quartiere erano le filiali delle note multinazionali pro-israele, nella giornata dell’11 sono stati segnalati tutti i negozi aperti al grido di 

esquirol

 (crumiro). 




A Gràcia, quartiere ribelle fino a 10 anni fa ed oggi mangiato dagli expats e svuotato della maggior parte delle sue occupazioni, ci sono tre diversi picchetti che si muovono avanti e indietro per le strade principali, costringendo a chiudere piú o meno gentilmente ogni serranda. Piano piano gli animi si vanno scaldando e la fantasia cresce: piante ornamentali di hotel tirate per terra, farina sulle casse dei supermercati, immondizia all’entrata dei negozi, scritte, manifesti e pressioni in ogni porta illuminata o aperta. I lavoratori lasciano le proprie attivitá con piú o meno buona volontá, la maggior parte chiudono poco prima che arrivi la piccola manifestazione, alcuni si nascodono al buio mentre altri litigano e si confrontano con lə manifestantə, a cui viene tirata farina, uova e costretto con la forza a chiudere il negozio. Vengono risparmiate farmacie e altri servizi minimi, particolare accanimento avviene contro i negozi piú gentrificatori. Un lavoratore, mentre trasporta un pallet di prodotti a un supermercato, scappa alla vista del picchetto e i prodotti vengono distribuiti tra tuttə, dal succo ai pannolini. In altri quartieri il confronto è piú violento. A Nou Barris un compagno viene investito e fatto volare svariati metri piú avanti da una macchina, che subito dopo scappa via. Al Carmel viene fatto chiudere il Park Güell e, con la scusa di alcune scritte su elementi del patrimonio storico, avviene un’esagerata azione di polizia contro il pranzo di quartiere, identificando tuttə lə partecipanti. Due persone che si erano allontanate per andare al bagno vengono fermate violentemente, una di queste viene arrestata con accusa di violenza a pubblico ufficiale, in quanto l’agente dei Mossos d’Esquadra che è uscito dalla volante correndo per fermarlo, è inciampato per terra e racconta di essere stato preso a calci dal militante. È l’unico detenuto prima della manifestazione del pomeriggio e il primo a essere rilasciato all’ora di pranzo del giorno dopo.




È evidente qui un’altra differenza tra l’Italia e la Spagna (o almeno Barcellona). I quartieri hanno un ruolo centrale nella vita personale e politica delle persone, dalle feste di quartiere autogestite una settimana all’anno ai sindacati per il diritto all’abitare specifici per ogni quartiere. Lo sciopero generale non consiste quindi solo di una grande manifestazione centrale ma di centinaia di atti per la cittá che prevedono dai picchetti familiari con i bambini disegnando sull’asfalto al picchetto centrale a plaça Catalunya delle 12. Una costellazione infinita di lotte che è impossibile racchiudere in un solo testo.  

 Dopo poche ore di riposo, verso le 3 iniziano le prime concentrazioni nei vari quartieri per formare le colonne per raggiungere la manfestazione centrale. Tutti si muovono a piedi, i mezzi pubblici non funzionano tutto il giorno e neanche i servizi minimi annunciati riescono a venire garantiti. Molte delle concentrazioni convergono in tre colonne principali di zona nord, sud e centro. Quelle che in altre giornate di lotta sono colonne di poche centinaia di persone, diventano qui vere e proprie manifestazioni con migliaia di 

partecipantə

. Solo da Nou Barris, quartiere periferico, storicamente marginalizzato e popolato da classi operaie e migranti, arrivano piú di 4000 persone al grito di “

Sense Nou Barris no hi ha revolució”

. 




Il percorso previsto dai soliti che chiamano ufficialmente le manifestazioni, senza prendere in considerazione la necessitá di azioni e sfogo della rabbia popolare, è il solito noioso percorso di sempre. Passeig de Gràcia, plaça Catalunya, dove ancora si mantiene l’

acampadaper la vivienda

, via Laietana. Le strade con piú camere di riconoscimento facciale e biometrico di tutta la cittá. Lə manifestantə peró non si lasciano intimidire e la rabbia è impossibile da contenere. In poco tempo si forma un gruppo di black bloc, la maggior parte raggruppati dietro lo striscione “

Ni publica ni privada, vivenda autogestionada

”. Inizialmente è formato da poche centinaia di persone, probabilmente per il mancato afflusso atteso e sperato dei piú  giovani, soprattuto di seconda generazione, arrestati massivamente nel corteo di 

Blocus

 del 24 ottobre. 

Blocus è

 un gruppo avvolto nel mistero, nato improvvisamente sui social in emulazione delle rivolte giovanili di Francia e Italia. Nonostante molti abbiamo ipotizzato ci fossero elementi dell’estrema destra, non si puó nascondere il carattere di rabbia giovanile diffusa nella partecipazione, che ha dato luogo ad un saccheggio massivo nel centro di Barcellona. Nelle settimane precedenti c’erano state anche varie discussioni tra le sigle sindacali: le piú combattive come la Coshac avevano preso in considerazione fino all’ultimo di separarsi e iniziare un percorso alternativo perchè non volevano rimanere in una manifestazione con alla testa la UGT e 

Comissiones Obreres

. In questo tutti i Paesi europei ci assomigliamo un po’, la UGT è un sindacato riformista che, per dirne una, ha chiuso un accordo vergognoso col governo durante l’ultimo sciopero di massa dei docenti di quest’anno, non garantendo nessuna delle richieste delle piazze.  Alla fine, si è deciso di seguire la manifestazione unitaria, ma la pace sociale è durata neanche una mezz’ora. I primi scontri si sono verificati in una traversa di Passeig de Gràcia. Il blocco nero è avanzato diversi centinaia di metri facendo retrocere cellerini e camionette grazie a petardi, fuochi d’artificio, transenne e tavolini dei bar. Si nota che non esiste lo stesso livello organizzativo e strategico di molte cittá italiane, qui gli scontri avvengono in modo molto piú spontaneo e anarchico e sono frequenti incursioni con ritirate fulminee, non è molto abituale mantenere la posizione. Dopo un piccolo spostamento di alcune camionette e il suono di una sirena, lə manifestantə battono velocemente in ritirata, forse anche per l’ignoranza della situazione dietro di loro e la paura che sia una trappola per farlə separare dal resto del corteo.  Tornato sulla via principale il blocco nero, comincia a rompere le prime vetrine. Vengono rimossi i plafon di legno che le proteggono, il primo è un Victoria Secret da cui cominciano a volare per aria mutande. Forse anche per ribaltare la narrativa che i negozi vengono assaltati senza scopo politico, solo per voler rubare beni di lusso, lə black block fanno arrivare quasi tutti i resultati dell’esproprio al resto dellə manifestantə, accoltə da grida di giubilo. 




Arrivatə a Catalunya, come molti dei cortei accesi dell’ultimo anno, tutto degenera e diventa confuso. La piazza ha troppe entrate, la grande parte centrale pedonale impedisce una vista globale dello spazio e divide in diverse parti il corteo. Da quanto si legge sui giornali, una parte di questo arriva davvero a via Laietana. Nel frattempo, il fuoco si espande e divampa velocemente, la piazza viene difesa con pirotecnia e pietre fino a circa le 8, quando gli agenti antisosommosa iniziano a disperdere violentemente la manifestazione con proiettoli di foam e manganellate. Da qui in poi è ancora difficile capire esattamente quello che è successo. Sicuramente una parte è confluita verso la Rambla, un’altra è stata spinta verso plaça Universitat difendendosi con barricate e incendi. È iniziata una caccia all’uomo, il bilancio della serata è di piú di cinquanta arrestatə e innumervoli feritə. L’accanimento poliziale è brutale, vecchiə e giovani vengono colpite da manganellate indiscriminate e gli scontri continuano per ore. 

Els agents dei paisá, la secreta

, piú o meno l’equivalente della nostra digos, sono tantissimi e si muovono per le strade bardati e facendo credere allə manifestantə di star scappando insieme per poi arrestarlə. Alcuni dei 

secreta

 hanno maglietta e bandiera della CGT.

 Nonostante questo, la sensazione generale è quella di una vittoria totale e intergenerazionale, a parte alcune voci di fascistə e riformistə. La manifestazione è rimasta entusiasta accanto alla rivolta e considera la giornata come solo l’inizio di quella che si prospetta come una lunga lotta per una casa e una vita 

digna.

Le scritte fatte per i muri della cittá non parlano infatti solo di diritto all’abitare ma anche di Palestina, del costo della vita troppo alto, dell’insostenibilitá della precarietá e di una cittá sempre piú venduta alla turistificazione e alla gentrificazione. Una Barcellona che sta perdendo progressivamente la propria anima e il cui carattere si sta vendendo come una marca, facendolo perdere di significato. In attesa di sapere il destino dellə detenutə, per cui il sindaco Collboni sta invocando il pugno di ferro, gioiamo per una giornata indimenticabile, che rimarrá nella storia di una 

urbe

 dal cuore anarchico. Una Barcellona 

ribelle e mai domata,

 che non china la testa di fronte all’ennesimo tentativo capitalista di sottomissione. Determinata a recuperare le case che le vengono rubate da banche e fondi d’investimento, i suoi parchi e le sue strade.

title: Families of seriously ill prisoners launch vigil in Ankara
content:
Families of seriously ill political prisoners began an indefinite sit-in outside the Turkish Ministry of Justice in Ankara on Tuesday. Together with members of parliament from the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) and human rights organizations, they are demanding the release of ill prisoners and access to adequate medical treatment. The participants announced that they would continue their protest until concrete steps are taken.




The vigil was organized at the call of DEM Party MPs, the Association of Lawyers for Freedom (ÖHD), and the Human Rights Association (IHD). Among the participants are relatives of Newroz Bozkurt, who was transferred from Sincan Women’s Prison to Etlik City Hospital, and Evin Zapsu, who is imprisoned in Kayseri Bünyan Women’s Prison with stage four cancer.




The demonstrators unfurled a banner bearing the names of seriously ill prisoners and the words: “We stand at the gates of justice. Through resistance, we will open the prison gates – Freedom for sick prisoners.” Slogans demanding the release of political prisoners were repeatedly chanted.




“People must no longer die in prisons”




Şirin Altay, the Ankara representative of the Federation of Solidarity Associations for Prisoners’ Families (TUHAD-FED), stated that the situation of seriously ill prisoners had not changed despite numerous protests and public appeals outside the Ministry of Justice. For this reason, the families have decided to launch an indefinite protest, Altay said and called on the authorities to facilitate the immediate release of prisoners and thereby strengthen public confidence in the ongoing peace process.













“People must no longer die in prisons. They must be able to receive medical treatment under appropriate conditions. The Ministry of Justice must hear our voices,” Altay said. She questioned the authorities’ responsibility for the deaths of political prisoners and demanded an answer as to how a peace process could move forward while people continued to die in detention. She stressed that the families would remain outside the ministry to fight for the lives of their loved ones.




“We cannot bear any more news of deaths”




DEM Party MP Ali Bozan recalled political prisoner Tuncer Sağlam, who recently died. He remarked that the continued refusal to release prisoners and provide adequate medical care was not only a human rights issue but also placed a burden on the social peace process. “We cannot bear any more news of deaths from prisons,” Bozan stated. Pointing out that the public was right to question how peace could be discussed while seriously ill people continued to be held in prison, he stated: "The vigil is therefore also intended to contribute to the peace process by drawing attention to the urgently needed humanitarian measures. Where rights violations continue indefinitely, protests will also continue indefinitely."




Mother of Newroz Bozkurt demands treatment outside prison




Sultan Bozkurt gave a particularly moving account of her daughter Newroz’s situation. She said her daughter had been seriously ill for a year. "Although she is now in hospital, she remains under prison conditions. When this process began two years ago, we hoped that we might be able to embrace our children again in good health,” she stated.




Sultan Bozkurt said she had traveled from Istanbul to Ankara and had been allowed to see her daughter for only ten minutes over the course of two days. "My daughter's health has deteriorated significantly. She is in a terrible condition. Her blood levels have dropped to zero,” Bozkurt said. She demanded that her daughter be transferred to a regular hospital ward and receive treatment under appropriate conditions.




She emphasized that no new law was needed to ensure medical care and the release of seriously ill prisoners. "Those affected must be given the opportunity to continue their treatment outside prison and in a family environment. We said that mothers would no longer have to cry when there is peace. We will do everything in our power to ensure that mothers no longer cry. Tears have no color. Now, concrete steps must finally be taken.”













Evin Zapsu can barely manage her daily life




Mecit Zapsu, the husband of seriously ill prisoner Evin Zapsu, also appealed to the Ministry of Justice. He criticized the apparent treatment of medical care for prisoners as a concession, even though it was a fundamental right. He said his wife is suffering from stage four cancer in Kayseri-Bünyan Prison, with her health deteriorating steadily. According to Mecit Zapsu, attempts are being made to manage her symptoms with painkillers rather than ensuring adequate medical care.




"Evin Zapsu is now unable to meet her daily needs independently. “We are here to remind the Ministry of Justice of its responsibility. The denial of adequate medical treatment worsens the prisoners’ conditions and endangers their lives. Our protest will continue until the prisoners receive treatment and are released," Mecit Zapsu stated..

title: Numerous politicians detained in operation against Kurdish party alliance Hevbendî in Turkey
content:
Numerous Kurdish politicians have been detained in Turkey as part of a large-scale operation targeting the newly formed party alliance Hevbendî. Among those detained is Bayram Bozyel, chairman of the Socialist Party of Kurdistan (PSK). The public prosecutor’s office in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır) accuses members of the alliance of endangering the unity of the state and Turkey’s territorial integrity. According to Hevbendî, the investigation covers all 51 members of the alliance’s council.




Hevbendî was founded on November 7 in Amed as the “National Alliance of Kurdistan.” Its members include the PSK, the Kurdistan Democratic Party/North (PDK-Bakur), the Patriotic Party of Kurdistan (PWK), Pêlkurd, Vejîn, and the Kurdistan National Initiative. The alliance aims to strengthen cooperation among Kurdish parties and political movements.




House raids in five cities




Police raided homes in Amed, Ankara, Mardin, Batman, and Istanbul in the early hours of November 17. According to Hevbendî, those detained included Bayram Bozyel, PSK deputy chairman and lawyer Hasan Dağtekin, Pêlkurd spokesperson Fuat Önen, PWK deputy chairman Mehmet Can Azbay, as well as Sevgi Çelik, Aryan Serhed, Ali Öncü, Rojbin Bükün, Ali Çeven, and Ali Aydın.




The home of PWK chairman Mustafa Özçelik was also raided and searched. According to the alliance, an arrest warrant has also been issued for him. Those targeted are accused under Article 302 of the Turkish Penal Code of “disrupting the unity of the state and the territorial integrity of the country.” The offense carries a sentence of aggravated life imprisonment. According to the alliance, the investigation files have been placed under a confidentiality order, and those detained have been denied access to their lawyers for 24 hours.




PSK: “This repression will not intimidate us”




The PSK condemned the detentions and announced that it would continue its political activities. “These and similar repressive measures, as well as the detention of our officials, will not intimidate us. We will continue to struggle alongside all patriotic forces until the Kurdish people achieve their national and democratic rights,” the party stated. It also called on democratic organizations and the public to oppose the measures and show solidarity with Hevbendî. “We will not be intimidated and will continue to stand up for Hevbendî.”




Solidarity appeal criticizes criminalization of peaceful political activity




In a joint appeal titled “Shoulder to Shoulder: Solidarity with the Hevbendî Detainees,” intellectuals, writers, academics, and artists condemned the operation. They pointed out that the accusations concerned a political conference, a joint program, and a press conference, none of which had involved acts of violence or calls for violence.




The signatories described the detentions as a violation of freedom of expression and association under the Turkish Constitution and the European Convention on Human Rights. They also referred to the case law of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR), according to which peaceful advocacy for the right to self-determination was not in itself a criminal offense.




‘Those who expected division have strengthened unity’




The signatories stated that the repression had fostered solidarity among different Kurdish political movements, some of which had previously had significant differences. “The national unity that the Kurdish people were unable to achieve through their own efforts over the years has now emerged on its own as a result of a single arrest warrant. People of different views and traditions who long kept their distance from one another are now signing the same declaration.”




They emphasized, however, that their previous objections to the establishment, working methods, and structures of Hevbendî remained unchanged. In light of the detentions, however, solidarity with those affected took precedence. “We will conduct our discussions on procedural matters among ourselves and on our own terms, just as a family discusses its affairs within the family. We will not allow these debates to become material for prosecutors’ investigation files or indictments.”




Alliance for national rights and political self-determination




Hevbendî emerged from a prolonged process of political rapprochement. The starting point was a conference on Kurdistan’s national unity held in Amed on March 14, 2026. At another conference on November 7, a joint program was adopted, before the alliance was publicly introduced on November 9.




In its founding declaration, Hevbendî calls for recognition of the collective rights of the Kurdish people, the right to self-determination, and political status for Kurdistan. Its objectives also include constitutional recognition of Kurdish identity, the use of Kurdish as an official language and a language of education, and stronger cooperation among Kurdish political forces in all four parts of Kurdistan.




The alliance elected a 51-member council to coordinate joint political activities. Following its establishment, PSK chairman Bayram Bozyel stated that political status for the Kurds could be achieved within Turkey’s existing borders, for example through a federal system or another model.
