author: Jenny Brown
title: Labor Mobilized for ‘Many vs. Mighty’ Midterms
content:
Something different was in the air as the labor movement mobilized for the midterms.




More than usual, unions were willing to support insurgent candidates who refused corporate donations and bucked the Democratic Party establishment. They championed a Bernie Sanders-style list of working-class issues: Medicare for All, a higher minimum wage, union rights, immigrant rights, stopping war, and taxing the rich. Many are union members themselves. And they won.




United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain called the election “the many versus the mighty.”




In Michigan, the UAW was a key backer of the victorious Abdul El-Sayed, who earlier defeated the party’s depressing primary choice for U.S. Senate.  “You had a lot of rich people who tried to… buy a seat, to buy these races,” Fain told 

Michigan Advance

. “Michiganders… are telling these people they’re not for sale.”




Logger and union member Troy Jackson won a Senate seat against 30-year incumbent Republican Susan Collins in Maine after the UAW and the Maine AFL-CIO helped defeat the establishment choice in the primary there. In Ohio, labor stalwart Sherrod Brown faced a river of crypto lobby cash but recovered the Senate seat he lost in 2024.




In Texas, the Communications Workers (CWA) mobilized for union-member candidates up and down the ticket, asking candidates to commit to a 

“Contract with Working Texans.”

 Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa signed on—she’s a labor lawyer, member of Texas State Employees Union/CWA, and the first Democrat elected Texas governor since 1990.




Various union members and leaders are headed for Congress. Ironworker Brian Poindexter won in Ohio. Pennsylvanians elected firefighter and union president Bob Brooks. Forest Service smokejumper and local union vice president Sam Forstag won in Montana. VA nurse and union member Mitchell Berman beat a Republican incumbent in Wisconsin. 




In New York, UAW members and Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) congressional candidates Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier defeated establishment Democrats in the primary, then romped November 3.




Richard Ojeda, a champion of the West Virginia teachers’ strike of 2018, won a Congressional seat in North Carolina, beating the head of the National Republican Congressional Committee. "We were elected to elevate the lives of working people across this country,” 

said Ojeda

. “We're coming in LASER FOCUSED on the mission. Help people. Hold anyone who has hurt people accountable. Tax the billionaires. The end.”




Others lost, but came way closer than expected. In Nebraska, Kellogg’s strike leader and independent Dan Osborn came up short (44-50) for U.S. Senate. He faced ferocious attack ads, with $24 million in ‘independent’ spending. In Florida, former SEIU organizer and DSA member Angie Nixon defeated the establishment Democrat in the primary and almost won (48-50) a Senate race the pundits had written off. She got zero support from the national Democratic Party.




CORPORATE DEMS UNDER FIRE




Now some unions have come out swinging, demanding more from the party. The Machinists (IAM) sent a letter 

urging Senator Chuck Schumer to resign as party leader

. OPEIU 

did the same

.




The IAM “is through with any member of leadership, in any political party, who stops one iota short of being a ferocious, unyielding and unbending champion of working people,” said President Brian Bryant. “This means… sweeping economic policy changes that will recalibrate the vast, immoral, economic injustice in this country.” 




The United Electrical Workers concurred: “The credit for these wins belongs not to the Democratic Party—whose leadership has offered at best tepid resistance to the Republican agenda over the past two years—but to the working people across the country who have spent the last two years organizing and fighting back in their communities and workplaces.”  




UE set out an ambitious agenda

: a $25 minimum wage, Medicare for All, dismantling ICE, taxing the rich, protecting Social Security, and passing labor law reform including the PRO Act and card-check recognition for speedier union recognition. National Nurses United said voters expect a stop to health care cuts, stat. 




President Trump can veto most bills Congress passes, but Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders 

insisted

 on November 9 that Congress needs to do its job and pass a bold working-class agenda. If Trump vetoes the bills, that’ll raise the stakes in 2028 to elect a president who will sign them.




It’ll take a lot of pressure get corporate Democrats to defy their paymasters. So plans are afoot for 

May Day 2028

, when the Auto Workers and other unions have important contracts expiring. The plan is to keep the focus on working class demands, backed by a season of contract campaigns and strikes.

author: Mehran Khalili
title: What’s next for Europe’s autumn of protests?
content:
This article 

What’s next for Europe’s autumn of protests? 

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.







It was a Wednesday afternoon in late October, and several marches were converging on Syntagma Square in Athens, the epicenter of Greek protest. There were teachers on strike, university students who’d camped in the square overnight, and high schoolers holding painted banners that read “From Greece to France, we’re fighting for modern schools.” Parents pushed strollers through the growing crowd, their toddlers looking on in wonder.




But not everyone was there for the same reason. Groups of black-clad young men ducking in and out of the march, faces covered, were play-fighting each other in a way that looked like a rehearsal. Riot police were lining the side streets, watching over it all with the bored expression of men waiting for their shift to end. And photojournalists were circling, hoping for the youths and the police to meet in a burst of violence that would pay for their day.




The violence didn’t happen this time. According to the 

police count

, 10,000 people marched peacefully through central Athens. Afterwards, people hung around, arguing about politics and passing water bottles in the autumn sun. 




I keep thinking about those bored riot police, though, because they seemed to understand what organizers sometimes don’t: A government that has seen a lot of marches knows how to wait one out. The question for the teachers and students in Athens — and in Paris, Milan, Brussels, Lisbon, Madrid, Berlin, Vienna, Tirana and every other city caught up in Europe’s autumn of protest — is how to make saying no cost their governments more than saying yes.




An autumn of anger




The energy in Europe’s streets is bigger than many realize.  Young people have been protesting in at least nine European countries this autumn, most of them since mid-September. 




In France, a walkout over the lack of teachers at one high school in Créteil in September 

spread to hundreds of schools

 within weeks. By mid-October, about 550,000 people (by the 

government’s own count

) were marching in cities and towns across the country. In Spain and Portugal, the anger is about housing. Protesters set up camps in 

Madrid’s Puerta del Sol

 and 

Lisbon’s Rossio,

 and on Nov. 11, Spain’s tenants’ unions, backed by the big trade unions, held the country’s 

first general strike in 14 years.

 It came after Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old widow in fragile health, was forcibly removed from the Madrid apartment she had lived in for most of her life. She 

died in hospital

 two weeks later.




Demonstrators march for the right to housing  after the eviction of  an 87-year-old woman from the home where she had lived for around seventy years in Madrid, Spain. (Wikimedia Commons)




The grievances overlap without being the same. It’s about schools in France and Greece, university tuition in 

Belgium

 and 

Albania

, university budgets in 

Austria

, military conscription in 

Germany

, and rent in Portugal and Spain, where the average rent is now 

98.7 percent

 of what a young person earns in a month. But running beneath most of them is a familiar story: governments that say there’s no money for schools, or for people who are struggling, always, somehow, manage to find it for something else, often weapons.




In France, Germany and 

Italy

, protesters have made that link. France’s 

2027 budget

 adds $7 billion for defense and just $1.2 billion for schools, while 

cutting 1,588 teaching posts

. In Germany, young people marched in more than 30 cities on Oct. 31, angry, as 

Al Jazeera reported

, that military spending is rising while education funding is cut. 




The protests have achieved some modest wins. On Oct. 26, France’s government promised to 

replace Parcoursup

, the hated university admissions system, cap first-year high school classes at 28, and add 500 teaching posts. And in Serbia, a student movement that began after a railway station canopy 

collapsed in Novi Sad two years ago

 turned itself into an electoral list and, on Oct. 25, 

beat Aleksandar Vučić, Serbia’s strongman of 14 years

. 










Sign Up for our Newsletter




We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.
































































 










Facts like these are why, in my organizing circles, there’s a lot of talk of a “European wave.” I think we should be careful with that phrase, though, because it suggests a level of coordination and a plan that doesn’t — yet — exist. The reporting I trust describes these protests as 

“largely unconnected”

: common causes, solidarity marches and viral calls, but no shared target, no joint demands, and nobody deciding anything together across borders.




The closest thing to coordination is an 

international student strike

 on Nov. 20, which I’ll come back to. Because I think it shows both what this moment could become, and what it’s missing.




Why “no” is cheap




So why, with so much energy on the streets sustained over two months, has so little been won? Serbia is the exception, because its movement is two years old and has organized itself, faculty by faculty, from the start. Elsewhere, I think it comes down to two things—one that is out of protesters’ hands, and one that isn’t entirely. 







A government can wait out a crowd that hasn’t said what it wants, from whom and by when, or what it will take away if it doesn’t get it.







First, European governments have learned how to absorb a crowd. There’s no evidence they’re coordinating, but they have landed on remarkably similar responses. Italy sent 

500 troops to Milan after riots in October

 and passed an emergency decree that makes it easier to hold youth 14 and older criminally responsible. France 

deployed soldiers to guard public buildings

, 

banned protests in several cities

 and imposed a curfew in parts of Paris. By Oct. 8, French police had taken 

6,877 people into custody

, about 80 percent of them children. Portuguese police 

cleared the housing camps

 in Lisbon and Porto before dawn.







And most governments have found a way to say no to protesters’ demands: France 

opened a “consultation”

 and made 

partial offers

, Portugal said it “will not give in to 

shouts from the street,

” and Greece 

pointed to money

 it says it’s already spending.




Behind all this is the fact that time is on the government’s side in most of these countries. As Arundhati Roy 

put it

 in a recent essay about India’s Cockroach movement, states have the power to wait, but people don’t. Erica Chenoweth’s research found that even as nonviolent campaigns became more popular through the 2010s, their 

success rate fell

, partly because states got smarter, and partly because movements leaned on mobilizing people rather than organizing them. 




The second thing is that a government can wait out a crowd that hasn’t said what it wants, from whom and by when, or what it will take away if it doesn’t get it. And from observing what most of these protests do in public, that’s where they are. Their demands keep getting lost, and few of their actions seem aimed at the person who can say yes, or timed to a moment when that person needs something. (Spain and Belgium are the exceptions, and I’ll come back to both.)




And when a movement doesn’t define itself, everybody else gets to define it for them. The mainstream press focused mostly on the violence, and even sympathetic commentators turned the protests into a 

test of the EU’s survival

. Donald Trump announced that 

“the migrants have taken over France.”

 An 

AI-generated photo

 of an elderly couple supposedly stripped by rioters got 

a million views

 and was 

shared by a French police union

. Albania’s prime minister, Edi Rama, blamed “

foreign hands

” and said the protests were “not a student phenomenon.” And parts of the left, my own corner included, did the same thing from the other direction, arguing that a crowd that had come out over missing teachers was actually protesting about Gaza, or arms dealers, or capitalism.




That fight decides who turns up at the next protest and, critically, who gets to position themselves as the answer. In France, Marine Le Pen gave a 

solemn address in front of a French flag

 after the Oct. 17 riots, and the first poll afterwards put her at 

36 percent, up from 32 in September

. If the students don’t define their movement, the candidate of “order” will.




Four old questions




When faced with an organizing problem, I go back to the oldest questions in campaigning: Who can give you what you want — in other words, who decides? What exactly are you asking them to do? By when? And what leverage can’t they ignore?




1. Who decides?




The default answer to “who decides” is almost always “the government.” That isn’t wrong, but it’s too vague to be useful, because a government is hundreds of people with different jobs. And the decision-maker who can say yes to a particular demand may not be the one people are marching against. Take two of the French students’ demands: smaller classes and more teachers. Class sizes, it turns out, the government could change itself, and it 

offered a cap within weeks

. But teaching posts are in the budget, which is up to parliament, and the next vote is in the 

Senate on Dec. 9.

 Two demands, two different targets.




Students in Belgium worked this out early. The tuition increase at French-speaking universities wasn’t set by the federal government, but by 

the parliament of the French-speaking community

. So that’s where they took the fight: they 

protested

 before the decree passed in June, and now they’re 

taking it to the Constitutional Court, which can overturn unconstitutional laws.

 They haven’t won yet — but they are fighting in the right venue.




Working out exactly who decides takes more work than it sounds. But the point is: It’s usually done by a few people around a laptop on a Monday night, rather than in the streets on a Saturday. 




2. What are you asking?




When I went hunting for what the French students were actually asking for, I had to find their national coordination’s communiqué on 

an activist website

 because almost no English-language outlet had reported it. It mixed things a minister could grant tomorrow, like scrapping Parcoursup, with things no one could grant at all, like an end to inequality between rich and poor neighborhoods. When I 

posted about this

, several people messaged me to say these weren’t even the demands most of the movement backed. 




Movements with clear demands mostly arrive at them the same way: They put them to a vote among the people doing the marching, or at least consult them. Serbia’s students decided theirs in 

open assemblies at every faculty

, by show of hands.  In Spain, the Tenants’ Union didn’t pick the date for its general strike on its own; it 

talked to the protesters first

, then brought it to the big unions. A list people have voted for is much harder for anyone else to rewrite. 




Previous Coverage

 

How Serbian students toppled an authoritarian




And a list that is short, fixed and public is much harder for governments to dodge. Serbia’s protesters held to 

four demands

 for months — so when the government claimed it had met them all, they could rebut it point by point. But France’s “yellow vest” movement in 2018 had 

42 demands

, which let Emmanuel Macron pick the ones he liked — and launch a national debate that split the movement. 




Last, the demands that stick are usually the most concrete ones. “Maximum class sizes of 25” is something you can measure and chase; an end to inequality is a vision nobody can grant, so a government can wait it out forever. I’ve 

made this argument before:

 Keep the end goal, but give people a fight they can win on the way. Or, as 

Mark and Paul Engler put it

, make demands that are “both practical and visionary.” 




3. By when?




Then there’s the date. On Oct. 18, the first weekend of the school holidays, France’s student coordination 

set its next national day of protest

 for Nov. 3, just after the holidays end. This was a smart move, because people who go away need to know when to come back. The harder part, though, is pointing that protest date at a decision:  a vote, a deadline, a meeting where someone has to say yes or no. Belgium’s students did that with the June vote; Spain’s tenants, below, did it with an election.




4. What can’t they ignore?




This is the pressure point. I don’t mean public pressure, which is a tactic; I mean something your target 

needs

, from someone specific, at a particular moment. Whose vote do they depend on? Who are 

they

 asking for something? The date tells you when they decide; the pressure point is what would make them decide your way.




Spain offers the clearest example of getting this right. The Tenants’ Union, which has spent nearly a decade building rent strikes, 

picked Nov. 11

 for the general strike, 18 days before Spain’s snap election. Pedro Sánchez’s Socialists are 

trailing in the polls

, and what they need is for voters who care about rent to turn out for them. By putting housing at the center of the campaign, the strike makes every party compete for those votes.




The union has also refused to let any party 

identify with the strike or frame it

 as an attack on rival parties. It isn’t against “the other side,” said its spokesperson, but against “the rentier system.” That makes it much harder for anyone to relabel.
















Support Us




Waging Nonviolence depends on reader support. Make a donation today!




Donate













And a strike asks just a day’s pay of the people taking part while costing the economy dearly — by one bank’s estimate, 

up to 0.2 percent of annual GDP

. “We, the workers — who are also renters or who also pay mortgages — are the ones with the power to halt production and bring the economy to a standstill,” Sandra Mora of the Madrid Tenants’ Union 

told Spanish radio

. Organizers say about four million people took part.




Of course, none of this guarantees a good result on Nov. 29, and the right may still win. But the point is: Spain is what a protest looks like when it’s attached to something a government can’t wait out.




And when there’s no pressure point to find, some movements build one. Serbia’s students spent two years marching for demands that were never fully met. In the end they stopped asking Vučić for anything and simply built the thing that could take power from him: 

a list of candidates

 with no party, no leader and one material grievance — corruption. That took two years, not two months.




From a date to a target




Which brings me back to Nov. 20. For the first time, if it all goes to plan, students in a dozen or so countries will walk out on the same day. The walkout was called by a small network of 

student and left-wing groups

, months before the French protests began. But this autumn’s movements have since picked it up: Italy’s national student organizations have 

adopted it

, Italy’s biggest union has 

called a general strike

 for the same day, and in Berlin, high school students will be 

marching with teachers’ unions

.




The youth strike’s first demand

 is the one that runs through almost every protest this autumn: “Investments in welfare, public education, healthcare and youth instead of weapons and militaries.” That’s an answer to the “what.” But it doesn’t yet have a “who” or a “when.”. Money for weapons and schools is decided in budgets, by parliaments, on dates set well in advance. And a budget vote is a moment when a government needs something it may not have: the votes in parliament. Whose votes are in doubt, and what would make them think twice, is the last question. And it’s what turns a date into a target.




Those riot police in Syntagma could afford to look bored, because they knew the march would be over by evening. A crowd on its own can be waited out. A crowd that keeps coming back — to the right decision-makers, at the right moment, and able to take away something they need — is much harder to ignore. 




The march shows how many people care. But the campaign is what you do with them.




This article 

What’s next for Europe’s autumn of protests? 

 was originally published by 

Waging Nonviolence

.

author: Unknown
title: İran: 13 petrol işçisinin trafik cinayetinde ölümüne öfke rejim karşıtı gösteriye dönüştü
content:
İran'ın batısındaki İlam eyaletine bağlı, ağırlıkla Kürt nüfusun yaşadığı Abdanan kentinde otobüsle işe giden 13 petrol ve gaz işçisinin ölümüne yol açan trafik cinayeti, yerel yöneticilerin istifasının talebiyle başlayan protestoların ardından İslam Cumhuriyeti yönetimine karşı gösterilere dönüştü.




14 Kasım Cumartesi akşamı Dehloran Petropalaj Şirketi'nin NGL 3100 projesinde çalışan işçi ve mühendisleri taşıyan servis otobüsü, Deşt Abbas–Murmuri yolunda, Segar köyü yakınlarında devrildi. Kazada 13 kişi yaşamını yitirdi.




Yaralıların sayısını Radio Farda 15, Hengaw ve Kürdistan İnsan Hakları Ağı 17 olarak bildirdi. 




Yas töreninden protestoya




17 Kasım Salı günü Abdanan'da kazada ölen işçilerden birinin cenaze töreninin ardından bir araya gelen yüzlerce kişi, yolların güvensizliğini, ulaşım altyapısındaki eksiklikleri ve yetkililerin ihmallerini protestoya girişti.




Rejimin militan kolluk gücü Devrim Muhafızları'na yakın Fars Haber Ajansı, Veli Asr Meydanı'ndaki gösteride başlangıçta 200–300 olan katılımın giderek 1.000'e ulaştığını bildirdi.




Göstericiler  “Bugün yas günü” ve “İstifa, istifa” sloganlarıyla başladıkları gösteriyi cinayetin sorumlularının hesap vermesi talebiyle sürdürdüler. Ancak gösteri ilerledikçe protestolar yerel yöneticileri aşarak ülke yönetimine yöneldi. Sosyal medyada yayımlanan görüntülerde “Diktatöre ölüm” ve “Liyakatsiz yetkililere ölüm” sloganlarının duyulduğu bildirildi.




Euronews Farsça, bazı görüntülerde seslerin sonradan eklenmiş veya değiştirilmiş olabileceğini belirterek sloganları bağımsız kaynaklardan doğrulayamadığını açıkladı. Ancak rejim yanlısı Fars ajansı da gösterilerin ilerleyen saatlerde siyasal nitelik kazandığını kabul etti.




Bazı görüntülerde de istihbarat bakanlığı ve Besic milis örgütünün propaganda afişlerinin indirildiği görüldü.




Güvenlik güçleri gazla müdahale etti




Kürdistan İnsan Hakları Ağı'nın 18 Kasım'daki açıklamasına göre, özel polis birlikleri göstericilere göz yaşartıcı gazla müdahale etti. Kentte özel müdahale birliklerinin ve Besic güçlerinin yoğun olarak konuşlandırıldığı ve internet bağlantısında kesintiler yaşandığı bildirildi.




Iran International'a konuşan görgü tanıkları, motosikletli güvenlik görevlilerinin havaya ateş açtığını ileri sürdü. Kürdpa ise göstericilere havalı silahlarla müdahale edildiğini bildirdi. 




Abdanan Savcısı Amrollah Meysaei, gösterilerden sonra yaptığı açıklamada olaydan yararlanarak kamu düzenini bozmak isteyenlere karşı sert önlemler alınacağını söyledi.




Gözaltına alınanlardan beşinin nerede olduğu bilinmiyor




İnsan hakları örgütü Hengaw, 18 Kasım'da yayımladığı güncellemede en az 7 kişinin gözaltına alındığını açıkladı.




Örgütün belirlediği isimler şöyle: Sina Dervişi (15), Said Abdullahî, İrec Haydari (51), Muhsin Bavir, Asgar Ekberi, Armin Süleymani ve Behnam Muradi. 




Hengaw'a göre 15 yaşındaki Sina Dervişi ile Muhsin Bavir birkaç saat içinde serbest bırakıldı. Diğer 5 kişinin tutulduğu yerler ve durumları hakkında bilgi edinilemedi.




Kürdistan İnsan Hakları Ağı 6 gözaltıyı teyit edebildiğini duyururken, Hana İnsan Hakları Örgütü de gözaltıların sürdüğüne ilişkin bilgiler yayımladı.




Associated Press'in aktardığına göre, bir eyalet milletvekili gözaltı yaşandığını reddetti.




Trafik cinayetnin sorumlusu kim? 




İlam Trafik Polisi, ilk incelemelerinde otobüs sürücüsünü, aracı kiralayan şirketi ve yol bakımından sorumlu kurumu kusurlu bulduğunu açıkladı. Radio Farda'nın aktardığına göre savcılık, Dehloran taşımacılık şirketinin genel müdürü ve eyalet yol bakım müdürü hakkında adli işlem başlattı.




İlam Valiliği eyalet genelinde bir, Abdanan ilçesinde 2 günlük yas ilan etti.




Mehr Haber Ajansı, hayatını kaybedenlerin ailelerinin trafik cinayetinin nedenlerinin açıklığa kavuşturulmasını ve sorumluların belirlenmesini istediğini; ayrıca kendi adlarına gösteri düzenlenmemesi çağrısı yaptığını bildirdi.




Ocak protestoları hafızalarda 




Yaklaşık 24 bin nüfuslu Abdanan, Ocak 2026'da İran genelinde yaşanan protestoların önemli merkezlerinden biriydi: 9 Ocak'ta Tahran'daki gösterilerde güvenlik güçlerince öldürüldüğü bildirilen 16 yaşındaki Alireza Sayyedi, Abdananlıydı. Cenazesinin 11 Ocak'ta memleketine getirilmesi üzerine kalabalık gösteriler düzenlenmişti.




Kürdistan İnsan Hakları Ağı, cenaze törenine katılanlara gerçek mermiyle ateş açıldığını bildirmişti.




Şubat ortasında Sayyedi'nin ölümünün kırkıncı günü dolayısıyla Abdanan'da yeniden protestolar düzenlenmişti.




17 Kasım'daki gösterilerde de Sayyedi anıldı. Protestocuların “Alireza, ruhun huzur bulsun” sloganını attığı bildirildi.




(AEK)

author: Rory Mir
title: Outage Chaos: When Tech is too Big to Fail
content:
Outages happen, but we deserve a resilient internet where no one outage at one company can put people at risk and disrupt the global economy. We can only get there by addressing an over-reliance on a few cloud monopolists through effective antitrust laws and interoperability requirements.

Service outages, like we’ve seen recently at Microsoft, Apple*, banks, courts, airlines, and elsewhere, can be more than an annoying hurdle. Losing a vital service due to an error can cause the same impacts as a government-ordered internet shutdown—people losing access to vital information and lines of communication. As usual, the greatest harms are faced by people on the margins globally.

There’s not much hope in companies out-nerding these issues either. Technical errors will always exist, whether it’s a bug, negligence from an administrator, or a malicious attack. The problem is an over-reliance on any one company or system when these inevitable outages occur. It’s a matter of public safety and economic stability that policymakers mitigate the impact of these disruptions before they occur.

In order to do so, we must ensure antitrust prevents providers of key technical systems from becoming too big to fail.

The harms inflicted by tech monopolies go beyond monetary costs to the end user. In fact, monopolists can often offer lower prices, or even offer free services, thanks to their greater scale and incentive to shut out competitors using free-flowing investment capital. The problem is this puts a few tech companies in a position of incredible influence. The true cost is a loss of control when our private data, access to knowledge, and free expression all become mediated by tools owned by a handful of billionaires.

Losing diversity in our digital infrastructure creates a less stable and less resilient internet for everyone.

This isn’t just a bad deal for us as individuals. Losing diversity in our digital infrastructure creates a less stable and less resilient internet for everyone. When everything from daily tasks to national security is reliant on a few digital monocultures, one mistake or exploit can cascade into an explosive impact. The risks multiply in the current investment climate, where financial markets reward companies that strip-mine redundancy and resiliency from critical systems. Even if you see the problem coming, an outage that hits clients, suppliers, collaborators or loved ones proves just as disruptive. We need to remove these chokepoints for good, which means a digital sovereignty movement that makes the web more free by design—not just importing existing levers of control into another nation's borders.

Central to this effort must be undercutting platform control by fostering interoperability, i.e. when tools are made to be compatible among competitors. When this is done carefully, it’s not only easier to switch to better alternatives, we wind up with more alternatives as it becomes more viable to compete or offer complementary tools alongside existing systems.

This is what made systems like email great. You could choose your own apps and services, even using several simultaneously, and never lose touch with a contact. Early architects of the internet did not take reliable hosting for granted. Services were often on a machine a few rooms over, and needed to be prepared for the occasional interruption of service.

But in the age of hyperscalers and massive data centers, the infrastructure underlying the web isn’t owned by many scattered IT departments, it’s rented from a handful of “cloud” providers. These providers managed to scale up quickly and replace interoperability with walled gardens, enticing customers with lower costs while making it costly to leave and tightly controlling how services behave. Once in control, these platforms have every incentive to enshittify their services and devalue their workers, delivering an increasingly shoddy and restrictive service.

This context makes building interoperability an act of defiance—often coming from the sweat of open source developers. These projects may be tolerated by monopolists in the short term, but can be one boardroom decision away from being broken entirely. A better internet means championing these creators through funding, liability protections, and requiring big players to cooperate. Here is what lawmakers should do:

Federal and state legislators should—

Defend competitive compatibility. Developers merely providing alternative interfaces for tools should be shielded from liability. In the U.S., that means explicit protections under DMCA, CFAA, and corporate Terms of Service agreements. These protections should cover shared protocols and APIs as well as automated content retrieval through scraping.

Encourage interoperability. Lawmakers should force open key aspects of platform infrastructure by requiring big tech to support: (1) data portability, so users can move to a new service (2) back-end interoperability, to support more tools with competitive compatibility and (3) delegability, so people are not prevented from having code act on their behalf. So far, the Digital Markets Act in the EU has provided some positive examples of such legislation

Fund open source. In order to be sustainable, interoperable tools and standards cannot rely solely on corporate interest and volunteer labor. Programs like the EU Sovereign Tech Fund could help create viable alternatives within and beyond the borders of the EU.

Municipalities and institutions should—

Buy interoperable services. At any level, government agencies should set minimum interoperability requirements in procurement and hold a competitive bidding process to evaluate vendors’ privacy, security and lock-in risks. Agencies dependent on a sole provider, including through cooperative purchase agreements, are stuck with corporate price-gouging and even higher switching costs.

Fund Departments of Information Technology. Cloud services are often adopted to offset spending on IT professionals but, when these departments atrophy, institutions become even more reliant on the cloud providers. Maintaining in-house talent prevents this cycle of dependency and improves emergency responses to outages.

Adopt a plus-one approach to public communications. Institutions shouldn’t force citizens into walled gardens just to access public communications. In addition to posts to corporate social media, government agencies should share the same information on an open protocol—whether it’s bluesky, the fediverse, or just an RSS feed. By putting these in the open, more people will have access to urgent alerts and can create new useful tools.

Building a more resilient and democratic internet is possible, and many people are already hard at work doing just that. Above are some necessary steps to get corporate and government interests out of the way of rewilding the net with greater community and individual controls. The dream of the internet as a digital commons operating for the public good is not dead yet, and is worth fighting for.

*Apple is an EFF donor. EFF donors do not influence our agenda or our positions.

author: Jenny Brown
title: ‘Delay, Deny, Discipline’ Is Amazon’s Real Pregnancy Policy, Workers Say
content:
Willamina Barclay was working as a picker at Amazon’s fulfillment center in Rochester, New York, when she felt lightheaded again. “She pleaded with a manager for a seat… He refused: ‘No, because you don’t have a [pregnancy] accommodation. If I give you a chair, I have to give everybody else a chair,’” he said, according to a recent lawsuit.




But Barclay, who learned she was pregnant in March 2025, had already asked managers many times for accommodations—a seat, extra breaks to drink, eat, pee (or throw up) in the bathroom, no ladder-climbing or squatting, and no heavy lifting.




Amazon—a company known for fast delivery—had failed to answer for weeks, demanding medical documentation. Even after Barclay provided it, Amazon still refused most accommodations, permitting her four breaks a day, but no chair. She was moved to a different position, but still required to lift heavy packages. 




Amazon counted her new breaks against her unpaid time off (UPT), a leave bank that workers accumulate at five minutes per hour and that maxes out at 80 hours. She went to Human Resources several times to try to rectify the situation, but stopped because they were also counting those visits as UPT, the lawsuit says.




The heavy lifting led to sharp pains. At one point she left the warehouse in a wheelchair headed for the hospital. Amazon also counted that time against her unpaid leave bank. On another occasion, she had to leave due to uncontrolled vomiting. Despite a doctor’s note, that was also counted against her. Her UPT thus used up, Amazon fired her.




Under the law, workers cannot be penalized for taking pregnancy-related leave 

(see box at end of article)

.




Barclay’s ordeal is detailed in a lawsuit filed September 8 by 

A Better Balance

, a nonprofit focused on work policies affecting families. It’s a proposed class action on behalf of all U.S. workers whose rights under the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA) have been violated by Amazon.




SYSTEMATIC VIOLATIONS




Barclay’s harrowing experience is common, said Sultana Hossain, recording secretary of the Amazon Labor Union (ALU) on Staten Island: Under the law “pregnant workers don’t have to give in paperwork,” she said. “They only have to verbally say, ‘I’m pregnant and I need to be accommodated.’ But we’re seeing Amazon systemically violate that.




“Even if workers get an accommodation eventually, it can take several weeks,” said Hossain. “So people really don’t have any choice but to keep working in their regular role, which is really dangerous if they actually need an accommodation.”




Key’Asia, a worker at Amazon’s fulfillment center near Wilmington, Delaware, said that Amazon management twice rejected a note from her doctor, once because it had an e-signature, and then again when she got an ink signature. (For privacy to discuss medical matters, some workers asked that last names not be used.)




Managers said the signature looked fraudulent and still refused to accommodate her pregnancy, Key’Asia said. “They are making you do the things that your doctor told you that you’re not supposed to be doing,” she told attendees at an online Jobs With Justice event in October. “They’re making you do things that are putting yourself and your baby at risk.” She said Amazon fired her twice, both times when she was pregnant.




PATTERN OF ILLEGALITY




Workers have noticed a pattern: When they request accommodations, Amazon managers ask if they are “safe to work.” If they say “yes,” they are forced to continue to work without accommodations. If they say “no,” Amazon puts them on 

unpaid leave

, which rapidly runs out.




Marissa, who worked at Amazon’s fulfillment center in Rossford, Ohio, said that after her accommodations were denied, she was forced out on unpaid leave, and she ended up losing her apartment. “I was out $1,700… I couldn’t pay for my vehicle. I couldn’t afford to eat.




“Amazon doesn’t care about whether or not you’re in pain,” she said. “They care about whether or not you can get their packages out on time.”




Hossain said it was typical for workers to get fired for “job abandonment” because “they ran out of time-off options because they were just not given the accommodation.” (A Better Balance 

has also sued

 Amazon for this practice on behalf of a disabled worker.)




TRAGIC RESULTS




Hayat Bzezi was working at Amazon’s Staten Island JFK8 warehouse during the busy holiday season of 2024, when all workers were required to take an additional weekly 10-hour shift. She had asked for lighter duty, and management said she could use a chair, but then she was denied it. 




She was “lifting heavy products, climbing up and down the stairs, despite having a high-risk pregnancy,” said her husband Wajdy, an elected ALU trustee who works at the same warehouse.




Hayat worked through pain, but it got worse and finally she had to go to the hospital, where she miscarried. It was the second time she had miscarried while working at Amazon. After that the couple decided to 

speak out

. Since then, she has stopped working at Amazon and has been able to bear a child.




LAW REDUCES MISCARRIAGES




When the PWFA went into effect in 2023, 

a study found

 that it reduced miscarriages by 9.6 percent. This suggests that many more miscarriages could be avoided if Amazon, the country’s second-largest private employer, started following the law.










 Pregnant 

With

 A Contract 







Postal workers move packages like Amazon warehouse workers do, but they have a union contract. It makes all the difference when you’re pregnant, said Postal Workers (APWU) national field organizer Lori Cash. 




She hired into a heavy job at the Postal Service in 1998 while pregnant with her third child. After a couple of months, her doctor told her she needed to stop work, but she had no sick leave or vacation time accrued. “I went to my union steward, and I said, ‘This is what my doctor is telling me, I’m scared.’ I had no idea what my rights were. I’d never been in a union before.” 




Her steward explained that she could take leave without pay, under the contract, and could not be fired: “We have a just cause process in our contract. They have to prove that they had a just reason to fire you, and just using too much time off without being paid is not justified.”




After the birth, Cash came back to work, but it was too hard: “I had two toddlers and a newborn. I was trying to go back to work with all those shenanigans going on at my house with all these babies.” She told her steward she was thinking of quitting. But her steward fought for her to get the option to come back with fewer hours and gradually increase them, which was also guaranteed in their contract.




“Pregnancy is stressful,” said Cash. “You have so much to worry about.” But during her next pregnancy, she felt “much more confident that I was going to be able to get the accommodations I needed. I had a whole union behind me, fighting to make sure that those rights were given to me, and to make sure that I had a healthy pregnancy and was able to take the time that I needed for me, and for my baby to be taken care of.”





But there is every indication that Amazon is ignoring it. Last year, New Jersey’s attorney general 

filed a lawsuit

 against Amazon after reviewing thousands of worker requests for accommodations. Amazon is New Jersey’s largest private employer, with around 50,000 workers.




“When Amazon’s pregnant workers and workers with disabilities request accommodations, Amazon stonewalls them,” the suit charges. “It forces them through a byzantine accommodations process, imposing rigid and unnecessary paperwork requirements and subjecting workers to unexplained weeks-long delays.”




Rosa, a worker at Amazon’s fulfillment center in Akron, Ohio, said she asked for pregnancy accommodations because she was working in Ship Dock, a role that requires heavy lifting, pushing, and pulling. She was hospitalized for dehydration four times, but managers still kept her in that role, she said.




“Eventually my symptoms became so severe that I had to take an unpaid leave of absence,” she said. “I found out afterwards that I could have done paid short-term disability leave, but these options weren’t told to me.”




Amazon denies this. “The suggestion that we routinely deny or don’t support pregnancy accommodations is simply untrue,” said Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel. She said “99.9 percent” of pregnancy accommodation requests this year had been approved.




But New Jersey investigators found that Amazon regularly fired workers for requesting accommodations, in violation of New Jersey’s Law Against Discrimination and the PWFA. New York State 

has also sued

 Amazon for this.




Hossain said the medical forms that Amazon requires for pregnancy, injury, and disability accommodations are so comprehensive and invasive that doctors have objected that they violate medical privacy laws.




Amazon wants such detailed medical documentation, Hossain said, because “they want to claim that if workers ever get injured, it’s because of conditions they came to work with, and it’s not workplace injuries.” Asked about this, an Amazon public relations representative declined to respond.




PACE DRIVES INJURIES




The worker justice group 

Warehouse Life

 has been tracking and protesting Amazon’s health and safety record since 2023, and helping injured workers who have to “fight through a lot of misinformation and lies that they received from [Amazon] managers about workers’ comp,” said Chloe Sigal, campaign manager for the group.




Sigal said Amazon’s rate system, along with “time off task” (TOT) policies, make the work unsafe: “Amazon is pushing people to work as fast, as hard as humanly possible—or really outside what is humanly possible. That’s what’s driving this 

injury epidemic

.”




In 2021 the California legislature found that injuries in Amazon warehouses were driven by its rate system. Workers were forced to work faster and faster because if they fell into the lowest 25 percent they could experience discipline, and the bottom 5 percent risked termination.




California passed a law requiring warehouses to publish stable quotas and not constantly accelerate them. In 2024 the state 

fined

 Amazon $6 million for violating it. 




Workers also accumulate TOT when surveillance detects a pause in their package scanning. Fear of too much TOT pushes workers to cut short their breaks, skip bathroom breaks (and reduce liquid consumption to match), and push on through pain. Dehydration is particularly risky during a pregnancy. “The reason that people are miscarrying at Amazon is because of this rate system,” said Sigal.




Doctors agree. Jenny Fish is a Santa Rosa, California, physician who provides prenatal care. “Prolonged standing, going the whole shift without water, lifting more than 15 to 20 pounds, working night shifts regularly,” she said, “all of this has been irrefutably linked to higher risk of miscarriage, preeclampsia, increased maternal fatigue, preterm delivery, low birth weight, and just in general adverse birth outcomes.” Preeclampsia is potentially fatal.




IS THERE A POLICY?




Sigal said that soon after Warehouse Life started, several Amazon workers came to the group reporting pregnancy issues. But when the group put out a call on social media for experiences working at Amazon while pregnant, it was flooded with stories. Two thousand women from 40 states responded, and 81 described loss of a pregnancy. (To talk to Warehouse Life, 

schedule a call here

.)




Now some of these workers are leading the charge to get changes at the company. They have put pressure on New York City’s Mt. Sinai Health System to terminate Amazon Board of Directors member Edith Cooper as a hospital trustee, given Amazon’s dismal safety record.




Warehouse Life members have also met with Amazon management. Sigal said that during those meetings Amazon claimed to have a policy on pregnancy that was only available to workers. But no workers were able to access it. “Nobody has it. We’ve heard from managers that they don’t have it either, that they don’t receive training on what to do,” Sigal said.




When Labor Notes asked Amazon for its pregnancy policy and any training materials, no documents were forthcoming. Warehouse Life counters that the company’s real pregnancy policy is 

“Delay. Deny. Discipline.”




MARCH ON H.R.




The Amazon Labor Union organized on Staten Island in 2022, and in 2024 affiliated with the Teamsters. But Amazon refuses to negotiate with the union at the 5,000-worker warehouse, despite being ordered to do so by the National Labor Relations Board in April.




The union can still help, though. “Just a few weeks ago a pregnant worker came to our union hall saying she wanted help getting an accommodation at work,” said ALU’s Hossain. The worker had already told her manager that she was pregnant.




The union sent several workers to accompany her to H.R., saying “that should be enough, and Amazon needs to start the process of accommodating her,” Hossain said. “And they actually did listen, but only because a group of workers accompanied her.” A contract could provide additional protections 

(see box at upper right)

.




The union isn’t waiting for workers to seek it out. Union activists distribute fliers with a QR code to a reporting form that goes to the union. Half of the reports “are unfair discipline, the other half is workers who are dealing with injuries or the accommodation process or need workers’ comp or whatever,” said Hossain. “It’s such a big issue.” 




“It really does feel like we’re all just numbers,” said Rosa in Akron. “I want them to take more accountability. They make it so hard when it comes to a life-changing thing.”			     










 Pregnancy Rights 







It has been illegal to discriminate against pregnant workers since 1978, when feminist agitation won the 

Pregnancy Discrimination Act

 (under Title VII of the 1964 Civil Rights Act), which says employers can’t discriminate based on pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions. Before that, many employers had a policy of terminating workers when they got pregnant, and pregnant women often weren’t eligible for unemployment insurance.




In 2023, the 

Pregnant Workers Fairness Act

 strengthened pregnancy rights. Now employers are required to make reasonable accommodations.




The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission has found that reasonable accommodations which don’t require a doctor’s note include: a seat; additional breaks to eat, drink, or use the bathroom; adjusted uniforms and safety equipment; and changes to your job duties or your schedule to make it possible for you to keep working safely while you’re pregnant or recovering from a birth.




Additional accommodations that might require a doctor’s note include limits on weight you have to lift, bending, and ladder use. “But you still have the right to get those accommodations quickly and have them implemented effectively,” said Katherine Greenberg, attorney with 

A Better Balance

. 




“It is illegal for employers like Amazon to force workers to take a leave of absence if there’s an on-the-job accommodation that would keep them safe and allow them to keep working and earning an income,” said Greenberg. Also, employers can’t punish workers for asking for or needing accommodations.




“If you need to pump milk for your baby, you have the right to take a lactation break without being punished for too much time off task,” said Greenberg. “Or if you experience a miscarriage and you need to miss work to recover, you have the right to take that time without being deducted UPT or assigned points for your absence.”




Your state or city may have additional protections; 

check here

. Have a question or concern about your pregnancy at Amazon? 

Schedule a call with Warehouse Life here

.

title: Animal Freedom Library!
content:
We couldn’t be happier to announce this. The Talon Conspiracy was a website that archived hundreds of animal liberation and earth liberation magazines, providing a platform to look into the past, learn from what the movement did decades prior, and plot the next steps for total liberation.

For a while, Talon was not available. Now, a new website has been launched, allowing you to read all the content Talon had. Go and check it out, from single zines from the 80s and 90s to long running publications like HOWL or the ALFsg magazine, there are heaps and heaps of material to read and learn from, for free, available to download or read online!

Go visit the Animal Freedom Library right now, and share far and wide, everybody should know about this!

author: Stelinsky
title: Η ισλαμοφοβία και η γιαγιά μου
content:
Η μεταψυχροπολεμική εποχή άφησε τα δυτικά κέντρα εξουσίας, και κυρίως τις ΗΠΑ, χωρίς αφορμή για να δικαιολογούν τις ιμπεριαλιστικές επιχειρήσεις τους στις περιοχές της βόρειας Αφρικής και της Νοτιοδυτικής Ασίας. Αυτό το κενό, και με τη χρήση των οξυμένων μεθόδων προπαγάνδας που είχαν ήδη κερδίσει έναν πόλεμο, καλύφθηκε από τη «μουσουλμανική απειλή» και τη νέα εποχή ισλαμοφοβίας που διανύουμε μέχρι σήμερα, με σημαντικό σημείο καμπής την επίθεση της 11ης Σεπτεμβρίου και των εισβολών των ΗΠΑ σε Ιράκ και Αφγανιστάν. Ο μουσουλμάνος εξτρεμιστής αναδύθηκε ως ο νέος εχθρός του καπιταλιστικού κέντρου, και η μουσουλμάνα γυναίκα ως παίκτρια μπαλαντέρ για κάθε λογής προπαγάνδα των εμπόρων θανάτου. Οικεία για την εξουσία η τεχνική από τις εποχές της αποικιοκρατίας, η στροφή έφυγε από το υλικό, τις παραγωγικές σχέσεις, και γύρισε προς το πολιτισμικό και την κατασκευή μίας κατώτερης ή οπισθοδρομικής ετερότητας: Οι βάρβαροι και απολίτιστοι μουσουλμάνοι άνδρες καταπιέζουν τις γυναίκες τους, οι οποίες είναι ταυτόχρονα άβουλα θύματα αλλά και ενεργοί φορείς της ιδεολογίας, και έχουν ανάγκη από το δικό μας δυτικό χέρι – είτε με τη μορφή βομβιστικών επιθέσεων, είτε με τη μορφή φεμινιστικών διδαγμάτων, για να απελευθερωθούν από τα φονταμενταλιστικά δεσμά τους. Το απόλυτο σύμβολο αυτής της καταπίεσης αποτελεί η μαντίλα, η οποία στον καθημερινό λόγο θα ονομάζεται μπούρκα ανεξαρτήτως του είδους της (αν είναι δηλαδή μπούρκα, η παραδοσιακή κάλυψη των γυναικών των Παστούν που επιβλήθηκε αργότερα στις Αφγανές γυναίκες, τσαντόρ, χιτζάμπ ή ο,τι άλλο μπορεί κάποια να φοράει).

Υπάρχουν πάνω από τριάντα διαφορετικοί τύποι κάλυψης της κεφαλής ως ισλαμική πρακτική με διαφορές στο ύφασμα, την κάλυψη, την περιοχή και την ιστορία. Η μπούρκα είναι ένα μακρύ ύφασμα που καλύπτει ολόκληρο το σώμα και το πρόσωπο, με ένα κέντημα στην περιοχή των ματιών, και χαρακτηριστικό μπλε χρώμα. Το τσαντόρ είναι ένα μακρύ ύφασμα που καλύπτει το κεφάλι και τυλίγεται ή πέφτει γύρω από το σώμα, το οποίο συνήθως κρατείται με τα χέρια και θεωρείται ένδυμα προσευχής. Το χιτζάμπ, πέρα από τη χρήση του για να περιγράψει γενικά την κάλυψη της κεφαλής, είναι ένα μαντήλι το οποίο καλύπτει τα μαλλιά και τυλίγεται γύρω από τον λαιμό, αφήνοντας ακάλυπτο ολόκληρο το πρόσωπο. Μία βασική ερμηνεία που έχει το χιτζάμπ είναι η δημόσια ένδειξη σεμνότητας, ευσέβειας και δήλωσης της επιθυμίας να βρίσκεσαι κοντά στον Θεό. Έδινε στις γυναίκες τη δυνατότητα να κινούνται στον δημόσιο χώρο σε περιόδους και περιοχές που η παρουσία τους περιοριζόταν εντός του ιδιωτικού. Παρ’ όλα αυτά θα ήταν μεγάλο λάθος να εγγράψουμε μόνο μία ερμηνεία στο χιτζάμπ, ή και ακόμη να θεωρήσουμε ότι η σεμνότητα και η δήλωση εγγύτητας με το θείο μονοπωλούνται από την ισλαμική πρακτική.

Για να δώσουμε μερικά παραδείγματα, οι γυναίκες εβραϊκής πίστης Χασίντ, αν και φαινομενικά. έχουν τα μαλλιά τους λιτά, στην πραγματικότητα φοράνε περούκες, κρατώντας τα φυσικά του μαλλιά για την ιδιωτική σφαίρα. Σε μέρη του Πακιστάν, του Μπανγκλαντές και της Βόρειας Ινδίας, Ινδουίστριες γυναίκες καλύπτουν το κεφάλι τους με το duppata. Δεν χρειάζεται όμως να πάμε μακριά για να βρούμε αντίστοιχες πρακτικές, αφού η Ελλάδα έχει μακρά παράδοση στην κάλυψη των μαλλιών των γυναικών, από την αρχαία Ελλάδα, τις κατά τόπους παραδοσιακές φορεσιές πριν την ίδρυση του ελληνικού κράτους, τις σημερινές καλόγριες αλλά και πολύ πιο κοντά μας, τις προγιαγιάδες και τις γιαγιάδες μας. Η Καινή Διαθήκη θεωρεί ότι η γυναίκα που έχει ακάλυπτο το κεφάλι της το «ντροπιάζει», ότι είναι ένδειξη ανυπακοής στον άνδρα και έλλειψη σεμνότητας (Παύλος προς Κορινθίους 11:4-8). Το μαντήλι είναι χαρακτηριστικό ένδυμα της Βαλκάνιας και της Σλαβικής μπάμπουσκα της υπαίθρου. Είναι επίσης έκφραση πένθους σε πολλές περιοχές της ελληνικής επαρχίας, όπως η Μάνη και η Κρήτη (όπου αντίστοιχη λειτουργία έχει και το ανδρικό σαρίκι).

Η κρητικιά προγιαγιά μου η Χρυσούλα δεν θα έβγαινε ποτέ από το σπίτι με τα μαλλιά λιτά. Όταν πήγαινε σε αγροτικές εργασίες προστάτευε τα μαλλιά της με τσεμπέρι, και όταν πήγαινε στην εκκλησία έβαζε πάνω στο κεφάλι της ένα λευκό κεντητό μαντήλι. Η γιαγιά μου έχει ένα συρτάρι με τα τσεμπέρια της και τις μαύρες μουσελίνες που φοράει σε τελετές πένθους για να δείξει την απόσυρσή της στο ιδιωτικό. Ή άλλη μου προγιαγιά από τη Δαμάστα, χωριό της Κρήτης που λεηλατήθηκε και σφαγιάστηκε σε αντίποινα Γερμανών της κατοχής, δεν έβγαλε ποτέ το μαντήλι, όπως και οι υπόλοιπες γυναίκες του χωριού. Επιστρέφοντας στην περίπτωση του χιτζάμπ, μπορούμε ακόμη και να βρούμε καταστάσεις όπου αυτό συνδέθηκε με την αντίσταση στην αποικιοκρατία. Χαρακτηριστική είναι η περίπτωση της Γαλλίας, η οποία με το προσωπείο του φιλελεύθερου ανεξίθρησκου κράτους με σεβασμό στα δικαιώματα, έχει μία μακριά παράδοση καταπίεσης και ρατσισμού. Κατά τη διάρκεια του πολέμου για την ανεξαρτησία της Αλγερίας (1954-1962) από την αποικιοκρατική επιβολή της Γαλλίας, η μαντίλα έγινε σύμβολο της οπισθοδρόμησης των Αλγερινών από τη γαλλική προπαγάνδα. Τον Μάιο του 1954, οι γαλλικές στρατιωτικές αρχές οργάνωσαν δημόσιες τελετές στο Αλγέρι, όπου Γαλλίδες γυναίκες αφαιρούσαν τα πέπλα των Αλγερινών γυναικών μπροστά σε κάμερες, παρουσιάζοντας το ως απόδειξη του καλωσορίσματος της γαλλικής κυριαρχίας. Η συμμετοχή των Αλγερινών γυναικών σε αυτές τις τελετές ωστόσο γινόταν μέσω εκβιασμού και απειλών. Ο επαναστάτης και θεωρητικός Φ. Φανόν έχει υποστηρίξει ότι η στάση αυτή της εξουσίας ανέδειξε τη μαντίλα ως σύμβολο αντίστασης, μεταφορικά αλλά και κυριολεκτικά, αφού γυναίκες εντός του απελευθερωτικού αγώνα χρησιμοποιούσαν τη μαντίλα τους για στρατηγικούς σκοπούς. Σήμερα η Γαλλία, όπως και πολλές άλλες χώρες της Ευρώπης, συνεχίζει να διατηρεί τη στάση του κρατικά ελεγχόμενου ντυσίματος των μουσουλμάνων γυναικών, απαγορεύοντας τη μαντίλα σε δημόσιες υπηρεσίες και σχολεία, περιορίζοντας έτσι τη ζωή και την κίνηση πολλών γυναικών.

Φυσικά καμιά από εμάς δεν αρνείται ότι η κάλυψη έχει υπάρξει και εξακολουθεί να αποτελεί σημείο ακραίας καταπίεσης για πάρα πολλές γυναίκες ανά τον κόσμο. Θα ήταν τεράστιο σφάλμα να αφήναμε στα ψιλά γράμματα αυτής τη συζήτησης τις καθημερινές αντιστάσεις στην πατριαρχική επιβολή, αλλά και τις αιματηρές εξεγέρσεις στο όνομα της αυτονομίας του σώματος, με πρόσφατη αυτή που ακολούθησε την δολοφονία της Κούρδισας Mahsa Amini το 2022. Όλα αυτά λέγονται για να δείξουν πώς μία πολιτισμική πρακτική είναι πολλά παραπάνω από μία μονοσήμαντη ερμηνεία, είτε αυτή είναι η αντίσταση είτε αυτή είναι η επιβολή και καταπίεση – ειδικά για τις περιπτώσεις που ο εν λόγω χαρακτηρισμός της καταπίεσης βγαίνει από το στόμα των ΗΠΑ, του Ισραήλ και οποιοδήποτε άλλου παράγοντα ακόρεστης πολεμικής λύσσας.

Εμείς ως μέρος του αντιπατριαρχικού αγώνα οφείλουμε να καταστήσουμε σαφές ότι η κρατική εξουσία με τη συνοριακή θανατοπολιτική της, οι ταξικοί μας εχθροί, οι πολεμοχαρείς απελευθερωτές, και το κάθε κυρίαρχο καταπιεστικό καθεστώς θα μας βρίσκουν πάντα απέναντί τους. Να αφήσουμε στο παρελθόν τις λογικές του λευκού σωτήρα και τις υποδείξεις για τη δική τους φεμινιστική χειραφέτηση, και να βοηθήσουμε τις αδερφές μας και τις αντιστάσεις τους, επιτιθέμενες στα δικά μας δυτικά κράτη και το κεφάλαιο του παγκόσμιου βορρά, που αποσταθεροποιούν και βομβαρδίζουν τις χώρες τους για ενεργειακά και μονοπωλιακά συμφέροντα, που τις πνίγουν στα σύνορά τους, που εκμεταλλεύονται την φθηνή και αόρατη εργασία τους. Οι ετερότητες που φτιάχνουν είναι πλαστές και παρελκυστικές. Οι εχθροί μας κοινοί, ο αγώνας μας ένας.

author: Daron Letts
title: Kotierk family competes on Family Feud Canada
content:
Wednesday night’s episode of 

Family Feud Canada

 on CBC features the Kotierk family of Nunavut competing for up to $30,000 in cash prizes.




“It was a lot of fun,” said team captain Kunuk Kotierk, who caught up with Nunatsiaq News ahead of the episode’s première. “We did it on a whim.”




The whim was his.




This past spring, he submitted an application for himself and four family members to compete on the show.




The rest of the Kotierk team includes Kunuk Kotierk’s uncle 

David Joanasie

, aunt 

Emily Joanasie

, aunt 

Jessica Kotierk

, and mom 

Aluki Kotierk

.




On each episode, two families of five face off to determine the most popular answers to survey questions.




The application process included three interview stages, held weeks apart, leaving some in the family to doubt whether they would be selected.
















“I had confidence the whole way that we were going to make it,” Kunuk Kotierk said. “I was like 

—

 this is a sure thing.”




The family practised over the summer by watching 

Family Feud

 reruns while trying to out-guess the on-screen contestants, he said.




“We also would look up a lot of 

Family Feud

-type questions online,” he added.




His sibling, Siku Rojas, the team’s understudy, played the role of show host Gerry Dee during these sessions.




“And then ‘lo and behold, we end up getting flown to Toronto and filming for a weekend,” Kunuk Kotierk said. “When we came on for our episode, everything was lit up, and it looked magical.”




The show is co-produced by CBC and Zone3 and shot in the national broadcaster’s downtown Toronto studio. The family was put up in a nearby hotel.
















During the taping, Rojas sat in the audience.




“It was really surreal,” Rojas said about watching the family on set. “It’s edited, so I am excited to see what they keep in the show.”




Their brother shares that curiosity.




“Me and my family like to talk a lot and so we were definitely chatty with Gerry Dee,” he said. “There was moments where he would go off script and it was like, ‘Oh this is something only we can see because this is not going to be on the show.'”




Wednesday’s episode is titled 

Who’s the Sexiest Game Show Host?
















The Kotierks are the third Nunavut 

family on the show. 

Their episode airs at 7:30 p.m. Wednesday on CBC and is also watchable on the CBC Gem app.

author: Stelinsky
title: Η φαντασμαγορική γοητεία της μπουρζουαζίας
content:
Skincare ρουτίνα, ούλτρα βία, και το ανάθρεμμα της κενότητας

I used to think that the day would never come I’d see delight in the shade of the morning sun

Το American Psycho είναι ένα φιλμ μαύρης κωμωδίας τρόμου που γυρίστηκε το 2000, σε σκηνοθεσία της Mary Harron, βασισμένο στο ομώνυμο μυθιστόρημα του Bret Easton Ellis.

Νέα Υόρκη, τέλη της δεκαετίας του ‘80: Η εποχή του χρυσού θερισμού, μέσω της εγκαθίδρυσης των νεοφιλελεύθερων πολιτικών του Ronald Reagan, και ο αμερικανικός πολιτισμός μας δείχνει τα δόντια του. Ιταλικά κουστούμια, μάχες για ένα τραπέζι σε κάποιο δημοφιλές εστιατόριο, έκρηξη της αστεγίας και δημιουργία μιας νέας κοινωνικής τάξης, των λεγόμενων «yuppies».

Αυτό το συμπύκνωμα του οικονομικού μετασχηματισμού, μέσα από μεγάλα, απανωτά «κραχ» και «μπουμ», φέρνει στην οικονομική και πολιτισμική επιφάνεια τη Μεγαλόπολη της Νέας Υόρκης σαν έναν νέο τόπο λατρείας, με πρωταγωνιστή το κοινωνικό status. Η εικόνα, οι τάσεις και οι γενικόλογες, ψευδοκοινωνικές κλισέ συζητήσεις για τις ευκαιρίες του αμερικάνικου ονείρου δείχνουν να είναι η προμετωπίδα της «μικρής» οικονομικής ελίτ των «mergers and acquisitions», δηλαδή των golden boys που δουλεύουν σε εταιρίες «συγχωνεύσεων και εξαγορών».

-Με λένε Νάρκισσο, Νάρκισσο Μοναχό. -Και μένα Ηχώ.

Ο πρωταγωνιστής της ταινίας ονομάζεται Patrick Bateman, είναι 27 χρονών και μας εξιστορεί -αφού κάνει τα πρωινά του push ups- με εμμονική λεπτομέρεια τα προϊόντα περιποίησης που χρησιμοποιεί, ξεκινώντας ευλαβικά από κάποιο προϊόν βαθύ καθαρισμού και φτάνοντας μέχρι τον ορό αντιγήρανσης. Καθώς τελειώνει την εξαντλητική του ρουτίνα, γεμίζει το υπαρξιακό του κενό μπροστά στον καθρέφτη με τον παρακάτω εσωτερικό μονόλογο:

Υπάρχει μια «ιδέα» για το ποιος είναι ο Patrick Bateman, κάτι αφηρημένο, δεν υπάρχει κάποιος πραγματικός εαυτός, παρά μόνο μια οντότητα αυτού, μια ψευδαίσθηση.

Κι ενώ μπορώ να κρύψω το ψυχρό μου βλέμμα δίνοντας μια χειραψία, θα νιώσεις τη σάρκα μου να σφίγγει τη δική σου, ίσως ακόμα και να αισθανθείς πως ο τρόπος ζωής μας είναι πιθανώς συμβατός· όμως εγώ, απλώς δεν είμαι εκεί.

Παίρνοντας τη συμβατότητα του Patrick σαν εννοιολογικό σχήμα, παρατηρούμε την ομοιομορφία αυτής της νέας αστικής τάξης των yuppies. Ίδια ρούχα, ίδια μαλλιά, ίδια γούστα εν γένει: Είναι τόσο ίδιοι, που πολλοί μπερδεύονται με το ποιος είναι ποιος, δημιουργώντας μία σύγχυση που θα παίξει μεγάλο ρόλο αργότερα στην πλοκή. Με κορυφαίο σαρκαστικό παράδειγμα την ψυχική κατάρρευση του πρωταγωνιστή στη σκηνή όπου όλα τα άτομα στην παρέα δείχνουν τις καινούργιες επαγγελματικές τους κάρτες, οι οποίες είναι φαινομενικά ίδιες. Η σκηνή αυτή αποτελεί το σημείο εσωτερικής ρήξης στην ψυχοσύνθεση του Patrick, που από εκεί και μετά ξυπνάει η σαδιστική και δολοφονική του δίψα.

Ο Ellis έπλασε αυτό το τρομακτικό ανδρείκελο σατιρίζοντας τόσο τη νέα αστική τάξη των golden boys, όσο και την πατριαρχική αρρενωπότητα και το hustle culture. Αυτή η ταινία θα έπρεπε να μείνει στην ιστορία σαν κωμωδία των από τα κάτω που γελάνε με τους από τα πάνω, και αντ’ αυτού βρίσκει οπαδούς του πρωταγωνιστή. Έτσι, τα τελευταία χρόνια εγκαθιδρύεται η εικόνα του Patrick Bateman σε σύμβολο επιτυχίας και alpha-sigma ανδρισμού, τη στιγμή που μια ολόκληρη γενιά μεγαλώνει εκκολάπτοντας τις κοινωνικές της δεξιότητες μέσω των social media.

Προσπερνώντας τα ειρωνικά meme και τις προτάσεις αυτοβελτίωσης, η λεγόμενη alt-right κατάφερε να εδραιωθεί ξεφεύγοντας από τον «στείρο», παραδοσιακό, αμερικάνικο συντηρητισμό και περνώντας στον αποχαυνωμένο νεοφασισμό της «εναλλακτικής δεξιάς». Μετατράπηκε σε πυροκροτητή και δεκανίκι του κεφαλαίου και του κράτους του. Έφτιαξε μία πλατφόρμα που, αντί να δραστηριοποιείται περισσότερο στον δρόμο όπως συνηθίζει η ακροδεξιά, κάνει τη βρωμοδουλειά στα μέσα κοινωνικής δικτύωσης.

Αυτό που διαφαίνεται από το σενάριό, είναι πως ο Patrick δεν είναι ένας πραγματικός άνθρωπος, μα περισσότερο ένα αρχέτυπο. Όχι ένα στατιστικό λάθος σε μια κατακερματισμένη κοινωνία, αλλά ο ακριβής κλώνος της επιτυχημένης κάστας της Wall Street, όπως ο «κουλ» τότε Donald Trump, όπως αναφέρεται στο σενάριο. Είναι λυπημένος και αποξενωμένος, σαν να τον θλίβει οτιδήποτε δεν του επιφέρει κέρδος. Είναι ένα πρότυπο της τοξικής αρρενωπότητας που, 40 χρόνια μετά, φαντάζει επίκαιρο.

Από την αχόρταγη υλιστική όρεξη για μόδα, ακριβό φαγητό, κοινωνική επιβεβαίωση και εξαντλητική περιποίηση, περνάει στο «τελευταίο» στάδιο του καπιταλισμού, την εξόντωση. Στην προσπάθειά του να γεμίσει το κενό του γιάπικου τρόπου ζωής, που σε υλιστικό επίπεδο τα έχει όλα σε αφθονία, περνάει σε μια αδηφάγα πείνα να σκοτώσει.

Η προσέγγιση της Mary Harron φέρνει οργανικά τη σάτιρα μέσα στο φιλμ, με απλότητα και ειλικρίνεια, χωρίς να εκβιάζει. Πλασάροντας κάποιο έτοιμο προϊόν, συμπυκνώνει εκεί που πρέπει την ψυχική κατάσταση του Bateman, είτε με εσωτερικό μονόλογο, είτε με την αποτύπωση ενός μωσαϊκού συμπεριφορών και συνηθειών.

Τον κανόνα της ταξικής ανέλιξης του «πατάω επί πτωμάτων», ο Bateman εδώ τον μετουσιώνει με περίσσιο κυνισμό, χύνοντας ποτάμια αίματος και στοχεύοντας κυρίως στα προλεταριακά σώματα, όπως άστεγοι ή σεξεργάτριες. Εξαίρεση αποτελεί ο Paul Allen, συνεργάτης του Bateman, και μεγαλύτερος αντίζηλος, επειδή βρίσκει πάντα τραπέζι στο πιο δημοφιλές εστιατόριο του Μανχάταν, το «Dorsia». Ανοίγοντάς του το κεφάλι με ένα τσεκούρι, υπό τους ήχους των Huey Lewis and the News, ο πρωταγωνιστής δεν διαπράττει ακριβώς κάποια δολοφονία, παρά σπάει τον εσωτερικό του καθρέφτη, κάνοντας μπάνιο σε ένα ντεμπορικό λουτρό αίματος.

Αρκετά ρε μαλάκες με την κονόμα και τις μαλακίες, μας γαμήσατε

Ο Bateman βρίσκεται σε ένα διαρκές επεισόδιο, μέχρι που κάποια στιγμή σπάει και θέλει να εξομολογηθεί τις ειδεχθείς πράξεις του. Εδώ, η ταινία θολώνει τα νερά σχετικά με το ποιες κτηνωδίες έχουν όντως συμβεί και ποιες μπορεί να είναι προϊόν του μυαλού του. Έχοντας –ίσως– διαπράξει ένα πλήθος από ανθρωποκτονίες και γυναικοκτονίες, ο πρώτος που θα επιλέξει να επικοινωνήσει είναι ο δικηγόρος του. Ο δικηγόρος δεν τον πιστεύει, επειδή ούτε ξεχωρίζει τα golden boys μεταξύ τους, αλλά ούτε και θέλει να τον πιστέψει. Τη δεύτερη εξομολόγηση την κάνει στον εαυτό του και παραδέχεται πως, παρ’ όλο τον πόνο που έχει προκαλέσει, δεν βρίσκει καμία λύτρωση, καμία ανακούφιση και δεν κατάφερε μέσα από αυτόν να γνωρίσει τον εαυτό του καλύτερα. Ο Bateman δεν έχει σύστημα να τον τιμωρήσει, γιατί είναι οργανικό μέρος του συστήματος, αν όχι το ίδιο το σύστημα. Και αυτό ξέρει να αναπαράγεται αδιάκοπα, εις βάρος μας.

author: Chris Walker
title: Mary Peltola Wins Alaska Senate Race Despite Trump’s Efforts to Halt Count
content:
Peltola won outright in the first round, negating the need for a second round of ranked-choice voting.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) has been declared the winner of the Alaska U.S. Senate race, following weeks of ballot counting since Election Day, which President Donald Trump had sought to derail.

The Associated Press called the race on Tuesday night, determining that, with 99 percent of the ballots counted, Peltola had secured around 50.1 percent of the vote. While Alaska employs instant ranked-choice voting, secondary ballot counts will not be necessary, as Peltola secured a majority of votes in the first round of tabulation.

Peltola defeats incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), who garnered just 45.8 percent of the vote. Her victory ensures that Democrats (and aligned independents) will have 56 seats in the Senate, while Republicans will have just 44 members.

While some votes have yet to be counted, the AP explained why it was calling the race.

“Very few ballots remain to be counted, most of which are absentee ballots,” the news outlet said. “Peltola has handily beaten the incumbent Sullivan among absentee votes, which suggests her vote share will remain above 50 percent.”

The result of the race comes despite Trump’s attempts to end vote counting sooner, when it had appeared that Sullivan was closer to Peltola’s totals. The matter was complicated by the fact that a separate Dan Sullivan, running as an independent, had received a few thousand votes, too.

The president, citing a New York Times investigative report that accused the Peltola campaign of recruiting the second Dan Sullivan in an effort to confuse reporters, cried foul in a Truth Social post just two days after Election Day. (The Peltola campaign denies the conclusions drawn from the Times report.)

“The vote totals for the Fake Dan Sullivan, plus the other ‘slug’ that the Dems put on the Ballot, should be immediately given to the REAL Dan Sullivan, and the Election is over — He easily wins,” Trump wrote in his post. “There is no other fair solution!”

At the time of Trump’s post-election demand, fewer than three-quarters of all votes had even been counted. Had Alaska officials attempted to do what Trump wanted, potentially hundreds of thousands of voters would have been disenfranchised.

Trump had also complained about the other Sullivan candidate before the election. In response, the Department of Justice (DOJ) took the unprecedented action of requesting that Alaska delay certification of the Senate race if the incumbent Sullivan lost.

“It is vital that Defendants not certify any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion,” the DOJ asserted in its filing.

A federal judge dismissed the lawsuit, but the DOJ said that it was going to pursue an appeal. However, due to Peltola’s outright win (without purported “confusion” affecting the race’s outcome), the lawsuit is likely to be dropped, or dismissed again as moot in an appeals court.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $21,000 in the next 24 hours. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.
