author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Overcoming police brutality, protests continue vs. Trump, Pax Silica
content:
Kampuhan Kontra Pax Silica, a UP Diliman-based formation, together with progressive groups, students, faculty members, and rights advocates held an indignation protest along Katipunan Avenue in Quezon City on November 15, 2026. Photo by Carlo Manalansan/Bulatlat

“Even if we see police harassment, it does not deter us. We will persevere and fight back.”

No amount of police brutality could hold back the progressive groups from continuing their protest today, November 16. They gathered at the Liwasang Bonifacio and strongly condemned the Marcos Jr. administration for its subservience to foreign interests.

“We feel more courage now that there are many people who chose to stand alongside our fight for our ancestral lands,” Ayta elder Nelson De Guzman told Bulatlat in Filipino. “Even if we see police harassment, it does not deter us. We will persevere and fight back.”

De Guzman is among the delegation of the Ayta-Hungey community from Capas, Tarlac who went to Manila to join the series of protests against the arrival of U.S. President Donald Trump and the reported signing of the Pax Silica framework agreement.

He said, “They are lying when they said that indigenous peoples will not be affected [by Pax Silica]. We are here to prove them wrong and stand for what is right.”

The first day of the 49th ASEAN Summit on November 15 began with a series of arbitrary mass arrests of close to 300 activists, students, journalists, and community leaders.

Hundreds of the arrested individuals were part of the Lakbayan Southern Tagalog who were supposed to hold a campout in Liwasang Bonifacio to attend the series of protests in Manila.

They have been detained for more than 24 hours at Camp Bagong Diwa in Bicutan.

Read: Police violently disperse, arrest hundreds in Muntinlupa protest

Article 125 of the Revised Penal Code limits detention without charges to 12 [light penalties], 18,[correctional penalties] or 36 hours [capital penalties]. It also guarantees the accused’s right to legal counsel at any time.

Lawyers, paralegals, and human rights investigators were only allowed entry to Camp Bagong Diwa after six hours of negotiation with the police.

“From the first day since we started our lakbayan (collective march), the repression never stopped. They tried to sabotage our program, the wheels of our vehicles, up to the massive deployment of police officers within our camp-out area,” human rights defender Paul Tagle, who is part of the Southern Tagalog delegation, said in Filipino in a press conference.

He said that detained individuals are being threatened with charges under the Public Assembly Act (Batas Pambansa Blg. 880), a remnant of Ferdinand Marcos Sr.’s dictatorship, which he described as a complete “madness” since it is the police who exercised violent intervention.

Read: Bayan hits ‘Marcosian’ tactics against protesters

At least 500 policemen are reportedly stationed in the entry and exit points in University of the Philippines Diliman in Quezon City, where some 200 Ayta and their supporters held a campout.

Cristina Palabay, secretary general of human rights group Karapatan, demanded accountability from police officers and commanders who ordered the violent interference. She emphasized that the denial coming from state security forces, particularly the National Police Commission (Napolcom), rings hollow as the police brutality was properly documented by the journalists and activists, publicized in the social media.

“The fact is,” said Palabay, “the PNP has long been besmirching the uniform. Yesterday’s incidents of police brutality have not been the first, nor will they be the last, given the vociferous statements issued by the PNP’s talking heads, and their consistent denials of the truth.”

Moreover, the National Union of Peoples’ Lawyers (NUPL) said that neither the ASEAN Summit nor Trump’s visit guarantees the suspension of peoples’ right to protest and peaceful assembly.

“The Constitution guarantees the people’s right to protest. Peaceful assembly is no crime, while the law requires maximum tolerance and protects participants in otherwise peaceful assemblies from criminal liability,” the NUPL said in a statement.

The group also demanded release of the detained individuals, the police to pull back from UP’s gates to allow the protest delegation to reach the assembly sites unharmed, and the accountability of state security personnel responsible for unlawful arrests and assaults.

The Philippine National Police deployed more than 23,000 personnel coming from the National Capital Region Police Office (NCRPO), Armed Forces of the Philippines, Bureau of Fire Protection, and other concerned agencies.

Igorot youth leader Funa-ay Claver, secretary general of indigenous group Katribu, said that they have long prepared for the protest actions.

“The repression of the administration is in full force, all to stop our Indigenous Peoples from asserting their rights and aspirations. But we see that most of us reached here in Manila to fight together despite the long, tedious journey,” said Claver.

Another youth leader, Lance Alba of Anakbayan, said during the protest today: “The violence, repression, and arrests never stopped. But so are we. Our camp-out remains. And we are ready to continue this until November 18.”

“Protest marches that attempt to go beyond designated spaces or barricades, are still protected by the right to peaceful assembly, and must not be forcibly or violently dispersed,” said Ritz Lee Santos III, Section Director of Amnesty International Philippines.

Article 5 of the United Nations Code of Conduct for Law Enforcement Officials states that it is prohibited to inflict, instigate, or tolerate any act of torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, nor they can invoke superior orders or exceptional circumstances as a justification.

“The PNP must take steps to practice restraint and strict adherence to international standards on the use of force. Any use of force must be a measure of last resort, and should be in line with the principles of necessity and proportionality,” said Santos.

Meanwhile, for Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan) “now is the best time to speak out and hold Marcos accountable for his treasonous sell-out of the country’s resources when the country is under international spotlight.”

The group said the world needs to know that farmers and Indigenous Peoples are being evicted from their lands because of the US-led Pax Silica initiative.

“While Marcos is rolling out a red carpet welcome for war criminal Donald Trump, the Filipino people are opposing his state visit. After his party’s embarrassing defeat in the midterm polls, Trump is being greeted by a gigantic ‘protest wave’ in the Philippines,” Bayan said.

“People’s protests are not organized for the convenience of those in power. We protest to inconvenience those who abuse their power like the fascist puppet Marcos Jr. regime,” they added. (AMU, RVO)

author: Aaron Ernest Cruz
title: ‘Unconstitutional’ — lawyers on checkpoints blocking, delaying protesters
content:
Southern Tagalog delegates negotiating with the police who block their way going to Liwasang Bonifacio. Photo from UPLB Perspective

“These rights have primacy in all constitutional rights. This is the highest constitutional right that the government should protect at all cost.”

As police continue to block protesters from different places using checkpoints, progressive lawyers said the police are interrupting not only the rights of the people to protest but also of Filipinos who are working during the 49th ASEAN Summit.

Delegates from Southern Tagalog who held the Lakbayan ng Timog Katalugan (Southern Tagalog caravan) starting on November 12, faced police brutality during their march to Liwasang Bonifacio.

Previously, they have been repeatedly blocked by police forces. Reports from UPLB Perspective shows punctured tires from the vehicles used by the delegates. The harassment continued where police disrupted the delegates when they barricaded the road at midnight to prevent them from moving forward.

On November 15, police brutality took over as they violently arrested almost 270 delegates while holding a peaceful mobilization. As of this writing, the National Union of People’s Lawyers and Koalisyong Makabayan have gained access to those arrested.

In the University of the Philippines, hundreds of police were deployed to man checkpoints at the exit points. The PICC and nearby areas were also heavily guarded. Aside from these checkpoints, there are also other checkpoints conducted in the borders of several provinces and the National Capital Region.

In an interview, National Union of Peoples’ Lawyer (NUPL) Ephraim “Rey” Cortez underscores that mass deployment of checkpoints within the area violates freedom of expression and right to peaceful assembly that is protected under the Philippine constitution.

“These rights have primacy in all constitutional rights. This is the highest constitutional right that the government should protect at all cost,” Cortez asserted.

Cortez also explained that freedom of expression should include the right of people to protest not just in any designated freedom park such as the Liwasang Bonifacio but anywhere without needing to secure a permit.

In Batas Pambansa Bldg. 880, going to freedom park to protest does not need a permit or any travel pass. Lawyers like the NUPL argue that blocking protesters while officials cannot identify clear and present danger is unconstitutional.

The said law has been facing criticism by NUPL stating that “this dictatorship-era law that places constitutional rights of the people to collective action under a system of prior state approval.”

Aside from rally permit arguments, Cortez added that traffic regulations should not also be used as a tool to suppress or stop the people going to freedom park where they can protest to amplify their call against police brutality and opposition to Pax Silica where thousands of Ayta and local farmers will lose their livelihood.

“As long as there is no clear and present danger, [it] cannot prevail over the exercise of constitutional guaranteed rights,” Cortez explained.

As there are no specific laws on checkpoints, the Supreme Court has previous decisions such as the Valmonte vs. De Villa, which states that checkpoint is not illegal but law enforcement shall be limited to visual search.

In Aniag Jr. vs COMELEC, it is stated that police should only have access to a vehicle if they have probable cause or voluntary consent. None of the ruling states that checkpoints can be used to block protesters, especially going to freedom park.

“You are conducting a checkpoint because there is an impending criminal act to be committed. But if the checkpoint is used because of protest, it violates their constitutional rights […] You can’t put the blame on protesters as they are continuously moving and exercising their rights,” Cortez said.

According to Cortez, it is not the people who participated in the rally causing traffic, the blame should fall on the police who continuously block the protesters’ way to raise their legitimate concerns.

As police brutality continues, progressive groups vow to push through with their protests to amplify the call of the marginalized groups especially to Indigenous and local communities who will be affected once the Pax Silica is officially constructed. (AMU, RVO)

title: Groups condemn police brutality, state repression against anti-Pax Silica protesters
content:
Police officers arrest a protester during a protest in Liwasang Bonifacio on November 15, 2026. Photo by Adrian Puse/Altermidya

MANILA — “Trump was given a red carpet but the Filipino people are given fascism and repression, and are prevented from expressing their opposition to Pax Silica.”

This is the statement of Dr. Ganni Tapang, leaf convener of the Network Opposed to Pax Silica.

Representatives of different progressive groups condemned the state’s attacks against Filipino activists, journalists, and Indigenous people in a press conference at Vinzon’s compound at the University of the Philippines–Diliman.

Around 500 personnel of the Philippine National Police (PNP) were spotted surrounding the perimeter of campus. They were stationed around the entrance and exits of campus, along Katipunan Avenue, University Avenue, and College of Science among others.

Tapang, also the former Dean of the College of Science, condemned the collusion of the Philippine government with the US, specifically Marcos Jr.’s enabling the Pax Silica Initiative to plunder the country.

“The PNP should be defending our rights and not curtailing them, and following the orders of Donald Trump and President Marcos,” Tapang said.

The Kampuhan Kontra Pax Silica launched on campus on Friday, November 13, and will continue until November 16. This was participated by 200 Ayta, including 50 from Cordillera, 500 farmers and youth from Central Luzon, and many volunteers and community members.

Although UP is a sanctuary campus, student journalists from the College of Mass Communication covering the protests suffered from attempted arrests.

Dr. Ma. Diosa Labiste, dean of the UP College of Media and Communications, said that this is the police’s attempt to prevent legitimate dissent in the course of the ASEAN summit.

“We demand the police to recognize the citizens to participate in protest actions,” said Labiste. “We will hold the police accountable if our students are harmed when they are doing their job as campus journalists.”

“Journalism is not illegal,” said Yvo Asis, multimedia editor of the Philippine Collegian. He shared about a student journalist from UP who was arrested in Sucat, Muntinlupa while on the ground.

The police did not read to them the Miranda rights and later on brought a truck full of people to Camp Bagong Diwa. Over 300 were arrested, with the largest contingent coming from Southern Tagalog.

“It is the democratic right of the Filipino masses to spread the developments of Pax Silica.” Paul Viuya, Chairperson of BAYAN Central Luzon, said that these arrests expose the true face of fascism in our country.

Of those arrested, twelve were injured, including someone who fainted and was still kicked in the head by the police, according to Teacher Kat Ortega, president of the All UP Academic Employees Union.

Ortega also condemned the arrest of three students of the University of Makati while participating in the November 13 nationwide student walkout. “They are not criminals. They are just peacefully expressing their indignation,” she said.

Activists in Liwasang Bonifacio shared to Ortega how the police scattered human feces and urine around Freedom Park on November 15. They also took the rallyists’ belongings, and slashed the tires of the activists’ trucks while they were setting up for the protest.

The Philippine government allotted P22.9 billion (US$358 million) for hosting the ASEAN Summit.. Ortega said that these could have been used for social services and building classrooms that serve the Filipino people. Instead, it is used for the advancement of Pax Silica, which will take the country’s water, electricity, and labor power.

“We call on the PNP. Arrest Atong Ang, Zaldy Co, Bato dela Rosa, and all of the corrupt politicians. Block Donald Trump, who wages war against the people of the world,” said Ortega. “They are the true criminals who destroy peoples’ lives.”

Amid repression, Erich Jones Escototo, convener of UP Against Pax Silica (UPAX) said that nothing could silence the voices of the oppressed Filipino masses.

“The Filipino people continue to resist.” Escototo called on fellow students to join the protests in Liwasang Bonifacio on November 17 where different sectors from all over the country will express their indignation.

“What the masses want is the freedom to protest,” said Tapang, calling on the Filipino people to stand for their right to protest and to convey their demands and opposition. (RVO)

title: Surfers organise Paddle out for Palestine in Torquay
content:
About 120 people gathered at Cosy Beach in Torquay at dawn on November 15 to hear from speakers and highlight the ongoing genocide in Gaza.

Organised by Surfers for Palestine, the group donned wetsuits and paddled out into the ocean with Palestinian flags. They formed a circle of peace and chanted “From the River to the Sea”.

Tihan Abeywickrema from Surfers for Palestine said that they were delighted with the turn out as it showed that people are still prepared to campaign for Palestinian rights.

The paddle out was supported by the Independent and Peaceful Network Geelong and Victoria Southwest and Socialist Alliance Geelong.

Freya Hedley, Socialist Alliance candidate for South Barwon in the Victorian elections, told Green Left "it was great seeing so many new and familiar faces, and we only recieved positive response from passersby.

"It's inspiring how long and determined the fight for Palestinian liberation has been in the wider community, and there are more and more people recognising that all these different struggles are interlinked.”

title: By suppressing Pax Silica foes, gov’t lost
content:
The Marcos Jr. administration should stop acting with unctuous servility to Donald Trump by whitewashing the metropolis, putting up Potemkin villages where the ragged people live and sabotaging protest actions against Pax Silica by destroying the brakes of vehicles used by the Lakbayan marchers, mauling three students of the University of Makati, rounding up 278 workers, farmers and activists in Muntinlupa, Paranaque, arresting nine protesters in Laguna, stopping DLTB buses from plying the UP Los Banos-UP Diliman route out of fear that they would ferry protesters to Metro Manila, preventing a delegation from Bulacan to enter the metropolis and nabbing 21 activists at Liwasang Bonifacio.




Why do we have to engage in *scurryfunge and give Trump a tongue bath when he was resoundingly repudiated by the US electorate in the midterm elections by giving to the Democrats 28 statehouses, 56 seats at the Senate and majority of the House of Representatives, with the margin at 140, the worst beating suffered by addled Republican politicians in history.




For the edification of the foremost defenders of Pax Silica and the data centers that it requires, US voters rejected data centers, with potential $68-billion investment going up in smoke in many states. If this Pax Silica castle in the air were a cornucopia of investment that would eliminate poverty (and about 29% of Americans are now dirt-poor), create millions of jobs and usher in a Golden Era facilitated by Trump, why did hundreds of millions of US voters junk it? Pax Silica may well be phantasmagoria.




Malacanang has broken the record for mass arrests by suppressing the right of the Filipino people to organize, protest and seek redress of grievances as guaranteed by the 1987 Constitution. There is no legal justification at all for suppressing civil and political liberties just to please the lawless Trump, who has inflicted the worst economic burden on humanity when he, at the instigation of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, launched a war against Iran and caused oil and gas prices to skyrocket. Trump, who barely reads, only operates to line his pockets and those of his tech pals led by Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Peter Thiel, Jensen Huang and other billionaires who have secured subsidies, tax breaks and favorable policies from Trump, who has enriched himself to the tune of $5-billion in his unlamented return to the White House.




Government has mobilized thousands of policemen and soldiers to secure the venue of the ASEAN Summit and the hotels housing delegates to the summit in a vain attempt to show that Filipinos will not protest the opaque Pax Silica Initiative that many insist was 

inilista sa tubig

. Nobody has seen the ghost of the purported framework agreement for Pax Silica and nothing has been reported about the negotiations between the Philippines and the US on what exactly this animal really is. As reports go, this program was conceived in December 2025 and included the US demand that for Pax Silica to be implemented, diplomatic immunity must be granted to US personnel. This is standard demand by US exceptionalism, which is akin to the erroneous assertion by Zionists that international laws do not apply to them because they belong to the chosen race, even if only 10% of Ashkenazi Jews can trace their maternal line to the Levant, or Palestine.




The US appears to argue that such immunity was necessary to guarantee US investments in Pax Silica. Americans always wanted to make it appear that Filipinos have no choice but to accept US **importuning without question, harking back to the days of US colonialism, when Washington DC controlled all resources and provided Americans with parity rights, making them more equal than Filipinos in their own country. It is true that the US belatedly understood that it committed a fatal error when it sold the technology to mine, extract, process and refine rare earth elements more than four decades ago, thus losing their domination of the market. As the saying goes, 

nagdadalang-hiya si Trump sa kapalpakan ng Amerika

. Today, US share in lithium production is barely one percent and they pin their hopes on the Arkansas-East Texas geological formation that purportedly holds a huge deposit.




Police also tried to suppress protests against Pax Silica in Cebu City, Baguio City and many towns and cities where various organizations registered their opposition to the US military initiative disguised as the collective effort of 24 nations. For starters, Trump and his ilk could not even agree on what the Pax Silica Initiative really is and no one knows exactly how the scheme was hatched in Washington D.C., hive of the Washington Consensus that had punished developing countries with punitive economic policies, not only higher interest rates but punishing conditionalities, from depreciating their currencies and inflicting austerity measures that worsened poverty levels. The Philippine National Police (PNP) was condemned by the National Union of People’s Lawyers (NUPL), lawyers from the Alpha Phi Beta fraternity and the entire UP community, along with the United Methodist Church (UMC), the UPLB community, Kilusang Mayo Uno (KMU), Karapatan and even unnamed government lawyers who criticized the refusal of the PNP to let in investigators from the Commission on Human Rights (CHR) and the lawyers representing the 278 detained protesters.




The US is trying to impose Pax Silica and its bigger project called the Luzon Economic Corridor (LEC) to give a semblance of generosity on a plan to ensure that its military supply chain that guarantees the processing of rare earths and lithium to produce military-grade magnets and chips for use in US fighter jets, warships, aircraft carriers, radars, drones (aerial and marine), as well as electric vehicles (EVs), turbines and others. The LEC would connect Central Luzon and Southern Luzon through expressways to hasten the transport of various products to Batangas. They are not yet contemplating on creating a canal that would link the Pacific Ocean to the South China Sea (one senator, now deceased, was enamored to do just that, making Quezon and Pangasinan close to each other.)




As things stand, there is no truth to the claim that at least 900,000 jobs would be created by Pax Silica since highly chips production require fewer workers but would demand huge power plants and continuous water supply to cool the servers in data centers. The 1,619-hectare Pax Silica hub at Clark Freeport has already led to the destruction of Aeta farms and traditional cemeteries, with government insisting that the ancestral domain is within the Freeport. Power plants would need to be built, which explains the campaign for nuclear power plants to be constructed has gone full-blast. Two such plants are mulled. How will Pax Silica provide water for its facilities? They can immediately employ dowsing to find “interminable” water sources, ***doodlebugging to find oil, and explore the entire 1,169-hectare hub with divining rods.




Central Luzon has been bugged with perennial shortage of irrigation water and with Pax Silica, the shortage would worsen. The Indonesians have found out that data centers made it hard for them to brush their teeth and cook their meals. Yet, government wants to welcome a water crisis with open arms. Capisce? #

author: Bulatlat Staff
title: Int’l groups condemn police brutality
content:
Police officers forcibly grab human rights activists and multisectoral leaders during a protest in Cebu City on November 16, 2026. Screengrab from Bulatlat's video

By Dominic Gutoman and Anne Marxze Umil

International groups denounced the police brutality on November 15, the first day of the 49th ASEAN Summit.

In a statement, the International Association of Democratic Lawyers (IADL) expressed strong condemnation over the violent dispersal and mass arrests of the activists.

They said that instead of arresting international offenders like Sen. Ronald “Bato” Dela Rosa who has an outstanding International Criminal Court warrant, “the Philippine police and military are using their superior force to harass and arrest peaceful demonstrators and protestors and to stifle dissent and lawful redress of grievances.”

The group stressed that the police brutality and mass arrests are overkill, violating the Philippine Constitution and the country’s laws in the presence of ASEAN member-states, other heads of state, and the United Nations Secretary General.

“The IADL in particular is holding the police Chief PGen Jose Melencio Nartatez, Jr., Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla, and President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. himself as well as identified individual members of security forces responsible,” the group said in a statement.

The events of the 49th ASEAN Summit happen at the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City until November 18, bringing leaders from 11 member-states and representatives of nine dialogue partner-countries.

The Asia Pacific Forum on Women Law and Development (APWLD) stressed that police brutality and state-sanctioned harassment are blatant attacks on fundamental rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly which violates Articles 19 and 21 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR).

“The Philippine government’s actions also violate their international obligations under the UN Declaration on Human Rights Defenders and the UN General Assembly resolution which calls upon all States to take concrete measures to protect human rights defenders and recognise the vital work they do,” APWLD said in a statement. “We call on the international community, civil society organisations and feminist movements across Asia and the Pacific to amplify their demands, release statements of solidarity and support ongoing legal and humanitarian aid for those detained.”

In a press conference on November 16, Jheri Lising, representative of International League of Peoples’ Struggles (ILPS)-US, said that these arrests are part of a broader pattern of repression against people who stand up to US imperialism and its wars of aggression. “The Philippine government is once again demonstrating its willingness to trample on people’s democratic rights to protect US interests. We stand with the Filipino people in opposing Pax Silica, Trump’s visit, and the continuing US intervention in the Philippines.”

June Colcol of Bagong Alyansang Makabayan-US said that “the Filipino people, including our diaspora, have every reason to oppose Trump’s visit and the US economic and military agenda behind it.”

Colcol said that Pax Silica serves US strategic interests, deepens the Philippines’ dependence on foreign capital and technology, and offers no real path to national development. “The Marcos government will not silence us for exposing this agenda. We will not allow these mass arrests to set the tone for the international week of action. We remain indignant and determined to push through with our planned actions and mobilizations, in the Philippines and around the world.”

Arnold Padilla, secretary general of ILPS-Philippines said that the Marcos government will not succeed in silencing them.

“We will not allow yesterday’s arrests to dictate the course of this international week of action. We remain indignant, and we will push through with our plans to expose and oppose the agenda of Trump and Marcos. The demand for accountability will continue to be heard in the streets of the Philippines and across the world,” Padilla said. (DAA)

author: Kodao Productions
title: Two Conferences, Two Distant Venues, One Unilateralist US Policy
content:
Nearly nine years ago, in November 2017, I faced criminal charges for joining a protest against the visit of then US President Donald Trump to the Philippines. He was in Manila for the 31st ASEAN Summit hosted by then President Rodrigo Duterte. What should have been an exercise of our constitutional right to protest ended in a violent police dispersal.




Water cannons, truncheons and even a sonic weapon were used against protesters trying to march toward the summit venues. I was among the progressive lawmakers and protest leaders charged with violating the Public Assembly Act, direct assault and disobedience to persons in authority. The police accused us of inciting protesters to breach barricades.




I considered the charges politically motivated, particularly since I was a sitting member of Congress exercising my right to dissent against a visiting foreign leader. The assault and disobedience charges were eventually dropped for lack of evidence that we had personally attacked police officers.




That experience exposed a familiar contradiction: government readily invokes democracy and national sovereignty in dealing with foreign powers but becomes intolerant when Filipinos exercise those same rights to question our relationship with a powerful ally.




Trump is back in Manila, nearly nine years later. His return brings into focus issues far bigger than the visit itself: military access, economic dependence, geopolitical rivalry, climate responsibility and Philippine sovereignty.




Two international conferences in distant venues provide a useful lens through which to examine these issues: COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, and the 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila.




Their agendas differ, but both reveal the unilateralist character of Trump’s foreign policy — one that puts American strategic and economic interests ahead of multilateral commitments and the concerns of less powerful nations.




America’s retreat from climate responsibility




While Trump is welcomed in Manila, the United States is drawing criticism in Türkiye for its absence from international climate negotiations. For the second consecutive year, his administration has declined to send an official government delegation to the UN climate conference.




Trump has dismissed climate change as a hoax while his government retreats from international commitments and rolls back domestic environmental protections.




This is no minor diplomatic snub. The United States is among the world’s largest historical contributors to greenhouse gas emissions and possesses enormous economic and technological resources.




Its withdrawal weakens efforts to secure climate finance, adaptation support and compensation for loss and damage — commitments particularly vital to developing countries that have contributed little to the crisis but suffer its worst consequences.




Washington’s retreat also creates space for China and other powers to present themselves as defenders of multilateral cooperation. But for countries like the Philippines, the issue is not which superpower fills the diplomatic vacuum. It is whether the international community will deliver the resources and concrete commitments needed to confront a crisis already devastating vulnerable communities.




Trump’s return: Military dependence and strategic alignment




The concerns raised in Türkiye are not disconnected from what is happening in Manila. Opposition to Trump’s visit has brought together progressive lawmakers, church groups, people’s organizations, farmers, workers, Indigenous communities, professionals and student activists.




Their protest is directed not simply at Trump but at the policies and agreements associated with his administration and the Marcos government’s unquestioning alignment with Washington.




The Makabayan bloc has filed House Resolution No. 1593 opposing the administration’s reception of Trump. At the heart of the protest is the concern that the Philippines continues to grant Washington military and diplomatic concessions without adequately examining what the country gives up in return.




The expansion of American military access under the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA), additional military sites and increasingly frequent joint exercises risk drawing the Philippines deeper into the strategic confrontation between Washington and Beijing.




We have every right to defend our territorial integrity and maritime interests in the West Philippine Sea. But defending these rights should not mean surrendering our independence in determining our security and foreign policy. An expanded US military presence does not automatically guarantee Philippine security. It could just as easily make our territory a staging ground for a wider conflict, exposing our people to dangers over which we have little control.




The question is not whether we should maintain relations with the United States, but whether these relations genuinely serve Philippine sovereignty and the Filipino people.




Aeta leader Tatay Elmer makes clear what they wish to do with Pax Silica. (Photo by Nuel M. Bacarra/Kodao)




Pax Silica: Development for whom?




Beyond military cooperation, Trump’s visit brings another major concern: Philippine participation in Pax Silica, a US-led initiative to build allied supply chains for critical minerals, semiconductors, artificial intelligence infrastructure and advanced manufacturing.




The Marcos administration promotes it as an opportunity to attract billions in investments, create jobs and move the country up the global value chain. But the projected economic gains must be weighed against the social and environmental costs.




The proposed industrial hub in New Clark City raises serious questions about the allocation of land, ancestral domains and agricultural communities.




Aeta communities in Tarlac and farmers whose land claims may not be adequately reflected in formal titles deserve particular attention. Experience has shown how large development projects can displace communities that have occupied and cultivated their land for generations. Promised investments and jobs may come later; the loss of land and livelihood can be immediate and irreversible.




The environmental costs also deserve scrutiny. Semiconductor manufacturing and critical mineral processing require enormous amounts of water and electricity, potentially placing additional pressure on the Sacobia watershed and encouraging destructive mining elsewhere.




More fundamentally, will Pax Silica strengthen domestic industries, build technological capabilities and provide decent jobs? Or will it primarily give foreign corporations access to our land, resources and cheap labor while technology, intellectual property and profits remain in foreign hands?




The same questions apply to the Luzon Economic Corridor and related infrastructure initiatives. Our opposition is not to development or foreign investment. It is to a development model that sacrifices land rights, food security, environmental protection and economic independence for promises whose benefits may largely accrue to foreign corporations.




Sovereignty must come before alignment




What connects the conferences in Türkiye and Manila is the same fundamental question about American power. In one, Washington retreats from its responsibility in addressing a global crisis to which it has contributed enormously. In the other, it expects allies to accommodate its military and economic priorities while reserving the freedom to act unilaterally.




For the Philippines, this is not an abstract debate. It concerns access to our territory, control over our natural resources, the direction of our economic development and our ability to chart an independent course amid intensifying geopolitical rivalries.




This does not mean rejecting bilateral cooperation. Relations between nations must rest on mutual respect, not unquestioning obedience. The Marcos administration must answer – must be made accountable – for the military access it grants, the economic commitments it enters into and the communities that may bear their costs. A high-level summit cannot place these decisions beyond public scrutiny.




Nearly nine years ago, I faced criminal charges for protesting the visit of an American president. Today, the same struggle for democratic rights and national independence confronts us in a different form.




Whether the issue is climate responsibility in Türkiye or military and economic cooperation in Manila, we must ask whose interests our government is really serving.




Our foreign policy and development priorities should be measured not by how closely they advance Washington’s geopolitical and corporate agenda, but by how well they protect our people, resources and future.




National sovereignty and peoples’ interest trump Pax Silica! #

Two Conferences, Two Distant Venues, One Unilateralist US Policy

Kodao Productions

author: CMI Argentina
title: Recuerdos del futuro del fentanilo
content:
El fentanilo surgió de las farmacias y sanatorios de Estados Unidos como una oferta auspiciada por ese estado y construyó el mercado consumidor millonario en personas y multimillonario en dólares. Las muertes por fentanilo son consecuencia de un negocio paraestatal y multinacional.







Donald Trump inventa carteles en Venezuela para quedarse con el petróleo y lo seguirá haciendo en México, Brasil, Argentina y Colombia para explotar de manera irracional los bienes comunes de los pueblos del sur.




En su reinvención de la historia apela a los principios de la guerra fría, las doctrinas de seguridad nacional y continental.




Hacer de los ejércitos de los pueblos por debajo del Río Bravo los guardianes pretorianos de la concentración y extranjerización de riquezas con la excusa del combate al narcotráfico.




Lo lleva adelante con la complicidad de los presidentes electos por el voto popular aunque cada vez es más notorio que el capitalismo desprecia esas formas republicanas.




En esa revisión del relato norteamericano, Trump falsifica los hechos que dieron origen a uno de los principales problemas sanitarios del pueblo de los Estados Unidos que es el mercado negro del fentanilo.




El actual presidente acusa a los carteles mexicanos de los hijos del Chapo Guzmán de ser los causantes de la epidemia cuyos efectos pueden verse en distintos sitios de Youtube, personas degradadas a ser zombis que deambulan sin sentido en las principales calles del imperio.




La realidad histórica es que el fentanilo emergió de las farmacias y sanatorios de Estados Unidos como una oferta auspiciada por el estado norteamericano y construyó el mercado consumidor millonario en personas y multimillonario en dólares.




Las muertes por fentanilo son consecuencia del negocio del fentanilo, paraestatal y multinacional, como lo es el narcotráfico, la venta de armas, los medicamentos, la trata de personas y ciertas vertientes del increíble comercio del petróleo y derivados.




Cuando aparecieron las muertes por fentanilo contaminado en Argentina, las diferentes dimensiones de la justicia apuntaron a lotes que se perdieron de su trazabilidad.




Lo cierto es que mientras avanza el tiempo van apareciendo noticias que confirman la repetición de aquellas etapas del negocio tal cual surgió y se consolidó en Estados Unidos.




Desde los laboratorios, sanatorios, hospitales y farmacias a las calles, al surgimiento y posterior consolidación de un mercado negro de fentanilo que será la base del consumo de miles de personas.




El 23 de octubre de 2026, fueron allanados tres sanatorios de Rosario por la venta ilegal de fentanilo y morfina.




“La investigación sobre la venta y uso ilegal de fentanilo y morfina en Wheelwright se actualizó después de cuatro meses. La Justicia federal ordenó una serie de allanamientos en tres sanatorios de Rosario para profundizar la pesquisa que comenzó con una denuncia de fraude en Pami.




La Policía Federal Argentina (PFA) inspeccionó distintos centros de salud privados de la ciudad y también de Acebal. Esta última es una de las dos localidades donde se enfocó la causa penal por el suministro ilícito de los fármacos por parte de un médico y un enfermero. En total, el Ministerio Público Fiscal (MPF) solicitó ocho allanamientos en busca de evidencia. De esta manera se secuestraron medicamentos sin recetas como diazepam, ondansetrón y dexametasona. Además, los encargados del procedimiento identificaron a siete nuevos sospechosos vinculados con la causa que tomó estado público a principios de junio en el departamento General López. La División Unidad Operativa de Investigaciones Especiales (DUOIE) de la PFA fue a las oficinas de los sanatorios Norte, Laprida y Delta. También revisaron inmuebles particulares de Rosario y una farmacia de Acebal, entre otros domicilios”, informaron los medios de comunicación regionales.




Esta información va repitiéndose no solamente en la provincia de Santa Fe sino también en otros lugares de la Argentina.




El fentanilo no es consecuencia de una “tragedia”, si no de la planificación de un negocio a escala internacional y cuya matriz está en los Estados Unidos.







Fuente: Diario “La Capital”, Rosario, viernes 23 de octubre de 2026; “Geografía narco 10”, del autor de esta nota.

author: Victoria Python
title: EFF’s AI Cybersecurity Policy Framework
content:
The news has been filled with stories recently of AI breaching the security of websites. And while it may feel like a new problem because of AI’s involvement, it turns out that there are longstanding existing cybersecurity safety best practices that these companies—some of the largest tech companies in the world—could and should have taken to prevent these breaches.




Recent cybersecurity incidents have shown that some of the world’s largest tech companies have failed to take basic security precautions when testing frontier AI systems on internet-connected systems. Unfortunately, these failures resulted in breaches of numerous third-party websites, including an AI research-sharing platform called Hugging Face and the Australian healthcare system’s website. Even worse, AI developers failed to detect most of the incidents until long after they occurred due to inadequate monitoring of the AI systems during testing. Had the companies abided by basic, common sense security protocols, these incidents likely would not have occurred.




While the White House and leaders of major AI companies have claimed that no action is necessary, understandably, lawmakers at all levels and of both parties are proposing legislation to create new, additional safety protocols. These incidents may warrant legislative action. However, the good news is that post-incident reports indicate 

new

 protocols are largely unnecessary. Following 

existing

 best practices would have been enough to prevent the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident and others like it. In other words, responsible AI developers can take immediate action to protect the public by implementing well-established security precautions as they develop and test their systems.




Lawmakers should start by referencing existing legal protections, including claims like negligence, gross negligence, trespass to chattels, Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), and computer trespass statutes like the Consumer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) and analogous state law provisions, such as Section 502 of the California Penal Code.




Policymakers can help protect the public by requiring AI developers to follow established security protocols—and creating legal liability for failing to do so. These policies would protect the public from irresponsible actions by AI developers without impeding innovation. To the extent that gaps in existing laws warrant new legislation, EFF recommends the following policy framework:







STATUTORY SECURITY REQUIREMENTS: 

Lawmakers should enact legislation that requires AI developers to adhere to well-established cybersecurity best practices when testing AI systems, such as strong sandboxing and network isolation, least-privilege access, effective logging and monitoring, and clear incident-response procedures




REGULATORY STANDARDS: 

Congress should require an existing federal agency, such as the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)

1

, to adopt safety standards for pre-deployment development and testing of generative AI systems, based on the established best practices referenced above. The agency should be required to update the standards every 2 years, or earlier as needed due to reported security incidents and/or major technological advancements. These standards should be developed in consultation with academic and nonprofit AI researchers, civil liberties organizations, and commercial AI developers, and adopted through formal agency rulemaking following a notice and comment process. That consultation should include an assessment of potential adverse impacts on competition, with the goal of ensuring that regulatory standards do not effectively lock out potential competitors.




LIABILITY: 

The law should provide for civil liability for AI development and testing that results in unauthorized access to a third party system, if performed under conditions that do not satisfy cybersecurity standards adopted by NIST, or another federal agency responsible for adopting these regulations, unless the company proves it acted reasonably under the circumstances to prevent unauthorized access to third party system 




ENFORCEMENT: 

Both federal and state authorities should be able to hold AI developers accountable where they have failed to meet the minimum standards adopted by the designated federal agency, such as NIST. Providing for state—in addition to federal—enforcement power reduces the risk of regulatory capture. Regulators should require independent investigations and notification of affected parties in the event of a security incident involving unauthorized access to a third party’s computer system. Finally, legislation should include an appropriately targeted private right of action.







The public shouldn’t have to worry about the risks of reckless AI development—or give up the benefits of AI just to prevent irresponsible developers from causing harm. By adopting policies that address demonstrated risks, lawmakers can provide meaningful public protection without hampering the development of useful tools.




1

NIST, the NSA, and CISA have recently issued a set of 

voluntary practices

 for managing security incidents during the training and evaluation of AI agents. Those practices may inform but do not substitute for the regulatory standards that should be developed according to the public, participatory process outlined here.

author: Valerie Anne
title: LGBTQ+ Representation in Television Hits Devastating Lows
content:
As I’m sure you’ve noticed, LGBTQ+ representation in media is at the lowest it’s been in over a decade.

GLAAD’s latest Where We Are in TV study showed some bleak results that reflect the state of the country due to the hateful administration we live under and the wealthy conservatives who own most of the media conglomerates. Trans representation took the biggest hit, going from 33 characters to a measly SEVEN, and since three of them were on shows that were cancelled and four are from limited series, none of those seven will be returning next season. NONE. Devastating.

Twenty-five percent of LGBTQ+ characters have left our screens since last year, which brings the stats to their lowest point in over a decade. Cable television hit a 16-year low. BLEAK.

Streamers have more queer representation than cable and broadcast characters put together, but we have lost almost 100 characters from streamers as well, so even that isn’t great news. And combining streaming, cable, and broadcast, of all LGBTQ+ characters, 44% of them are characters of color, which is the lowest percentage since GLAAD’s 2017-2018 report.

Pride points out that it seems wild to imagine because some of the buzziest shows of the last few years feature queer characters: The Hunting Wives, Hazbin Hotel, Pluribus, Stranger Things, Heated Rivalry. I don’t think this show made it into the count, but we also have Sterling Point and now The Body. Queer people show up for shows that feature them, and queer people are great at telling unique stories. Alas, too many higher-ups lean on outdated Christian ideals and won’t invest in us in an effort to silence us.

This is especially wild because, while it reflects what the political times want you to believe (that queer people are outsiders, among other things), it doesn’t reflect the actual statistics. Every generation reports identifying as gayer than the last, so representation should also be at a steady increase to reflect reality, not a drastic decrease.

The actual numbers of LGBTQ+ characters on broadcast and cable shows are harrowing to look at. There are dozens of characters on any given TV show, and dozens of shows on each network, and yet the highest number among them is HBO with 15 characters. The second-highest is a big drop down, with Fox and Starz coming in with 10 characters each.

The numbers start off a little more promising for streaming, with 116 on Netflix, but then they also start dropping dramatically, with 68 on Prime Video and then again a steep drop to Hulu with 24.

I’m sure you, like I have, felt the shift even before you saw these numbers. Here at Autostraddle, we used to have to have a weekly TV roundup because there were so many queer characters on cable and broadcast shows that we couldn’t keep up with individual recaps. We used to do Pop Culture Fix twice a week to keep up with the news coming at us from all angles. And now there aren’t enough recurring characters for a weekly roundup and barely enough news for 10-15 links a week in a pop culture roundup.

It’s disheartening to see these numbers go down more and more every year when we were in such a steady incline for so long, but the fact is: We’re still here. We’re still out here writing well-rounded characters and telling our stories and watching and supporting the LGBTQ+ characters we DO still have on TV. We will not go quietly into the night. We will keep shouting and keep showing up for the queer shows doing it right until these numbers make sense again.

+ Phoebe Bridgers was the musical guest on this weekend’s SNL

+ Former wee lesbian (on Derry Girls) Nicola Coughlan doubles down on her pro-trans, anti-Harry Potter stance and we love her for it

+ Beanie Feldstein had nothing but lovely things to say about working with Ariana Grande on Focker-In-Law

+ Kate McKinnon and Queen Latifah are among those listed to be part of the NBC100 Live Celebration next month

+ Sarah Paulson and Holland Taylor have no plans to marry; Sarah Paulson doesn’t even like the idea of someone calling her a “wife”

+ The Hunting Wives stars Brittany Snow and Malin Akerman play fuck, U-Haul, kill in an interview, which eventually devolves into them complimenting each other’s past performances

author: CMI Argentina
title: Santa Fe: el río Paraná superó el nivel de evacuación
content:
El crecimiento del nivel del agua en Santa Fe genera preocupación en distintas localidades y barrios de la zona. Desde el jueves pasado, la crecida avanza a un ritmo de aproximadamente 15 centímetros por día y ya obligó a evacuar familias en Arroyo Leyes, ubicada a 23 kilómetros de la capital provincial.










Escuchar el reporte de Radio Chalet de Santa Fe




“Estamos complicados y evacuando a las familias”, advirtió Eduardo Lorinz, presidente comunal de Arroyo Leyes, quien explicó que hasta el jueves la situación se mantenía tranquila, pero que desde entonces el ingreso de agua se aceleró.




“Nos tuvo todo el fin de semana ocupado, realmente, un poco las corridas, porque, a diferencia de otras emergencias, esta fue muy rápida”, relató.




El funcionario también manifestó su preocupación por la situación de uno de los barrios de la localidad, que habitualmente resiste las crecidas, pero que esta vez se encuentra “bastante colapsado”.




La situación también es compleja en Alto Verde, otro de los sectores de la ciudad de Santa Fe históricamente afectados por las inundaciones. Luis Alba, presidente de la vecinal del barrio, informó que el domingo pasado quedó cortado el camino que constituye la única vía de ingreso a ese sector.




Alba advirtió además sobre el riesgo que implicaría una eventual rotura de la defensa ubicada del lado del canal de acceso. Según explicó, si eso ocurriera, entre el 80 y el 90 por ciento de Alto Verde podría quedar bajo el agua, con niveles de entre un metro y medio y dos metros dentro de las viviendas.




El vecinalista señaló que el barrio no cuenta con maquinaria propia para responder ante una emergencia de esas características y alertó sobre el tiempo que demandaría la llegada de equipos, camiones y materiales para contener una posible rotura.

author: Cierra Bettens
title: InFocus: Is adopting permanent daylight saving time a mistake?
content:
Many of us know how we feel when it’s time to change our clocks back in the fall and forward in the spring. Sleepy – maybe even a little disoriented.

Well, on Nov. 1, citizens in six provinces and territories didn’t experience any of that because their governments scrapped the dreaded seasonal time change.

Governments had two choices: stick with standard time or daylight saving time. Standard time gives you more sun in the morning – while daylight time gives you extended sun in the evening.

Most chose to extend daylight into the evening.

But will they regret their decision?

This week on InFocus, David Prerau, one of the world’s foremost experts on daylight saving time, explains why they might.

“What happened in the U.S. anyway is nobody was much against it until it actually occurred in January 1974,” Prerau, the author of Seize the Daylight, told host Cierra Bettens. “We had an incident in 1974 where there was an energy crisis, an unexpected energy crisis. And so they put in daylight saving time year-round for a two-year period, which they thought would cover the energy crisis. And most people thought it would be good until it happened.

“Everybody saw they had to get up in the pitch dark, go to work in the pitch dark, and most people thought the worst thing was that to send their kids to school in the dark, walking on dark city streets or waiting at the bus stop on dark country roads. And so it lost popularity very quickly in the US, and I think 1974 and even though it was only a two-year plan, they got rid of it after one year because it was so unpopular.”

Anishinaabe health scholar, Dr. Amy Shawanda, said if the government wants to adopt one particular time, she supports standard time. But she added, there are impacts of changing the clocks.

“It’s not natural to our circadian rhythms,” she said. “A lot of people will feel off when the clocks change because it’s not natural to our circadian rhythms. As Indigenous Peoples, we never had to change the clocks. We just lived on the land, and so it’s not natural to who we are.

“We should really move away from the daylight saving time and not adopt it at all, because it does really go against our own circadian rhythms. It goes against our biology.”

Cierra is the host and co-producer of the of the weekly APTN News InFocus podcast. She joined APTN in 2024 as a reporter-correspondent in Winnipeg after working in campus and city news. She’s currently completing her Master of Arts in Media Studies at Concordia University in Montréal. Cierra has mixed settler and Red River Métis roots and is a member of the Manitoba Métis Federation.

title: Kongra Star mobilizes against violence against women in Rojava
content:
The women’s movement Kongra Star has mobilized against gender-based violence and discrimination in several cities across Rojava. As part of activities marking the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on November 25, a demonstration was held in Dêrik, while political gatherings took place in Til Temir and Dirbêsiyê. Alongside the struggle against patriarchal violence, the events focused on women’s social self-determination, the right to education in their mother tongue and demands for constitutional guarantees of women’s rights in Syria.




The events are part of a joint campaign organized by women’s movements and organizations in Rojava. Under the slogan “Jin, Jiyan, Azadî” (Woman, Life, Freedom), they are linking the struggle against violence against women with demands to safeguard the social and political rights won during the Rojava Revolution within Syria’s future constitutional framework.




Demonstration in Dêrik: Enshrining women’s rights in the constitution




In Dêrik, Kongra Star organized a march from Freedom Square to the city center. Participants chanted slogans highlighting the role of women in society and opposing violence and gender-based discrimination. Following a moment of silence in memory of those who had lost their lives, Wefa Elî spoke on behalf of Kongra Star. She reaffirmed that the women’s movement would continue its struggle against all forms of violence and support women in their pursuit of self-determination.




Elî described women’s social and political participation as a fundamental prerequisite for a democratic society. She emphasized that the achievements of the women’s movement must be defended and protected through binding legal guarantees. In particular, she called for women’s rights to be explicitly enshrined in the Syrian constitution.




She also recalled the leading role of women in the Rojava Revolution. Elî stated that the women’s movement had developed its organization and resistance on the basis of Abdullah Öcalan’s ideas and philosophy and would continue along this path.




Violence against women goes beyond physical assault




Student Aya Hesen brought a broader perspective on the different forms of gender-based violence to the demonstration. She read out a statement emphasizing that violence against women was not limited to sexual harassment, physical assault or domestic violence.




“The systematic silencing of women, the denial of their identity and the deprivation of their right to speak and receive education in their mother tongue are also forms of social violence and oppression,” she said. Hesen stressed that the Kurdish language was an essential part of Kurdish women’s identity and social existence.




The female students also spoke out against the segregation of girls and boys in education. They argued that such practices were rooted in patriarchal attitudes and reinforced existing gender inequalities. They called for an education system that guaranteed equal rights for girls and boys and enabled their shared development within society.




Til Temir: Self-determination as the result of organized struggle




In Til Temir, Kongra Star organized a gathering ahead of November 25. The meeting, held in the hall of the Council of Families of the Martyr, was attended by representatives of political parties, staff members of civil society organizations, women’s organizations and numerous other interested participants.




Hedla Yûnis, head of the Til Temir Women’s House, addressed the social changes women had achieved through their organizing efforts and political struggle. She highlighted the connection between patriarchal notions of ownership and domination and the historical denial of women’s rights.




“Women have freed themselves from the notion that they are the property of men. Today, they can determine their own destiny and make decisions about their future,” Yûnis explained. She attributed this development in large part to engagement with Abdullah Öcalan’s ideas.




For a long time, families and society have denied women the right to make independent decisions about their own lives, Yûnis said. “Men thought and acted on their behalf. Overcoming these conditions was the result of years of struggle and considerable sacrifice. Women have gone through many stages, fought and paid a heavy price. They have developed a will of their own, become decision-makers and taken their place in political and social life,” Yûnis said.




Despite these advances, she said, women in many societies continued to face oppression and violence. The struggle for equality must therefore continue at the social, political and legal levels.




Calls for constitutional guarantees also raised in Dirbêsiyê




In Dirbêsiyê, another gathering organized by Kongra Star also focused on the connection between the struggle against violence against women and Syria’s future political order. Under the themes “No to Violence against Women” and “Guaranteeing Women’s Rights in the Syrian Constitution,” participants discussed the legal and social changes needed.




The women emphasized that protection against gender-based violence could not be guaranteed through public declarations alone: “Binding legal rights and their effective enforcement are essential. Women in other parts of Syria also have a crucial role to play. They need to organize and demand their rights for themselves within the political process.”

author: Unknown
title: Former long-term political prisoner Abdulvahap Adsoy dies
content:
Former political prisoner Abdulvahap Adsoy has died of cancer in Kızıltepe, in Mardin province. Adsoy had spent more than 30 years in Turkish prisons and was released from Bandırma Prison in the western Turkish province of Balıkesir on April 28, 2024. He had developed cancer during his imprisonment.




Adsoy was arrested in Kızıltepe in 1993 and subsequently sentenced to life imprisonment in an arbitrary trial by one of the notorious State Security Courts (DGM). Following his release, he underwent medical treatment for his illness. He died at a private hospital in Kızıltepe.




Upon his release, Adsoy had stated: “I made a promise, and I will live to fulfill that promise. I spent 30 years behind bars, but my heart was always with you. I will fight until the last drop of my blood. We draw our strength from our people. As long as our people stand behind us, no one can harm us. I thank you all.”




Following the completion of the necessary formalities, Abdulvahap Adsoy was laid to rest at Heci Hasan Aksoy Cemetery in Kızıltepe.

title: 16 trees planted in Amed in memory of murdered women
content:
Since Monday, 16 newly planted trees in Peace Park in Amed (Turkish: Diyarbakır) have stood in memory of women murdered by men in the city in 2026. Through this symbolic initiative, the city administration is taking a stand against femicide and promoting social solidarity ahead of the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on November 25.




The tree-planting event in the Seyrantepe neighborhood was organized by the Women’s Council and the Department of Women’s Policies of the DEM Party-run metropolitan municipality. It is part of a series of events held under the slogan “Now Is the Time for Women – Fighting Violence Through Organized Struggle.”




Co-Mayor Serra Bucak recalled that the municipality had commemorated victims of gender-based violence with a similar initiative last year. The trees planted at the time were intended to grow and symbolize hope for a society free from violence, exploitation and discrimination.




Bucak emphasized that this year’s initiative reflected the same vision. “Our struggle against violence against women will continue until we achieve a world where femicides and massacres no longer occur,” she stated.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Reports Say Trump Lied About Ending Aid to Israel, Funding Will Be Maintained
content:
Israeli outlets report that officials are, in fact, working to renew the funding for another five or 10 years.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

President Donald Trump’s claim on Election Day earlier this month that the U.S. was ending its annual funding to Israel at the end of 2026 was a lie, Israeli outlets have revealed, catching Trump in a last-ditch effort to boost Republicans that was seemingly nothing more than a PR stunt.

According to reporting by Israeli outlets Times of Israel and Ynet, several Israeli and U.S. officials say that there is no such deal in place between the countries. In fact, the current agreement being hashed out is for the U.S. and Israel to enter another memorandum of understanding (MOU) when the current one ends to continue sending Israel aid.

Details have yet to be worked out, but the general outline consists of a 5- or 10-year deal to phase out the U.S.’s annual $3.8 billion in annual aid sent to Israel. One version of this, according to Ynet, is for the U.S. to maintain current funding levels — with $3.3 billion of that funding allocated under the Foreign Military Financing program — for five years, after which it would be cut off.

The goal of striking a new deal, as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has openly acknowledged, is for the U.S. to wind down such financial support of Israel while further integrating the U.S. and Israel’s military sectors, with some measures to do so currently slated for passage by Congress. This would allow the countries to maintain a more secretive technology- and intelligence-sharing relationship with less public oversight.

The current MOU would continue to be funded through its end date in 2028, the reports said. Both Israeli and U.S. officials were taken aback by Trump’s announcement on November 3, reports have found, and Israeli Finance Ministry officials told members of Israel’s parliament, the Knesset, on Monday that they were not informed of the announcement nor do they know when the funding will be cut off.

Ynet and Times of Israel are right-wing outlets that often support ultranationalist movements in Israel. However, the reports add credence to suspicions that Trump was bluffing when he made his announcement. At the time, Trump openly said that he was making the announcement in order to stave off attacks from the left about Republicans’ fervor for supporting Israel, as polls portended his party’s major losses in the midterm elections.

Experts and advocates for Palestinian rights had cast doubt on the announcement. U.S. taxpayers could still be on the hook for $10 billion in outstanding military orders from Israel in coming years if Trump ends the MOU early, according to a State Department letter sent to Rep. Joaquin Castro (D-Texas) and reported by The Wall Street Journal on November 4. This is because the MOU is structured so that Israel orders U.S. weapons and equipment in advance, and is later provided the money by the U.S. to pay for it.

“It’s not plausible there will be a total cut-off starting January 1,” said Josh Paul, a former State Department official working on foreign arms procurement, to The Intercept shortly after Trump’s initial announcement. “My guess is that he was speaking off the cuff with the next 10-year memorandum of understanding between the U.S. and Israel in mind, but did so in a way that is at best inaccurate or imprecise.”

title: İstanbul'da uyuşturucu operasyonu: 6 milyon 200 bin hap bulundu
content:
Jandarma Genel Komutanlığı, İstanbul'da uyuşturucu madde imalatçılarına yönelik düzenlenen operasyonda iki imalathanenin ortaya çıkarıldığını, 6 milyon 200 bin sentetik ecza hapı ile 165 kilogram ham madde ele bulunduğunu açıkladı. Operasyonda 5 şüpheli yakalandı.

Gaziosmanpaşa Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığı ve Jandarma Genel Komutanlığı Narkotik Suçlarla Mücadele Daire Başkanlığı koordinesinde, İstanbul İl Jandarma Komutanlığı ekiplerince düzenlenen operasyonda 5 kişi gözaltına alındı.

Jandarma Genel Komutanlığının açıklamasına göre, şüphelilerin uyuşturucu ticareti yürüttükleri ve uyuşturucu madde sevkiyatı yapacakları tespit edildi.

Operasyonda iki imalathane ortaya çıkarılırken 6 milyon 200 bin sentetik ecza hapı, uyuşturucu hap üretiminde kullanılabilecek 165 kilogram pregabalin ve 1 milyon boş kapsül bulundu.

Aramalarda ayrıca bir kapsül dolum makinesi, bir karıştırma makinesi, iki tabanca ve çeşitli malzemelere el konuldu.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

title: Verilen sözler tutulmadı: Medical Hospital işçileri ikinci hastane önünde eylem yaptı
content:
Elif Ekin Saltık [email protected]

Elâzığ’da faaliyet gösteren Özel Medikal Hospital Hastanesi çalışanlarının iş akitleri 9 Kasım 2026 itibarıyla feshedilmişti. Doktorların dört aylık, diğer sağlık çalışanlarının ise 69 günlük maaş alacakları ile tazminat ve izin haklarının ödenmemesi üzerine işçiler eylem başlatmıştı. İşverenle yapılan görüşmeler sonucunda 16 Kasım Pazartesi gününe kadar süre istenmiş, çalışanlar da bu talebi kabul etmişti. Ancak verilen sürenin dolmasına rağmen ödemelerin yapılmaması üzerine emekçiler eylem yaptı.

Medikal Hastanesi önündeki eylemlerini kesintisiz sürdüren sağlık emekçileri, verilen sözlerin tutulmaması üzerine patrona ait ikinci hastane olan Anadolu Hastanesi önünde protesto eylemi düzenledi.

Anadolu Hastanesi önünde sloganlar ve ıslıklarla yönetimi protesto eden çalışanlar, "Alın terimiz olan hakkımızı istiyoruz, sadaka değil" diyerek tepkilerini dile getirdi. Eyleme Elâzığ Yeni Parti İl Başkanı da katılarak işçilere destek verdi.

Eylemin ardından işçilerle yeniden masaya oturan hastane yönetimi, ödemeler için 17 Kasım Salı günü saat 12.00’ye kadar ikinci bir ek süre istedi. Emekçiler ise haklarını tam olarak alana kadar eylemlerine kararlılıkla devam edeceklerini belirtti.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Carey Gillam
title: Environmental Groups Warn Nitrate Pollution Is “Urgent Threat to Public Health”
content:
A petition sent to the EPA calls for tighter restrictions on a contaminant increasingly associated with many cancers.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Sixteen environmental and public health groups filed a legal petition with U.S. regulators on Monday seeking new restrictions on nitrate contamination — a type of water pollution the groups say is driving a “public health crisis across the country.”

The petition calls for the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to slash the Maximum Contaminant Level (MCL) for nitrate in drinking water to 1 milligram per liter (mg/L), down from the current federal standard that allows for up to 10 mg/L. The groups are calling for the Maximum Contaminant Level Goal (MCLG) to be set at 0 mg/L, which essentially would acknowledge that no amount of nitrate is considered safe for human health over lifetime exposure.

Such moves are warranted because scientific research shows that current levels of contamination pose “an urgent threat to public health,” including increasing the risk for certain cancers, the petition states.

The petitioners cite analysis showing that surface water levels of nitrate across the nation are increasing while nitrate monitoring is decreasing.

“One of the things we have sought to do here is to do the EPA’s job for it,” said Tyler Lobdell, an attorney with Food & Water Watch, one of the groups leading the petition effort. “One hundred and twenty million on people being serviced by public water systems are told the water is perfectly safe when the science says it is not.”

The petitioners include the Environmental Working Group, the Center for Biological Diversity, the Center for Food Safety, Food & Water Watch, Sierra Club, Natural Resources Defense Council, among others.

The petition blames not only the EPA but also federal, state, and local lawmakers and other public officials for failing to address nitrate pollution, which is linked to cancers and other health problems.

The groups cite excessive application of synthetic fertilizers, the “over-application” of animal waste from concentrated animal feeding operation (CAFO) onto farm fields, inadequately treated sewage and industrial discharges, and failed septic systems as culprits for the nitrate-laden water.

The legal petition for rule making requires a response by the EPA and could set in motion further legal actions, Lobdell noted.

When asked about the petition, the EPA said it would review it and said it is “committed to ensuring all Americans have access to clean drinking water.” However, the agency noted it completed its most recent review of drinking water regulations, including the regulations for nitrate, in July 2024, evaluating available studies and applicable data. And based on that information, there was no need for a revision of the MCL, the agency said. The agency said it will consider new studies for its next review.

The current standard of 10 mg/L for drinking water was initially set in the 1970s and finalized in 1991 at a level that was set to avoid causing methemoglobinemia, also known as blue baby syndrome. All public water systems are required to monitor for nitrate contamination to determine compliance with that MCL.

But research on nitrate health impacts has grown over the past 35 years and there is now a large and growing body of evidence that consuming even low levels of nitrate-contaminated water is associated with colon and rectal cancers, and ovarian cancer, bladder and kidney cancers, as well as other adverse health impacts such as neural tube defects and low birth weights in babies.

The petitioners said they identified 3,205 community water systems serving roughly 119.7 million people that recorded at least one nitrate sample at or above 1 mg/L between 2021 and 2023.

The petition comes as many U.S. states, including key farming states, wrestle with concerns about nitrates. Iowa, in particular, has drawn national scrutiny for its high levels of nitrate in prominent waterways and climbing rates of cancer.

Scientists point to farm operations as largely to blame for nitrate contamination, both because of the runoff of fertilizer applied to fields of corn and other crops, and the runoff of liquified manure generated by large livestock operations that is also often spread on farm fields. The runoff carries nitrates and phosphorus into surface and groundwaters, and ultimately into drinking water.

Iowa tops the list of U.S. states with the highest mean levels of nitrate in surface waters from January 2015 through August 2026, according to the petition, which cites analysis of water quality data from multiple national, state, and local monitoring systems. Iowa is followed by Minnesota, Delaware, Illinois, Indiana and Kansas.

People who get their drinking water from wells are at particular risk as nitrate is commonly found in groundwater.

“For decades EPA has given industrial agriculture a free pass to pollute, and now one in three Americans is drinking water with dangerous levels of nitrates, JP Rose, director of soil health at the Natural Resources Defense Council, said in a statement. “Tackling agricultural pollution at the source and improving treatment will help ensure all Americans have access to safe drinking water.”

One of the primary drivers of agricultural nitrate pollution is overapplication of fertilizer; synthetic nitrogen fertilizer is the largest nitrogen source in 41% of U.S. watersheds, the petition states.

Along with lowering the allowed levels of nitrate in drinking water, the EPA should take new steps to address the source of the nitrate pollution by implementing greater controls at the source point, the petition states. The petitioners point to cover cropping, wetlands protection and restoration, riparian buffers or field border strips, and crop diversification as practices that can help reduce nitrate pollution.

The petitioners noted that stricter regulations on nitrate pollution would also benefit ecosystems and fish and wildlife. Dozens of species listed under the Endangered Species Act are at risk due to the water pollution the petition notes.

The Iowa Environment Council (IEC), which has been pushing for stronger controls on nitrate contamination in that state, supports the call for strengthening the MCL, said IEC general counsel Michael Schmidt. But he noted a lowered MCL would not affect private wells, many of which exceed the 10 mg/L limit that applies to public water supplies. The state should take steps to help protect private well users in the near-term without waiting for EPA to act, he said.

Lowering the MCL for nitrate in drinking water could prove very costly for water utilities if the sources of the contamination are not significantly restricted. The current cost of nitrate treatment is “a substantial financial burden on water utilities,” according to recent research. Utilities spent up to 9% of their overall operating budgets just on nitrate treatment, according to a 2018 study by the Northeast-Midwest Institute.

The Association of Metropolitan Water Agencies did not respond to a request for comment on the petition. Neither did the the American Water Works Association.

The groups petitioning the EPA argue that their analysis demonstrates that an MCL of 1 mg/L is both “technically achievable and economically justified.”

They also say that the human health benefits of a lower MCL more than justify the costs of compliance. They say their analysis shows a nitrate MCL of 1 mg/L would “conservatively result in approximately $364.1 billion in present-value health benefits, compared with approximately $94.5 billion in compliance costs, yielding approximately $269.7 billion in net benefits over the 50-year analysis period.”

Nancy Stoner of the Environmental Law and Policy Center said in a press conference that the federal government should provide financial support to utilities to help them comply with a lowered standard.

“Americans should not suffer the adverse health outcomes resulting from drinking nitrate contaminated water because funds are not available to ensure safe drinking water, nor should communities be burdened with the full costs of reducing nitrate contamination driven by underregulated industrial agriculture,” the petition states.
