author: Hudson Hongo
title: Donate Equity to Support Digital Rights: Stocks, DAFs, and Giving
content:
Do the holidays have you thinking about how you can support your favorite nonprofit?

For 35 years, the Electronic Frontier Foundation has been advancing our digital rights, including defending security researchers, encrypting the web, and fighting illegal surveillance. Donating equity to EFF can help support this important work.

Perhaps your family has taken advantage of the new tax law around giving by creating a Donor-Advised Fund.

Perhaps your employer has gone public and you now own stock.

Perhaps you’ve seen some of EFF’s recent successes and thought, Man, imagine what they could do with more.

A gift of equity can help your contribution go farther and offer tax savings. When you donate appreciated stock, you avoid paying capital gains tax on any increase in its value. You also receive a charitable income tax deduction for the fair market value of appreciated stock on the date it is transferred. Also, more and more companies are offering gift-matching programs that can double your impact at no additional cost.

If you have owned the stock for less than a year, your gift will not qualify for all of these potential tax advantages. And gifts of appreciated stock are fully deductible—up to a maximum of 30% of your adjusted gross income. Please check with your accountant or tax advisor regarding your particular tax status.

We have helpful information here to facilitate the transfer of securities. Please email us if you have any questions. And let us know in advance if you are transferring securities. We’ll need to know the amount and type of shares that you will be donating in order to provide a tax receipt.

As a 501(c)(3) organization, EFF can also receive distributions through your Donor-Advised Fund (DAF), including one-time gifts or recurring donations. Simply inform your DAF provider you would like to make a gift to: Electronic Frontier Foundation (EIN 04-3091431) 815 Eddy Street San Francisco, CA 94109 Please note that many DAF providers do not provide the donor’s name to the recipient organization. If you would like to be recognized for your gift, let us know the amount of the gift and the fund name. And due to IRS regulations, we may not be able to provide a thank you gift in line with your giving level. The DAF provider is responsible for your tax receipt.

The rules that govern technology shape our freedom. Help us write those rules today!

author: Unknown
title: Agricoltori e studenti: un dibattito in università sui temi del carovita, della PAC, delle mobilitazioni sociali
content:
A partire dall’introduzione al dibattito 

Agricoltori e studenti: un’unica terra

, riportiamo qui i punti toccati e invitiamo a riascoltare gli interventi contenuti nel video allegato. 







Un incontro tra agricoltori e studenti per condividere esperienze e individuare prospettive comuni contro il carovita.




Prima di iniziare, faremo una breve introduzione per presentarvi gli ospiti, presenti per la prima volta all’Università di Torino e a Palazzo Nuovo: Gabriele Ponzano, allevatore e agricoltore ad Alessandria, Samantha Sonaglio, allevatrice di bovini di razza francese, anche lei in provincia di Alessandria, e Andrea Maggi, risicoltore nel Vercellese. Invece, dal lato della moderazione e per aiutarci a dare un quadro al dibattito, nonché discutere del perché ci troviamo qui insieme proprio in questo periodo, Andrea di 

Italia in piazza 17.




Sia Gabriele che Samantha fanno parte dell’associazione 

Agricoltori Autonomi Italiani

, che è aderente a un’associazione ancora più grande che si chiama 

COAPI

, Coordinamento Agricoltori e Pescatori italiani.




Questa introduzione si concentra sulle motivazioni che hanno portato alla nascita di queste associazioni nel 2024, perché se oggi attenzioniamo quelle che sono le proteste in corso è importante anche tracciare la storia di queste realtà e delle mobilitazioni degli agricoltori – le cosiddette “rivolte dei trattori” o “mobilitazioni dei trattori”.




Sono associazioni, le loro, che nascono nel 2024. In quel periodo avrete tutti sentito parlare dei “trattori”, attivi anche qui a Torino con vari presidi, ai quali avevamo partecipato insieme ad altri compagni e compagne che avevano seguito queste mobilitazioni. In particolare a Febbraio a Torino Sud, con più di 300 trattori per 5-6 giorni in protesta.







Sostanzialmente i temi che venivano portati già allora nel dibattito pubblico erano quelli di una produzione sottocosto a livello italiano sostanzialmente per tutte le aziende agricole, anche quelle medio-grandi, con la conseguente difficoltà di arrivare a coprire le spese di produzione ed assicurarsi un margine minimo di guadagno.




Il sistema attuale sta infatti andando a schiacciare anche le aziende storicamente più integrate nella produzione capitalistica, quindi con una produzione su vasta scala e inserite nella GDO (grande distribuzione organizzata): anche questi soggetti all’oggi vivono la fine del vantaggio economico di cui hanno potuto godere nel tempo. Questo a causa dell’apertura dei mercati e delle politiche agricole europee sempre più concentrate verso la grande e grandissima produzione.




Ma, tra gli altri temi portati allora, c’era anche quello della mancanza di rappresentanza.




Quindi la frattura che si è creata nel 2024 con i sindacati agricoli, Coldiretti e non solo, ha portato alla creazione di queste nuove associazioni: un modo, come gli ospiti ci racconteranno meglio, per  dare voce direttamente alle proprie rivendicazioni di agricoltrici e agricoltori.I sindacati nel tempo si sono trasformati da enti di supporto alle istanze di chi lavora e di chi produce a CAF territoriali che sostanzialmente aiutano i produttori solo dal punto di vista burocratico. Anche la burocrazia è sicuramente un tema importante, soprattutto per quanto riguarda i sussidi europei ma anche, ad esempio, per le normative sanitarie.




Anche oggi, le aziende che si stanno mobilitando in tutta Italia sono sia relativamente piccole che di media dimensione, come ad esempio quella di Andrea che si estende per 116 ettari. 

Nel complesso non si tratta di piccoli produttori tagliati fuori dal mercato, ma è il mercato stesso che è arrivato a una crisi profonda

 

ancora più evidente con l’aumento dei costi del carburante.




Oltre alla questione del sistema produttivo, esiste quella relativa alla 

Politica agricola comunitaria

 (PAC), su cui volevo darvi un paio di dati.È attualmente in discussione la nuova programmazione della politica agricola europea , nello specifico  la prossima fase che inizierà  dal 2027 (quadro PAC post 2027), e su cui è evidente che c’è pochissimo spazio di voce in capitolo da parte di chi lavora tutti i giorni in questo settore.




Nel periodo 2021-2027 la PAC ha concentrato 

oltre 378 miliardi di

 

fondi pubblici

 europei.

 Guardando alla suddivisione di questo budget tra imprese agricole, capiamo che questo è un 

esempio di concentrazione estrema anche dei finanziamenti pubblici

, perché come ci spiegheranno tra poco, è vero che questi finanziamenti sono divisi su vari ambiti, ma sappiamo che il grosso va alle produzioni gigantesche, talvolta anche attraverso la mediazione di prestanome societari. Le grandi multinazionali si stanno inserendo nella produzione del cibo ma non solo, perché un altro tema che tocchiamo oggi è quello del controllo dei territori e di una sottrazione di decisionalità sui territori che ci circondano.




Ne parleremo anche in relazione all’

agrivoltaico

, andando a capire come la questione energetica si intreccia con un accaparramento delle terre nelle mani, anche qui, di grandi multinazionali che davanti a un settore in crisi, davanti ad agricoltori e agricoltrici in crisi, cercano di comprare terreni per produrre energia. Energia che, spesso e volentieri, non viene neanche poi distribuita sul territorio. Analogamente, i territori ora vanno a confrontarsi anche con tutta la questione dei 

data center

.La risposta spesso è l’abbandono delle aree rurali, il che significa l’abbandono della produzione agricola, una sempre minore sovranità alimentare e capacità di produrre.




In conclusione, accenniamo a una questione che verrà ripresa sicuramente negli interventi: quella dello 

sfruttamento dei braccianti

 agricoli, cioè dei lavoratori stagionali in agricoltura, che è un altro elemento che si sta cercando di attenzionare sul territorio piemontese, e in particolare a Saluzzo.Ci sono nuovi coordinamenti che stanno nascendo intorno a questo tema e l’idea è di portarlo all’attenzione oggi e in generale nelle prossime mobilitazioni per far emergere come lo sfruttamento che si riproduce nel lavoro stagionale è figlio di quello sfruttamento economico della GDO e delle grandi multinazionali che si inseriscono in una dittatura di prezzo, in aste al ribasso, in dinamiche imposte che danno luce a questo fenomeno e alla sua riproduzione nel caporalato.




Arriviamo così al 2026, e ai temi a cui ho accennato si somma anche la questione del 

caro carburanti

, che di nuovo accende anche per agricoltori e agricoltrici un segnale di crisi importante e viene raccolto come occasione ulteriore di mobilitazione.A partire dal caro carburanti abbiamo visto soprattutto dal Centro-Sud Italia quella che è una sorta di alleanza nascente tra le mobilitazioni degli autotrasportatori, di vari settori del lavoro e della logistica, di agricoltori e agricoltrici e l’intera mobilitazione studentesca contro il carovita e il governo Meloni, che vediamo oggi anche qui a Palazzo Nuovo occupato.




Su questo, oggi, vorremmo interrogarci insieme.

author: Unknown
title: Памяти Ивана Хуторского
content:
Публикуем рассказ об Иване Хуторском. Автор - антифашист Олег Волин.

17 лет прошло как с нами нет нашего друга и товарища, известного антифашиста и анархиста Ивана Хуторского.

Его подло убил со спины ублюдок неонацист Коршунов из БОРН. Иван сделал очень многое для развития антифашистского движения в Москве и в России. Вечная слава героям!

16 ноября 2009 года был убит антифашист Иван Хуторской по прозвищу Костолом. Иван зашел в подъезд своего дома на окраине Москвы, привычно заглянул в почтовый ящик, и в это время нео-нацист Алексей Коршунов выстрелил ему в затылок. Спустя два года после совершения преступления этот ублюдок погиб, подорвавшись на собственной гранате.

Иван был добрым и отзывчивым человеком, всегда был готов прийти на помощь друзьям в любой ситуации. В наше смутное время этот человек для многих был примером несгибаемой воли и мужества. Иван до конца оставался предан своим убеждениям. Его уважали друзья и боялись враги.

Иван закончил юридический факультет МГАПИ и после смерти отца, оставшись единственным кормильцем семьи, работал в московском городском центре профилактики безнадзорности, преступности, алкоголизма, наркомании и СПИДа среди несовершеннолетних «Дети улиц» по специальности, юристом.

Иван занимался армрестлингом и самбо, участвовал в организации безопасности множества левых акций и музыкальных концертов. Был одним из организаторов антирасистских турниров по смешанным единоборствам «Не сдавайся!». Этот турнир собирает бойцов, разделяющих антирасистские взгляды, а также участников леворадикального движения.

Иван едва ли не первым среди столичных анархистов и антифашистов понял, что боевая подготовка и дисциплина должны стать одним из главных приоритетов антифашистского движения, и фактически выстроил нынешнюю модель спортивной подготовки «антифа». Первый такой турнир прошел в октябре 2009 года также в Москве в память об убитом нацистами антифашисте Фёдоре Филатове.

К несчастью, за время своей активной работы на благо движения Иван успел завести не только друзей, но и врагов.

Его адрес и имя, как и адреса и имена многих других известных антифашистов, таких как Станислав Маркелов и Николай Гиренко, неоднократно вывешивались на пронацистские сайты с призывами к его уничтожению. Первый раз на него напали нацисты в 2005 году и порезали бритвой голову. Второй раз нападавшие праворадикалы ждали его в подъезде. Ивану чудом удалось выжить. Он получил множественные ранения отверткой в область шеи, а также многочисленные удары бейсбольной битой. И уже в январе 2009 года во время уличной драки ему был нанесен удар ножом в живот, после которого Иван снова еле выжил. И вот только с четвертого раза нацисты добились своего, выстрелом из пистолета в затылок. Подло, исподтишка. Похороны Ивана в своей статье «Красные мартенсы» описал его знакомый, один из лучших журналистов России Андрей Лошак:

«Власть торжественно провожает Ивана Хуторского в последний путь „почетным караулом“ из десятков бойцов ОМОНа, перекрывших все подъезды к кладбищу. Опасаются терактов и провокаций. Возле крематория несколько сотен молодых людей, с первого взгляда напоминающих футбольных хулиганов. Хотя встречаются и панки…

Наконец все собираются возле гроба. Родственники, обычные русские люди, плачут. Друзья пока держатся. Тетенька говорит казенную фразу про последнее прощание с усопшим (какое неточное слово!). Первый ставит диск, и ритуальный зал взрывается жесткими звуками панк-рока. Тимура тоже хоронили под его любимую музыку. Кажется, это был Эллиотт Смит. С Ваней прощались под Stage Bottles, песня „Солидарность“. Вообще-то эта вещь в свое время была написана в поддержку польского рабочего движения. Но замени Polish на Russian — и песня станет идеальным саундтреком к яркой, честной и мужественной жизни Ивана:

Give them hope, give them strength, give them live like a candle burning in the black of night, we’re all with you in our hearts and in our minds, and we’ll pray for our nation through its darkest times

Под конец песни слезы текут у всех, включая молодых мужчин, явно не склонных к сантиментам. В их жизни уже давно все по-взрослому. Взаправду и очень серьезно. Они сделали то, что в их силах: очистили панк-культуру от коричневой грязи. Вымели, вышвырнули нечисть из своих клубов и подвалов. Теперь практически в одиночку ведут кровопролитную войну на улицах. Настоящие психи: их убивают, а они продолжают сопротивление. Нет чтобы играть вместе со всеми в „секретики“.»

Антифашисту Ивану Хуторскому в этом году было бы 43, но он навсегда остался 26 летним. Помним!

Фильм об Иване на английском языке можно посмотреть с субтитрами.

author: Natalia Viana
title: Deu a louca nos bots
content:
Quer receber os textos desta coluna em primeira mão no seu e-mail? Assine a newsletter Xeque na Democracia, enviada toda segunda-feira, 12h. Para receber as próximas edições, 

inscreva-se aqui.







Outro dia estava em Santiago do Chile, e quis compartilhar com os colegas chilenos 

este artigo

, no qual listo as maneiras como os EUA intervieram nas eleições brasileiras e, portanto, pedi ao Deepseek para traduzi-lo para o espanhol. 




O robozinho chinês realizou meu comando com presteza, mas foi além. Abaixo da tradução, após um emoji de alerta, ele avisou: “Nota importante: Se trata de um artigo de opinião/denúncia jornalística com uma linha editorial muito definida, não de um relato neutro”. Prosseguiu, dizendo que as afirmações eram interpretações, “não fatos confirmados independentemente”. E terminava: “Se você necessita deste resumo para um trabalho acadêmico ou uma decisão importante, convém contrastá-lo com outras fontes”. 




Não fiquei ofendida com a interpretação do robozinho, mas pasma – assustada é a palavra – com o fato de que 

ele não se limitou a cumprir o meu

 

prompt

, mas decidiu me alertar sobre o conteúdo do material

 que eu forneci a ele. 




As implicações disso são tremendas. Se você está acompanhando as notícias recentes sobre desenvolvimentos da IA, está pelo menos um pouco alarmado. 




Esta escapadela do Deepseek funciona mais como uma anedota interessante – não é o caso de que o robô decidiu agir sozinho, deve ser alguma nova atualização do chatbot que pretende ajudar a alertar sobre desinformação – e como um ponto de partida para uma reflexão sobre as consequências da adoção de tecnologias que evoluem rapidamente, são obstinadas e, falando em bom português, 

ninguém sabe bem como funcionam

: nem seus criadores, nem seus engenheiros, nem seus donos. 




A consequência do que fez o Deepseek é exatamente o que os 

tech bros

 fingiram não querer por tanto tempo: eis que o robozinho agora se arvora em dizer o que é verdade e o que não é. Isso, em um contexto privado, em uma relação desigual, onde uma pessoa/humana se volta para um robô/ferramenta em busca de conhecimento, ou seja, se portando como aprendiz. 

Nós, diante dos chatbots, estamos vulneráveis. E é perigosíssimo que eles façam um juízo de valor – sem serem requisitados a isso – sobre a informação que consumimos.

 




Na mesma semana em que o Deepseek me dizia que minha coluna é enviesada, jornais 

publicam

 que o correio da França foi hackeado e os dados de 22 milhões de franceses – um terço da população – foi comprometido. 




Apertem os cintos, essas notícias serão cada vez mais comuns. 




A verdade é que chegamos a novembro com um novo paradigma do desenvolvimento da IA, no qual agora somos obrigados a lidar com as consequências de termos jogado no mundo essas ferramentas que tomam decisões por si sós e que portanto, por princípio, não temos como controlar ou prever totalmente. Mudou de vez o paradigma da segurança digital. Tudo está sob ameaça. As câmeras do Smart Sampa. O Tinder. O E-gov. Os alertas da Defesa Civil. Tudo. 




Na imprensa internacional, os eventos de quebra de segurança recentes foram chamados de “outubro sombrio”. 




Um dos mais graves foi a descoberta de vulnerabilidades na linguagem de programação chamada PHP, amplamente usada por sites que vemos todos os dias, o que 

pode ter deixado

 70% de todos os sites na internet sob risco de serem invadidos – 

pessoas (ou robôs) poderiam assumir controle dos servidores, roubar dados, tirar os sites do ar.

 Antes do anúncio da vulnerabilidade, 

experts

 em cibersegurança já estavam detectando um aumento de ataques tentando explorar a falha em todo o mundo. Em resposta, a NSA (de triste memória) do governo dos EUA emitiu um alerta e diversos sites governamentais saíram do ar para implementar as correções. 




Um 

relatório

 do centro Halcyon, especializado em sequestro de dados digital, detectou um aumento de 40% de ataques do tipo entre julho e setembro deste ano, se comparado com os meses anteriores. É só um exemplo; diversos especialistas estão alertando para o fato de que 

estamos vivendo uma onda sem precedentes de ataques de segurança a sites do mundo todo. 




Jason Clinton, vice-diretor de segurança da informação da Anthropic, 

chamou

 de desastre o que o que estamos começando a vislumbrar. “O tsunami de vulnerabilidades está chegando em apenas alguns meses e não haverá tempo suficiente para corrigir a infraestrutura crítica”, escreveu no X.




Criminosos, agências de inteligência e segurança, governos autoritários, empresas corruptas, todos estão testando o que pode ser feito com os LLMs (Large Language Models)

 

disponíveis no mercado.

 




E em termos de explorar falhas em segurança na arquitetura do mundo digital, eles são imbatíveis. 




Uma reportagem recente da 

Reuters

, que tem como fonte o especialista em segurança Snorre Fagerland, traz com muita clareza como funciona este novo mundo. Ele conta que conseguiu mapear a ação de um cibercriminoso chinês que usou agentes para invadir sites de mais de 100 empresas, incluindo uma fabricante de eletrodomésticos e uma de motores da China. 




Segundo a Reuters, o que ele fez foi definir os alvos e passar aos seus agentes de IA uma instrução concisa – “invada” – e uma lista das suas táticas de intrusão preferidas. Incansáveis, os robozinhos passaram horas a fio em busca de vulnerabilidades em diferentes sites. Quando não encontraram, eles passaram a explorar vulnerabilidades em outros provedores de serviços ou infraestrutura associada. 




A busca pode ser infinita. 




Alguma vulnerabilidade, haverá.  




O 

expert

 entrevistado pela Reuters se disse “impressionado” pela capacidade dos agentes de resolver problemas complexos como esses. Ele diz ter comprovado que os agentes de IA que já existem no mercado podem fazer invasões complexas sem intervenção humana. 




Como sabemos, 

é bem difícil estabelecer limites para a IA.

 Se os robôs recebem uma ordem, vão buscar obstinadamente encontrar a solução. Não têm sono, não têm sede, não têm problemas familiares com que se preocupar; e são baratos. 




Fagerland estimou que a atividade do hacker chinês usava uma combinação do DeepSeek com o Claude Code, da Anthropic, e gastou apenas US$ 5.000 em tokens.




Os robôs, ainda por cima, não têm bom senso, apenas lógica. 




Assim como na emergência climática, à qual fomos jogados pela ganância de gerações de homens no poder, é este o mundo em que vivemos agora. 




Se os robôs só têm a lógica, seria bom que pelos menos os homens que comandam essas empresas – e os governos – tivessem algum bom senso e se unissem para regular de uma vez essa tecnologia

, decretando uma moratória imediata. 

Como comentei na semana passada

, é o que estão pedindo os votos nas urnas. 




Não me parece que é o que vai acontecer, infelizmente.

author: Mzi Velapi
title: Western Cape hit with tighter water restrictions
content:
The water and sanitation department has issued a warning to residents and businesses in the Western Cape that it will implement a 7% reduction in domestic and industrial water allocations as well as a 15% reduction in water for irrigation. Addressing the media on Monday, Minister of Water and Sanitation, Pemmy Majodina said that the current water in storage in the province is below the preferred operational threshold of 80%.




“While the major dams remain at acceptable levels overall, some key components of the system have recorded significant declines compared to the previous year. Storage levels remain significantly above those experienced during the severe drought period of 2016-2017; yet, the current water storage is below the preferred operational threshold of 80% and approximately 11.9 % points below the ten-year average of 84.49%,” Majodina said.




According to the minister, the decline in stored water resulted from below-average winter rainfall in the province while the looming El Niño event is increasing temperatures and evaporation.




Municipalities are expected to restrict water supply to residents and can impose further restrictions, but by no more than the 7% that the national government has imposed. The department is expected to write a submission to the director general who will approve the restriction and get it gazetted.




“Modelling undertaken by water resource specialists reveals that if water users continue to utilise their full allocations without intervention, the risk of water shortages and mandatory restrictions will increase substantially from 2027 onwards,” said Majodina.




The City of Cape has announced that it will introduce level 1 water restrictions from 1 December 2026.




Rural taps already dry




The Kannaland Local Municipality that covers Ladismith, Calitzdorp and Zoar are already on level 4 water restrictions. Water in the municipality is available for human consumption only.




Carmelitta Juries lives on a farm near Ladismith. While the farm dam is full, the water isn’t safe to drink without first disinfecting it with bleach. Carmelitta said they have no choice but to rely on the unsafe dam water as the municipality offers no alternative. “The municipality promised that they would put up water tanks. One tank could sustain a couple of homes. For example, 10 homes can use one tank, but to date we haven’t heard anything further,” she said.




Zoar resident, Irene Isaacs said that it is harder for the village to access water in summer. Community members without water storage tanks must wait for municipal trucks to deliver water. Elderly residents are especially vulnerable in these circumstances, she said, and depend on members of the community to carry water in buckets to their homes. 




Kannaland Municipality is already on level 4 restrictions. File photo by Mandla Mnyakama




Bergriver, Swartland and Saldanha Bay municipalities have been flagged as key areas where water scarcity and aging infrastructure pose significant constraints to future growth unless supply and bulk infrastructure are urgently upgraded. Hendrix Van Wyk from Vredenburg, which falls under Saldanha Bay Municipality, told 

Elitsha

 that in poor neighbourhoods like Hopland, Louwville, Selbou and Yskor, the water pressure in the taps is low. “It takes up to 30 minutes to fill up a 5-litre bucket and a 20-litre bucket takes about 2 hours to fill up,” he said.




According to Majodina, construction of the Clanwilliam Dam, which will increase water availability for the West Coast District Municipality, is 40% complete.




Partnership, not privatisation of water

 insists DWS




A 

new amendment to the Water Plan

 states that if a municipality is not delivering a clean, safe supply of water, the national government can hand that function over to the private sector. The government has already implemented this in the City of Tshwane where a public-private partnership is taking effect. According to 

BusinessTech

, Coca-Cola has partnered with the government to invest R500-million in municipal water infrastructure to stop service delivery from collapsing.




During Cape Town’s severe drought between 2015 and 2018, marked by the 

Day Zero Campaign

, water rights groups protested against water guzzlers, and the soft drink manufacturer was one of their targets. At the time, Coca-Cola drew about 530-million litres of water annually from the City of Cape Town to manufacture its products. A litre of Coke requires about 2 litres of water to produce.




Minister of Water and Sanitation, Pemmy Majodina during the opening of parliament this year. File photo by Mzi Velapi




The involvement of the private sector is seen by water rights groups as an early sign of water privatisation and exclusion of the poor.




During the media briefing, the acting director general, Dr Risimati Mathye denied that partnership with the private sector is ushering in the privatisation of water. “Government has never, in any way, taken a decision to privatise water. Yes, there is partnership that the government undertakes with the private sector, most especially integrated with their corporate social responsibility programmes but that is not necessarily privatisation of water. The government always invites the private sector to work with us to ensure that access to water is done but that is not privatisation,” Mathye said.

author: Dominique Gené - Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Beatrice Deer honoured for album of Inuit legends
content:
Beatrice Deer has two more awards for her mantle.




On Nov. 8, the Nunavik singer-songwriter brought home Félix awards from the Adisq Gala in Montreal for her album 

Inuit Legend

. She won Indigenous Artist of the Year and Album of the Year – Indigenous Languages.




 Adisq — or 

Québec Association for the Recording, Concert and Video Industries — celebrates the best of the province’s music and art.




Released in April, 

Inuit Legend

 features 11 songs inspired by Inuit stories and legends, reimagined through rock music.




In an April 

interview

 with 

Nunatsiaq News

, Deer, an Inuk-Mohawk artist originally from Quaqtaq, said her research for the album was rooted in conversations with elders. She wanted to preserve stories passed down through generations and share them as music.




“It’s a way of honouring our elders,” she had said. “It’s important to keep telling our stories, to keep the imagination running.”




During the gala, Deer performed 

Aukkauti

, a song inspired by a real-life hunting accident in Nunavik in 1899 that led to a series of deaths and a cycle of revenge.

author: Sonali Kolhatkar
title: With Dems on the Rise, Organizers Ramp Up Push for Paid Family and Medical Leave
content:
Organizers say guaranteed national paid leave is possible — and a tax on corporations and the wealthy could pay for it.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The United States is one of the only nations in the world without a federally guaranteed paid family and medical leave policy. As U.S. workers continue to be caught between stagnant wages and rising costs, a single emergency such as an unexpected illness can put them into the untenable position of choosing between their physical health and their financial health.

In June 2025, Jasmine White of Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, found herself in exactly such a situation when she became injured and unable to walk. The single mother of four had no safety net to sustain her catering business, Jazzy Good Eats & Catering. “I was forced to step away because my body wouldn’t allow me to keep going,” she said. “I didn’t have paid leave, disability coverage, or a safety net to fall back on.”

In the absence of federal action, a state-by-state movement for paid family and medical leave has spent years painstakingly pushing for policy changes — and has enjoyed growing success. According to Paid Leave for All, a nationwide coalition of organizations working on the issue, “fourteen states and the District of Columbia have passed laws to guarantee paid family and medical leave, while 18 states and D.C. along with several municipalities have paid sick time laws.”

With Pennsylvania not yet on that list of states, White was forced to take unpaid leave for four months while recuperating from her injury. “When I couldn’t work, the business couldn’t operate the way it needed to,” she said. The resulting financial precarity forced her to pivot her business model from a restaurant and catering operation toward exclusively catering, and she switched from employing full-time employees to hiring contract workers as needed.

“It feels like a never-ending cycle of working just to survive,” said White. “If you don’t work, you don’t eat. If you don’t work, you can’t pay your bills. If you don’t work, your children are affected. That reality keeps me in a constant state of work mode.”

Jennifer Driscoll of Coopersburg, Pennsylvania, experienced a similarly difficult situation when her daughter Lily was born seven weeks premature in 2007 and she needed to stay at home to care for her fragile newborn. “That decision came at a tremendous financial cost to our family,” said Driscoll. “We went into serious debt because of my extended time away from work.”

Driscoll and her husband started a nonprofit called Lily’s Hope Foundation in 2013. In her words, her goal was “to support families facing the unexpected challenges and financial hardships that come with having a premature baby or a child in the NICU.” While the organization has supported thousands of families across the U.S., Driscoll believes that “these families need more than care packages and emergency assistance.” They need state support.

According to Dawn Huckelbridge, founding director of Paid Leave for All, “the United States is one of the only countries in the entire world that doesn’t guarantee any kind of paid leave.” This includes vacation, sick leave, parental leave, or time off to care for an ailing family member.

In stark contrast to workers in the U.S., workers in Europe have a guaranteed right to four weeks of paid vacation, and varied but generous amounts of paid sick leave and parental leave depending on the country where they live.

It isn’t that Americans don’t want paid leave. A large majority of the public supports paid family and medical leave, regardless of political affiliation. “Literally any kind of demographic you could try to poll, a supermajority does support this issue,” said Huckelbridge.

It’s hard to believe that until relatively recently, working Americans didn’t even have the right to take unpaid leave for emergencies. The 1993 Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) allowed workers to take up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave per year without the risk of losing their job.

When the COVID-19 pandemic struck in 2020, advocates pushed lawmakers to expand on the FMLA with the passage of the Families First Coronavirus Response Act, enabling eligible workers to access paid leave, and self-employed workers to get tax credits in very specific cases of COVID-19 infections. That law’s paid leave provisions lasted barely a year.

Then, under President Joe Biden and with the backing of Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-New York), advocates worked to include provisions for four weeks of paid leave in the 2021 Build Back Better bill. While the bill passed the House of Representatives, it failed in the Senate by one vote: Sen. Joe Manchin (D-West Virginia) refused to vote for the bill, effectively killing it.

The lack of guaranteed paid leave disproportionately impacts low-income women and people of color. Huckelbridge thinks that part of the reason why the U.S. has no federally guaranteed paid leave is that Congress has historically been white male-dominated. “There’s this bias of people who do less of the caregiving,” she said. “Issues that have disproportionately impacted women and people of color have often been sidelined; they’ve often been sort of cut and compromised because they haven’t been framed as fundamental and economic kitchen table issues, when in fact they are.”

In the wake of Manchin’s exit from politics, and historic Democratic Party congressional wins in the November 2026 midterm elections, Wendy Chun-Hoon, president and executive director of the Center for Law and Social Policy, is optimistic: “With the clear majority in both chambers of Congress, we expect Democrats to move swiftly to show voters ‘message received,’ and focus their first hours and days on advancing paid leave and child care for all,” she said.

Having come within a single vote of winning federally guaranteed paid leave in 2021, the Paid Leave for All coalition is now focused on passing a new bill introduced by Senator Gillibrand called the Family and Medical Insurance Leave (FAMILY) Act. Huckelbridge explained that if it were to pass, the bill would ensure paid leave for things like “serious health events, new babies, injuries, illness [in] your family.”

The question that routinely arises with such safety net proposals is how to pay for them and if businesses would suffer. According to Huckelbridge, “It would be administered by the federal government, it would be funded by the federal government, and it would in that way be very much a business support.”

The funding could come from general revenues or from a modest payroll tax. But, given that big corporations and wealthy individuals continue to be enriched from lower taxation, Huckelbridge suggested one simple funding source could come from “taking taxes from the wealthiest and big corporations to make them pay their fair share.”

When asked about the likelihood that President Donald Trump would veto every piece of Democratic Party-supported legislation landing on his desk, Chun-Hoon said, “If this White House chooses to continue to ignore families’ needs — if they veto paid leave — then Congress will have it ready for the next president to sign it in 2029.”

In the meantime, advocates in Pennsylvania, where there is no statewide paid leave, are continuing to push for legislation. Dan O’Brien, the family economic stability policy director at the Pennsylvania-based organization Children First, has been working on passing a state bill called the Family Care Act.

If passed, that act would establish an insurance fund to cover paid sick leave to recover from major surgery, as well as parental leave for the birth or adoption of a new child, and to care for children recovering from serious illness or for elderly parents needing critical care or rehabilitation.

That bill, which has passed the Pennsylvania House of Representatives, has bipartisan support in the Pennsylvania State Senate but, as of this writing, has not yet been introduced for a vote. O’Brien explained that “[state] senate leadership has decided to side with the big business lobbyists in Harrisburg who have been opposing our efforts.” He is confident that if it is brought to a vote in the state senate, it will pass.

Pennsylvania has traditionally been a politically “purple” state, swinging between support for Democrats and Republicans. O’Brien is hopeful that if Pennsylvania lawmakers pass the Family Care Act, it could be a “blueprint for conservative states and the federal government to do the same.”

Workers like White and Driscoll are among those for whom a paid leave guarantee would offer desperately needed relief. “Paid family and medical leave is about dignity, stability, and the ability to take care of ourselves and the people who depend on us,” said White. “We shouldn’t have to reach a breaking point before we’re allowed to rest.”

Driscoll concurred, saying, “No one should have to choose between being there for their family and being able to pay their bills.”

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $28,000 in the next 72 hours. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

author: C.J. Polychroniou
title: We’ve Reached the 31st Global Climate Summit and Have Yet to Phase Out Emissions
content:
COP31 is making clear yet again that the world cannot simply rely on summits to solve the climate emergency.

COP31 is making clear yet again that the world cannot simply rely on summits to solve the climate emergency.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

With the 31st annual UN climate summit (COP31) currently underway in Antalya, Turkey, and deadly heat waves and catastrophic floods having been a hallmark of 2026, a year set to be the hottest on record, this is a propitious time to take stock of the progress made on climate change and the environment and reflect on the challenges of a world beyond fossil fuels.

No one anticipates any breakthroughs in negotiations at COP31, which concludes on Friday, November 20. Climate change is not even a major issue regularly getting the attention of global leadership, and global banks, including the largest U.S. banks, are dropping their climate commitments. If there was ever an international consensus in fighting climate change, it is surely gone, as British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told COP31. Indeed, recently re-elected Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva scolded fellow leaders at the UN climate summit in Turkey by saying they are interested in “talking more about weapons and tariffs than the survival of future generations.” It is thus not surprising that the leaders of major countries around the world (Germany, France, Italy, Canada, Japan, India, and China) skipped the event. U.S. President Donald Trump of course is also not attending since he (again) withdrew the United States from the Paris Climate Agreement.

Short-term political concerns have dominated past global climate summits, and it is no different this time around. COP31 has exposed yet again the deep divisions among developed and developing countries over adaptation funding and climate finance accountability. And Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodriguez objected to calls for an end to the age of fossil fuels by telling the conference that “we reaffirm our sovereign right to strengthen our energy and oil industry as a driver of our national development.” Sadly enough, this is a view that is now openly shared by many leaders around the world, including Turkey, the host of this year’s climate summit which remains heavily dependent on fossil fuels, especially coal-fired electricity generation. So while electrification has emerged as a major theme of this year’s summit, it seems more than likely that oil and gas could dominate for decades.

Moreover, like in all previous climate summits, the formal agenda of COP31 does not include an item on the relationship between militarism and climate action. No mention of the long-term environmental costs of war, militarism, and occupation — including the destruction of Gaza, which has unleashed massive greenhouse gas emissions — is expected to feature in COP31’s final text. In sum, COP31 will make clear yet again that the world cannot simply rely on summits to solve the climate emergency. Radical and legal activism are the best hopes for our future.

James K. Boyce is an author, naturalist, and a leading scholar of environmental economics and climate policy. In this interview, Boyce discusses the evolution of the political economy of the environment and of environmental movements, the opportunities and failures of global climate summits, and he highlights the links between climate change and inequality.

Boyce is professor emeritus of economics and senior fellow at the Political Economy Research Institute at the University of Massachusetts Amherst. He is the author of many books, including Economics for People and the Planet: Inequality in the Era of Climate Change. He is also the recipient of major awards including the 2025 Common Wealth Prize, the 2024 Global Inequality Research Award, and the 2017 Leontief Prize for Advancing the Frontiers of Economic Thought.

The interview that follows has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

C.J. Polychroniou: Climate change is the defining crisis of our time. We have also been in an environmental crisis since the late 1960s. Indeed, the first Earth Day took place in 1970 as a response to rising environmental concerns. Shortly thereafter, we also had the establishment of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), further evidence that the environment was becoming a top issue for voters. Now, you have devoted much of your career to investigating the dynamics of environmental degradation, including the link between inequality and the environment. Can you discuss a bit how the study of the political economy of the environment has evolved over the past 50 years?

James K. Boyce: Dirty air, polluted water, and depleted natural resources put environmental issues on the political map. As so often is the case, the economics profession was behind the curve. When I went to Oxford to study for my doctorate in 1980, the university did not offer a single course in environmental economics.

As the importance of environmental “externalities” — impacts of production and consumption that do not show up in market prices — became more evident, the new field of environmental economics developed with its focus on how to restore “efficiency,” in the cost-benefit analysis sense of maximizing net present value, once externalities are factored into the mix via “shadow prices.”

Initially, few economists connected the dots between environmental degradation and inequality. In part this reflected the times: The field emerged during the heyday of free-market fundamentalism, when most economists dismissed inequality as a non-issue. But two more things contributed to that neglect. One was the ideological axiom that the economic well-being of a society can be measured by summing the dollar value of output (adjusted, perhaps, for the imputed dollar value of environmental impacts) without considering how those dollars are distributed; that is, ignoring the elementary fact that a dollar is worth less to a billionaire than to a worker struggling to make ends meet. The second was ignoring the role of power — political power as well as purchasing power — in shaping how markets and governments alike function, including the role of power in shaping decisions on environmental policy.

Over time, this too has begun to change.

What about the evolution of the environmental movements? How has environmental activism evolved over the years, and what have been its main achievements so far?

There have always been diverse strands in environmental movements, within and across countries, so generalizations should be taken with a grain of salt. In the United States, I would say that in its early years the environmental movement saw the basic problem as one of protecting nature from people. “People” were seen as the problem. In practice, this often meant poor people who supposedly could not “afford” to care for the environment. This notion went hand-in-hand with the rampant Malthusianism of the time which portrayed population growth as the root of all ills.

Things began to change in the 1980s with the birth of the environmental justice (EJ) movement. Its initial focus was the disproportionate siting of hazardous waste facilities in communities composed primarily of Black people. Gradually, the movement widened its scope to disparities across a wide range of environmental impacts, along lines of class, ethnicity, and gender as well as race. Environmental justice reframed the environmental narrative not simply as protecting nature from people but protecting some people from environmental harms caused by the actions of other people.At the same time, the international women’s health movement effectively challenged the axiom that overpopulation is the main cause of poverty and environmental degradation.

In the U.S., race and ethnicity often are even stronger than income as predictors of exposure to environmental hazards.

A milestone was achieved in 1994 with the executive order issued by President Bill Clinton that directed federal agencies to address disproportionate environmental impacts on minorities and low-income people. The political fortunes of the environmental justice movement have risen and fallen over time — the Trump regime marks a nadir in this as in so many other respects — but environmental justice has made a lasting imprint on environmental activism.

Much has been achieved. Air quality and water quality have improved greatly, reducing illnesses and premature mortality from pollution. The Montreal Protocol, an international agreement that went into effect in 1989, protected the stratospheric ozone layer from depletion by chlorofluorocarbons. The decline of biodiversity has been arrested, though by no means halted. And a start has been made on the historic transition from fossil fuels to cleaner sources of energy. Much remains to be done, but it is important to recognize these achievements, if only to take heart from their evidence that we are on the right side of history.

Inequality is one of the biggest and most troubling issues of our time. What are the mechanisms by which economic inequality can lead to environmental degradation?

Economic inequality and the accompanying inequalities of power make it easier for those on top of the economic ladder to impose environmental costs on everyone else, and especially on those at or near the bottom.

This would be the case even in the ideal world of neoclassical economic orthodoxy, where maximizing the dollar value of net benefits is the touchstone for welfare optimization. Standard cost-benefit analysis is guided by the principle of “one dollar, one vote,” not “one person, one vote.” Under this formula, those people with more dollars have more votes. The cost of environmental harms is measured by willingness to pay to prevent them. If those who suffer the harms are poor — while those who reap the benefits from environmental degradation, via higher corporate profits and lower market prices, are relatively wealthy — then the so-called “efficient” level of environmental protection is weaker than would otherwise be the case.

The impact of inequality does not stop there, however. Political power often mirrors purchasing power. The result is to distort environmental policy-making even further by biasing decisions against those with less political voice. This helps to explain why in the U.S., race and ethnicity often are even stronger than income as predictors of exposure to environmental hazards.

It has been argued that climate change also increases economic inequalities. How so, and what can be done about that?

Like other kinds of environmental degradation, climate change tends to hit the poor harder than the rich. In part, this is because lower-income people have less ability to withstand environmental costs than do high-income people. If climate change led to a 10 percent decline in incomes that was equally distributed across the board, it would be a bother to the rich, a bigger deal for the middle class, and potentially fatal for some of the poorest people in the world. But it is also due to the fact that the costs of climate change are not, in fact, evenly distributed. Lower-income people often live in more vulnerable locations, and they are less able to afford house insurance, health insurance, air conditioning, and other means of escaping the worst effects of extreme weather events. This was vividly illustrated, for example, by the impacts of Hurricane Katrina in New Orleans in 2005, a disaster that has been described as “environmental injustice in a fast-forward mode.”

In principle, climate adaptation investment should and could be preferentially channeled to those at most risk. All too often, however, scarce resources for this purpose flow to those with the most economic and political power.

What can be done about this? The first order of business is to move as quickly as possible to phase out the use of fossil fuels, doing so in a way that enhances the energy security for working people in the short run by increasing the money in their pockets, and in the long run by freeing them from periodic shortages and price gouging on the world markets for oil and gas. The second task is to make those most responsible for climate destabilization — the world’s biggest fossil fuel corporations — shoulder a fair share of the costs of disaster response and climate adaptation, and to ensure that funds for these purposes reach those in greatest need. Both of these things are possible, but only if working people exercise their democratic rights to call the shots rather than leaving environmental policy in the hands of oligarchs.

The COP31 summit is happening this month in Antalya, Turkey. How much impact do these global summits have?

The fact that we are now on the 31st summit and have yet to phase out emissions of greenhouse gases shows that their impact has been limited. But this is not to say that summits are useless. They raise the visibility of the issues across the world, and to some extent, they offer a forum for concerted action in reducing emissions and funding investments for climate adaptation and for compensation for losses and damages that have not been averted.

Local and national action to combat climate change does not have to wait for an international agreement.

Much more needs to be done. The fact that the U.S. administration today has chosen to obstruct progress rather than cooperate (let alone play a leading role in addressing climate change) only makes matters worse.

But it is crucial to recognize that local and national action to combat climate change does not have to wait for an international agreement. Curbing carbon emissions is often depicted as a textbook collective-action problem: Why should any country reduce emissions if others fail to do so? This was the argument invoked by President George W. Bush when he refused to ratify the 1997 Kyoto Protocol. This pretext for inaction rests on the misleading premise that the transition from fossil fuels to clean energy necessarily is a cost rather than a benefit to the country and its people.

In reality, proactive climate policies can bring enormous health benefits to the public thanks to cleaner air, for the simple reason that fossil fuels spew out multiple toxic pollutants along with carbon dioxide. Moreover, fossil-fuel phasedown policies can be designed to raise the purchasing power of working people through energy security cashbacks. These benefits of cleaner air and higher incomes accrue regardless of what other countries do. In addition, being a leader in the development of clean energy technologies will confer a strong competitive advantage to the country’s economy in coming decades. So national moves to cut emissions need not be held hostage to decisions by other countries.

Are you optimistic about humanity’s chances in curbing the climate crisis before it destroys civilization as we know it?

Well, “civilization as we know it” today has deep flaws in terms of obscene economic inequality and needless environmental degradation. To improve human well-being, we need to fix both.

Rephrasing the question in terms of curbing the climate crisis before it irreparably damages human well-being, I am optimistic that is possible. There is no scientific or technical reason it cannot be done; instead, there are political obstacles. These are formidable, but when it comes to politics, I take inspiration from Antonio Gramsci’s optimism of the will.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $28,000 in the next 72 hours. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

content:
This petition was written by Amazon workers and shared internally on Nov 16, 2026 in response to The Guardian’s revelations of Amazon Rekognition’s complicity in ongoing the “israeli” genocide in Gaza.

Sign Worker Petition Sign Public Petition

The Guardian has revealed that “israel” uploaded 3.5 million photos of Palestinians into Amazon’s cloud to be run through AWS Rekognition, the company’s facial recognition technology. The photos include the ID photos “israel” forces every Palestinian to take at 16. After the ground invasion in Gaza, the IOF aimed this system at its own checkpoints, where cameras scanned Palestinians as they fled “israeli” bombing and matched their faces against Rolling Stone, described by an IOF soldier as the system “where all the information relevant to the control of the Palestinian civilian population is centralised”. A military IOF source said Amazon’s cloud was used precisely because of the “very large scale” of images collected at those checkpoints, which became sites of mass detention and enforced disappearance, as documented by UN bodies.

Under Project Nimbus, the company constructed a segregated, fortified “walled garden” inside its Tel Aviv data centers for IOF military and intelligence data, and hosted IOF soldiers at its own offices in “israel” as they explored how to run the Gaza facial recognition programme on AWS. Rolling Stone’s plan, in the words of a military source, was to migrate “pictures, videos, all the confidential intelligence information — everything.”

Since October 2023, “israel” has carried out a sustained bombardment that has caused daily suffering and the murder of countless Palestinians, enforced a deliberate starvation blockade, continued bombing Gaza despite the so-called “ceasefire”, and damaged or destroyed 82% of all structures, including schools and hospitals. Behind this carnage, Amazon serves as the technological backbone of “israel’s” surveillance and bombing apparatus in Gaza.

Through contracts like Projects Nimbus and Sirius, Amazon facilitates A.I. targeting systems that use mass amounts of surveillance data to identify and strike Palestinian civilians. When data volumes, including billions of audio files, exceeded military server capacity, the IOF turned to Amazon Web Services (AWS) and its “endless storage” for information on almost “everyone” in Gaza. IOF personnel testified that data stored in Amazon’s cloud was used to confirm aerial assassination strikes, many firing munitions from “israel”-owned weapons firms that Amazon has sold cloud and A.I. services to throughout the genocide.

In June 2025, a UN report formally categorized Amazon, Google, and Microsoft as part of a “joint criminal enterprise” actively transforming colonial occupation into genocide by providing “israel’s” essential tech and A.I. infrastructure. By September 2025, Microsoft was exposed storing 11,500 terabytes of intercepted Palestinian phone calls for Unit 8200 on Azure, and the IOF swiftly planned to move the trove to AWS. A month later, it was revealed that as part of Project Nimbus, Amazon and “israel” agreed to a secret “winking” mechanism: coded payments that alert “israel” of any incoming legal demands or investigations from foreign governments for “israeli” data. Similar to Microsoft, Amazon has engineered a scheme to buy the IOF time to move evidence of its genocide hosted in AWS.

Amazon Rekognition is just one tool in the digital arsenal powering “israel’s” ongoing genocide of Gaza.

While the Guardian leak is abhorrent, it should not be shocking. It is not the first time Amazon has knowingly profited off of human rights abuses using Rekognition facial A.I. technology.

In 2018, the ACLU revealed that Amazon was selling Rekognition to U.S. police departments despite its documented racial bias that frequently misidentified Black and Brown members of Congress as criminal suspects. During the George Floyd protests in 2020, there was public outcry about police use of facial recognition technology to surveil protestors. Facing public and shareholder pressure, Amazon announced a one-year moratorium on sales to local law enforcement, later extending it “indefinitely”.

Despite the moratorium, Amazon continued to pitch and sell Rekognition to federal entities like ICE and the FBI, cementing its position as “the largest provider of facial recognition technology to U.S. law enforcement, including federal immigration agencies and the FBI.” ICE now uses facial recognition to scan individuals on the street without consent, instantly checking their immigration status against federal databases to identify targets for detention and deportation. This surveillance infrastructure has already been used against Amazon’s own workers: ICE detained two Amazon Flex drivers at the company’s Hazel Park, Michigan facility in February 2026.

Now, the same infrastructure used to surveil and deport migrants in the U.S. is being leveraged to target and murder Palestinians in Gaza. Amazon did not learn from the police scandal; they simply moved up the chain of command, finding new markets here and in Palestine for the same dangerous facial A.I. technology.

Amazon has imposed a moratorium on Rekognition sales to U.S. police before; we demand similar restrictions on “israel”. We did not consent to building the tools used to murder Palestinians, and we refuse to stay silent any longer. Therefore, we demand that Amazon:

Stop Selling Facial Recognition Technology to “israel”: End all sales of Rekognition to “israel” to prevent its continued use in the ongoing genocide in Gaza and the occupation and apartheid in Palestine.

Conduct an Investigation: Conduct and release the results of a transparent, independent investigation of how Amazon customers, including “israel” and ICE, are using Rekognition in violation of international human rights law, the AWS Responsible AI Policy, and the AWS Acceptable use Policy.

Protect Worker Speech: Guarantee zero retaliation—no suspension, firing, or harassment—for any worker who wants to discuss or engage in moral discourse about the Guardian article or this petition on internal platforms like Slack or email.

We, the workers, made these demands before. In May 2021, after “israel” murdered more than 250 Palestinians in Gaza, more than 500 of us wrote to Andy Jassy and Jeff Bezos demanding Amazon cut all ties with “israel” and protect pro-Palestinian speech. That October, 300 workers sent a petition to the executives demanding Amazon pull out of the Nimbus contract and cut all ties with the IOF. Amazon ignored both. In 2023, after “israel” began its genocidal onslaught in Gaza, 1,700 of us again demanded Amazon cancel its contracts with the IOF. Again, silence.

This time, our petition comes from an organized Amazon worker resistance movement—and for the fourth time, we are here because Andy Jassy (Amazon CEO) and Matt Garman (AWS CEO) are murdering Palestinians with our labor, all while expecting us to remain silent. They are not alone. The leaders of Rekognition—Peter DeSantis (SVP), Vishal Sharma (VP), Srini Veeravanallur (Director), Helbert Fonseca Maich (Senior Manager), and Palak Mehta (Senior Manager)—authorize the sign-offs, the high server capacities, and the shipment of Rekognition code to the IOF. We will continue to escalate until all our demands are met. We want material change, and we want it now.

author: Ames Alexander
title: EPA Plane for Chemical Detection in Toxic Emergencies Can No Longer Do Its Job
content:
Former agency employees who worked on the airborne detection effort say the program has unraveled.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

When an ammonia leak outside a hotel in Weatherford, Okla., injured 74 people last November, the federal government’s chemical-detection plane stayed on the ground.

When a fire tore through a Valero refinery in Port Arthur, Texas, in March, the plane sat idle.

And when massive blasts killed two workers at an industrial recycling plant in Toledo, Ohio, in August, it stayed put, despite a fire surrounding tanks of flammable solvents.

“Ten years ago, it would have gone to all of them,” said Mark Thomas, a former EPA official who for years managed the airborne detection effort.

The program, known as ASPECT, was designed to respond around the clock to emergencies involving toxic chemicals, oil spills and radiation. The plane’s sensors could identify chemicals in the air within minutes, giving emergency responders crucial information about the dangers nearby communities face.

For more than two decades, the plane has flown over many of the country’s worst disasters, from New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina to the deadly West Fertilizer explosion in Texas to the Deepwater Horizon oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico.

But since early 2021, the single-engine Cessna has responded to just seven emergencies. And former ASPECT scientists said two of those missions — the 2023 train derailment that sent toxic clouds over East Palestine, Ohio, and the 2025 fire at Smitty’s Supply in Louisiana — were badly mismanaged.

At Smitty’s, the EPA declared the air safe, but a former ASPECT scientist later found toxic chemicals the agency had missed. And the agency’s Inspector General is now auditing the response to the East Palestine derailment, including the data behind its public assurances about air quality.

Now — at a time when chemical emergencies are increasing — the plane can no longer do its job. In June, the EPA Inspector General found the plane’s systems can’t identify chemicals within minutes, as designed. Instead the process takes about a week, far too long to help anyone on the ground who’s deciding whether to evacuate.

The EPA said the plane’s chemical sensors are wearing out and expects replacements to be working by mid-2027.

But five people who helped build and run the program told Floodlight that the EPA is fixing the wrong problem.

The old sensors still work, they said. What the agency lost, in their view, is the initiative and expertise that made the program a powerful tool when disaster struck. Replacing the old sensors, they warn, could leave the EPA even less capable of detecting hazardous chemicals in an emergency.

“I fear that the public is at risk,” said Robert Kroutil, a longtime ASPECT scientist who helped develop the program and later became a whistleblower. “It’s such an important program, and they’ve allowed it to waste away to nothing.”

The EPA did not respond to Floodlight’s requests for an interview or questions about ASPECT’s decline, its handling of emergencies, the replacement of its sensors and allegations of mismanagement by former program scientists and managers.

The country’s need for a chemical-sensing plane grew from the smoldering, toxic debris in Manhattan on Sept. 11, 2001, when the EPA’s monitoring trucks were stranded on the wrong side of the Hudson River, unable to cross after bridges and tunnels into the city closed.

Kroutil was a program manager for the Department of Defense at the time, leading a research team that had developed the technology that would become ASPECT, short for Airborne Spectral Photometric Environmental Collection Technology. The military transferred the program to the EPA for use in detecting hazardous chemicals during civilian emergencies.

It became a critical tool for emergency responders over the next 20 years.

For 72 hours after Hurricane Katrina struck, it was the only emergency response aircraft flying over New Orleans, where it helped locate a missing 55-gallon drum of potentially lethal chloroacetic acid.

During the Deepwater Horizon disaster, it became a key tool for tracking oil slicks in the Gulf of Mexico.

And when a fire engulfed 15 massive tanks at a chemical storage terminal east of Houston in 2019, the ASPECT plane helped emergency responders track the plume, which contained the carcinogen benzene.

Richard Lawhorn, an assistant chief with Harris County’s hazardous materials response team in Texas, said the plane could detect chemicals at elevations beyond the reach of ground crews and survey a much wider area in a short time.

“They’re monitoring the products we can’t reach,” he said.

The program’s success lay in its intellectual rigor: Kroutil and the program’s radiological lead held PhDs, as did Mark Thomas, the former EPA official. The team wrote the code, designed the mounts that held gear, and analyzed the raw data themselves.

“We were very, very hands-on and intimately familiar with every part of that aircraft,” said Thomas, who later went to work for a company that develops chemical-sensing technology.

The decline began with the departures of key ASPECT personnel during President Donald Trump’s first administration.

As part of an agency reorganization, the EPA told the program’s staff in 2019 that they had to relocate to Texas, where the plane was based, or face termination, documents show.

The mandate was unnecessary, according to Thomas, because the program had been designed for remote operation. Rather than leave his elderly parents in Kansas, he retired. Then, ASPECT’s radiological lead left the division, and the engineer who helped build and manage the plane’s sensors accepted a demotion to stay in Kansas.

According to Kroutil and two of his former colleagues, the EPA then failed to fill those vacancies with scientists who had any experience with airborne chemical detection.

“They lost the institutional knowledge of the program, and quite frankly, lost the momentum of the program,” Thomas said.

During its first two decades, the plane flew almost 80 emergency missions — an average of roughly four a year. In the past five years, however, it has flown an average of just one a year.

In October, hundreds were evacuated — and more than 50 were treated at hospitals — when a 5,500-gallon industrial tank in Toledo leaked glycidyl methacrylate, a chemical used in making plastics that is a likely carcinogen suspected of causing genetic defects. It was one of at least 80 chemical emergencies this year that the plane did not respond to.

The decline comes as accidental chemical releases are becoming more common. The U.S. Chemical Safety Board tracked 133 last year, up from 83 in 2021. The Trump administration, meanwhile, is proposing to roll back federal safeguards designed to prevent chemical disasters, including requirements for some plants to undergo independent safety audits and provide hazard information to nearby communities.

Former ASPECT program managers said they used to actively track chemical emergencies and urge EPA on-scene coordinators — who manage environmental emergencies — to deploy the plane. After they left, that proactive approach vanished: The plane stayed in a Texas hangar until coordinators requested it, they said.

Scott Smith, an independent environmental tester who’s often called on by local communities to investigate chemical contamination after industrial accidents, said ASPECT could help him target his soil and water testing by mapping the path of chemical plumes. Deployed regularly, he said, the plane could save lives.

Instead, “It’s being shut down and not used.”

On Feb. 3, 2023, a Norfolk Southern freight train carrying the carcinogen vinyl chloride and other hazardous chemicals derailed in East Palestine, Ohio, near the Pennsylvania border.

As fires from the derailment smoldered, emergency responders feared an explosion — and made the controversial decision to vent and burn five railcars containing vinyl chloride, sending a towering plume over the town.

ASPECT missed the vent-and-burn operation, and its services weren’t requested until more than two days after the initial disaster. Even then, it was used sparingly. Despite the derailment being one of the nation’s worst chemical disasters in years, Kroutil said, the plane collected just eight minutes of chemical data when it finally flew over East Palestine on February 7 — a fraction of what it typically gathered during an emergency.

Had the plane been deployed earlier — or flown over the site en route to Pittsburgh, the nearest major airport — its thermal detection equipment might have helped determine that the tank cars were not in danger of exploding, Kroutil later said in an affidavit.

The National Transportation Safety Board later concluded the vent-and-burn operation had been unnecessary. It found no evidence of the dangerous chemical reaction that Norfolk Southern and its contractors said threatened an explosion. Temperature readings showed the railcars were cooling.

An EPA Inspector General investigation later found a series of errors in the East Palestine response: The agency had poorly documented its procedures and failed to adequately inform emergency responders of the plane’s capabilities. The on-scene coordinator, who didn’t request the plane until two days after the derailment, wrongly believed ground-level monitoring would provide better data.

Frustrated by how EPA officials were running the program, Kroutil retired. Two of his colleagues also left, further draining the program’s pool of experience and expertise.

On Aug. 22, 2025, a massive explosion ripped through Smitty’s Supply, a facility that blended and packaged oil and other engine lubricants in Roseland, La.

Less than four miles away, Ronnie Polezcek and his family heard something hitting their roof that afternoon. At first, they thought it was raindrops.

But when they walked outside, Polezcek said, “It was just like it was raining oil.”

The dark residue covered the family’s 23-acre farm. Polezcek said he had to burn his hay, move his cows temporarily to Mississippi and replace a metal roof that could not be scrubbed clean. Two of his cows miscarried soon afterward, he said, and a veterinarian found arsenic in one of them. Polezcek sued Smitty’s in September 2025. The lawsuit has been consolidated with an ongoing class-action case.

The Smitty’s fire burned for nearly two weeks, sending a huge plume of smoke into the air. Local authorities ordered a one-mile evacuation around the plant, and the EPA dispatched ASPECT — the plane’s first emergency deployment in 19 months.

The agency didn’t publicly post findings from the ASPECT flights until August 31, nine days after the fire began. Those reports show the air around Smitty’s contained ozone and three other pollutants — but at levels considered safe.

A later analysis of the raw flight data, though, told a very different story.

Working with the Government Accountability Project, a nonprofit that advocates for whistleblowers, Kroutil obtained data from ASPECT’s third flight over the disaster area. He said it took him weeks to analyze it, doing by hand what the plane’s software was designed to do in minutes.

Kroutil identified high concentrations of the neurotoxicant toluene and the carcinogens trichloroethylene and naphthalene, among other toxic chemicals. He concluded that the levels of toluene were so high they could have put nearby communities at risk.

Many of the findings also matched what Smith, the independent environmental tester, detected in soil and water after the fire. The EPA later acknowledged a similar problem, according to records that the Government Accountability Project obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request.

In a May 2026 email, an EPA manager said some target chemicals might have been present in data from the third flight but weren’t flagged at the time the data was collected. The manager suggested that deterioration of the aging sensors might have contributed to the failure.

More than a year later, Polezcek said, the residue still coats much of his property. When his grandchildren play outside, he said, they come back inside with “little black feet.”

“That’s my biggest concern,” he told Floodlight. “What is it doing to them?”

Polezcek believes officials should have evacuated a larger area.

“I really think it was a pitiful job,” he said. “They just kept saying, ‘There’s nothing to worry about, you’re good to go.’ ”

In June, the EPA Inspector General confirmed that Kroutil’s warnings were justified: The plane could no longer provide chemical-monitoring data within five minutes.

Instead, scientists had to conduct manual analysis that would take about a week. The EPA also failed to tell on-scene coordinators that the program isn’t working as designed.

EPA officials blamed the delays on old sensors. The agency bypassed competitive bidding to award a Canadian company, Telops, a $1.7 million contract for replacement sensors designed for several applications, including gas detection and mineral mapping. Integrating the new sensors won’t be complete until “early to mid-2027,” according to the EPA.

In contract documents, the EPA cited peer-reviewed studies showing the Telops sensors had been field-tested and proven. But much of the research on the new equipment has focused on tracking methane leaks, not the wide range of toxic chemicals released during complex industrial emergencies.

Five people formerly involved with ASPECT have raised concerns that the new sensors will be less capable than the old ones at detecting hazardous chemicals during industrial emergencies.

Exosens, the parent company of Telops, told Floodlight that its system and the old one use “different measurement architectures.”

The new sensors, it says, can identify hundreds of chemicals and distinguish chemical plumes from surrounding objects.

Chris Manning, an infrared spectrometer expert with no ties to Telops, the EPA or the firm where Thomas now works, said the new Telops sensors could complement ASPECT’s older sensors but would be a poor replacement. They are slower, less sensitive, and less suited to moving targets, he said.

“To say, ‘We’re just going to replace these other two instruments’ … I mean, that’s ludicrous,” he said.

The old sensors had problems, too. Their artificial intelligence software had not been retrained after an electrical malfunction several years ago, Kroutil and Thomas said. In early 2023, contract scientists with the program presented the EPA with a plan to retrain the software, emails show. But the EPA never took the required steps, Kroutil said.

He and his former colleagues said they have no confidence that the new sensors will fix the problem. They expect the program to deteriorate further.

In the affidavit submitted to the Government Accountability Project, Kroutil offered a dim prognosis: “Unless major changes are made at EPA and with the ASPECT program, it is not going to get any better and EPA will be flying blind.”
