title: ᐱᓕᕆᔨᒻᒪᕇᑦ ᓈᒻᒪᒃᓴᙱᓗᐊᖅᑐᑦ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ‘ᒪᑦᑐᑎᑐᐃᓐᓇᖅᓯᒪᔭᖓ’ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᖃᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᕐᒥ ᓱᕈᓯᕐᓂ
content:
To read the English version of this story, please see 

Experts decry Nunavut’s ‘Band-Aid’ approach to foster care

.







ᓱᕋᒃᓯᒪᔪᖅ ᓱᕈᓯᕐᓂ ᐃᓄᓕᕆᓂᖅ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐱᒋᐊᕐᕕᖃᕐᒪᓐ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᓄᓇᓕᙳᖅᑎᑕᐅᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ ᒪᓕᒃᑕᐅᓯᒪᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᓈᒻᒪᙱᓕᐅᕈᑎᖃᓗᐊᕐᒪᑕ, ᐃᓚᖏᑦ ᐅᖃᕐᓯᒪᔪᑦ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᒐᓴᖕᓂ ᑕᒪᑐᒥᖓ ᐊᑐᕐᓯᒪᓂᑰᔪᑦ ᓱᕈᓯᓕᕆᓂᕐᒥᑦ.




“ᓄᓇᖃᖅᑳᖅᑐᑦ ᓱᕈᓯᖏᑦ ᐱᔭᐅᖃᑦᑕᕐᓂᖏᑦ ᓄᖅᑲᖅᓯᒪᙱᒻᒪᑦ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕆᐊᕐᕕᐅᕙᓚᐅᖅᑐᓂ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᔨᐅᕆᒥ ᔭᖕ, ᐊᓈᓇᖓᓂ ᐱᔭᐅᓂᑯ ᓱᕈᓯᐅᑎᓪᓗᒍ. “ᑲᔪᓰᓐᓇᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᓱᕈᓯᕐᓂ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᕆᙱᑕᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᐅᑎᑕᐅᓕᕌᖓᑕ.”




ᔭᖕ ᐅᖃᓪᓚᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᓄᓇᑦᓯᐊᕐᒥ ᐱᕙᓪᓕᐊᔪᓄᑦ ᐊᑐᖃᑦᑕᖅᓯᒪᔭᕕᓂᕐᒥᓂᒃ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᕆᙱᑕᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᐅᖃᑦᑕᕐᓂᐅᔪᒥᑦ ᓄᕕᐱᕆ 5-ᒥ ᐅᖃᐅᓯᖃᖅᖢᓂ ᑭᖑᓪᓕᖅᐹᒥ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᕙᓪᓕᐊᔪᓂᒃ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖅᑎᓄᑦ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᑉ ᐅᓂᒃᑳᓕᐅᓚᐅᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᖃᕈᓯᖏᓐᓂᒃ ᐃᓅᓱᒃᑐᓂ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᐅᑎᑕᐅᔪᓂᒃ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᕆᙱᑕᖏᓐᓄᑦ.




ᐱᓇᓱᐊᕈᓯᐅᓚᕐᑐᒥ ᐅᓂᒃᑳᓕᐊᕆᔭᐅᔪᖅ, ᑕᓪᓕᒪᒋᔭᐅᔪᖅ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᑦ 15 ᐃᓗᐊᓂ, ᓴᖅᑭᑎᑦᑎᓯᒪᖕᒪᑦ ᐊᓯᔾᔨᖅᓯᒪᓗᐊᒋᓐᓂᖓᓂ. ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᐅᑎᑕᖏᓐᓂ ᓱᕈᓯᕐᓂ ᖃᐅᔨᒪᓗᐊᙱᒻᒪᑕ ᖃᔅᓯᐅᓂᖏᓐᓂ, ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖃᑦᑕᙱᓗᐊᖅᖢᑎᒡᓗ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᒃᓴᕆᒐᓗᐊᖅᖢᒍ ᑕᒪᒃᑯᐊ ᓱᕈᓰᑦ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᕆᙱᑕᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᑲᒪᔨᒋᔭᐅᔪᑦ ᓈᒻᒪᒃᑐᒥᑦ ᐊᖏᕐᕋᕆᔭᐅᔪᒧᐊᕋᓗᐊᕐᒪᖔᑕ.




ᔭᖕ, ᒫᓐᓇ 26-ᓂ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᖃᓕᕐᑐᖅ ᐊᓈᓇᖓᓂ ᐱᔭᐅᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᖕᒪᑦ ᓱᕈᓯᐅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᐸᓐᓂᕐᑑᒥ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᖃᑦᑎᐊᕋᓱᒃᑲᓗᐊᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ, ᔭᖕ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.




ᐱᔾᔪᑎᖃᓗᐊᕋᓱᒋᓚᐅᕐᑕᖓ ᐃᓄᒋᐊᓗᐊᖅᑐᒦᓐᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓂᕿᖃᕈᓐᓇᑦᑎᐊᙱᖢᑎᒃ ᐃᓚᒌᑦ, ᐅᖃᖅᖢᓂ ᐊᓈᓇᖓ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᓂ 12-ᓂ ᐃᒡᓗᑖᕋᓱᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᓂᖓᓂ ᐃᓚᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᑭᓯᐊᓂᓕ ᐊᔪᖅᑎᑕᐅᖏᓐᓇᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ.
















“ᓄᓇᖃᑎᒌᓕᕆᔩᑦ ᓄᓇᖃᖅᑳᖅᑐᓂ ᐃᑲᔪᙱᓗᐊᕐᒪᑕ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ. “ᑕᐃᒪᓐᓇ ᐊᔪᕐᓴᑲᑕᓗᐊᖅᐳᒍᑦ. ᑕᐃᒪᓐᓇ ᐊᒃᓱᕈᕐᓇᖅᑐᒃᑰᑲᑕᓚᐅᖅᑐᒍᑦ.”




ᔭᖕ ᐃᓱᒪᔪᖅ ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᓇᖕᒥᓂᖅ ᒐᕙᒪᖃᕐᓂᖓ ᓈᒻᒪᙱᓕᐅᕈᑎᓂ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᕈᑎᐅᔪᓐᓇᖅᑐᖅ ᓱᕈᓯᕐᓂ ᑲᒪᒋᔭᖃᖃᑦᑕᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ. ᑲᖏᖅᖠᓂᖅᒥ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖅᑎ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᑐᓕᕆᔨ ᐲᑕ ᕗᐃᓕᐊᒻᓴᓐ, ᐊᒻᒪ ᐋᓖᓐ ᕼᐊᓯ, ᐊᕐᕌᒍᒐᓴᖕᓂ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑐᐃᔨᐅᔪᖅ ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑎᖃᖅᐸᒃᖢᓂ ᓄᓇᖃᖅᑳᖅᑐᑦ ᐊᕐᓇᖏᓐᓂ ᑕᒪᑐᒥᖓ ᐊᖏᓚᐅᕐᒥᔪᖅ.




ᕗᐃᓕᐊᒻᓴᓐ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᕐᒥᔪᖅ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᕙᓪᓕᐊᔪᓄᑦ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖅᑎᓄᑦ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᕐᒥ ᑐᓵᓪᓚᕆᓕᖅᐸᑕ ᐃᓱᒪᓕᐊᖏᓐᓂ ᓱᕈᓯᓕᕆᓂᖅ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᑕᐅᖁᔭᐅᓪᓗᓂ, ᑖᓐᓇᓗ ᐃᓚᖃᖅᖢᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖑᕙᓪᓕᐊᔪᑦ ᑐᓴᐅᒪᔭᐅᑦᑎᐊᕈᑎᒃᓴᖏᓐᓂ, ᑕᒪᓐᓇᓗ ᐱᒋᐊᕈᑎᐅᔪᒥᑦ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᕈᑎᐅᓇᔭᙱᖢᓂ ᒪᑯᓂᖓ ᓱᕈᓯᕐᓂ ᐃᓚᖏᓐᓂ ᐊᕐᓵᖅᑕᐅᖃᑕᕐᓂᕐᒨᖓᔪᓂ. ᑕᒪᓐᓇᓕ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᕈᑎᑐᐃᓐᓇᐅᖕᒪᑦ.




“ᓇᓗᓇᐃᕐᓯᑲᑕᖕᒪᑕ ᒪᑦᑐᑎᑐᐃᓐᓇᕐᓂ ᐋᖅᑭᒋᐊᕈᑎᓂ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᓐᓂ ᐱᒋᐊᕈᑎᖏᓐᓂ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᓯᙱᖔᖅᖢᑎᑦ ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓂ,” ᕗᐃᓕᐊᒻᓴᓐ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.




ᐃᒡᓗᖃᑦᑎᐊᙱᓗᐊᕐᓂᖅ, ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᓯᒪᑦᑎᐊᙱᓗᐊᕐᓂᖅ, ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔮᒃᓴᖃᙱᓐᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᔪᕐᓴᑲᑕᖕᓂᖅ ᐅᓗᕆᐊᓇᕈᑎᐅᖕᒪᑕ ᓱᕈᓯᕐᓂ ᐃᓚᖏᓐᓂ ᐊᕐᓵᖅᓯᖃᑦᑕᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ, ᕗᐃᓕᐊᒻᓴᓐ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ, ᐅᖃᐅᓯᖃᖅᖢᓂ ᕿᒥᕐᕈᐊᖃᑦᑕᕐᓂᕐᑯᑦ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖅᑕᐅᓯᒪᔪᓂᒃ ᓄᐊᑦ ᐊᒥᐊᓕᑲᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐅᑭᐅᕐᑕᖅᑐᕐᒥ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖅᑎᓄᑦ.




“ᐅᑯᐊ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐃᓗᐊᕐᒪᑕ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.
















ᐊᓈᓇᒋᔭᐅᔪᑦ ᑐᐊᕕᕐᓇᖅᑐᓕᕆᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᖃᖅᑎᑕᐅᔪᑦ ᐅᓗᕆᐊᓇᖅᑐᒦᓐᓂᕐᓴᐅᖕᒪᑕ ᓱᕈᓯᖏᑦ ᐱᔭᐅᓇᔭᕆᐊᒃᓴᖏᓐᓂ, ᐅᖃᒃᑲᓐᓂᖅᑐᖅ.




ᕼᐋᓯ ᑕᒪᑐᒥᖓ ᐊᖏᓚᐅᕐᒥᔪᖅ, ᐅᖃᖅᖢᓂ ᒫᓐᓇ ᐱᓕᕆᔾᔪᓯᐅᔪᖅ “ᑐᖁᕋᐃᓂᕋᖅᖢᓂᒋᑦ” ᓄᓇᖃᖅᑳᖅᑐᓂ.




“ᐅᑯᐊ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᖅᑎᖏᑦ ᐃᓚᒌᓄᑦ ᐅᐸᒍᑎᔭᕌᖓᑕ ᐅᕝᕙᓘᓐᓃᑦ ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓄᐊᖅᐸᑕ ᑕᒪᑐᒃᑯᓂᖓ ᕿᒥᕐᕈᐊᖃᑦᑕᕐᒪᑕ ᓈᒻᒪᙱᓕᐅᕈᑎᐅᕙᒃᑐᓂᒃ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ. “ᓲᖃᐃᒻᒪ ᐃᓱᒪᖏᑦ ᐃᓄᒋᐊᓂ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᓱᐃᓯᒪᓇᓱᖕᓂᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᓅᖃᑎᒌᙱᑕᖏᓐᓂ ᐱᐅᒃᓴᖃᑦᑕᙱᓐᓂᕐᒧᑦ.”




ᐊᓯᐊᒎᕈᑎᐅᔪᓐᓇᖅᑐᕐᓕ ᐃᓄᖕᓄᑦ ᐊᐅᓚᑕᐅᔪᓂ, ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓃᑦᑐᓄᑦ “ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑐᐃᓂᕐᒥ ᐃᓚᒌᓂᒃ, ᖃᐅᔨᒪᓗᑎᒃ ᐱᒻᒪᕆᐅᓂᖏᓐᓂᒃ ᐊᒻᒪᓗ ᒪᒥᓴᕈᓐᓇᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂᒃ, ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑐᐃᕙᒡᓗᑎᒃ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᔪᕈᓐᓃᕐᓴᖅᐸᒡᓗᑎ,” ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.




“ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᖃᐅᔨᑎᑕᐅᔭᕆᐊᖃᕐᑐᑦ ᐱᕈᕈᓐᓇᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂ ᒫᓐᓇ ᐅᐸᒃᓯᒪᔭᖏᓐᓂ ᓄᑖᒦᖔᓕᕈᑎᒃ. ᑕᐃᒪᓐᓇ ᐃᓐᓇᐃᑦ ᐃᓱᒪᖕᒪᑕ ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᓄᓇᖏᓐᓃᑦᑐᑦ.”
















ᓄᓇᕗᑦ ᐱᒋᐊᓕᓵᕐᓯᒪᑎᓪᓗᒍ 1999-ᒥ, ᓄᓇᒥᑦ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᖃᐃᖁᔨᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᖕᒪᑕ ᕼᐋᓯᒥ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᐳᓚᕋᖁᔭᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᑕᒪᓐᓇ ᑐᓴᐅᒪᔭᐅᔪᖅ ᑐᓴᖅᑕᐅᑎᓪᓗᓂᒋ ᒪᑐᒧᖓ ᓱᕈᓯᕐᓂ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᖏᓐᓂ ᐊᖅᓵᖅᑕᐅᓯᒪᔪᑦ ᒥᒃᓵᓄᑦ, ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.




ᐅᓇ ᐃᓱᒪᒋᔭᐅᓕᓵᙱᑦᑐᖅ. ᐋᖅᑭᒃᓱᐃᓂᖅ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᑐᓕᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᖅ ᕼᐊᕗᐊᐃᒥ 1979-ᒥ, ᓱᓕ ᒫᓐᓇ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᖕᒪᑦ.




“ᐅᓇ ᖃᐅᔨᓇᓱᕈᑎᑦᑎᐊᕙᒃ ᓄᓇᕐᔪᐊᕐᒥ ᓄᓇᖃᖅᑳᖅᑐᓂ ᑐᑭᓯᓯᒪᔭᐅᓂᖓ ᐃᓚᒌᑦ ᒥᒃᓵᓄᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᓱᕈᓯᕐᓂ,” ᕼᐋᓯ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ. “ᐅᓇ ᑕᐃᒪᐃᖃᑦᑕᕐᓯᒪᔪᖅ ᐅᕝᕙᓘᓐᓃᑦ ᓄᑖᖑᙱᖢᓂ. ᑭᓯᐊᓂᓕ ᐅᑭᐅᕐᑕᖅᑐᕐᒥ ᑕᐃᒪᐃᖃᑦᑕᓕᑕᐃᓐᓇᕐᒪᑦ ᐃᓄᒋᐊᓃᓕᖅᑕᐅᓯᒪᙱᑉᐸᑦ.”




ᓄᓇᕗᑦ ᑖᔅᓱᒥᖓ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᕙᒃᓯᒪᔪᒥ ᐊᑐᖁᔨᓚᐅᙱᑦᑐᑦ.

title: ¿Y ahora qué? Ahora a seguir
content:
Imagen

: 02:4055h. Piquete informativo en Mercavalencia | Fuente: CNT




La huelga general del 11 de noviembre ha sido un éxito. Pero, sobre todo, ha sido una demostración de que cuando quienes sostenemos la sociedad con nuestro trabajo decidimos organizarnos y salir a la calle, tenemos mucho que decir y mucho que hacer.




Desde CNT valoramos muy positivamente el desarrollo de la huelga y, especialmente, la respuesta que han tenido las movilizaciones en las calles. Miles de personas han expresado su hartazgo ante unas condiciones de vida cada vez más difíciles, en las que trabajar ya no garantiza poder vivir dignamente. La precariedad, los salarios insuficientes, la pérdida de poder adquisitivo y la imposibilidad de acceder a una vivienda digna no son problemas individuales: son problemas colectivos que requieren respuestas colectivas.




Pero ahora viene la pregunta inevitable: ¿y ahora qué?




Ahora, a seguir.




No podemos permitir que el 11N se quede en una fecha señalada en el calendario, en una jornada de protesta que se recuerde durante unos días y después se olvide. La huelga ha sido un paso, pero no puede ser el último. Necesitamos mantener la movilización, extenderla a más centros de trabajo, barrios y sectores, fortalecer nuestras organizaciones y construir espacios de lucha y solidaridad.




Las huelgas feministas de 2018 y 2019 nos enseñaron algo importante. Fueron capaces de sacar a la calle a millones de personas, visibilizar las desigualdades que atraviesan la vida de las mujeres y situar en el centro del debate social problemas que durante demasiado tiempo se habían considerado asuntos privados. No acabaron con el machismo ni con las desigualdades, pero abrieron un camino y demostraron la capacidad transformadora de la movilización colectiva. Su éxito no estuvo en resolverlo todo en un día, sino en poner en marcha un proceso que continúa.




El 11N debe ser también un comienzo.




Y tenemos claro algo más: 

esto no lo va a solucionar ningún Gobierno.

 No porque no existan responsabilidades políticas, sino porque el problema va mucho más allá de quién ocupa los despachos. Vivimos en un sistema en el que las decisiones económicas están condicionadas por los intereses de quienes concentran la riqueza y el poder. Cambian los gobiernos, cambian los discursos, pero la economía sigue organizada para garantizar los beneficios de unos pocos a costa de las condiciones de vida de la mayoría.




No vamos a delegar nuestros problemas en ningún político a sueldo de los millonarios. No vamos a esperar a que quienes administran este sistema tengan la voluntad de cambiarlo. Nuestra fuerza no está en las promesas electorales ni en confiar nuestro futuro a representantes profesionales. Está en nuestra capacidad de organizarnos, apoyarnos mutuamente y conquistar nuestros derechos mediante la acción directa y la solidaridad. En nuestra ilusión por crear un nuevo mundo, más justo y con más respeto a la vida.




La vivienda, los salarios, las jornadas, las pensiones y unas condiciones de vida dignas no son cuestiones separadas. Forman parte de una misma realidad: la de una economía que antepone el beneficio a las necesidades de las personas.




Por eso, desde CNT hacemos un llamamiento a continuar las movilizaciones, a mantener viva la organización en los centros de trabajo y en los barrios, y a convertir la indignación expresada el 11N en fuerza colectiva y capacidad de lucha.




No hemos salido a la calle para pedir que nos escuchen y volver a casa a esperar una respuesta. Hemos salido porque sabemos que nuestros derechos dependen de nuestra capacidad para defenderlos.




El 11N no es un final. Es un comienzo.




¿Y ahora qué? Ahora a seguir.




La entrada 

¿Y ahora qué? Ahora a seguir

 se publicó primero en 

Confederación Nacional del Trabajo

.

author: Sicilia Libertaria
title: La politica tra piazze e maranza
content:
Mobilitazioni e decreti.




La classe politica italiana (ma si potrebbe benissimo estendere in generale alla classe politica europea, per tacere ad esempio di Trump) mostra tutta la sua incapacità a comprendere le gravi falle che il sistema capitalistico ha provocato nella società oppure, che forse è più vicino al vero, la sua pervicace volontà a mantenere a tutti i costi il sistema esistente.




Lo scatenamento dei più tremendi spiriti animali del capitalismo e del sistema politico mondiale degli ultimi anni si traduce in guerre, instabilità economica, crisi sociali, peggioramento progressivo delle condizioni di vita delle classi sfruttate. La risposta da parte delle classi dirigenti è ovunque la repressione, la criminalizzazione delle mobilitazioni che la società esprime, il fomentare l’odio sociale e l’anestetizzare l’opinione pubblica con opportuni diversivi.




Quanto sta accadendo in queste settimane in Italia è la perfetta fotografia di questo stato delle cose. Le piazze piene di una protesta spontanea e incontenibile, animata principalmente da giovanissimi e studenti, i blocchi e le manifestazioni promossi da agricoltori ed autotrasportatori contro il caro carburanti e il carovita, in particolare al Sud, hanno provocato nel governo una reazione che qualcuno ha definito infantile-adolescenziale, definizione corretta se vivessimo in un mondo giusto ma così non è, e che si è tradotta nell’ennesimo decreto sicurezza e nell’introduzione nel codice penale dell’ennesimo reato, con cui si tenta di imbrigliare le proteste degli ultimi anni. Questo per quanto riguarda in prima istanza i cosiddetti maranza, termine comodo per liquidare la profonda insoddisfazione che investe il mondo giovanile, mentre nei confronti di autotrasportatori e agricoltori i fascisti al governo hanno fatto ricorso al più classico dei metodi: il bastone e la carota. Dapprima sono state mandate le forze dell’ordine per identificare camionisti e agricoltori che bloccavano le strade, il giorno successivo è stato varato un decreto che distribuisce briciole per sedare momentaneamente la protesta.




Dall’altra parte, l’opposizione parlamentare rappresentata dal centro sinistra non ha saputo neppure cavalcare la protesta, anche solo per mettere in difficoltà un governo in palese affanno che pur vuole battere alle prossime elezioni politiche. Senza considerare l’incredibile presidio milanese convocato dalla Cgil e dal Pd per dire no alla violenza, in generale leader ed esponenti del “campo largo” si sono limitati a criticare il governo per i provvedimenti presi, precisando che alla repressione dei comportamenti violenti vanno affiancate politiche sociali che affrontino il malessere giovanile e diano una risposta al carovita e alla crisi di salari e retribuzioni. Senza peraltro entrare nel merito delle questioni, tutto chiuso in un linguaggio ormai logoro e stereotipato, rappresentazione di un teatrino veramente distante dalle questioni sociali e dalla gravità della crisi che ci attanaglia. A cosa servono dichiarazioni di principio, prese di posizioni, manifestazioni di solidarietà, quando va bene, se tutto ciò rimane un flatus vocis, buono per i media e per animare uno sterile dibattito?




Il governo della destra fascista, o delle destre destre, come preferiscono definirlo i benpensanti convinti così di poter continuare ad alimentare il mito della destra liberale e ragionevole, che tanto ragionevole nella sua storia non è stata quando si è trattato di difendere l’ordine costituito, esprime al meglio la sua idea di società gerarchizzata, ordinata, controllata e prona al volere dei potenti. Naturalmente la maschera democratica viene adattata al caso. Quindi se la destra fa quello che ha sempre fatto, qualche interrogativo potrebbe suscitarlo quella parte politica che continua a definirsi sinistra (tolto l’alibi del centro). Pierluigi Bersani, uno degli esponenti più in vista di quella “sinistra” che si è fatta investire dalla furia neoliberista, ha sostenuto in un noto programma televisivo che di fronte alla gravità della crisi mondiale in atto occorrono risposte radicali. Non ha poi chiarito in cosa consistano e soprattutto come dovrebbero attuarsi queste decisioni radicali, tuttavia ha ragione. Eppure le menti più illuminate della sinistra italiana, come Bersani, continuano a pensare che correttivi al capitalismo cosiddetto selvaggio e un nuovo protagonismo statale siano sufficienti a ridare vita ad un rinnovato patto sociale di stampo socialdemocratico che contenga le disuguaglianze e le ingiustizie. Ma anche questo obiettivo, di un riformismo tenue, richiede prese di posizione che né Bersani né la sinistra più ampia sono disposti a prendere in considerazione. A cominciare da una politica che riequilibri le gravi disuguaglianze sociali e che non può prescindere dall’introduzione di una vera tassazione progressiva che faccia pagare di più a chi ha di più. Da questo punto di vista il massimo che sono disposti a concedersi è la proposta di tassare gli extraprofitti energetici o invocare, con molta cautela, come una tantum o con un prelievo infimo, l’introduzione di una patrimoniale. Legittimando in tal modo il profitto, come se non scaturisse dallo sfruttamento dei lavoratori. Ma la parola sfruttamento non usa più e l’imprenditore, figura mitica del nostro tempo, assurge a benefattore della società, da trattare con riguardo. Altra riflessione profonda dovrebbe essere fatta riguardo all’Unione europea, artefice massima delle politiche di austerità che hanno garantito al capitalismo la possibilità di scaricare le proprie contraddizioni e i propri limiti sulle classi subalterne. Infine si dovrebbe affrontare di petto la profonda crisi della democrazia rappresentativa, rimettere in discussione il feticcio della governabilità, aprirsi alle istanze e alla conflittualità sociali, come momenti di vivificazione della politica e della società e come espressione di una decisionalità che promani dalle realtà territoriali. Limitarsi a legittimare, come fanno gli esponenti del centro sinistra, manifestazioni e proteste di piazza, facendo attenzione a distinguere tra buoni e cattivi, tra quello che è concesso e quello che esula dal consesso “civile”, è segno di una debolezza politica e di una visione che non si discosta dalle tendenze dominanti.




Le proteste, gli scioperi, i cortei di queste settimane testimoniano della possibilità di una ripresa di parola da parte delle classi subalterne. Le componenti più avvertite delle mobilitazioni in corso hanno posto l’esigenza di una politicizzazione delle proteste che dovrebbero compattarsi in un progetto di trasformazione sociale. Non sarà facile ma è ineludibile. Tuttavia per provare ad evitare, come oramai accade da tanto tempo, che le contestazioni vivano di fiammate occorrerà trovare luoghi, modalità, espressioni capaci di resistere alle insidie del tempo e di distendersi in una prospettiva di cambiamento.




Angelo Barberi

author: Sicilia Libertaria
title: La guerra come forma della crisi
content:
Il capitalismo oltre la promessa della crescita infinita




La guerra contro l’Iran racconta qualcosa di più di un nuovo conflitto per il controllo delle risorse energetiche e degli equilibri geopolitici mondiali. Racconta la crisi di un modello economico che ha fatto della crescita senza fine la propria ragione d’essere e la propria promessa di benessere. Un modello che, incontrando i limiti materiali del pianeta, sembra sempre più orientato a trasformare la stagnazione in rendita, la scarsità in profitto e l’instabilità in una condizione della propria sopravvivenza.




Il 13 luglio 2026 l’OPEC ha comunicato, per la terza volta consecutiva, una revisione al ribasso delle previsioni di crescita della domanda mondiale di petrolio: da 970.000 a 780.000 barili al giorno. Nello stesso periodo il prezzo del greggio continuava a subire le violente oscillazioni provocate dalla guerra iniziata il 28 febbraio con i bombardamenti congiunti degli Stati Uniti e di Israele contro l’Iran.




Sono due dati che raccontano aspetti differenti di una stessa contraddizione. Il prezzo del petrolio ci parla della guerra; il rallentamento della domanda ci parla delle difficoltà di un sistema che ha costruito la propria riproduzione sull’espansione permanente dei consumi.




Il secondo numero, insomma, ci dice perché la guerra possa diventare una risposta alla crisi del sistema. Non necessariamente una risposta capace di rilanciare lo sviluppo, ma certamente una possibile occasione per continuare a produrre profitti.




Già nel 2024 il World Energy Outlook dell’Agenzia internazionale dell’energia collocava entro il 2030 il possibile picco della domanda mondiale di petrolio. Per decenni l’ossessione degli analisti era stata quella del picco dell’offerta: quando avremmo esaurito le riserve disponibili? Oggi la questione si è rovesciata. Il problema non è più soltanto quando finirà il petrolio, ma quando il suo consumo smetterà di crescere.




La saturazione di alcuni mercati, la diffusione della motorizzazione elettrica, soprattutto in Cina, i miglioramenti nell’efficienza energetica e lo sviluppo delle fonti alternative stanno modificando le prospettive dell’industria petrolifera. L’Agenzia internazionale dell’energia è arrivata a prevedere per il 2026 una contrazione complessiva dei consumi mondiali, aggravata dalle conseguenze economiche della guerra.




Non siamo ancora alla fine del petrolio, naturalmente. Ma siamo di fronte alla possibilità che uno dei principali motori materiali dell’espansione capitalistica non possa più garantire una crescita indefinita.




Il paradosso più grande è che nemmeno la guerra è riuscita a rianimare questo mercato. Il conflitto ha moltiplicato i prezzi senza produrre una corrispondente ripresa dei consumi. Ha creato occasioni di guadagno per chi riesce a vendere a prezzi maggiorati, mentre ha aggravato i costi per chi deve acquistare energia.




Ci troviamo così di fronte a un capitalismo nel quale la produzione di profitto può separarsi sempre più nettamente dalla crescita della ricchezza sociale. Un sistema che, quando non riesce a espandere sufficientemente i mercati, cerca di aumentare la quota di ricchezza che può appropriarsi.




Non più soltanto produrre, dunque, ma estrarre.




E l’instabilità può diventare una risorsa. Il blocco dello stretto di Hormuz, la sua parziale riapertura, le nuove interruzioni e le continue oscillazioni dei prezzi creano condizioni nelle quali alcuni operatori economici e finanziari possono realizzare guadagni indipendentemente dall’aumento della produzione.




Per produrre occorre stabilità. Per appropriarsi di determinate rendite, invece, l’instabilità può diventare conveniente.




Per comprendere questa trasformazione dobbiamo tornare indietro, alla fine della Guerra fredda e all’emergere della crisi climatica come questione politica mondiale.




Rio de Janeiro, 1992. Durante il vertice internazionale sull’ambiente, il presidente americano George Bush senior ribadì che lo stile di vita degli Stati Uniti non era negoziabile. Quella dichiarazione conteneva una promessa destinata a entrare in contraddizione con i limiti materiali del pianeta.




L’American way of life aveva, e conserva, un presupposto fondamentale: la disponibilità di energia abbondante e a buon mercato. La politica energetica americana si trova davanti a una contraddizione: deve garantire ai propri cittadini la continuità di un modello di consumo che ha dichiarato intoccabile, mentre le condizioni economiche, ambientali e geopolitiche della sua riproduzione diventano sempre più difficili.




Le possibilità sono sostanzialmente tre: riconoscere il limite e trasformare il modello di sviluppo; trasferire su altri paesi e altre popolazioni i costi dell’aggiustamento; oppure trasformare la scarsità e il controllo delle risorse in nuove occasioni di reddito.




Le ultime due strategie possono convivere e rafforzarsi reciprocamente.




È qui che acquistano un’importanza crescente i cosiddetti chokepoints, gli snodi obbligati attraverso i quali passano le grandi rotte energetiche e commerciali mondiali. Lo stretto di Hormuz, attraverso cui transita una quota enorme del petrolio commerciato via mare, rappresenta uno dei punti più sensibili di questo sistema.




Il controllo delle risorse non coincide più soltanto con il possesso dei giacimenti. Diventa anche controllo delle rotte, delle infrastrutture, delle condizioni di accesso ai mercati e, in definitiva, della possibilità stessa che le merci circolino.




In questa prospettiva la guerra contro l’Iran assume un significato che va oltre gli obiettivi militari dichiarati dagli Stati Uniti e da Israele. L’Iran è a sua volta uno Stato impegnato a difendere il proprio potere regionale e la rendita derivante dalle risorse petrolifere. Non siamo di fronte a uno scontro fra un sistema di sfruttamento e la sua negazione, ma a una competizione fra poteri differenti per il controllo di una parte decisiva della ricchezza mondiale.




Naturalmente non tutti guadagnano dalla guerra. Molte imprese vedono aumentare i costi, interi settori produttivi subiscono danni, popolazioni intere pagano il prezzo della distruzione. Ma proprio questa differenza è essenziale: ciò che rappresenta una perdita per la società può costituire un’occasione di profitto per particolari gruppi economici.




La questione allora non è soltanto perché sia scoppiata la guerra contro l’Iran, ma perché la sua prosecuzione possa risultare compatibile con gli interessi di settori importanti del capitalismo contemporaneo.




Forse siamo davanti a una trasformazione più profonda di quanto siamo abituati a riconoscere.




Un sistema che ha promesso crescita illimitata e benessere futuro incontra i limiti della propria espansione. Ma invece di riconoscerli e trasformarsi, cerca di convertire la crisi in nuove possibilità di appropriazione. La rendita sostituisce una parte dello sviluppo, la speculazione accompagna la stagnazione, la forza militare interviene a regolare i rapporti economici.




La guerra non appare più soltanto come un’interruzione del normale funzionamento dell’economia. Può diventare uno dei modi attraverso cui l’economia continua a funzionare, distribuendo profitti e potere anche in assenza di un corrispondente sviluppo sociale.




Stefano Capello

author: James Crump
title: Spain Caps Rents and Protects Tenants After Four Million Join Protests
content:
Spain’s parliament has approved a package of reforms aimed at making housing more affordable, a day after four million took part in a 

nationwide general strike

 over the country’s housing crisis.




The measures, proposed by prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s government, include extending eviction protections for vulnerable tenants and restricting speculative property purchases by preventing companies from buying homes for less than 70% of their assessed value.




Rent increases will also be capped at 2%, while those already above the government’s neighbourhood reference index will be frozen. A 10% tax on flats rented to tourists will also be introduced. 




The conservative Popular Party said it will repeal the reforms if it takes power in the 29 November elections, which were called by Sánchez after his government failed to pass similar housing measures.




“Yesterday, the right to housing won on the street and in workplaces, and I hope it will win again at the ballot box,” said interim housing minister Isabel Rodríguez after the vote on Thursday.




Spain has witnessed weeks of housing protests following the eviction and subsequent death of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who was forcibly removed from the flat she had lived in for 70 years in September after she couldn’t afford rent increases.




The country has a deficit of 750,000 homes, which is set to grow to over a million by 2028. The average rental price of a home, €1,176, is equivalent to 98.7% of the average young person’s monthly salary, according to the Youth Council of Spain.




“We won’t stop until we transform this country’s housing model from top to bottom,” said Alicia del Rio of the Madrid Tenants’ Union.




Trade unions reported 90% turnouts among dockworkers and carmakers for the 24-hour strike on Wednesday – Spain’s first general strike in 14 years – 

with “total stoppages”

 at Volkswagen’s factory in Navarre and SEAT’s in Barcelona, organisers said.




Around 85% of meat industry workers, 82% of waste collection employees and 75% from the energy sector also took part. In healthcare and ⁠social services roughly 38% went on strike, while 35% of postal service workers also joined.

author: Randi Beers
title: Fresh face in cabinet expected to receive portfolio Monday
content:
Fred Pedersen, the newest appointee to Nunavut’s cabinet, will receive his portfolio assignments on Monday, says Joanna Awa, press secretary for Premier John Main.




The Cambridge Bay MLA was selected by his colleagues on Nov. 5 to replace Brian Koonoo, who 

resigned

 from his ministerial duties on Nov. 2.




“I just want to thank the members again for putting their trust in me by selecting me to sit on the executive council,” Pedersen said in his Nov. 5 members statement to the legislative assembly.




“I want to assure my constituents in Cambridge Bay that I will continue to advocate on your behalf.”




He said as well that he’s looking forward to “in-depth” conversations with the premier, and finding out what portfolio he’d receive.




Koonoo was minister of environment, energy, languages and culture and heritage.




Cecile Nelvana Lyall, the minister responsible for the Nunavut Housing Corp., took on environment and energy in Koonoo’s absence. Human Resources Minister Annie Tattuinee took on the languages and culture and heritage assignments.
















Koonoo, the Tununiq MLA, listed a number of personal reasons for his resignation, including that he missed his family and hunting.

author: CMI Argentina
title: “Vaca Muerta no derrama ni en Vaca Muerta”
content:
La extracción de petróleo marcó un récord con 973 mil barriles diarios en septiembre de 2026; en el mismo semestre, la pobreza alcanzó el 32,3% a nivel nacional según las cifras oficiales. El famoso “efecto derrame” jamás llega a los hospitales ni al bolsillo de las familias trabajadoras, apuntaron desde la Federación de Profesionales de la Salud (Fesprosa).







 




Compartimos el comunicado de Fesprosa, SiProSaPuNe y ASSPUR:




Vaca Muerta no derrama ni en Vaca Muerta




La producción petrolera crece, pero el sistema público de salud de Neuquén y Río Negro está roto.




Fesprosa, junto a sus sindicatos de base SiProSaPuNe (Neuquén) y ASSPUR (Río Negro), denuncia que las ganancias generadas de Vaca Muerta no llega a los hospitales ni a las familias trabajadoras de las provincias que la explotan.




La extracción de petróleo marcó un récord con 973 mil barriles diarios en septiembre de 2026; en el mismo semestre, la pobreza alcanzó el 32,3% a nivel nacional. Detrás de los discursos oficiales sobre el “boom energético” y las proyecciones exportadoras, hay una brecha dolorosa: hidrocarburos transitan por nuestras rutas y costas, pero el mentado “efecto derrame” jamás llega a los hospitales ni al bolsillo de las familias trabajadoras.




Es que Vaca Muerta no derrama ni en Vaca Muerta:




Neuquén.

 La propaganda del Gobierno de Rolando Figueroa pretende mostrar una provincia donde todo funciona de maravillas, pero la realidad de la salud pública neuquina está muy lejos de ese relato. En la provincia de Vaca Muerta, el sistema público atraviesa una profunda crisis. No son problemas aislados: es un deterioro que compromete la capacidad de respuesta y pone en riesgo el derecho a la salud. Plottier, una de las ciudades de mayor crecimiento demográfico, es un ejemplo contundente. En menos de 15 días, pacientes que requerían derivación urgente debieron permanecer intubados más de cuatro horas en la guardia, con una red de referencia y contrarreferencia seriamente deteriorada, fragmentada y burocratizada. Se redujo el número de camas por falta de nombramientos de enfermería. Faltan insumos, medicamentos y reactivos, y los proveedores reclaman deudas millonarias que comprometen el abastecimiento. El Gobierno provincial debe responder.




Río Negro.

 Detrás de los anuncios del gobierno provincial de Weretilneck sobre el Oleoducto Vaca Muerta Sur y el desarrollo industrial, la economía extractiva impone alquileres, alimentos y servicios atados al “dólar petrolero”, mientras el sistema público sufre un vaciamiento progresivo y sistemático. El presupuesto recortado y la escasez de recursos humanos ya son una constante: faltan decenas de agentes, y el equipamiento y los insumos están lejos de lo deseable, con ausencia de equipos básicos e instalaciones seguras. Hay déficit de enfermería en Viedma y Bariloche, localidades enteras sin cobertura de ginecología y pediatría, y hospitales donde sostener una terapia intensiva a pleno o cubrir guardias y traslados es un desafío diario. Se reducen consultorios y horas de atención porque los profesionales dejan el sistema o pasan a part-time para compensar los magros salarios.




Salarios.

 En Río Negro, la pérdida acumulada del poder adquisitivo bajo las gestiones de La Libertad Avanza a nivel nacional y Weretilneck en la provincia supera el 24%. Los sueldos de ingreso en la salud provincial rondan $1,5 millones, mientras la Junta Interna de ATE-INDEC señala que un hogar tipo necesita más de $2,6 millones, y la Canasta Básica Total oficial marca el encarecimiento desmedido de la vida en la Patagonia. En Neuquén, el salario deteriorado no cubre el costo de vida en una de las provincias más caras del país. La sobrecarga de trabajo y la falta de reconocimiento empujan a muchos profesionales a abandonar el sector público.




El modelo.

 El extractivismo hidrocarburífero deja impactos ambientales de largo plazo y una inflación local insostenible, sin contraprestación en infraestructura social básica. La explotación de recursos no renovables es una lógica transitoria: cuando los capitales privados agotan el recurso o reducen su rentabilidad, se retiran y dejan un territorio devastado.




En este contexto, no hay sistema de salud posible sin profesionales, sin salarios dignos, sin insumos, sin infraestructura y sin una red sanitaria integrada que funcione. No alcanza con los anuncios, las estadísticas ni la propaganda oficial. No vamos a naturalizar el deterioro.




Por ello, exigimos:







La apertura inmediata de la paritaria sectorial de salud en Río Negro y espacios de participación sindical en Neuquén.




Salarios iniciales que respondan al costo real de la vida.




Un presupuesto adecuado para sostener el sistema sanitario.




Nombramientos de enfermería, insumos, medicamentos y reactivos, y el pago de las deudas con proveedores.







¡Que el famoso BOOM energético no termine por reventar nuestros hospitales y centros de salud!




LA SALUD PÚBLICA NO PUEDE SEGUIR ESPERANDO.




POR UNA SALUD PÚBLICA GRATUITA Y DE CALIDAD PARA NEUQUINOS Y RIONEGRINOS, Y POR CONDICIONES Y SALARIOS DIGNOS PARA SUS TRABAJADORES.




La entrada 

“Vaca Muerta no derrama ni en Vaca Muerta”

 se publicó primero en 

Indymedia Argentina Centro de Medios Independientes (( i ))

.

author: kelsie kilawna
title: The taste we’ve been missing
content:
Graphic by Lauren Marchand




The clanking of pots and pans and the ringing of laughter while moving around the kitchen were always calming sounds to me growing up. 




The most important lessons I’ve learned about food came as I stood at the hips of my grandmothers, watching them peel potatoes and listening to their stories.




I am a culinary storyteller of syilx foodways. In my work at 

Smoke on the Plateau

, I teach through food. I share stories about my syilx/Okanagan homelands through a fully embodied experience bringing together taste, sight, smell and sound. My research has been lifelong and has taken place in kitchens, in berry patches, and while waiting for salmon and deer to return so I could help prepare it for the people. 




There is a beauty to this way of knowing and living, because it is what taught me to be slow and patient with the offerings of our land.




The work I do honours the relationships that collapse time and place into story. It is a way of ensuring we never forget the importance of our Four Food Chiefs system. In essence, this is a reaffirmation of our governance system. 




Now, today when you enter the Okanagan Valley, you see another food story being told. A palate cleanser for the gentrification of our foodways.




What’s missing from culinary discussions




A rising culinary hotspot, the Okanagan has dressed itself in words like “local,” “seasonal,” “farm-to-table.” While wine glasses clink and tasting notes are murmured, words like “terroir” roll off the tongue as a somewhat promise to its authenticity.

It is a beautiful and comfortable story.




Terroir is a French term embraced by the culinary industry to speak to “the taste of place.” The concept itself describes how the climate and land conditions of an area affect the flavour profile of local food crops. 




In the Okanagan this is popularized through the wine industry. It’s often the terroir of a wine that is showcased through wine tastings. It speaks to the soil, weather, topography and tradition that shape what consumers taste. 




“Local” has now become a premium label, “farm-to-table” has become marketing copy, and “terroir” has become a way to charge more for the same soil that syilx Peoples have been tending since the time of our Creation, without acknowledging who did the tending, or what was given back in return.




This is gentrification. 




Not just through the extractive wine industry, but it’s become the gentrification of taste itself. 




When terroir is extracted from its French roots and planted in the Okanagan, it lands on soil that is already alive with syilx knowledge and responsibility. 




First Foods Board, Smoke on the Plateau Catering, An assortment of homesmoked deer and elk sausages, cedar smoked candied salmon, accompanied by homemade xusem raspberry compote, and siya jam. Photo by kelsie marchand (kilawna)




As a syilx culinary storyteller, I am responsible for reminding people of this, that our foodways should not be minimized for the sake of an entertaining evening.




Our foodways have and always will be prayed over. Ceremonies of health, and gratitude are held for all our homelands offer us. Young people go through their Coming of Age ceremony learning to pray for the health of our waterways. All of this is the missing spirit of the term terroir.




So I’ve been working to name what’s missing. One word, something that can hold the weight of kinship, of reciprocity, of generations coiled into one. Something that reminds us we are part of the land, not separate from it.




So I call it by it’s name, tmixʷ.




tmixʷ is the nsyilxcen word for life-force, the aliveness of every being that makes a place what it is, it speaks far beyond just soil and climate. Rather it speaks to the kinships between all of it, our reciprocity, and our syilx/Okanagan obligation to give back, so that what you take can live again.




The syilx/Okanagan understanding of place is through tmxʷulaxʷ, which speaks to the life-force-place. It is a dynamic, regenerative relationship between all beings, which the culinary industry’s shallow “local” label cannot contain.




The Okanagan culinary industry wants you to taste place, so what they’re selling is terroir, but what its missing is tmixʷ.




What tmixʷ tastes like




Let me tell you a story about xusem (soapberries).




There’s a small spot in the Okanagan mountains that has the sweetest soapberries my family has ever tasted. 




The oldest person in my family shared that those berries are special, he’s had xusem berries from all areas of the Okanagan Valley, and these are unique because of their sweetness. xusem is typically a rather bitter berry. But from this one particular spot, they are very sweet.




They hold memories for their sweetness. Our family talks about that spot and visits it every year just to give it thanks.




As I research the micro-climate of that place each year, I notice a specific dappling of sun unique to that area. It is rather open, so the berries get enough sun to sweeten but not so much that it kills them, because xusem loves its darker, cooler places.




The taste comes from the sun in that area, but it also comes from the water that feeds that place. I know the families who carry the ceremonial responsibility to caretake it, to pray over it, to give thanks for it, to ensure it remains healthy so that the berries can continue to sweeten, year after year, generation after generation. I know the specific prayer and ceremony said over that place.




And this is data — or knowledge — sovereignty. We have a story now about that particular place in our homeland, a story that helps us understand the relationship between land, its specific environment, and the taste of place. 




But more than that, we have a responsibility. We know who holds the ceremonies, we know who carries the prayers, and we know that the taste of that berry is inseparable from the health of that water, and the health of that water is inseparable from the people who tend it with reverence.




That taste, the taste of that specific dappling of sun, of the hands that harvest, of the water that was prayed over, of the generations who knew to return, that is tmixʷ. That is the kinship I am speaking of that is missing from terroir.




Terroir speaks to what the land gives.




tmixʷ speaks to the responsibility, love and gratitude we have for how we are built into the system of a place.




skʷəkʷiw̓ (Rosehip) gathered from my great great grandmother, Julia Tonaskets rosehip bush, I make a cranberry and rosehip sauce and share stories of her life while serving it. Photo by kelsie marchand (kilawna)




The missing spirit




But to fully understand tmixʷ, you have to understand its shape.




In syilx-centric understanding, time and relationship do not move in straight lines. They coil, they spiral, and they return. Like a rope being twisted, strand by strand, year after year, generation after generation. 




tmixʷ is often described as the action of many strands continuously being bound and unified with each other to form one strong rope or thread, this coiling over time is what creates a living future.




Our name, syilx, carries this image. It loosely translates to those-who-twine/coil-(many)-into-one. This is who we are, and this is what we do as people, we coil the strands of life into a thread that carries us forward, so we may move into the future unbroken, generation after generation.




And there is another word that is used to describe us, sqilxʷ. It is the word for our people. And it translates as “to dream in a spiral.”




We are the ones who dream in spirals. We have the mind power to envision what could be, to create into reality whatever we can dream. So, unlike salmon, unlike roots, unlike bears, we humans do not automatically know how to live in ways that contribute to the wellbeing of future generations. It’s our responsibility  to learn it, to dream it, and to choose it, again and again, this is our spiraling forward.




This is what it means to be syilx/Okanagan. We are the coil and the spiral, and we hold the past while we dream the future. We are the ones who must remember, and in that remembering, we create.




So when we harvest, we are coiling, and when we give thanks, we are coiling. As part of our agreement as people here it is up to us to ensure that what we take can be revived, we are adding our strand to the thread. And when we dream, when we envision a future where all life-forces can revive, we are spiraling, we are bringing the future into the present. This is how we collapse time and place and can share it as story.




The taste of place, through tmixʷ, is the taste of something being coiled, year after year, generation after generation, towards a time where all life-forces can revive. That rests on our responsibility as The People of this land.




People-eaters logic




The Okanagan culinary industry has taken the flavour of place and stripped it of the relationships that made it possible, but they don’t sell the obligation to give back. 




Because you can’t sell what you don’t know, and you can’t taste what you’ve forgotten.




When you forget that you are part of a coil, a thread being twisted, strand by strand, generation after generation, you begin to believe that you are separate. That the land is just resources and that food is a product, that taste is just flavour.




This is the logic of extraction. It is the logic of the people-eaters, nəɬnasqilxʷtn, the monsters that Coyote, our teacher and trickster, was sent to transform. They consume without giving back, they take without gratitude, and they believe they are the only ones who matter.




I do not want to say that the Okanagan culinary industry is Coyote, because it doesn’t mean to be a monster, however it is dressed in the same forgetting. It has adopted the language of terroir without adopting the responsibility of relationship, and it speaks of a place without knowing who ceremonies for the water.




And so the coil weakens. The thread frays. The spiral loses its way.




To be sqilxʷ, to dream in a spiral, is to remember that we are the ones who must keep it coiling, and we are the ones who must keep it turning. We are to remember that we are torn from the earth and that our responsibility is to return.




To remember that we are not the only ones, that the water, the berries, the salmon, they are our relatives. They have their own life-force, and they have their own right to regenerate.




My sister and I spend a lot of time in the mountains each year gathering different berries and medicines, a family favourite is st̓xałq (huckleberries), a berry that requires a very specific environment to grow, talking to the plants, laughing with our loved ones amongst our Plant People, clearing away debris so they can grow strong, praying with its water sources, we become kin. We are part of that ecosystem as helpers of our Plant People. Photo by kelsie marchand (kilawna)




To remember that we are not just consumers, but we are participants, we are co-creators, we are the ones who must give back.




So what I know to be true, is that the taste of tmixʷ is still here, has always been and will always be. It is reaffirmed in the xusem berries that my family harvests every year. It’s reaffirmed in our salmon relatives that still swim up the rivers, it’s reaffirmed by the roots that still push through the soil, it’s reaffirmed by the berries that will continue to sweeten in the dappled sun of a place that has been tended by syilx Peoples for generations.




It will all remain and stay alive, surrounded by the sound of pots and pans and laughter moving about the kitchen where our children learn to stand and watch at the hips of their grandmothers. It’ll remain alive in the stories that collapse time and place into a single moment.







A note on language




tmixʷ (pronounced tuh-MEE-kwuh) is the syilx word for life-force, the aliveness of every being that makes a place what it is.




sqilxʷ (pronounced skee-lkhw) refers to the syilx people. It translates as “the dream in a spiral.”




syilx (pronounced see-ilkh) means those-who-twine/coil-(many)-into-one.




xusem (pronounced hoo-sem) is the syilx word for soapberry.

The taste we’ve been missing

author: Aaron Hemens, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: ‘It’s all about taking care of people’: How a smǝlqmíx farmer is building food sovereignty at ntámłqən
content:
Dixon Terbasket, the founder of ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands, walks through the farm’s greenhouse on Sept. 15, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




The potato plants are so tall that their stems reach Dixon Terbasket’s eyes. 




He remembers walking through his family’s garden when he was three or four years old, more than 60 years ago, in a community where his mom, all his aunties and uncles, grew food in gardens and orchards — and stored them in root cellars, too.




Now, Dixon finds himself leading his own food sovereignty initiative that he hopes will equip the next generation of smǝlqmíx (Similkameen) people with the knowledge and skills to farm on their own.




“I want to give them at least a running chance, man,” Dixon told IndigiNews.




The ntámłqən garden is in unceded smǝlqmíx territory in the lower Similkameen Valley, in the southern Interior of “B.C.” It shares its nsyilxcən name with the adjacent community elementary school, meaning “gathering place.” Dixon said his people have gathered here since time immemorial.




The ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 28, 2026. Photo by Aaron Hemens




At ntámłqən, a 7.5-acre community garden and food hub on Lower Similkameen Indian Band (LSIB) land near “Cawston,” he works with a small but dedicated crew of staff and volunteers to teach people life skills — from growing their own food; to sharing it with the community; and how to preserve what they grow.




At the peak of the harvest season, the garden hosted a free barbeque for the community on Sept. 28, in collaboration with the Indigenous Food Sovereignty Association. 




Rumy Muenala helps prepare food for a community BBQ at the ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 28, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




Staff at ntámłqən Community Garden prepare salads during a community BBQ event at the farm in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 28, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




Dozens of people — Indigenous and non-Indigenous — came together around meals made with ingredients provided by the garden and its partners. Between all the mingling and laughs, they feasted on stuffed-peppers, colourful salads, watermelon, goat meat, apple pie and more.




“It’s all about taking care of people,” Dixon said, echoing the farm’s slogan of “For The People.”




Hannah Field, who co-manages the ntámłqən Community Garden as its coordinator, stands in a prayer circle before a community BBQ event at the farm in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 28, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




Community members fill their plates with food during a community BBQ event hosted at the ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 28, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




The garden is working towards giving the community the ability to make decisions about their food — and having the knowledge, land and facilities to provide for one another. A processing facility expected to be completed by March 2027 will add space to prepare and store harvests, with opportunities for community food businesses. 




Dixon’s niece, Coven Terbasket, joined the crew in 2024, a couple of weeks after moving back to her ancestral homelands. She was 29 and looking for work when she ran into Dixon at an insurance office in small-town Keremeos. 




For most of her life, Coven had lived south of the colonial border in “Spokane, Washington.” During childhood summers, her mom would send her up to “roam around” LSIB lands with family, usually in their ancestral community of nkʷrulauxʷ (Blind Creek, Place of Yellow Dirt). 




Like her uncle, she remembers family gardens all around Blind Creek, and the work that kept households fed beyond the growing season.




“Everyone had made the time to grow their own food, can their own food, to preserve,” she said.




Coven Terbasket, the administrative assistant at the ntámłqən Community Garden, is pictured at the farm in smǝlqmíx homelands on Oct. 5, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




Coven hadn’t seen Dixon since she was a child. As they reconnected in the insurance office two years ago, he learned she needed work and offered her a job at the community garden he had been building with a small crew of workers and volunteers for more than a year.




“He told me to show up at the garden the next day at 10 a.m., so I did,” she said.




Coven describes the encounter as fate, saying her uncle “found me” shortly after her return, during a difficult period in her life. 




“It’s freaky how crazy it worked out … me looking for a job; me freshly back in the homelands after years of not living here – and being stuck in a really dark spot in life,” she said.




“Needing something to prove to myself that it’s worth living. That it’s worth giving another try.”




Working at the garden over the past two-and-a-half years, she said, “has been the growth and the movement that I needed in my life to be able to move through some of that.”




“It’s providing support for those who have once gotten forgotten about. It provides a place of well-being,” she said.




“This is a place where people can come and get grounded.”




A view of the ntámłqən Community Garden from the farm’s food processing building in smǝlqmíx homelands on Aug. 31, 2026. In the distance to the left is the Lower Similkameen Indian Band Office, while the building to the centre-right is the ntámłqən Band School. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




Learning to feed one another




The garden’s published priorities include supporting Elders, single-parent families and households with low incomes. Produce is available free or by donation to Indigenous and non-Indigenous community members experiencing food insecurity.




For eight weeks, beginning at the end of August, more than a dozen Elders received weekly “Elder Boxes” full of fresh produce from the garden for free. The program was carried out in partnership with LSIB’s health department, who helped deliver the boxes to the Elders’ homes. 




Community members harvest produce from the ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 28, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




Staff at ntámłqən Community Garden prepare Elder Box deliveries in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 15, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




The garden also has a library of seeds — from flowers, to herbs and vegetables — that community members can have access to, so that they can plant and garden at their own homes.




Workshops extend that work into the community’s kitchens and pantries, teaching people how to process and preserve what is available locally. 




Canned pickles, salsa and other processed foods are labelled following a food processing and preservation workshop led by Rumy Muenala at the ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on Aug. 31, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




With support from the Indigenous Food Sovereignty Network (IFSA), ntámłqən has brought in Rumy Muenala of Ayapacha to lead harvesting, processing, and preserving sessions.




Participants learn to turn produce into meals, canned peaches, pickles, salsas and more. Muenala has also helped put on staff appreciation feasts and community dinners using ingredients from the garden. He was the lead chef at ntámłqən’s September community barbeque.




Baked potatoes for a community BBQ are prepared using a ground oven at the ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 28, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




“To me, that’s food sovereignty: you have to adapt, you have to get creative with what’s available — and not depend so much on going to a grocery store,” said Muenala, whom Dixon met through 

Tea Creek

.




Muenala, who is Quechua from Ecuador, delivers workshops and dinners at community farms around “B.C.,” most of them Indigenous-owned or Indigenous-led.




Rumy Muenala of Ayapacha at the ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on Aug. 31, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




“It takes more work … to go out and find these ingredients. But at the end of the day, that’s more important to me, because it builds relationships: relationships to each other; to the land,” said Muenala.




“For me, Indigenous food sovereignty is reclaiming that power of not feeling like you need to depend on somebody anymore. The only people you should depend on are your close relatives, your community, to help one another.”




Rumy Muenala and Dixon Terbasket spark up the grill during a community BBQ event at the ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 28, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




Before joining ntámłqən, Coven had spent about a decade working in hospitality. Her administrative job includes marketing and social media, but she spends just as much time out on the land, getting her hands dirty. She knows her way through the long rows of fruits, vegetables, sunflowers, tobacco and other plants.




“Harvesting, seeding, transplanting, weeding — all of it, man,” she said.




She arrived knowing little about farming. Over the past two and a half years, she has learned how to grow watermelons, squash and tomatoes, and to preserve what she harvests. Working on the land every day has been, as she put it in October, “probably the biggest culture shock I’ve ever experienced.”




A staff member in a tractor tends to the crops at the ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on Oct. 5, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




Coven sees the work as part of building a food system guided by the community’s needs and its responsibilities to the land. She envisions being able to feed one another on their own terms, so that “we don’t rely on the food systems that have been set up, as far as the whole capitalistic ideal.”




Learning to grow food has also changed how she understands her place in that system.




“I feel like there’s a sense of self in growing your own food. You identify with that food – you know what it took, and what it takes to grow.”




Staff prepare food for a community BBQ at the ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 28, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




The 

Okanagan Nation Alliance’s teaching resources

 describe syilx food knowledge learned through the territory’s seasonal changes. When saskatoon bushes first bloom, bitterroot is ready to harvest. Learning when to gather one food means paying attention to other life around it. 




“I’ve found this calling here at the garden,” Coven said. “To be a good person. And to give back – to have this reciprocal way of living. I give as much as I take, and find that nice balance between the two.” 




Returning to the simplicity of farming has taught Coven the patience and sustained care that living things need to thrive.




“To take care of the things that take care of us … a deeper appreciation and understanding of where food comes from, and how water feeds every source of life that surrounds us on a daily basis.”




Peppers grow in the fields of the ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on July 22, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




Staff at ntámłqən Community Garden sort through tomatoes as they prepare for Elder Box deliveries in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 15, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




Through the 

garden’s volunteer program

, people can help tend to crops, process produce or clean seeds, and leave with a harvest bundle. First-time volunteers receive a site and cultural safety orientation. 




Earlier this fall, Hannah Field, who co-manages the ntámłqən Community Garden as its coordinator, said more than 600 people — including volunteers and guests — had come through the farm this year alone. 




At an Okanagan Food System Summit gathering at Okanagan College in kiʔláw̓naʔ (Kelowna) in October, Field described ntámłqən as a place where people could find belonging and learn to “work together in a good way.”




“I’m from England. I showed up on Dixon’s doorstep in 2023, and became entwined in making this vision a reality,” she said.




Coven remembers how different community life felt while she was living south of the border. 




“That’s the beauty of it – you could be from any walk of life and come here, and feel comfortable and feel welcome,” said Coven.




“The sense of community is something that I very much lacked living in the States. I didn’t really know what that meant, as far as what it means to show up for each other.”




Hannah Field and Dixon Terbasket, the managers of ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands, pictured together at the farm on Sept. 15, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




A place to keep the harvest 




The garden’s development drew on years of community planning and consultation. LSIB has supported the project through core funding and an in-kind land lease, 

according to the garden’s published history

.




Funding includes a 

$193,873 grant through the federal Local Food Infrastructure Fund grant

 for the farm and food hub and $747,704 listed among the province’s 2024-25 rural development awards for the processing facility. A separate 

$289,759 federal contribution

 supports a well, irrigation equipment and facilities to preserve and store food.




The garden’s irrigation system is sourced from a well, which was implemented during the farm’s development.




About two acres of the site are devoted to infrastructure, including a greenhouse, chicken coop, office, workshop and community space above a root cellar. Some buildings are finished, while others are nearing completion.




The two-storey food-processing facility will have a walk-in cooler and freezer downstairs, with storage that can be used for commercial purposes. The commercial kitchen downstairs is equipped with meat grinders, dehydrators, and other tools to help support food processing and preserving.




A ramp leads upstairs to a rental kitchen, a podcast room and washrooms. 




Dixon Terbasket looks out towards the ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on Oct. 5, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




“You can start to imagine the kinds of things the community can do once they have these types of infrastructure in place,” said Field.




“You can chop a thousand pounds of peaches through there, can it, and take it up to the North Okanagan. Or store apples in the walk-in cooler. There are endless possibilities, really.”




Power for the facilities is currently being funded by grants. But Field said that within the garden’s operational business plan, they envision a future where diverse revenue streams can support the garden’s operation costs. 




Potential revenue streams include different workshop programming; wholesale produce distribution; and renting out the commercial kitchen and other facility spaces, like the freezer or cooler.




Kwantlen Polytechnic University’s 2021 Okanagan study

 describes how spending at locally owned food businesses can circulate among growers, suppliers and repair services. It also identifies concentrated supply chains as a vulnerability during disruptions.




The garden donates fresh produce to community members and gives people a place to spend time together. Dixon said people can learn to fix a chainsaw or take part in growing, processing and preserving their own food.




Staff harvest fruits at ntámłqən Community Garden as they prepare for Elder Box deliveries in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 15, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




The teaching model also helps democratize practical knowledge by offering paid training and describes every team member as a potential mentor, with local Knowledge Holders involved in particular tasks.




“That’s the whole thing — we want people to come here and just hang out,” said Dixon.




In a 

2026 YMCA online survey

, 64 per cent of people in “Canada” wished their communities had more “third places,” or informal gathering spaces outside of home and work.




Longtime residents and newcomers to the valley are welcome to 

volunteer at ntámłqən

, with no gardening experience required.




“A lot of people believe in — they want to help. There are a lot of settlers who want to do something, and feel like they’re contributing. This is an opportunity for that,” Field said.




Staff at ntámłqən Community Garden prepare Elder Box deliveries in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 15, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




In a 

2023 account published by the Economic Trust of the Southern Interior

, Dixon outlined a plan to feed the community first and sell surplus produce, with processing and storage eventually bringing in income to help keep the garden running. 




The 

garden’s apprenticeship

 program describes it as an organic operation. Its training plan includes cover cropping, composting and seed saving, alongside irrigation and food preservation. Keeping seeds gives growers something to sow the follow season; compost returns organic matter to the soil, helping it retain water and nutrients. Cover crops help protect the soil between harvests. 




A nursery for native plants is also in the works at the garden. Its 

2026 growing list

 includes native seedlings and cuttings intended to restore the territory, including black huckleberry and wild strawberry. 




Connections with Young Agrarians, Tea Creek and the Indigenous Food Sovereignty Association have also supported the garden’s development.




Dixon sees opportunities for the community to farm elsewhere on reserve land, too. He said soil mapping had identified 7,200 acres of Class 1 agricultural land, opening possibilities for community members to grow food for their families and earn a living from farming. 




Dixon Terbasket cruises through the ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on July 22, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




‘The garden was everywhere’




In 1978, when he was 21, Dixon planted his first garden at his mother’s place, next door to where he lives now by the ntámłqən garden. The plot was no bigger than his kitchen. 




He developed a business plan to farm on a larger scale and involve more of the community. On the same lands where ntámłqən garden would be built nearly 40 years later, he launched the Similkameen Native Organic Produce company in 1987, beginning as a market garden and later moving into commercial growing. 




“We had quite a few people — similar to what we’re doing right now — training people from the reserve,” he said.




Theresa Ann Terbasket, Dixon’s 93-year-old mother, leads the opening prayer of a community BBQ at the ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 28, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




They started with five acres of potatoes. With help from his staff and a 100–horsepower irrigation pumping system, they started growing “rows and rows of vegetables,” he said.




“Putting in 5,000 tomato plants and 4,000 pepper plants. It got bigger and bigger.”




The tomatoes they were growing were a major seller – not just locally, but even into the U.S., he said.




He highlighted that the Similkameen Native Organic Produce company was producing 40,000 to 60,000 pounds of tomatoes every season for at least four years.




“I became quite the market. After a while, sometimes, I’d run out of tomatoes,” he said.




Dixon Terbasket tends to his chickens at the ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on July 22, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




By the end of the 1990s, Dixon got busy raising a family and returned to a life of local governance. He later worked as a natural resource technician with the Okanagan Nation Alliance and retired in 2024 after more than a decade in that role.




But even before he announced his retirement, Dixon was already making plans to return to farming. 




In 2018, Dixon sought community support and permission to farm a piece of band land near his home. His request was approved. 




“I just thought I was going to retire here, grow some tomatoes and some peppers. The good life,” he said.




Now, Dixon has found his fourth wind in life, passing on the lessons that began at an early age in his family’s garden.




“I think you die after you slow down,” he said of retirement. 




Theresa Ann Terbasket, left, is embraced by a community member as she leads the opening prayer of a community BBQ at the ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 28, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




Farming runs deep in his family history. Dixon’s 93-year-old mother, Theresa Ann Terbasket, grew up farming on a ranch operated by his great-grandfather Paul Terbasket at nkʷrulauxʷ.




But farming isn’t the way his ancestors traditionally lived, Dixon said.




“Maybe my grandfather did — maybe his grandpa, too. It’s a couple generations back. But prior to that, it was hunting. Everything was there — berries were there; the roots were here; the deer were here; the fish were here. The garden was everywhere,” Dixon said.




“Then they started putting us on the Indian reserves, and then we became farmers. We were good farmers.”




Dixon Terbasket at the ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on Oct. 5, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




The Working Group on Indigenous Food Sovereignty describes the right to food as sacred, alongside responsibilities to care for the lands, plants and animals that provide it. 




As 

IndigiNews reported in 2022

, Paul was farming 50 acres by 1909, diverting water from Blind Creek through an irrigation ditch.




That year, the province’s Water Act asserted Crown ownership over water and required licences to divert it. Indigenous water licences were often improperly recorded, altered or cancelled, according to legal researcher 

Kathryn Gullason’s history of water regulation

.




Paul’s application for a water record was refused in 1911. Instead, the provincial Board of Investigation confirmed the Similkameen Fruitlands Company’s water record, historian Duane Thomson wrote in a 

1994 study in BC Studies.

 




Author and historian Harold Rhenisch, who grew up with Dixon, said the attempt to block Paul’s water use dates back to 1913. In his 

2022 account

, he wrote that Paul carried on using the land and water because “he had never relinquished title to it, and he had been promised water long before.”




In 1923, the dispute went to court, Rhenisch wrote. Paul continued watering his orchard and was eventually jailed for contempt of court. 




“We were banned from selling our food in the 1930s and ‘40s. They took away water licenses from us in the ‘50s and ‘60s. We were food sovereign until the end of the ‘60s – we were becoming reliant on a thing called social assistance,” Dixon said.




Dixon Terbasket, the founder of ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands, examines produce growing in the farm’s greenhouse on Sept. 15, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




What the next harvest depends on




Dixon and the ntámłqən crew worry about climate change, political instability, and disruptions to food supplies.




This fall, cyberattacks reportedly disrupted the refrigeration systems that grocery stores depend on to keep food safe. In October, attackers 

reportedly

 remotely took control of cooling systems at hundreds of supermarkets and independent stores in France, forcing some to discard food. 




Governments have also been emphasizing household preparedness. In 2025, the 

European Commission called for guidelines

 to help people meet their own needs for at least 72 hours during a crisis. 

Federal emergency guidance in “Canada”

 also advises households to keep enough food, water and other essentials for at least three days.




The federal 

National Food Security Strategy

 also calls for growing and processing more food domestically. It sets a target to increase the domestically produced share of healthy food available in “Canada,” measured against Canada’s Food Guide, from 75 to 85 per cent by 2032. 




Closer to the garden, preparing for disruptions begins with helping people grow food and keep the harvest available year-round. That ability depends, in turn, on the health of the territory where the food grows. 




Fresh melons harvested from the ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 28, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




Hannah Field helps prepare Elder Box deliveries at ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 15, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




In May 2026, the syilx Okanagan Nation 

declared a watershed emergency

 across the Similkameen and five other watersheds, citing drought, ecosystem decline and growing threats to water security. The Nation identified declining streamflows, threats to fish, and the early die-off of bitterroot as signs of a deepening crisis.




Nearby, nməlqytkʷ (the Similkameen River) winds through agricultural land and surrounding ecosystems. At nearly 200 km long, the waterway has been described as “the lifeblood of the valley” by LSIB Chief Keith Crow. 




Coven remembers swimming in its waters as a child.




“I’ve seen the changes (in the river) since I’ve been a kid. I’ve seen how it’s getting grittier, nastier – something that I preferably don’t want to swim in anymore, which is really sad,” she said. 




“We all have a responsibility to the land and to the water.”




Hannah Field leaves notes on the staff chalk board at the ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on Oct. 5, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




The region has also experienced how quickly transportation routes can fail. In November 2021, flooding and mudslides closed major highways and rail lines connecting the Lower Mainland and “B.C.’s” Interior, interrupting the movement of food.




“Food can become scarce. I think a lot of people don’t really know how much risk we’re at. How vulnerable we are. We take it for granted,” said Dixon.




In the event of an emergency situation where local food systems are disrupted, he explained that the garden would step-up and manage whatever food they have readily on-hand. Part of that process is to identify any food surpluses, which they would then compile into a “stockpile” to support the community’s needs.




“You have to manage it. You might even have to protect it,” he said.




Dixon Terbasket waves goodbye to a community member following a food pick-up event at ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 15, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




Emergency response also includes working with other nearby farmers and ranchers to see how they can pool their resources together for the community, he added.




“It’s dependent on the time of year,” Field emphasized in November. 




“If it’s now, obviously there’s nothing in the field. But what we’ve got in the cellar, or processed, would be what we would have.”




The food processing facility comes equipped with a back-up generator, so the community would still be able to access stored food and food processing equipment, in the event of an emergency food systems situation.




Dixon sees a “generational gap” in the knowledge needed to grow and preserve food. Teaching is his way of giving back to the community that taught and supported him through his years of farming.




“I care so much, man. … Why do I do it? I really think that people need to learn. As a young guy, I was trained. A lot of older men and women trained me. They showed me how to do these things.”




Passing those skills on is his way of giving back to the community that supported him through his years of farming.




“I didn’t realize how valuable it is, how to do that.”




Staff and crew at the ntámłqən Community Garden, following a community BBQ event they hosted at the farm in smǝlqmíx homelands on Sept. 28, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




In the garden, Dixon can see the results of his work. He contrasts that with years spent in board meetings.




“You sit there for 20 years and don’t get any results. At least here, it feels like I did something,” he said.




Coven described her uncle as “a git-r-done kind of uncle,” and called it a privilege to work and learn from him.




“I see a man that is very vision-led, vision-driven. I see a man of action. The man just does, and will figure it out in the process,” she said.




For Coven, caring for the ntámłqən garden is part of revitalizing smǝlqmíx food systems, culture and customs. She imagines that work extending into people’s homes.




“I see a lot of the community members being able to sustain their own fridges, to sustain their own pantries,” she said. 




The work gives her hope for a future in which her people can “survive and thrive.”




“The hope that we can do this as one people. Because it takes all of us.”




If there’s anything the community takes away from the garden, Dixon said that he hopes that people can develop the confidence to know that they can farm and grow food at home, too.




“You can do this. Grow a couple tomato plants. Grow some peppers. Grow a few potatoes. Grow some beets. Grow some carrots. Throw a couple onions in there – in your own little patch. That’s how I started,” he said.




Dixon Terbasket, fresh out of knee surgery, catches his breath at the ntámłqən Community Garden in smǝlqmíx homelands on Oct. 5, 2026. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




The post 

‘It’s all about taking care of people’: How a smǝlqmíx farmer is building food sovereignty at ntámłqən

 appeared first on 

Indiginews

.

author: CMI Argentina
title: Condenan a cuatro ex agentes de inteligencia por su participación en crímenes de lesa humanidad
content:
El Tribunal Federal 1 de Rosario dictó el veredicto en el cuarto tramo de la causa Saint Amant donde se juzgaba, entre otros imputados, a cuatro ex agentes de la Dirección de Inteligencia de la Policía de la provincia de Buenos Aires (DIPPBA) que prestaban servicios en la delegación San Nicolás. La justicia dictó para ellos penas de entre 6 y 3 años de prisión. La Comisión Provincial por la Memoria fue querellante y, durante el trámite de la causa, presentó documentación del archivo de la DIPPBA, que tiene bajo su guarda y custodia; ese material documental fue determinante para definir las responsabilidades de los agentes de inteligencia en los delitos imputados. También fueron condenados a la pena de prisión perpetua el ex mayor del Destacamento de Inteligencia 101 de San Nicolás, Omar Andrada, y con penas de entre 3 y 6 años el ex cabo de la delegación San Nicolás de la Policía Federal Adrián Domingo Meisner y el ex coronel Carlos Manuel Biglieri, del Batallón de Ingenieros de Combate 101 de San Nicolás. El también cabo de la Policía Federal Gregorio Florentino Mancilla fue el único absuelto.







El juicio Saint Amant IV se había iniciado el 14 de marzo de 2004 y, luego de muchas dilaciones en el trámite del debate oral, finalmente este miércoles el Tribunal Oral Federal 1 de Rosario leyó el veredicto en una sala que contó con la presencia de familiares y víctimas del terrorismo de Estado. Representantes de la Mesa por la Memoria de San Nicolás y la Asociación por la Memoria y los derechos humanos de Pergamino junto al secretario ejecutivo de la CPM Roberto Cipriano García y la directora general Sandra Raggio también participaron de la audiencia que concluyó con una absolución y siete condenas, una de prisión perpetua y el resto con penas que van de los 3 a los 6 años.




Entre los condenados, están los cuatro ex agentes de la delegación San Nicolás de la Dirección de Inteligencia de la Policía de la Provincia de Buenos Aires (DIPPBA) que llegaron a juicio: Enabel Otilio Cappa recibió la pena de 6 años de prisión, Miguel Ángel Amarillo, 4 años de prisión, y Oscar Alberto Parodi y Raúl Calabresi, 3 años de ejecución condicional por ser coautores de los delitos de privación ilegítima de la libertad agravada por mediar violencia y amenazas, y por los tormentos agravados por tratarse la víctima un perseguido político.




Además, el Tribunal dispuso la pena de prisión perpetua para el ex mayor del Destacamento de Inteligencia 101 de San Nicolás, Omar Andrada, y penas de entre 3 y 6 años para el ex cabo de la delegación San Nicolás de la Policía Federal Adrián Domingo Meisner, y para el ex coronel Carlos Manuel Biglieri, quien al momento de los hechos ocupaba el cargo de subteniente de la Sección Antisubversiva del Batallón de Ingenieros de Combate 101 de San Nicolás. El también cabo de la Policía Federal, Gregorio Florentino Mancilla fue el único absuelto.




En el juicio se ventilaron crímenes de lesa humanidad cometidos bajo la jurisdicción del Área Militar 132 -que estuvo bajo el mando del fallecido y múltiples veces condenados coronel Manuel Saint Amant- de la que resultaron víctimas 59 personas del noroeste de la provincia de Buenos Aires, con hechos cometidos en los distritos de Pergamino, San Nicolás y Baradero.




La Comisión Provincial por la Memoria fue querellante en la causa y, como organismo de custodia del archivo de la DIPPBA, presentó durante la instrucción y el debate oral documentación del archivo probatoria de la participación de los condenados en los delitos que se juzgaban. En ese sentido, la documentación del archivo de la DIPPBA permitió corroborar el doble accionar de los agentes de la delegación de San Nicolás tanto en la inteligencia sobre las víctimas como en la posterior participación en los grupos de tareas que las secuestraron.




Pese a la exigua pena, la condena a los integrantes de una delegación de la DIPPBA es un enorme avance en el juzgamiento de las acciones de inteligencia como parte constitutiva de los delitos cometidos en el marco del terrorismo de Estado.




Como viene sosteniendo la CPM, los documentos del Archivo prueban no sólo el rol fundamental que tuvieron las acciones inteligencia para la señalización de las personas a perseguir y, en muchos casos, eliminar, sino también la participación de sus agentes en los operativos represivos.

https://www.andaragencia.org/condenan-a-cuatro-ex-agentes-de-inteligencia-por-su-participacion-en-crimenes-de-lesa-humanidad/
