author: Anonyme Anarchist*innen
title: 20. November: Schulstreik – Generalstreik – Aufstand!
content:
Endlich kommt es zu großen Demonstrationen und Revolten. Mit der Jugend ganz vorne gehen in Frankreich, Belgien, Albanien, Italien und Spanien die Menschen in Massen auf die Straße. In den letzten Jahren ist nochmal ganz klar geworden, dass dieses kapitalistische System uns nichts zu bieten hat. Lockdowns, Krieg, Genozid, Waffenproduktion, Arbeitszwang, Armut sind dazu da, uns auszubeuten und die Reichen reicher zu machen und die Mächtigen mächtiger. Viel zu lange war es still in Europa, waren wir überfordert mit der ganzen Scheiße, die uns täglich vorgesetzt wird.




Auch hier in Deutschland haben die Proteste gegen die Wehrpflicht über das Jahr regelmäßig tausende von Leuten auf die Straße gebracht. Und jetzt gibt es die ersten Schulbesetzungen, die ersten militanten Demos und Aktionen, die sich an denen in Frankreich orientieren. Worum es geht ist klar: in Opposition zu diesem System zu gehen, dass uns gegeneinander ausspielt und ins Verderben jagt. Statt dessen solidarisch und selbstbestimmt leben. Wir brauchen keinen Staat und keine Herrscher. Wir brauchen eine Bewegung von unten.




Was als Schülerprotest begonnen hat, hat sich zu einer generellen Revolte entwickelt. Politik und Massenmedien wollen das hier in Deutschland verhindern, denn sie haben Angst um ihre Macht und ihr Geld. Es wird gehetzt. Gegen Migrant*innen. Gegen Erwachsene, die sich den Schülern anschließen. Gegen angebliche Extremist*innen.


Damit wollen sie uns gegeneinander aufbringen und eine generelle Revolte verhindern. Doch das soll nicht klappen!




Am 20. November wird es wieder einen bundesweiten Schulstreik geben und Europaweit ist zu Demonstrationen und Aktionen aufgerufen. Machen wir diesen Tag zu einem generellen Streik- und Kampftag! Lasst uns die Flamme der Revolte endlich auch hier entzünden! Gemeinsam können wir den Kapitalismus besiegen und uns zurückholen was sie uns geklaut haben, was uns aber immernoch gehört: unsere Straßen, unsere Viertel, die Kontrolle über unsere Leben und damit die Freiheit.




Am 20. November: alle auf die Straße!




Macht Pläne! Achtet auf Ankündigungen! Achtet aufeinander!

author: Michael Csaszkóczy (konkret 7/26)
title: Ein unpolitischer Prozess? In einem – wie das Gericht betonte – völlig unpolitischen Prozess ist Daniela Klette zu 13 Jahren Haft verurteilt worden.
content:
»Was ist ein Dietrich gegen eine Aktie? Was ist ein Einbruch in eine Bank gegen die Gründung einer Bank?«


Mackie Messer in der »Dreigroschenoper«




In der Berichterstattung über das Urteil gegen Daniela Klette kommt kaum eine Meldung ohne die Bemerkung aus, wer ihr Auftreten sehe, könne fast den Schilderungen der Nachbarn glauben, die sie als freundliche und nette ältere Frau beschrieben. Das müsse allerdings offensichtlich Verstellung sein: »Reue sieht anders aus«, tadelt die »Bildzeitung«, und die »Taz« bemängelt Klettes »schier unerträgliche Hybris«.




Denn anscheinend ist die 67jährige auch heute noch nicht bereit, sich pauschal von der RAF zu distanzieren. Ob Klette Mitglied der RAF war, ist – anders als es die Berichterstattung nahelegt – eigentlich überhaupt nicht Gegenstand des Verfahrens, in dem es ursprünglich um 13 teils versuchte, teils durchgeführte Raubüberfälle geht, die die Angeklagte gemeinsam mit ihren Genossen Burkhard Garweg und Ernst-Volker Staub begangen haben soll, um ihr Leben in der Illegalität zu finanzieren (Staatsanwalt und Gericht nennen das Habgier). Während des Prozesses wurde entschieden, dass fünf Taten nicht weiter verfolgt werden. Damit ging es vor Gericht nur noch um acht Überfälle. Erst in einem späteren Verfahren soll die mögliche Beteiligung an drei Anschlägen in den Jahren 1990 bis 1993 geklärt werden. Der Tatbestand der Mitgliedschaft in einer terroristischen Vereinigung selbst ist ohnehin seit geraumer Zeit verjährt.




»Wir führen hier kein Staatsschutz-, kein Terrorismusverfahren, auch wenn wir im Staatsschutzsaal verhandeln«, hatte der Vorsitzende Richter Lars Engelke gleich zu Beginn der Verhandlung betont und anlässlich der Urteilsverkündung sprang die »Taz« ihm noch einmal bei: Für eine politische Motivation des Verfahrens »spricht wenig. Auch andere wurden wegen ähnlicher Überfälle auf Geldtransporter zu vergleichbar langen Haftstrafen verurteilt.« Das ist insofern nicht völlig falsch, dass es bei erheblich vorbestraften Tätern für Raubüberfallserien schon vereinzelt ähnlich hohe Strafen gegeben hat – wenn es um erhebliche Geldsummen geht, versteht die Klassenjustiz keinen Spaß.




Dass aber der Prozess gegen Daniela Klette ein politisches Verfahren war, müsste selbst für einen »Taz«-Journalisten, für den die Weigerung, einen revolutionären antikapitalistischen Anspruch als Verfehlung einzugestehen, anscheinend eine permanente Provokation darstellt, offensichtlich sein. Dafür sorgt schon der Ort der Verhandlung: Eine ehemalige Reithalle in der Umgebung von Verden wurde eigens für mehrere Millionen Euro zu einem festungsartigen provisorischen Gerichtsgebäude umgebaut. Klette selbst war samt ihren Verteidigerinnen und Verteidigern in einem kugelsicheren Glaskasten plaziert, an den Ausgängen des Gebäudes waren Spezialkräfte mit Sturmhauben und Maschinengewehren postiert. Beim zweieinhalbstündigen Transport zur Verhandlung musste die Angeklagte eine schwere Bleiweste tragen und war an Händen und Füßen gefesselt.




Obwohl bei den verhandelten Raubüberfällen niemand verletzt wurde, beharrte die Staatsanwaltschaft auf dem Vorwurf des »versuchten Mordes«. Die »billigende Inkaufnahme tödlicher Verletzungshandlungen«, die die Bundesanwaltschaft (BAW) Klette vorwirft, ergibt sich allein aus der unterstellten früheren Mitgliedschaft in der RAF. Letztlich ist es auch diese vermutete Zugehörigkeit zu der längst aufgelösten Stadtguerillagruppe, mit der die Indizienkette, aufgrund derer das Urteil gefällt wurde, in irgendeiner Weise plausibel gemacht werden könnte. Die Argumentation beruft sich erkennbar auf die allgemein bekannte Kollektivität in der Entscheidungsstruktur der RAF. Die Zulässigkeit dieser Argumentation wurde 1998 vom Bundesgerichtshof bestätigt und dient nun dazu, Daniela Klette auch die Beteiligung an Raubüberfällen zur Last zu legen, bei denen es für ihre konkrete Tatbeteiligung nur wenige Indizien gibt: Zeugenaussagen oder Überwachungsvideos, die sie klar als Täterin identifizierten, sind nicht vorhanden, und die DNA-Mischspuren, die die Beweisaufnahme in Fluchtfahrzeugen festgestellt hat, sind für sich genommen nicht besonders aussagekräftig.




Obwohl das Thema RAF also den gesamten Prozess beherrschte, sollte es nach dem Willen von Staatsanwaltschaft und Gericht keine Rolle spielen. Erst in einem weiteren Verfahren am OLG Frankfurt wird es um einen versuchten Anschlag auf ein Gebäude der Deutschen Bank im hessischen Eschborn 1990, um Schüsse auf das US-Botschaftsgebäude in Bonn 1991 und schließlich um die Sprengung des Knastneubaus in Weiterstadt 1993 gehen. Bei keiner dieser Aktionen wurden Menschen verletzt. Im Jahr 1992 hatte die RAF angekündigt, sie werde »Angriffe auf führende Repräsentanten aus Wirtschaft und Staat für den jetzt notwendigen Prozess einstellen«. Sollte Daniela Klette tatsächlich ein »führendes Mitglied der RAF« gewesen sein, wäre sie daran beteiligt gewesen, die bewaffnete Auseinandersetzung zu beenden – ein Ziel, das die Repressionsbehörden der BRD selbst durch den Einsatz massiver Gewalt und die Aushöhlung rechtsstaatlicher Standards in über zwanzig Jahren nicht erreicht hatten.




Das Exempel, das an Daniela Klette statuiert wird, ist erkennbar weder einer realen Bedrohung geschuldet, noch der Anziehungskraft, die die Idee, bewaffneten Widerstand gegen den Kapitalismus zu leisten, derzeit auf jüngere Linke haben könnte.




Im August 1971 hatte die RAF in ihrem »Konzept Stadtguerilla« erklärt: »Wir sagen nicht, dass die Organisierung illegaler bewaffneter Widerstandsgruppen legale proletarische Organisationen ersetzen könnte und Einzelaktionen Klassenkämpfe, und nicht, dass der bewaffnete Kampf die politische Arbeit im Betrieb und im Stadtteil ersetzen könnte. Wir behaupten nur, dass das eine die Voraussetzung für den Erfolg und den Fortschritt des anderen ist. … Die Rote Armee Fraktion redet vom Primat der Praxis. Ob es richtig ist, den bewaffneten Widerstand jetzt


zu organisieren, hängt davon ab, ob es möglich ist; ob es möglich ist, ist nur praktisch zu ermitteln.«




27 Jahre später bilanzierte die RAF in ihrer Auﬂösungserklärung: »Die RAF war der revolutionäre Versuch einer Minderheit, entgegen der Tendenz dieser Gesellschaft, zur Umwälzung der kapitalistischen Verhältnisse beizutragen. Wir sind froh, Teil dieses Versuchs gewesen zu sein. Das Ende dieses Projekts zeigt, dass wir auf diesem Weg nicht durchkommen konnten.«




Wie im »Konzept Stadtguerilla« exemplarisch formuliert, verstand sich die RAF in den siebziger Jahren noch als Teil der vielfältigen Klassenkämpfe in der BRD. In den achtziger Jahren war dieses Selbstverständnis kaum noch aufrechtzuerhalten und wich zunehmend der Vorstellung, als Teil einer globalen antiimperialistischen Front zu agieren. Mit der Niederlage des sozialistischen Staatensystems 1989 war auch diese strategische Bestimmung obsolet geworden. In der Auﬂösungserklärung der RAF vom März 1998 bleibt letztlich vor allem der gleichsam existenzialistisch begründete radikale Bruch mit der kapitalistischen Gesellschaftsordnung, den die Entscheidung zum bewaffneten Kampf symbolisierte: »Der Kampf im gesellschaftlichen Riss, den unsere Feindschaft markierte, griff einer wirklich gesellschaftlich werdenden Befreiung nur voraus: der Riss zwischen einem System, in dem der Profit das Subjekt, der Mensch das Objekt ist, und der Sehnsucht nach einem Leben ohne den Lug und Trug dieser sich sinnentleerenden Gesellschaft.«




Die durch praktische Ermittlung gewonnene Erkenntnis, dass die Organisation bewaffneten Widerstands in der BRD in der gegebenen gesellschaftlichen Situation nicht möglich war, hätte also sicherlich schon sehr viel früher erfolgen können, hätte der Staat nicht die Mitglieder der Stadtguerilla, deren er habhaft werden konnte, in Geiselhaft genommen. Schon in den siebziger Jahren machte in der Linken die böse Rede von der »Befreit die Guerilla« die Runde – ohne dass freilich diejenigen, die so redeten, zu sagen gewusst hätten, wie denn mit der Situation der Gefangenen umzugehen sei, die teils unter menschenunwürdigen Haftbedingungen in den Hochsicherheitstrakten saßen und von denen etliche in der Obhut des Staates ums Leben kamen.




In ihrem Schlusswort bezog sich Daniela Klette auf die gesamte Palette dessen, was in der verbliebenen »linken Szene« weitgehender Konsens ist: auf den »Kampf gegen Militarisierung, Wehrpﬂicht und Aufrüstung«, gegen »Gewalt gegen Frauen, Queers, Transmenschen und Menschen mit Behinderung«, gegen das »repressive Abschottungssystem an den Grenzen zur Abwehr von Geﬂüchteten«, die »ökologische Zerstörung der Welt«, auf den Kampf gegen Antisemitismus und Rassismus ebenso wie – natürlich – auf den »gegen den israelischen Siedlerkolonialismus und die Apartheitpolitik gegen die palästinensische Bevölkerung«. Die Solidaritätsbewegung war dennoch kaum in der Lage, eine nennenswerte Breitenwirkung zu entfalten, auch wenn sich die bürgerlichen Medien begierig auf jedes Transparent stürzten, das als Beleg dienen konnte, wie real die Bedrohung durch die »Sympathisanten des linken Terrorismus« immer noch sei.




Unter Umständen könnte das Urteil – das sich nah an der Maximalforderung der Staatsanwaltschaft von 15 Jahren bewegt – dafür sorgen, dass das OLG Frankfurt sich mit den Daniela Klette zur Last gelegten politischen Delikten gar nicht erst befassen muss, denn eine höhere Strafe als 15 Jahre sind für Klette nicht möglich. Das könnte für die Repressionsbehörden durchaus eine attraktive Option sein, bliebe da nicht die offene Wunde Weiterstadt. Die Sprengung des Knastneubaus war die letzte Aktion der RAF und fand in der Linken eine lange nicht gekannte Zustimmung. Bis heute wurde niemand für diesen Anschlag verurteilt.




Sowohl die Staatsanwaltschaft, die auf den Vorwurf des versuchten Mordes, den das Gericht fallengelassen hat, nicht verzichten möchte, als auch die Verteidigung haben Revision eingelegt. Im Einstellungsantrag, den die Verteidigung zu Beginn des Prozesses stellte, wurde das Gericht aufgefordert, doch zu berücksichtigen, »welcher Anteil staatlichen und justiziellen Versagens dazu geführt hat, dass Menschen in den Untergrund gegangen sind und für sich keine legale Perspektive mehr gesehen haben«. Es ist kaum davon auszugehen, dass das Gericht sich davon beeindrucken ließ. Die gesamte Linke hingegen hätte allen Grund, an dieser Stelle ins Nachdenken zu kommen. Schließlich befinden wir uns in einer gesellschaftlichen Situation, in der kaum jemand zu prophezeien wagt, innerhalb welcher Frist die bürgerliche Demokratie in eine Situation kippt, in der Oppositionsarbeit in der Legalität nicht mehr möglich ist.




Im März 1972 – die Eskalation zwischen RAF und Staatsgewalt war in vollem Gange – veröffentlichte Heinrich Böll im »Spiegel« einen Essay, in dem er freies Geleit für Ulrike Meinhof forderte: »Haben alle, die einmal verfolgt waren, von denen einige im Parlament sitzen, der eine oder andere in der Regierung, haben sie alle vergessen, was es bedeutet, verfolgt und gehetzt zu sein? Wer von ihnen weiß schon, was es bedeutet, in einem Rechtsstaat gehetzt zu werden von ›Bild‹, das eine weitaus höhere Auﬂage hat als der ›Stürmer‹ sie gehabt hat?«




Es gibt heute, in einer Situation, in der keine linke Gruppe mehr existiert, die eine relevante Bedrohung des staatlichen Gewaltmonopols darstellen könnte, keine bürgerliche Zeitung mehr, die einen solchen Text abdrucken würde. Es gibt aber auch keine Intellektuellen von der Reichweite eines Böll, die die naheliegende Forderung aufstellen würden: »Amnestie für Daniela Klette und freies Geleit für Burkhard Garweg und Ernst-Volker Staub!«




 

passiert am 01.07.2026

title: İstanbul'da bazı vapur seferleri lodos nedeniyle iptal edildi
content:
Fotoğraf: Hüma H. Yardım/Unsplash

İstanbul - Meteoroloji Genel Müdürlüğü'nün uyarılarının ardından dün etkisini göstermeye başlayan lodos, bugün İstanbul'da şiddetini artırdı. Kuvvetli rüzgar nedeniyle deniz ulaşımında aksamalar yaşandı.

İDO tarafından yapılan duyuruda, olumsuz hava koşulları nedeniyle; Yenikapı-Yalova 09.45, Yalova-Yenikapı 09.45, Kadıköy-Yenikapı-Bandırma 11.30, Yenikapı-Yalova 11.45, Yalova-Yenikapı 11.45, Bursa-Armutlu-Yenikapı-Kadıköy 12.30 ve Kadıköy-Yenikapı-Armutlu Tatil Köyü-Armutlu-Bursa 14.50 seferlerinin iptal edildiği bildirildi.

Şehir Hatları'ndan yapılan açıklamada ise elverişsiz hava koşulları nedeniyle ikinci bir duyuruya kadar Bostancı-Moda-Karaköy-Kabataş, Büyükada-Sedef Adası, Maltepe-Büyükada-Heybeliada-Burgazada-Kınalıada, Beşiktaş-Adalar, Anadolu Kavağı-Rumeli Kavağı-Sarıyer, Sarıyer-Beykoz ve Bostancı-Adalar Ring hatlarındaki seferlerin gerçekleştirilemeyeceği belirtildi. Ayrıca 10.05 Kabataş-Kadıköy-Adalar seferinin de iptal edildiği duyuruldu.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Unknown
title: İBB davasında 8 tahliyenin ardından Çelik'ten çağrı: 'Tutuksuz yargılama esas olmalı'
content:
Tutuklu Cumhurbaşkanı adayı ve İstanbul Büyükşehir Belediye Başkanı Ekrem İmamoğlu’nun da aralarında bulunduğu İBB davasında 8 kişinin tahliye edilmesinin ardından Yeni Parti İstanbul İl Başkanı Özgü, tutuksuz yargılamanın esas olması gerektiğini vurgulayarak açıklamalarda bulundu.

Tahliye edilen isimler arasında Ekrem İmamoğlu'nun avukatı Mehmet Pehlivan, Medya AŞ Genel Müdürü Fatoş Pınar Türker, Kültür AŞ Genel Müdür Yardımcısı Onur Aldı, Fatoş Ayık, Serhat Kapki, Ahmet Köksal, Volkan Ateş ve Murat Or bulunuyor.

Cezaevinde bulunan diğer tutuklu sanıkların da serbest bırakılmasını isteyen Çelik, duruma ilişkin "Bugün verilen tahliye kararı, iki yıla yakın süredir devam eden hukuksuzlukları ortadan kaldırmadı" şeklinde değerlendirmede bulundu.

Çelik, sosyal medya hesabından yaptığı açıklamada şu ifadeleri kullandı:

"Bugün İBB davasında tahliye olan 8 yol arkadaşımız için sevindik. Hepsine hoş geldin diyoruz. Ancak, tutuksuz yargılama esas olmalıyken, yol arkadaşlarımıza ağır tecrit koşullarında tutsaklık reva görüldü.

Bugün verilen tahliye kararı, iki yıla yakın süredir devam eden hukuksuzlukları ortadan kaldırmadığı gibi, ailelerinden, sevdiklerinden, çocuklarından haksız bir şekilde uzak bırakılan yol arkadaşlarımız halen zindanlarda.”

Cezaevinde haksız yere tutulan tüm isimler için de tutuksuz yargılama kararının bir an önce verilmesi gerektiğini söyleyen Çelik, “Halkımızın her gece evinde kurduğu vicdan mahkemelerinden tertemiz çıkan biziz… Fon vurguncuları ise halkımızın vicdanında çoktan mahkum oldu, mahkemelerin yargılamaya başlamasını bekliyor” dedi.

Çelik, “Biz bu ikili hukuk düzeniyle mutlaka hesaplaşacağız. Gün gelecek, adaletin terazisi gerçek suçlularla, masumları ayıracak. Gün gelecek, kısa çöp uzun çöpten hakkını alacak. Hak kazanacak, halkımız kazanacak, Türkiye kazanacak" ifadelerini kullandı.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Unknown
title: Lula mohra xwe li roja çaremîn a COP31ê da
content:
Lûtkeya Rêberan a ku du rojan di civîna COP31ê ya li Antalyayê de domiya, bi dawî bû. Serokdewletê Brezîlyayê Lula da Silva mohra xwe li roja duyemîn a Lûtkeya Rêberan da. 




Lula di saetên êvarê de li salona duyemîn a mezin a desteya giştî ya bi navê Deryaya Spî (Akdeniz), bi nûnerên rêxistinên civaka sivîl ên Brezîlyayê re civiya û li Antalyayê hema bêje pîrozbahiyeke hilbijartinê jî li dar xist. Gotinên Lula û axaftvanên din gelek caran bi dirûşmeyan hatin birîn.



















Roja dawî ya Lûtkeya Rêberan




12 Mijdar 2026










Şandeya Brezîlyayê di saetên sibehê de jî civîneke bi heman rengî li dar xistibû. Brezîlyaya ku salek berê li Belemê mazûvaniya civîna COP30yê kiribû, li Antalyayê derbarê armanca devjêberdana sotemeniyên fosîl (petrol, komir û gaz) de nexşerêyek ragihand û bang li welatên din kir ku vê pêvajoya ku bi salan e tê paşxistin, bileztir bikin. 




Serok Lula jî di axaftina xwe ya di civîna êvarê de got ku Brezîlya dê di parastina jîngehê de bibe welatê herî baş û bal kişand ser nexşerêyê. Her wiha Lula behsa wê yekê jî kir ku di COP15a li Kopenhagê de bi Serokê berê yê DYAyê Barack Obama û Serokdewletê Çînê Wen Jiabao re axiviye û çawa alî razî kirine ku salane 100 milyar dolar bidin welatên di pêvajoya pêşketinê de ne.




Di saetên sibehê de çalakvana avhewayê Greta Thunberg, damezrînerê Enstîtuya Filistînê ya ji bo Stratejiya Avhewayê Mohammad Usrof, nûnera civakên herêmî yên ji Awistralyayê Rikki Dank û Celine Isimbi ya ji Rwandayê bi hev re civîneke çapemeniyê li dar xistin. 



















Tevî akredîtasyonê jî çapemenî di Lûtkeya Rêberan a COP31ê de hat sînordarkirin




11 Mijdar 2026










Greta Thunbergê di axaftina xwe ya vekirinê de bi van gotinan dest pê kir: “Em hemû li vir in ji ber ku em dizanin krîza avhewayê heye û ev êdî bûye meseleya jiyan û mirinê.”




Thunbergê diyar kir ku gavên ku kesên li vir desthilatdar in davêjin, bi temamî ji rastiyê dûr in û got ku em can, ekosîstem û cureyên biqîmet ên ku dê careke din qet venegerin, winda dikin. Thunbergê weha got; 

“Krîza avhewayê krîzeke bêedaletiyê ye ku kesên herî kêm berpirsiyarê vê krîzê ne, bi awayê herî dijwar û herî bilez jê bandor dibin”

 û destnîşan kir ku petrola ku ji Tirkiyeyê diçe Îsraîlê qirkirinê gur dike û xwest ku Tirkiye ambargoya enerjiyê deyne ser Îsraîlê. Mohammed Usrof jî di axaftina xwe de got ku baranên beriya hefteyekê 70 hezar malbat ji cih û warên wan kirine û wiha li axavtina zêde kir:







“Ji ber ku hemû di konên pînekirî û rizyayî de dijîn. Hefteya borî li Şerîaya Rojava di demekê de ku 3 hezar Filistînî ji cihên xwe dihatin koçberkirin, bi dehan kesan jiyana xwe ji dest da. Û tekane sedema vê yekê, encamên qirkirina ku bi piştgiriya DYA û Îngilîstanê û bi beşdariya petrola Tirkiyeyê ji aliyê artêşa Îsraîlê ve tê meşandin e. Ji ber vê yekê petrola Tirkiyeyê, ligel komira Kolombiya û Afrîkaya Başûr ku rasterast ji tora elektrîkê û sîstema leşkerî ya Îsraîlê re tê veguhestin, hêzê dide qirkirinê ku Îsraîlê didomîne.”







Tirkiyeyê di roja çaremîn a COP31ê de îmze avêt bin peymanên enerjiyê. Wezîrê Enerjiyê Alparslan Bayraktar bi rayedarên Komara Gel a Çînê re peymannameyeke lihevkirinê ya bi bihayê 15 milyar dolarî îmze kir ku santralên ba û rojê, tesîsên depokirina elektrîkê û xetên veguhastinê li xwe digire. Bi şîrketa AtkinsRealis a Kanadayê re jî ji bo lêkolîna pêkanbûnê (fîzîbîlîte) ya santraleke nukleerî ku dê ji 6 reaktoran pêk bê û bi giştî xwedî hêza 4500 megawatan be,peyman hat îmzekirin. Her wiha bi şîrketa ACWA ya Erebistana Siûdî re jî ji bo fînansekirina santrala rojê ya 2 hezar megawatî ya ku di encama peymana berê de avakirina wê dihat plankirin, îmze hatin avêtin.




Serokwezîrê Brîtanyayê Andy Burnham jî hat Antalyayê û raporeke bi navê Nexşerêya Elektrîkîkirina Paqij a welatê xwe eşkere kir. Rapor ji aliyê rêxistinên jîngehê ve hat rexnekirin ji ber ku nehatiye diyarkirin ka dê elektrîk ji kîjan çavkaniyan bê hilberandin û hat destnîşankirin ku divê hilberîna elektrîkê tenê ji çavkaniyên enerjiya nûjenbar bê kirin.




Greenpeaceya ku berê li Qada Şîn (Blue Zone) a ku muzakere lê didomin enstalasyonek vekiribû û nîşan dabû ku sotemeniyên fosîl berpirsiyarê germbûna 1,5 pileyî ne, dê roja Înê 13ê Çiriya Paşiyê ya 2026an jî li ber Şaredariya Konyaaltiyê peykerekî hespê Troyayê yê şeş metre bilind veke.




Şopînerê Çalakiya Avhewayê (Climate Action Tracker) dê di civîna çapemeniyê ya ku îro (13ê Çiriya Paşiyê) li dar bixe de, xebata xwe ya dawî ya ku hesab dike ka sozên heyî yên hikûmetan dê cîhanê ber bi germbûneke çend pileyî ve bibin,eşkere bike.




(ÖG/Mİ/AY)

author: Unknown
title: COP Bike Ride: 2 binden fazla bisikletçi, 20 bin kilometre yol kat etti
content:
COP Bike Ride, ulaşım kaynaklı karbon emisyonlarının azaltılmasında bisikletin daha etkin bir ulaşım aracı olarak kullanılmasını savunan, dünya çapında yurttaşların inisiyatifiyle oluşmuş uluslararası bir bisiklet topluluğu.




İstanbul’da buluştuğumuz COP Bike Ride ekibi şimdi Antalya’da.







COP30’un yapıldığı Brezilya Belém’den yola çıktılar, sıfır fosil yakıt tüketerek yelkenliyle okyanusu geçtiler ve bugün Antalya’dayız. 2 bin 200’den fazla bisikletçi rotaya katıldı, yaklaşık 20 bin kilometre yol bisikletle kat edilmiş oldu. Sadece Türkiye’de bin 300 kilometreyi kat ettik bisikletlerimizle. –

 Nihan Lafcı







Bisikleti iklim dostu ulaşımın temel unsurlarından biri haline getirmeyi amaçlayan topluluk, 10 maddelik talep listesini COP31 Başkanı Murat Kurum’a ulaştırmaya çalışıyor.




COP Bike Ride Türkiye Koordinatörü Nihan Lafcı ile bu kez COP31 alanında buluştuk; Brezilya’dan İstanbul’a uzanan yolculuğu ve bu süreçte edindikleri deneyimleri konuştuk.







COP Bike Ride’dan 10 talep




Ekip, 10 Ekim’de Kadıköy’de düzenlediği basın açıklamasında karar vericilere yönelik 10 talebini kamuoyuyla paylaşmıştı:







2030’a kadar, özellikle şehirlerarası ve günlük yolculuklar için çok modlu bağlantıyı da içeren temel bir bisiklet yolu ağı oluşturun. Temel zaten mevcutsa, daha iddialı olun!




Hem hızı hem de araç sayısını sınırlayarak araç trafiğini azaltın.




2030’a kadar bisiklet kullanımını geliştirmeye yönelik, tüm olanakları kapsayan özel planlar tasarlayın! (Bu planlar, özel bütçeyle desteklenmeli ve bisiklet topluluklarının da dahil olduğu düzenli uygulama inceleme süreçlerini içermeli.)




Okulların, toplu taşıma merkezlerinin, yerel işletmelerin ve yeşil alanların yakınında bisiklet ve yaya için ayrılmış alanları 2030’a kadar önemli ölçüde artırın.




2030’a kadar ulaşım merkezlerinde, alışveriş alanlarında (!), okullarda, ofislerde, evlerde (kargo bisikletleri dahil) uygun bisiklet depolama kapasitesini genelleştirin.




Bisiklet sürmeye yönelik bir zaman ve mekan yaratın: geniş bir kitleye hitap etmek için her yıl düzenlenen büyük bir bisiklet etkinliği + bisiklet tamiri, eğitimi, buluşması gibi etkinliklerin düzenleneceği bir “bisiklet evi”...




Özellikle 12 yaş altı çocuklar ve kadınlar için daha iyi bisiklet sürüş ve güçlendirme konusunda eğitim; bisikletin finansal faydalarının tanıtımı.




İlgili ekonomik sektörü (imalat, tamir, bisiklet turizmi, kiralama, paylaşım vb.) özel vergi teşvikleri/destekler yoluyla geliştirin.




“Son kilometre” teslimatları için kargo bisikleti lojistiği geliştirin.




Kaza oranları, memnuniyet anketleri, ayrılmış bisiklet ağı uzunluğu ve ulaşım türlerinin dağılımı gibi göstergeleri düzenli olarak ölçüp izleyerek kamuoyuyla paylaşın.










(CA/VC)

author: Coral Wynter
title: Standing with the women and girls of Afghanistan
content:
About 110 people from Australia and Britain joined Amnesty International (AI) in an on-line forum, on September 23, to hear about the human rights group's strategy to support women in Afghanistan. Kathy Allan from AI introduced the forum by saying that when Kabul fell on August 15, 2021, the United States handed over power to the Taliban, after the US Coalition, including Australian forces, had carried out a military intervention into Afghanistan for two decades.

The Taliban has 164 decrees targeting women and girls. Women have been barred from most jobs, and from working with non-government organisations (NGOs). Girls are banned from secondary school and university, parks, gyms and beauty salons. Women cannot speak publicly. LGBTIQ+ Afghans have been forced into hiding.

The Taliban is also attacking ethnic and religious minorities, as well as journalists and human rights defenders.

This institutionalised pattern of systemic domination and oppression based on gender has been labelled “gender apartheid”. Afghanistan is the only country in the world to impose this extreme form of gender discrimination.

Right now, international law has no statute that fully captures this situation. AI is calling for gender apartheid to be recognised as a crime under international law.

Muslima, an Afghan educator and writer, told the forum, “Almost overnight, the door to our classroom was closed. Just because you were a girl, you lost your classroom.

“I never imagined that my future would just mean I stay home ... simply because I was born a girl. Being at home every day felt like a prison, like being in jail. Where do I go? My human rights were wiped out.

“But now I have a computer, my classroom to the outside world. All that I have is a small screen in my room. If they find out, I can face charges.

“Thousands of girls have no access to a computer and internet, but I am lucky. Afghan women can’t talk about their stories, nor can they speak about these issues. Girls of 12 years of age are denied the simple right to education, to learn, to develop their skills, to make friends.

“The Taliban can’t build a strong future by excluding half of the population. Afghanistan is losing enormous [human] potential.

“I want the world to see something beyond our suffering. Women are still writing, working, advocating, creating, contributing and building. If you want to support Afghan women, you must listen to them.

“When the headlines disappear, Afghan women do not disappear.

“So my message is clear: make a space for us to speak. Share our voices.

“Sometimes solidarity begins with something as simple as a refusal to forget. Listen to the voices of Afghan women, who are denied their human rights,” Muslima concluded.

The next speaker was Shaharzad Akbar, a human rights activist from Afghanistan, currently living in exile. She talked about the Peoples Tribunal on Women of Afghanistan, which was held in Madrid, Spain, in October last year and hosted by four Afghan women’s organisations.

They are worried that the actions of the Taliban, as the de facto regime, are being normalised in the region. The Taliban currently have consulates in Germany, China, India and Turkiye, although only Russia officially recognises the Taliban government. Europe is now holding conversations with the Taliban regarding potentially deporting Afghan men and women.

Akbar said, “Women are not able to train as midwives or doctors ... Women will die from preventable diseases because there are not enough female health-care providers.”

Women are suffering from domestic abuse, but it is not considered a crime inside Afghanistan. Emotional, economic and physical abuses are not criminalised. Husbands are allowed by law to punish their wives for any offence.

Women can only go to a judge to make a complaint if they have obvious bruises or broken bones — and face many hurdles to do so. They are not allowed to leave the house alone and a male family member has to accompany them to the court. So a brother or father has to be convinced to support them.

The woman has to relay her message to the judge through a man. If she is believed and she has broken bones caused by her husband, he will be imprisoned for 15 days. He usually returns home only to repeat the abuse.

“We have had increased killing of women, increased suicides of women and a mental health crisis for women and girls in Afghanistan. They don’t see a future for themselves. They are imprisoned in their homes, suffering abuse and forced into early marriages. Despite all this, the Taliban are being normalised.

“We thought if we held a tribunal, where people could hear what is happening, we could slow down this normalisation process. Do we really want our governments to engage with a regime like this?

“Some 24 survivors, some who were refugees, spoke to the Tribunal by audio or written testimonies, for they feared for their own lives and that of their families.”

In December, a panel of eight judges declared that non-normalisation of the Taliban should occur. “So you should watch very carefully what the Australian government is doing in regards to their relationship to the Taliban,” said Akbar.

Two years ago, in September 2024, Australia, Germany, The Netherlands and Canada promised to hold Afghanistan and the Taliban accountable for violations of the Convention on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW). Afghanistan is a signatory to CEDAW. The countries said that if they didn’t get a satisfactory answer, they would take the Afghan government to the International Court of Justice (ICJ).

Afghani women have been asking these four countries each month when they are going to take the Taliban to the ICJ. “We receive vague answers. So please ask your government what happened to the CEDAW legal initiative?

“I know it won’t solve our problems but it will tell the women and girls of Afghanistan that the world stands with them. We need to tell the world to channel aid to Afghan women and force the Taliban to reverse the codification of gender apartheid,” concluded Akbar.

Azadah Raz Mohammad, one of the prosecutors who appeared before the Peoples Tribunal, and legal advisor to the campaign to end gender apartheid, told the forum: “The current objective is to codify gender apartheid under the current treaty we have before the UN, the crimes against humanity treaty.”

The phrase “gender apartheid” was first used in the period 1996 to 2001, when the Taliban was in power for the first time.

“We now have 14 states that have expressed support for codification of gender apartheid and seven states that have submitted formal proposals to the UN committee for inclusion of the practice in the crimes against humanity. These states include Australia, Timor-Leste, Luxembourg, Iceland, the former government of Afghanistan and Uruguay. This will go for negotiation to the UN in 2028.”

The final speaker, Fatima Frotan, is doing grassroots work with Afghan women in communities, including distributing menstruation pads in Daikundi and Uruzgan provinces, through personal contacts.

Frotan said men and boys in Afghanistan are getting educated in religious idolatry and misogyny and there has been a rise in the establishment of madrasas across the country by the Taliban.

Frotan was part of an organisation called Afghans for Progressive Thinking.

“We began talking to a number of youth. We started a pilot program for women and girls in Kabul. Afghanistan is a deeply religious country, and Islam is a big part of their identity. We introduced them to a more egalitarian interpretation of Islam, where they could find the agency and empowerment within their own identity, which was quite successful.

“In the western part of Kabul there have been targeted attacks on the Hazara neighbourhoods. Shiite education facilities have been taken over by the Taliban. LGBTQIA people are persecuted.

“We have to stop the campaign of genocide against Hazara peoples and other minorities. We want the West to expand the number of scholarships given to Afghani women and to expand the number of scholarships to overseas universities, and to help with the visas, especially for women at risk,” she said.

Amnesty International's 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence, from November 25 to December 10, is focussed on pressuring the Australian government to use its diplomatic influence to support recognition of gender apartheid under international law and follow through on accountability for the Taliban’s crimes against women and girls.

[For more information, visit: amnesty.org.au.]

International Court of Justice (ICJ)

author: Unknown
title: Ephéméride des luttes : 13 novembre
content:
Le 13 novembre de l'éphéméride des luttes parle aussi d'autres choses que de Paris. Elle parle effectivement de violence politique, mais de celle qui se veut émancipatrice et révolutionnaire.




1887 :

 - Au Brésil, abolition de l'escalavage.




 A Londres, des affrontements ont lieu entre une manifestation de travailleurs et la police, après que la manifestation soit interdite. De nombreux blessés sont signalés du fait de charges de la police montée, dont deux succomberont à leurs blessures.

 A Chicago, c'est l'enterrement des "martyrs de Haymarket". Plus de deux cent mille personnes sont présentes, portant une rose rouge.




1893 :

 L'anarchiste Léon Léauthier tente d'assassiner l'ambassadeur de Serbie Georgewitch à Paris. Léauthier a été élevé à Marseille, où il a appris le métier de cordonnier. Il sera condamné aux travaux forcés à perpétuité au bagne en Guyane, où il mourra lors de la répression de la révolte du 

22 octobre

 1894.




 

 

 

 




1909 :

 A Gijón en Espagne, parution du premier numéro du journal '

Solidaridad Obrera

'.




 

 

 

 




1974 :

 Aux USA, Karen Silkwood est tuée alors qu'elle s'apprêtait à révéler des informations sur des violations de sécurité dans les centrales nucléaires à un journaliste.




1979 :

 Dans les Alpes, les anarchistes Marco Camenisch et René Moser sabotent un pylône d'une ligne à très haute tension à l'explosif, contre le nucléaire.




1981 :

 A Londres, l'IRA fait sauter la maison du procureur général Michael Havers.




1991 :

 A Belfast, l'IRA mène toute une série d'actions explosives.




1992 :

 A Coleraine près de Derry en Irlande du Nord, l'IRA fait sauter un van piégé dans le centre, provoquant de gros dégâts matériels dans les principales rues commerçantes.




2015 :

 En Irak, les peshmergas et le PKK reprennent la ville de Sinjar à l'EI.




2016 :

 En Campanie en Italie, trois antennes radio sont incendiées en solidarité avec les anarchistes arrêté-e-s lors de l'opération de police 'Scripta Manent'.




Voir aussi 

l'éphéméride anarchiste

 du 13 novembre.

author: Mazin Qumsiyeh
title: Palestinian ecologist tells COP31: ‘Peace is an environmental necessity’
content:
Mazin Qumsiyeh, from the Palestine Institute for Biodiversity and Sustainability at Bethlehem University, delivered this speech to an ancillary meeting organised at the 31st Conference of Parties (COP31) being held in Türkiye.

We cannot seriously address the climate crisis while ignoring war, militarism, occupation, and the enormous environmental costs of colonisation.

Here in Palestine, the colonial genocide and ethnic cleansing of our people since 1948 has resulted in half a million killed, and now 8.5 million displaced or refugees.

We are working now to get the United Nations to pass an ecocide convention similar to the genocide convention.

The ecocide is global problem and goes beyond borders.

There is no other area where more bombs were dropped relative to population size than Western Asia.

The ecocide is more than just war effect and it does go beyond borders. The Zionist drying up of the Jordan River basin affects four countries; the uprooting of millions of trees and the pollution from the war on the people of Gaza is spreading along the Mediterranean coastline resulting affecting habitats and people.

War is also a climate issue as military activities consume enormous quantities of fossil fuels, destroy infrastructure, generate toxic pollution and release greenhouse gases.

These are often poorly reported or excluded from national climate accounting.

The destruction of Gaza has generated enormous greenhouse gas emissions, both directly through military operations and indirectly through the destruction and future reconstruction of buildings and infrastructure.

A study published in March reported that 33.2 million tonnes of carbon dioxide (CO₂) equivalent had been produced in the destruction of Gaza — a tiny area of 365 square kilometres.

This conservative figure does not take into account the destroyed trees (we studied those by remote sensing), nor the jet fuel burned in countless United States/Israeli sorties to bomb Lebanon, Yemen, Iraq, Syria and Iran.

The 2026 One Earth study estimated that US deliveries of military equipment to Israel between October 2023 and January 2025 involved approximately 50,000 tonnes of supplies transported through 507 aircraft and 107 ship journeys.

The US, which remains the largest single cause of climate change emissions — and it is exempted from reporting on these, has nearly depleted its stockpile of missiles via deliveries to Israel.

Military infrastructure, walls, fortifications and security installations also require enormous quantities of concrete, steel and energy.

The long-term environmental costs is catastrophic: Contaminated soil and water, destruction of agricultural land, damaged wastewater systems, loss of vegetation and even more people dying from diseases and deprivation than those killed directly by these weapons.

More studies and public attention are needed on all of this.

The destruction of ecosystems, like has happened in Palestine, makes communities less resilient to climate change.

Destruction of trees, agricultural land and natural vegetation reduces carbon storage. Soil degradation reduces water infiltration and groundwater recharge.

The destruction of wetlands and natural habitats undermines biodiversity and ecosystem services. Damage to water, sewage and electricity infrastructure increases pollution and dependence on burning wood and diesel for fuel.

The destruction of agricultural systems undermines food sovereignty and increases dependence on imported food.

The UN Environment Program’s September 2025 assessment provides particularly disturbing evidence. By May 2025, 97.1% of tree crops and 82.4% of annual crops in Gaza had been damaged. Approximately 61 million tonnes of debris would require management.

Climate justice requires accountability, not selective accounting.

There is a fundamental contradiction in international climate policy. Governments demand carbon reductions from ordinary citizens, farmers and industries, while military emissions remain inadequately accounted for.

The Paris Agreement climate framework does not impose a comprehensive mandatory reporting system for military emissions. Thus we demand mandatory, transparent reporting of military greenhouse gas emissions, including arms production, military logistics, combat operations and reconstruction.

We often speak about saving the planet for future generations.

But what does that mean to a Palestinian child growing up in Gaza, whose home, school, agricultural land, water resources and natural environment have been destroyed?

What does climate justice mean when billions are spent on weapons while communities struggle for clean water, food and the basic conditions for life? We cannot separate the climate crisis from militarism, colonialism and the unequal distribution of power.

We cannot talk about sustainability while financing destruction.

We, the ordinary citizens, have the burden of responsibility not only to report this climate abuse but offer alternatives.

Our Palestine Institute for Biodiversity and Sustainability provides practical on-the-ground community-led models for peace building, mitigation, adaptation, reduction and much more.

Our vision is sustainable human and natural communities and our motto is respect: For ourselves — empowerment — for other people and for mother nature.

Peace is an environmental necessity. Justice is a prerequisite for sustainability. Protecting nature means protecting the right of people to live in dignity, freedom and harmony with their environment.

[To follow Mazin Qumsiyeh, from the Palestine Institute for Biodiversity and Sustainability at Bethlehem University, visit his blog Popular Resistance.]

Palestine Institute for Biodiversity and Sustainability

author: Tamara Pearson
title: Journalism and news in times of catastrophe and enshittification
content:
I pace my small apartment for almost an hour after interviewing a fellow journalist in Mexico who was kidnapped by organised crime groups. Another day, a source has been arrested, another dies in a suspicious car accident. Others tell compelling stories of saving rivers and stopping powerful corporations. I feel alive when I work. But often also worried, deeply sad, and overlooked.

I also work as a global features editor, and the news comes in throughout the day, announcing more horrific events. Another oil spill, more destruction of the environment, of cultures, of people's youths and their futures.

Committed with such impunity, it sometimes leaves me questioning the impact of my work. The repetitive and ongoing nature of such injustices can also make journalism feel routine and close to pointless.

These are tough times for people reading or listening to the news, and for those real journalists who challenge economic and political power rather than aligning with it. But we must continue to stay informed—ignoring the bad news won't stop it.

Courageous journalism is needed more than ever, but it is being smothered by online platforms. Social media, search engines, and the web are increasingly enshitified—inundated with advertising, incorrect information, AI delusions, and mundane, vacuous viral videos.

It is an information crisis and a justice crisis all at once. But just as excessive consumerism and the approximately 48,000 overflowing landfills across the world are a clear call to only use what we need, these crises also embody within them a call for deep change, for a reckoning.

AI dominance begs us to return to everything that is humanising, creative, and real. Injustice and the climate crisis call for structural action and a strengthening of good journalism. The mainstream outlets beholden to corporations and in denial of empire and inequality are increasingly and obviously, useless.

Media outlets and other sources of information, like search engines and social media, are skewing perceptions about what matters. The amount of attention and space given to different regions, issues, and people forges a hierarchy of concerns.

Issues covered tediously can risk desensitising, normalising,and numbing. But overlooked news and silence numbs in malevolent and long-lasting ways, infusing populations with extremely high levels of tolerance and deflection.

Mass hunger in a world that produces an excess of food is a raging nightmare, deserving of daily coverage and strike action until it ends. Yet most people are accustomed.

For the journalists and outlets with integrity, at times it can feel like there is nothing left to say; that we've reported the injustices over and over. That all we are doing is documenting how the house is falling apart. This is indicative of a need to take things to the next level.

So how do we do good journalism, when everything is at stake and none of the polluting and warring criminals are held accountable? How can our news reading and news producing be useful, even as long-term worry exhausts us and narrows cognitive flexibility and creativity? How do we ensure clarity and care, without also falling apart?

The algorithmic boosting of low-grade and commercial content, accompanies the burying of critical insight and investigation. Amid catastrophe, injustice, and repression, the key sources of information — rather than enlightening — are calculated to numb and dull people.

The social media, information, book, and media landscapes are rapidly deteriorating as ad load is growing to ridiculous amounts. Every other post is sponsored content or online recipes. Many articles are unreadable without a browser or tools that remove all the ads. Our feeds are industrial swamplands of sponsored content and viral AI videos and stories. And for some demographics, objectified images of women.

Even newsletter spaces like Substack boost existing privilege (almost all the top newsletters are by men) and seek profitability. Meanwhile AI search engine summaries are discouraging direct reads of alternative media outlets. First page search results are likewise dominated by corporations like Expedia, United States outlets (even for users who aren't there), and mediocre click-bait websites. It's hard to compete, and our in-depth reporting can feel like feeble feathers in a hurricane.

Further, people expect shorter and short content. Two minute videos are now too long. Scrolling and short formats promote habits and standards that reject complexity, discomfort, intention, depth, process, and contemplation, and instead—especially when combined with e-consumerism—a desire for instant results is fostered.

Algorithmic curation and content recommendation based on predicted interests is understandably tempting for people who are overworked and exhausted. Intentional decision making is a mental load after a long day of work, caring for others, dealing with bureaucracy or discrimination, or working through trauma.

But being selective about news, information, and entertainment is practically a radical act amid such a deluge of crap and with companies like Meta supporting the right and suppressing alternatives and resistance (for example the restrictions Meta placed on Lula’s accounts during the Brazilian elections).

Intentionality is particularly necessary for international news, where regions like Latin America, Africa, and Asia have to wrestle for relevance in a rigid hierarchy of life that ranks them lower. Injustice here must be hundreds of times worse to capture interest. Indigenous towns drone bombed and eliminated aren't interesting enough. The recent gold mine collapses in Sudan and the millions forcibly displaced there, barely register.

Readers and reporters can gain back some control over their local and international news consumption with scheduled news time and short lists of strong pro-people, pro-planet media outlets and newsletters like mine, Excluded Headlines, which seek to re-balance world news coverage.

Well-written or produced news is actually good for us. It orders the chaos and gives it meaning. Depth and clarity around the causes and forces behind the horror is important for knowing how to put out the fire, as well as for our own well being and for informing our collective decision making.

Good journalism also restores a sense of freedom and relief after all the enshittification. It reminds us that not everything is garbage.

Avoiding the bad news won't help with handling reality. But the type of awareness matters, and a profound awareness of global and local forces is important for countering isolation, and for experiencing the patterns as history takes place that reveal connectedness between issues, resistance, and events, and for never falling into the trap of tolerating harm.

On the other hand, the banking system of education, AI, and low-quality media, by fostering an inability to think critically and under-representing oppressed peoples, can strengthen systemic class, race and nationality, gender, sexuality, and disability violence.

Hence, media and information isn't a side note to life, it is decisive. And the best journalism isn't done from the sidelines, but from the battlegrounds and fields.

Parachuting into another country or into an issue to cover them doesn't work. Reporting from a couch or a mansion, from the pinnacles of privilege, and from the corporate headquarters of empires isn't journalism.

We need reality — raw, and decoded.

Not greenwashing, not whitewashing, not spinning away the injustice, sugar-coating disregard and cruelty, justifying the intolerable. Not the naive glorifying of right-wing forces in Global South countries, or platitudes of balance and neutrality from outlets very much aligned with corporations and Euro or US-centric and pro-war perspectives.

Interestingly, despite the glut, most people (86% globally) do recognise climate change as serious, for example. And that is where the hope is. About 56% of people think about climate change on a daily or weekly basis, and a poll of ten European countries found 77% of respondents believe that companies should be held responsible for environmental harm.

The difficult next step is facing up to the fact that protecting the environment and building true global equality and justice involve some discomfort and uncertainty. Tweaking shower times and donating to charities won't cut it. Ending societal and structural addictions to petroleum involves effort, confrontation, and deep change.

Amid the oil spills and bombs, it can be hard to dream. Here in central Mexico, organised crime controls streets and transport, as well as extorting, forcibly disappearing, and tainting the air with tension and fear.

It feels close to impossible to imagine building some kind of nurturing community on these bruised and sunken streets. Yet we have to. We have to conjure up hope from the fish-scale-clogged drains and the potholes of life.

We have to free our imaginations from the bare and boring rooms of AI and 3am social media scrolling so we can remember the kite sky parties, the marigold fields, the precious art galleries in Havana overlooking the bay, the rainbow beetles and stealth caterpillars and mulberry silkworms that turn saliva into silk. Like magic.

We're magical too, but we often forget it. Our ability to turn the ordinary into the extraordinary is there, if dusty and atrophied.

I asked a few activists here if I should write another novel. "Is there any point?" I said, discouraged. Things feel too urgent for novels and stories and art. It is a time for strikes, roadblocks, shutting down and building anew. But they said yes, and of course one can do both.

"The harder times are, the more necessary art and creativity is. It provides hope, it keeps us humanised and sensitive to others," replied one friend. So, I've started writing another novel and it is pouring out of me. It will be the messy story of how people do away with borders, global inequality, environmental pillaging, and empire and build something more caring and nurturing than this selfish nightmare.

The AI boom is asking us what it means to be human. That question about our collective identity couldn't have come at a better time. We should refuse AI—not because technology is bad (it isn't) but because of who owns it and how they have looted our intellectual work to control what we know and how we think.

Build shields against the devaluing of life, of our work, of creativity. Turn AI off in search engines or use operators like -AI in searches (and other operators like site:.co to force results from a particular country rather than almost exclusively the US). Boycott corporate media and use search engines that are more neutral than Chrome like Mojeek (less big business but still very Eurocentric), Brave, and Qwant.

AI and billionaire-controlled social media, through the proliferation of so much AI-generated content and unverified or incorrect information, are planting distrust and disillusionment. I mentioned this to my friend.

“Exactly. AI takes away critical thought and dehumanises, and technology is inundating us so we don't feel the loss. When we're overstimulated, we don't pay attention to anything,” she said.

Our attention is everything right now. It is accountability and it is priorities. The news is hard to read, but don't stop. Just be strategic and selective. Let it connect and ground us, and inspire us.

There is so much bravery, beauty, kindness—and therefore such potential. Some media outlets will overlook that, others will highlight the resistances and generosity.

[Tamara Pearson is an Australian-Mexican journalist, editor, activist and literary fiction author living in Puebla, Mexico. Her latest novel is The Eyes of the Earth, and she writes the Global South newsletter Excluded Headlines.]

author: Daniel Avalos
title: Iglesia y Estado: una separación que todavía se reclama en la calle
content:
La consigna apareció este miércoles en la movilización de jubilados. La reciente visita del papa León XIV volvió a poner en escena el vínculo entre el poder político y la Iglesia católica, una relación que también se expresa en el presupuesto público.







La visita del papa León XIV terminó, pero la discusión sobre el vínculo entre la Iglesia y el Estado sigue abierta. En la movilización de los jubilados, volvió a aparecer un pedido que lleva años recorriendo las calles y que aún debe resolverse.




En medio de los reclamos por los derechos de nuestros viejos, la consigna puso sobre la mesa una discusión que suele quedar relegada. No se trata de cuestionar la fe de nadie ni el derecho de las comunidades religiosas a expresarse. La discusión pasa por otro lado: qué relación debe mantener el Estado con una institución religiosa y qué lugar ocupa esa institución en las decisiones y los recursos públicos.La visita del Papa dejó imágenes de cercanía entre las autoridades políticas y la jerarquía católica. Pero ese vínculo no se agota en los encuentros oficiales ni en las ceremonias. También tiene una dimensión económica.




 




El presupuesto nacional sigue contemplando partidas destinadas a la Iglesia católica. Es cierto que el financiamiento directo se redujo en los últimos años. En diciembre de 2023, los obispos renunciaron a las asignaciones mensuales que recibían del Estado. Sin embargo, eso no significó el fin de las transferencias.




Para 2026 se proyectaron 155 millones de pesos destinados a obispados, arzobispados y parroquias, según datos oficiales. También se mantienen mecanismos de asistencia a sacerdotes de zonas de frontera y a seminaristas. A esto se suman otros vínculos económicos que no resultan sencillos de dimensionar: el presupuesto no permite identificar de manera global cuánto dinero público llega a instituciones católicas a través de programas educativos o sociales.




Millones de pesos destinaron la Nación $20.400, CABA que no informó su aporte oficialmente pero que si quedó en la mira por su «carpa vip» con lujos extravagantes , la Provincia de Buenos Aires $12.000 y la Provincia de Córdoba $9.300. La iglesia solo aporto $5.400 que fueron acercados por empresas como Santander, Toyota, Techint, Corporación América y otras.




La discusión, entonces, no pasa por desconocer el trabajo que realizan esas instituciones ni por limitar la libertad religiosa. Pasa por preguntarse por qué una confesión en particular conserva un vínculo de financiamiento y reconocimiento institucional con el Estado, mientras este debe garantizar derechos para una sociedad con distintas creencias y también para quienes no profesan ninguna.




La fiesta de la Iglesia fue pagada casi en su totalidad por un Estado que no reconoce leyes ni atiende necesidades de su pueblo. Por eso el reclamo encontró su lugar en los carteles y las voces de los jubilados.




Hoy más que nunca. Separación de la Iglesia del Estado!

author: Bizzi Lavelle
title: Young Women, Pain, Mobility Aids
content:
Stories Contributors Pitch an Idea

To be sick, or have a health condition of any kind is not a moral failing. I know this and I hope that you do too. However, every time I find myself staying in or leaving something early because I’m in pain or I’m fatigued, I can’t help but feel the people around me are disappointed.

People wish they had a friend who could come to their fortnightly event like they said they would. They wish they could book a performer to MC an event without them withdrawing due to spending that week pain ridden in bed. They wish the friend they extended a birthday party invite made it instead of sending through an apologetic message. They wish their friend would be in the room cheering them on at their weekly drag comp or production show.

A common online talking point echoes in my head as I send my latest “I’m sorry” message; you have to inconvenience yourself a little for the sake of your community. You have to be someone’s villager if you want to have a village.

With the weeks or days I spend hidden away, inside, barely leaving the house I often ask myself, do I deserve to be in anyone’s village? Do I deserve my own villagers?

The words to Rina Sawayama’s ‘Bad Friend’ circle my mind as I spend another Saturday night in my pajamas, watching anime in bed: “So don’t ask me where I’ve been, been avoiding everything.”

As I’m lamenting my woes to my notes app and the friends who get it, an article from The Times UK comes across my feed. “Why are young women using walking sticks?” by Katherine Stock. And then another, this time from The Telegraph, “How having a disability became cool” by Poppy Coburn.

The themes of these pieces are misogyny and ableism, with sprinkles of transphobia and ageism.

In both of these pieces, the authors seem to believe that young women in increasing numbers are faking to be disabled for social clout. In the first piece, Stock declares young women using mobility aids and posting about being ill are victims of “social contagion” deems the pain they’re in as “unclear” and therefore “unclear” if these women “really have” disabilities.

It’s wild to me, that in 2026, anyone would partake in such ableist vitriol. Despite what both authors think, there are a wide range of ways to be disabled. Disability and chronic illness don’t always look like a wheelchair user. Sometimes disabilities and chronic illnesses are invisible. Sometimes they’re dynamic. The only criteria to being disabled is having a condition, injury or alike that impedes you and your ability to do day to day tasks.

Disability is the only minority group a person can become part of at a moment’s notice, and is the only minority group we will all be part of at some point in our lives. As my friend, Protect our NDIS rally organiser and activist Oriela says “You will become disabled. That’s a promise not just a threat”.

That one influencer you follow could one day be surfing and the next using a wheelchair or cane. You aren’t able to discern how much pain someone is in by simply looking at them. If that were the case, women wouldn’t be waiting years for their pain to be believed and diagnosed.

For Aboriginal women, seeking medical care has an extra layer of stress. Racial bias in medicine historically saw beliefs that bla(c)k people, particularly women, have a higher pain tolerance than their white counterparts. This, along with classic medical misogyny has led to Aboriginal women being mistreated, ignored or treated as though they’re only ‘drug seeking’.

In Allanah Hunt’s 2024 piece ‘The Good Patient’, she details her experiences of medical racism as she navigates dealing with endometriosis. Despite Allanah’s attempts to present to hospitals as the best and most polite patient, her pain was still disbelieved and she was still treated as a drug seeker. “Because the truth is, no matter how much I’m ‘the good patient’, I will never escape the racial judgement from healthcare providers” Allanah writes.

Similarly, Colleen Lavelle (my mother) discusses her experience of medical racism in her 2017 piece. “Death by racism: bigotry in the health system is harming Indigenous patients’”.

She notes from her own experiences and other First Nations people whose medical experiences she’s listened to that a common thread is wondering if you’ve been overly sensitive.

One memory I have from my teens is when I was at the shops with my mum and younger sister. I went out to the car to put some bags in the car and a man questioned me from his car since he saw a teen girl using a disabled parking spot. He grilled me and told me off for using the spot, not once considering or listening as I explained the car had a permit and I was bringing bags to the car so my mother, the owner of the permit, could stay inside and sit for a moment.

I didn’t look how he wanted or expected disability to look, and so I got chewed out. Aside from not listening, he didn’t consider I could’ve been the disabled person.

Through my own medical journey I’ve had some of the experiences both Allanah and Colleen have shared. It took 10 years and two laparoscopies for me to finally have an endometriosis diagnosis. I was discharged with zero pain killers, and consistently told by my doctor growing up that periods are a spectrum and some people have light and short ones and some, like me, have extremely heavy and painful ones.

I’ve had a doctor suggest the solve for my at the time undiagnosed chronic pain was to lose weight. Something a lot of people, women in particular, are told is the main cause for unrelated illness. Such a suggestion is to me, another clear example of medical misogyny. I was in chronic pain and had heavy periods when I was “average” weight, so it stands to reason I would still experience them even as my size fluctuates.

In her piece, Coburn writes that “the country (the UK) is sicker than before” and notes that often, the sick women she stalks on social media usually have more than one diagnosis. It’s confusing and worrying to me that Coburn not only doesn’t understand that concept of comorbidities, but she also doesn’t seem to understand that perhaps after a mass disabling event like the pandemic, that people would be sick after.

In 2023, content creator Sydney Towle was diagnosed with cholangiocarcinoma, an aggressive cancer of the bile duct. Sydney shared her diagnosis with her followers and began including content around living with cancer in her posts. Many watching online found it difficult to believe that Sydney would have cancer. She was so young and was still posting about the things that other people in their 20’s would be posting. As Sydney continued documenting her health, thousands of people accused her of faking cancer, and created subreddits for the sole purpose of picking apart her posts and proving she was faking for clout. In 2026, after Sydney’s cancer worsened, she passed away.

In an interview Sydney stated that “they are so angry that living with cancer can look different than they think it should”.

Which really, is the summary of all of this. There is so little to gain from pretending to be sick. When I use my walking stick or wear my sunflower lanyard I’m not suddenly receiving special treatment or oodles of social capital. It’s actually the opposite, as I wonder if my injuries or illnesses are “enough” to warrant taking a seat.

Sydney, (and any other disbelieved sick woman) deserved to be able to find love, document her holidays, have good days and bad ones, run marathons and surf and go to bed at night with a warm heart and deeper lines on her face from laughter and smiling.

Despite having a body ravaged by illness or pain, sick women deserve to be seen as whole people and not purely as their illnesses.

I have endometriosis, eczema, polymetabolic ovarian syndrome, a wonky knee and two wonky ankles but I also have a love of performing, laughing, protesting, anime and glitter. I deserve to be seen and known for the exciting things but still have my pain believed and acknowledged.

The day I was the first burlesque dancer to ever perform at the Women Deliver international conference was still the same day I lay in bed afterwards in more pain than I could explain.

What disbelievers miss is that often the things we love to do come to our own detriment. That we can’t simply just throw caution to the wind and go for a surf.

If I want to be social, or perform, I have to meticulously plan every detail. Will I have enough energy? Do I have enough pain killers on me, and will I be able to eat something so I can take them? Should I bring my stick just in case or will it be bulky in my bag and go unused if I don’t need it? Will I be able to rest that evening or the next day? What if I don’t pack something but then need it?

Disability and chronic illness look different than the general perception we expect. People like Coburn, Stock and Sydney Towle’s snarkers expect people to do nothing but be ill and speak of being ill. Chronic illness and disability doesn’t have to be frail, old and bed ridden. It can be a 20-30 year old woman in bright colours living a joyous life using a pink walking stick.

These people have no idea what it feels like to be betrayed by a body you grew up in.

To be stuck in a vessel that you know could at one point could do anything you wished it to only to now be exhausted by the smallest things. I wouldn’t wish disability or chronic illness on anyone, but what I do wish on Coburn, Stock and those that think alike is kindness, empathy, common sense and a modicum of comprehension.

Bizzi Lavelle is a Queer Wakka Wakka and Arrente writer and burlesque dancer. She was awarded 2nd Runner Up at the Australian Burlesque Festival’s “New Follies“ competition, “Out for Australia – 30 Under 30” Rising Star Award, and the First Nations Leadership and Engagement Award from the 62nd Annual Queens Ball Awards 2023. Her areas of expertise are gender, sexuality, and Bla(c)k feminism.

author: Ming-Yeh T. Rawnsley
title: Making Hope Credible: Puma Shen and the Politics of Access in Taipei
content:
A HOME THAT can be renewed without repeated moves, a cultural allowance that continues into working adulthood, and an exercise service that comes to the neighbourhood: these are tangible reasons to pay attention to Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) campaign for Taipei mayor. They also offer a way to test the comparison increasingly drawn between Shen and New York mayor Zohran Mamdani. Beyond the excitement surrounding an unexpected challenger, what would make the city more accessible to people with unequal resources?

Shen’s command of municipal policy has helped change how voters see him. Nathan Batto’s account dated September 28 describes how detailed answers helped him reach beyond his established image as a specialist in civil defence and Chinese information warfare. His appeal invites scrutiny of what that expertise could deliver for residents who find existing services difficult to use.

THE COMPARISON reportedly helped shape the contest itself. ETtoday’s Tao Ben-he (³³¥»©M) reported on October 29 that President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) drew inspiration from Mamdani’s unexpected rise when insisting on Shen’s nomination as the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) candidate. The reported connection poses a consequential question: if New York supplied inspiration for choosing a candidate, how much of Mamdani’s challenge to inequality has travelled with it?

Brian Hioe identified the distinction in New Bloom, also on October 29: Mamdani campaigned explicitly against socioeconomic inequality, while Shen has emphasised policy expertise and good governance. The proposals examined here suggest a distinctive contribution: reducing the practical burdens of using public provision. That could bring meaningful improvements, although its redistributive reach remains uneven, particularly where housing assistance depends on ownership.

Mamdani’s promises to freeze rents for rent-stabilised tenants, make buses free and provide universal childcare named household costs that government could reduce. His inaugural address on January 1 also connected childcare to taxing the wealthiest. Taipei need not reproduce those policies to learn from their political clarity: residents should understand whose circumstances will improve, who will contribute and what public authority will do.

Shen has offered a wide range of policy proposals. From that platform, I examine three areas—housing and urban renewal, cultural support for young adults, and neighbourhood exercise services for older residents—to assess how his proposals would change access to public resources. These examples reveal different relationships between administrative reform and inequality; they cannot establish the overall redistributive ambition of his platform.

HOUSING PROVIDES the hardest test. Taipei’s existing approach is not simply to leave residents to negotiate with developers. The city already promotes publicly led renewal and faster review through its urban renewal programmes. It also provides temporary accommodation and describes neighbourhood-based relocation as an objective, including arrangements involving social housing. Shen’s alternative must therefore demonstrate what it changes in practice.

His proposed circular urban renewal scheme (無限都更) changes the sequence of redevelopment. Willing owners would exchange existing property rights for a new home, or rights to use one, before their original site is rebuilt. The city would assemble an initial housing supply and manage the exchange; completed redevelopment would replenish resources for subsequent rounds. The objective is to avoid the familiar sequence of moving into temporary accommodation and moving again after reconstruction.

The scheme recognises disruption as a real cost, especially for older residents whose routines depend on nearby care and social relationships. It could make agreement easier without treating reluctant residents as obstacles. But Shen’s policy acknowledges limited initial supply. Its preference for nearby exchanges needs to be supported by identified sites and a realistic timetable.

Valuation is equally important. Shen’s scheme envisages settling differences between old and new property values, with loan assistance where needed. An older owner with little income may still struggle to bridge that difference. Independent valuations, accessible advice and safeguards against unaffordable debt would determine whether the exchange expands choice or mainly assists households already able to pay.

Property exchange also begins with ownership. Tenants cannot exchange an asset they do not own, and may remain exposed to displacement even when owners gain protection from repeated moves. Housing justice therefore requires affordable rental provision and safeguards for tenants affected by redevelopment.

Shen’s housing platform does address rental supply. It proposes using repair subsidies and tax incentives to bring approximately 4,000 underused homes into leasing and management arrangements, and obtaining additional social housing through renewal. However, Taipei already operates a government-backed leasing and management programme, whose current phase includes incentives for accessible accommodation for older tenants. The change is an expansion and reorientation of existing instruments, whose additional results need to be measurable.

Success should be measured by how many additional households secure suitable homes at sustainable rents, and for how long. Public resources also involve competing claims: allocating scarce homes to property exchanges has an opportunity cost for people waiting for affordable housing. Shen should explain those priorities alongside his plans to accelerate redevelopment.

HIS CULTURAL COIN proposal offers a more immediate and clearly defined extension. The national programme currently provides eligible 13- to 22-year-olds with 1,200 points annually, each worth NT$1, for approved cultural spending. Shen proposes a Taipei-funded extension covering ages 23 to 30 at the same annual amount. This would continue support after national eligibility ends, rather than increase the allowance for existing recipients.

Cultural participation need not cease to be a public concern when someone leaves education or starts work. Books, cinema and performance can become discretionary expenses for young adults meeting housing and employment costs. Continuing the allowance would make a modest portion of that spending a shared public responsibility.

The relevant test is whether the allowance brings additional people into cultural participation. A flat benefit may subsidise existing consumers more readily than it reaches people with little time, familiarity or confidence to participate. Outreach through workplaces and community organisations could help it reach beyond established audiences. Evaluation should therefore consider who begins attending or buying cultural work, alongside total spending.

Eligibility also matters. Young people may live, work or study in Taipei without sharing the same registration status. Clear rules would show whom the municipal extension includes and allow voters to consider exclusions they may not themselves encounter.

THE EXERCISE-BUS proposal addresses another barrier: distance. Shen proposes converting electric buses into mobile exercise classrooms, visiting community locations on regular schedules. Reported plans include professional coaching, fitness assessments, nutritional advice and health records. The service would bring supported activity closer to older residents rather than assume they can travel to a sports centre.

Taipei already offers older residents free access to swimming pools and gyms at district sports centres during designated hours, as its current provision shows. Bringing coached sessions into neighbourhoods could make that provision more useful to people deterred by the journey or unfamiliar equipment. The proposal’s contribution is to reduce the effort required to participate, complementing facilities that residents must travel to themselves.

A pilot could demonstrate that contribution by prioritising neighbourhoods poorly served by existing facilities and involving older residents in its design. Regular visits and consistent staffing would help turn an initial session into a sustained activity. Coordination with community providers should establish where a mobile service adds value, while evaluation should record whether it reaches people previously excluded, including those with limited mobility.

THE THREE EXAMPLES show why administrative reform can matter politically. Helping an older owner move with less disruption, continuing cultural support into adulthood and bringing coached exercise closer to home would expand practical choices. These gains deserve recognition on their own terms. Their limits are also specific: a property exchange cannot serve tenants directly, while an allowance or mobile service must reach beyond people already able to participate.

Delivery would require published budgets and a clear division of responsibility between Taipei and the national government. As the party holding the presidency, the DPP cannot treat national constraints as someone else’s problem. Progress should be measured against existing provision: additional affordable tenancies, new cultural participants and sustained exercise participation. Independent review should also record unsuccessful applications and complaints, making exclusion visible alongside headline results.

Residents should help determine those standards. Housing exchanges require independent advice and meaningful consent. Cultural policy should hear from young people who rarely enter established venues, and exercise services from older residents absent from organised activities. Their experience can reveal whether a programme removes an obstacle or simply relocates it. Participation gives the people affected some influence over how success is defined.

Matthew d’Ancona’s article in The New World on October 21 distinguishes hope from confidence in inevitable progress; James Ball, published in The New World on September 28 stresses visible improvements. Together, they suggest a useful standard for Taipei: hope requires both a commitment to act and evidence that action changes people’s circumstances.

The reported Mamdani connection is therefore illuminating without making Shen a Taiwanese equivalent. In these selected policies, Shen’s promise is a more active municipal government that helps residents use resources already available and extends provision where gaps remain. That is a credible basis for reform. A broader challenge to urban inequality would also require explicit choices about who pays, whose housing claims take priority and how people without assets gain security.

The campaign’s democratic significance lies in making those choices open to public judgement. Clear commitments would give residents something to defend, contest and improve after November 28, whoever wins. Shen has offered practical reasons to believe that government could make city life easier. Making that hope durable means giving residents greater influence over the resources and decisions that shape their lives.
